batch stats). the service must stay under the defined overhead budget and must not capture or emit customer data.nnprimary users: eng-infra on-call and release engineering during rollouts.nn---nn safe-disable procedures (kill switch)nuse to stop canary load quickly without impacting inference endpoints.nn d1. preferred: disable via control-plane confignthis is the safest path because it preserves deployment health while stopping workload generation.n1) set region enablement to disabled for perf-canary (control-plane flag).n2) confirm perf-canary acknowledges config refresh (logs/metric indicating targets0 or disabledtrue).n3) verify:n - qps to inference endpoints drops to 0n - metrics stop changing except for heartbeat/healthnn d2. secondary: set model list empty / qps notify security compliance.n- if due to overhead: capture before/after gpu utilization and canary qps for later tuning.nn---nn verification checklist (what good looks like)n healthn- pods delays.n - mitigation: do not tune thresholds based on delayed data coordinate with telemetry (logan wright / nadia rahman) to resolve lag.nn3) cardinality explosion / metrics cost spiken - symptom: metrics backend cost/volume alerts grafana queries slow.n - mitigation: disable offending metrics emission or rollback remove high-cardinality labels follow the metrics cardinality audit guidance.nn4) region-specific schedules.nn5) alerts flappingn - symptom: warning/paging repeatedly triggers and resolves.n - mitigation: increase min sample size extend dampening window ensure region/sku-aware thresholds if variance differs.nn---nn escalation and communicationn- if customer impact is suspected: follow the on-call incident process page sre on-call and notify eng-oncall.n- if regression is summary:nthis compact playbook is designed for first responders who need focused, action-oriented guidance for common redwood-serving incidents and a lightweight postmortem template to accelerate learning. it favors short, repeatable actions (micro-runbooks), clear decision points, and prewritten comms to reduce cognitive load during high-severity events. use this as the primary on-call cheat-sheet link to deeper runbooks when needed.nnscope:n- audience: first responders (on-call engineers), bridge operators, support leads.n- coverage: performance slo regressions, kv-cache/embedding full forensic investigations.nnhow to use this doc (quick):n1) identify the incident class using the incident quick classifier below.n2) run the micro-runbook for that class (13 remediation steps).n3) if unresolved in 20 minutes or customer-impacting, escalate to the appropriate on-call (pager escalation ladder).n4) publish a short customer-facing status update using the template.n5) after stabilization, fill the light postmortem scaffold within 72 hours and schedule a 3060 minute blameless review.nnincident quick classifier (decision tree):n- is the symptom increased latency or tenant? - treat as customer-impacting p2 open dedicated bridge with solutions/cs.n- are model-quality signals (eval infra or user reports) showing semantic regressions? - model quality incident.n- is burst traffic or constrained egress capacity.nngoalsnn- ensure predictability for tenant traffic when outbound (egress) capacity is constrained.n- maintain latency slos for high-priority tenants while playbook during:n1) pre-production validation for dedicated/private tenant cutovers.n2) go-live where tenant traffic patterns are unknown or have burst risk.n3) incidents where egress link saturation, proxies.n- does not modify customer data retention or encryption policies.nnprerequisites and config artifactsnn- tenant capacity profile created in capacity service (capacity-service v2): tenant_id, target_rps, burst_rps, expected_seq_len.n- ingress and egress proxies must expose the following metrics to metrics-ingest: ingress.rps, egress.bandwidth.bytes, proxy.queue_length, summarynthis playbook defines an experiment-driven approach for onboarding new developer customers to redwood inference with an explicit mapping between fidelity profiles, cost signals, and sla entitlements. the goal is to minimize developer friction while making unit economics predictable and measurable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.nnaudiencen- product managers and go-to-market leads running onboarding pilotsn- solutions engineers and customer success teams executing migrationsn- platform engineers implementing fidelity policy controls and telemetrynnscope and intentn- defines a set of onboarding experiment cohorts (a/b/c) tied to fidelity presets and priced trial credits.n- establishes measurable criteria to graduate customers between fidelity tiers.n- provides rollout steps, required product hooks, billing implications, and rollback guidance.nndefinitionsn- fidelity profile: a named bundle of runtime characteristics (model variant, quantization level, batching limits, streaming vs chunked responses).n- onboarding credit: time-limited usage credit applied to a tenant to cover trial costs.n- entitlement sla: explicit latency and availability guarantees associated with a pricing tier.nnhigh-level approachn1) create 3 onboarding cohorts:n - cohort a (exploratory): high-fidelity default model, minimal batching, extended latency budget (200ms p50 target), 1,000 onboarding credits.n - cohort b (balanced): mid-fidelity variant (int8 or mixed precision), moderate batching, standard latency budget (120ms p50), 2,500 onboarding credits.n - cohort c (economy): quantized variant with aggressive batching and prefix-caching, tight cost limits, relaxed p50 latency (220ms), 5,000 onboarding credits to demonstrate cost savings.nn2) instrument: telemetry hooks for per-request fidelity tags, credit burn-rate, per-route latency distribution, and quality regressions tied to shadow-eval prompt sets.nn3) gate graduation: customers must meet usage and quality thresholds in their cohort for n days before automatic promotion. promotion is governed by the fidelity promotion rule (fpr) below.nnfidelity promotion rule (fpr)n- inputs (measured over the last 7 days): 1) daily active tokens 10k, 2) regression rate against shadow prompts promote to next fidelity tier.n- if regression spikes 2x baseline for 3 consecutive days - immediate rollback to prior tier and open a fidelity incident.nnrequired product hooks (implementation checklist)n- tenant metadata: onboarding_cohort, onboarding_start, onboarding_credits_remaining (api console).n- runtime: fidelity_tag header on inference requests ability to map fidelity_tag to model variant and quantization profile.n- billing: trial credit ledger entries and reporting apis for credit burn by packaging implicationsn- trial credits should be delivered as non-billable ledger items that expire at onboarding_end 30 days.n- credits consumed beyond trial convert to regular billing at the tenants chosen pricing tier.n- cohort-specific uplift: if customer is kept at cohort a after trial, charge a 10 fidelity surcharge to reflect higher unit cost conversely, cohort c conversion includes a 5 low-fidelity discount.nnquick decision tablen- if customer requires regulated private deployment (vpc / on-prem): default to cohort b unless explicit cost-savings mandate - run cohort c only after security review.n- if the customer reports quality complaints within first 72 hours: escalate to csm consider one-time temporary credit and possible immediate promotion to higher fidelity for diagnosis.nnprd requirements (minimal viable set for q4 onboarding pilots)n- prd-1: new tenant fields (onboarding_cohort, onboarding_expires_at, onboarding_credits) exposed in accounts api and playbook, content: summaryn-------nthis playbook defines the lifecycle, versioning rules, testing gates, and rollout procedures for tenant-specific observability contracts used during enterprise onboarding and post-go-live operations. it standardizes how telemetry schemas, labels, and slo-related metrics are introduced, evolved, and deprecated for dedicated and private tenants. the aim is to reduce integration friction, preserve downstream slo integrity, and provide clear rollback and remediation steps for customers and internal teams.nngoalsn-----n- provide a predictable, auditable change process for tenant telemetry schemas (contract).n- minimize customer-side parsing and dashboard breakage during schema changes.n- ensure slo and billing signals remain consistent across contract versions.n- define operational runbooks for validation, rollout, and rollback.nnscopen-----nincludes: ingress metrics, request/response metadata, model-identifiers, latency/billing tokens, event tracing ids, and tenant-specific labels emitted by ingress-proxy, model-router, and telemetry-gatekeeper.nexcludes: internal-only debug traces and ephemeral dev-only flags.nnprinciplesn----------n1) backward compatibility first: additive fields only for patch/minor updates whenever possible.n2) explicit version header: every telemetry payload must include telemetry_contract_version and schema_version.n3) consumer-driven validation: create a consumer schema test harness prior to rollout.n4) slo continuity: any change that impacts token counting or latency buckets requires slo owner sign-off.nncontract versioning rulesn-------------------------n- versioning scheme: major.minor.patch (semver-like, but focused on consumer compatibility):n - major: incompatible changes (removal/rename of required fields, semantic changes to metric meaning). requires coordinated migration and 90-day deprecation notice.n - minor: additive fields and new optional labels. safe for rolling updates.n - patch: bug fixes in serialization, typos, or clarifications that do not change semantics.n- filesystem path / registry: contracts are stored in the telemetry registry (internal git repo: infra/telemetry/contracts/). each version has a manifest and migration notes.nntelemetry contract example (minimal json payload counts and latency buckets to ensure slos do not change 1.n c) dashboard smoke: run dashboard snapshots of top-10 queries for differences.nn3) canary (owner: cs sre)n - canary window (default 48 adjust based on risk and test results.nn5) complete and documentn - mark registry entry as active and update related onboarding docs and qbr templates.n - notify customer success contacts and tenant pocs.nnrollback and emergency remediationn----------------------------------n- hot rollback: flip ingestion to last-stable schema at the telemetry-gatekeeper layer. this is expected to be near-instant provide an automated, auditable safe-rollback path that returns the tenant to a verified last-known-good state within 60 minutes for p1/p2 incidents, with human-in-the-loop gating for production-critical changes.n- ensure rollback preserves data integrity and produces clear post-action telemetry for qbr review.nnscope and definitionsnn- configuration drift: any divergence between the expected, committed tenant config (control plane) and the live runtime state that affects routing, model selection, rbac, volume mounts, or network policies. examples: unexpected ingress rule changes, kv cache eviction policy flips, altered model pinning, quantization profile swap, unintended scaling min/max changes.n- last-known-good (lkg): an immutable snapshot of tenant configuration and service checksums created after a successful canary and synthetic acceptance gate. stored in the tenant-config-bucket (s3/gcs equivalent) with key format: tenant//lkg/.n- drift severity levels:n - s1 (critical): rtt/throughput regressions causing customer-visible sla breaches, or security-relevant changes (rbac, egress firewall).n - s2 (high): model mismatch or quantization change causing output-quality regressions or token-cost spikes.n - s3 (medium): non-critical tuning changes (batch sizes, non-critical autoscale tweaks).nnsignals and telemetry sourcesnnprimary signals (ordered by priority):n- control-plane-config-checksum: periodic (5m) checksum comparison between tenant lkg and live config.n- ingress-route-ttl-mismatch: delta between expected ingress certificates/routes and live (1m sampling).n- runtime-model-manifest-diff: difference between model version pinned in control plane and model manifest reported by the runtime.n- kvcache-hit-rate-drop: 40 drop vs baseline over 10m window.n- token-cost-surge: 2x baseline 30m token spend without corresponding throughput growth.n- customer-reported-llm-regression: triaged from support channel with trace id.nnalerting and oncall routingnn- all s1 alerts - pager rotation: customer success sre oncall - eng-sre escalation if not acknowledged within 5m. pager payload must include: tenant-id, signal, timestamp, lkg pointer, recent commit id, recommended rollback action.n- s2 alerts - routed to customer success queue and owner of the tenants onboarding cohort escalate to product ml for model regressions.n- s3 alerts - routed to csops runbook queue for scheduled reconciliation.nnautomated detection pipelines (implementation notes)nn1) config checksum worker (k8s job)n- runs every 5 minutes per tenant.n- compares canonical lkg yaml against /runtime/state/config via agent api.n- emits config-drift-tenant metric with tags drift_keys, delta_size.nn2) behavioral delta detector (streaming job)n- combines kvcache/latency/cost signals using a weighted anomaly model (weights maintained in infra config).n- triggers a synthesized alert with a reason code (e.g., model_pin_mismatch) and recommended play: inform, soft-rollback, hard-rollback.nn3) audit and snapshottern- on any detected config change, immediately create a snapshot in tenant-config-bucket with a unique id and set lifecycle tags: detected_by:checksum, severity.nntriage matrix and decision flow (short)nn1. alert received with severity sx.n2. run automated triage script (cs-triage --tenant --alert ) which returns: delta_scope (network/runtime/model), lkg_candidate (snapshot id), confidence_score.n3. if s1 or confidence_score 0.85 and delta_scope network, model, rbac: recommend automated rollback to lkg candidate with a safety hold of 5 minutes for human approval in production.n4. if s2 and confidence_score between 0.60.85: create a canary rollback in a single pod/replica and run synthetic tests for 3 minutes.n5. if s3 or confidence_score --reason rollback).n 2. create immutable incident record (incident-store create --tenant --type rollback --ref ).n 3. apply lkg patch to runtime via agent (agent apply --tenant --snapshot --mode dry-run) and validate (agent validate --checks smoke,models,ingress).n 4. if validation passes, agent apply --mode live.n 5. run post-rollback synthetic suite (synthetic-run --tenant --tests smoke,latency,kvcache) for 10 minutes and collect telemetry.n 6. if post-suite passes and no new s1 signals registered for 15 minutes, release control-plane lock and close incident with notes.n 7. if failure in any step, escalate to sre and preserve evidence bundle (logs, snapshots, traces).nn- commands (examples):n - check lkg list:n aws s3 ls s3://tenant-config-bucket/tenant/1234/lkg/ --human-readablen - trigger dry-run apply:n cs-agent apply --tenant 1234 --snapshot lkg-202602100730 --mode dry-run --output jsonn - promote snapshot to live:n cs-agent apply --tenant 1234 --snapshot lkg-202602100730 --mode live --reason auto-rollback:s1-driftnnhuman-in-the-loop gating rulesnn- production tenants with committed contract 50k mrr: require explicit cs director approval for any automated rollback that changes network/rbac or causes a service restart of more than 2 minutes. this approval can be provided via the ui or via signed cli token (one-time use).n- staging/non-critical tenants: automated rollback can proceed after a 5-minute pause with on-call notification.nnsafeguards and post-rollback governancenn- immutable incident record and snapshot ids are attached to the tenants qbr artifacts.n- every automated rollback triggers a post-incident rca template to be populated by the owner within 3 business days.n- for model regressions that triggered rollback, record: model id, quantization profile, kernel/md5 checksums, and prompt-set failure rate. attach to the model-onboarding queue for evaluation.nntesting and maintenance cadencenn- monthly: dry-run rollbacks for a randomly selected 3 of tenants in non-prod to ensure snapshot integrity.n- quarterly: tabletop exercise between cs, sre, and runtime teams verify lkg restore procedures under simulated production load.n- after any production rollback: follow-up 2-week monitoring window with elevated sampling of customer telemetry and weekly update to the account owner.nnrunbook appendix (quick reference)nn- immediate play (s1):n 1. acknowledge alert.n 2. run cs-triage --tenant --alert .n 3. if recommended: cs-agent apply --tenant --snapshot --mode dry-run.n 4. validate then cs-agent apply --mode live.n 5. post-rollback: synthetic-run and notify account owner.nn- canary rollback (s2):n 1. create canary flag: cs-agent apply --tenant --snapshot timestampsn - pre- and post-config checksumsn - agent logs (last 1h) and runtime metrics (last 24h)n - snapshot id and verification resultsnnroles and responsibilitiesnn- customer success (cs) ramirez).n, doc_id: dsid_4bfe055051b24a58bd94c173654dc6b0, source_type: confluence, title: enterprise self-heal automation playbook, content: summarynnthis playbook describes the standardized approach redwood customer success (cs) and support teams use to implement, validate, and operate enterprise self-heal automation for customer production incidents. self-heal automation refers to fully automated remediation actions that are safe to run without human approval when a monitored condition maps to a validated remediation recipe. the goal is to reduce mean time to recovery (mttr), lower toil for on-call engineers, and preserve customer slas while maintaining auditability and revertibility.nnwhen to use this playbooknn- enterprise customers with a dedicated or private deployment where the customer has agreed to automated remediation in their onboarding contract.n- routine, well-understood failure classes where automated remediation has been tested end-to-end and has a clear rollback path.n- situations where automation improves availability and cost predictability (e.g., autoscaling policies, model switchover, cache invalidation, connector restarts).nnscope and non-goalsnn- scope: networking reconnections, connector/ingest restarts, gk (gateway) route fallback, model variant switchovers, kv-cache warmup, automated quota adjustments with throttled rollback.n- non-goal: automated changes to customer data schema, irreversible data migrations, or actions that materially change billing without human sign-off.nnroles and ownershipnn- customer success (cs): negotiates automation consent, documents high-level workflows in the customer onboarding packet, approves business-level safety constraints.n- support (tier 1/2): triage alerts, confirm automation mapping, escalate when automation does not resolve incident.n- platform reliability (eng-sre): implements and maintains automation recipes and ensures telemetry coverage and safety gates.n- customer oncall: receives notices of automatic remediation and can request immediate pause/rollback.nnalerting and detection (signals)nnprimary signals that may trigger self-heal automation:nn1) service health metrics exceeding thresholdsn - api error rate 5 over 3 minutes and p95 latency 1.2s on critical routesn - model inference tail latency 2x baseline for 5 minutesn2) capacity saturationn - gpu pool utilization 92 sustained for 10 minutesn - pod eviction rate 1/min for 3 minutesn3) external integrations failingn - upstream telemetry forwarding http 5xx 2 for 5 minutesn4) data pipeline stallsn - connector lag 30 minutes and backlog growth 10 over 15 minutesnnevery trigger must map to a single canonical alert id (format: cs/selfheal/customer/alert-type) and include the following context: customer_id, tenant_type (hosted/dedicated/private), service, region, recent_error_snippet, and current_runbook_version.nnsafety gates and preconditionsnnautomation must not run unless all the following are true:nn- customer has opted-in in the onboarding contract and the opt-in record exists in the cs portal.n- the active slos for the customer are known and automation allowed for the slo class.n- at least one recent successful telemetry heartbeat from the effected service in the last 5 minutes.n- no active incident labeled major-outage for the same customer.n- automation run quota for the customer has not been exhausted (default 6 runs / 24 hours).nnautomation recipes and examplesnneach automation recipe is a small documented unit with: trigger definition, preconditions, exact steps, rollback procedure, runbook link, required rbac role, and audit metadata. examples below are canonical recipes we use as templates.nnrecipe: connector-restart-with-backoffn- trigger: connector http 5xx 3 for 5 minutes or connector crashlooping 3 restarts / 10 minutesn- preconditions: opt-in, recent heartbeat, automation quota availablen- steps (automated):n 1. create incident stub and link to customers cs record.n 2. annotate monitoring event with automation_run_id and start timestamp.n 3. graceful restart of connector (post /customer/id/connectors/id/actions/restart?modegraceful) with timeout 45s.n 4. wait for successful healthcheck: get /health/connectors/id (retry 3x @ 10s).n 5. if healthcheck passes, warm cache prefetch job (async).n 6. close incident stub with resolution code automated_restart_success.n- rollback: if healthcheck fails after step 3, perform a forced restart and escalate to support tier 2.n- audit: all steps produce structured events to /events/selfheal with policy_id and automation_run_id.nnrecipe: model-variant-failovern- trigger: model container oom or degraded token throughput 40 for 10 minutesn- preconditions: compatible fallback model available for customers deployment, model cost tier alignment checkedn- steps:n 1. mark route read-only for new non-essential low-priority requests for 60s.n 2. gradually shift 10 traffic to fallback variant and monitor quality/regression metrics over 5 minutes.n 3. if quality regression 25 - 50 - 100).n 4. notify customer and cs with rollout timeline and telemetry links.n- rollback: immediate rollback to pinned model if regression 3 at any step.nnimplementation patterns and safe primitivesnn- idempotent actions: all apis called by automations must be idempotent or have safe detect-and-noop semantics.n- circuit breaker: automations include a local circuit that prevents repeated runs against the same target if failure rate does not drop after 3 attempts.n- scoped throttling: rate-limit automation actions per customer and per resource to prevent cascading failures.n- audit trail: structured json logs for every automation run (fields: automation_run_id, policy_id, initiatorautomation, preconditions, steps, outcomes, timestamps, owner_contact).nnchange control and deployment process for recipesnn1. author drafts recipe as a pr in infra-selfheal repo. pr must include unit tests, enable policy with default disabled. cs will opt-in customers per onboarding workflows.nntesting and validationnn- unit tests: validate precondition checks and idempotency.n- integration tests: run simulated alert flows in the staging harness with injected failures.n- chaos tests: periodically run chaos scenarios (connector failures, model ooms) in a controlled environment.n- observability: every test run writes to a test-results index and dashboard with pass/fail and measured mttr impact.nnrunbook: manual handoff if automation failsnn1. alert hits support tier 1 with automation_run_id. recipe replaced with the suffix -manual (e.g., connector-restart-with-backoff-manual).n4. if remediation is not possible, initiate incident bridge and follow incident process in oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks.nncustomer onboarding checklist for self-healnn- confirm opt-in consent documented in contract and entered in cs portal.n- capture customer slos and forbidden deployments). it is intended for customer success, product, sre, serving runtime, and security teams. the goal is to reduce surprise regressions, keep customers informed, and make rollbacks telemetry gates.nnprimary stakeholders and ownershipn---------------------------------n- customer success (cs): final customer communications, risk assessment for accounts, qbr notes.n- product: configurable ttl,n 2) routed to a lower-cost model variant (quantized or smaller), orn 3) served from the customers best-effort cached response (for embeddings/long-running ops).n- deferrals must be title: regression cascade escalation and customer guardrails, content: summary:nthis playbook defines the observable triggers, triage steps, mitigation actions, and customer communications for simultaneous model-quality regressions and inference cost or token-spend spikes (a regression cascade). it is intended for customer success, first-line support (l1), sre, and runtime engineering to rapidly protect customer slas while preserving throughput and minimizing rollback scope.nnwhen to use this playbook:n- any time a customer, tenant, or cohort exhibits a quality drop (synthetic-eval delta or customer complaint) that co-occurs with a 30 increase in per-request cost or per-token compute time for the same time window.n- automated detection fires when both a quality metric and a cost/latency metric cross configured thresholds (see detection and triggers).nngoals and guardrails:n- protect customer-facing applications within 1560 minutes for critical customers.n- maintain availability slo: 99.9 request success for dedicated tenants 99.5 for hosted api customers.n- limit blast radius: prefer per-tenant or per-route mitigations before global rollbacks.n- preserve telemetry for postmortem and for qbr discussion.nnroles and responsibilities:n- customer success (owner): primary comms to customer, coordinate qbr follow-up and mitigations with engineering.n- l1 support: initial alert acknowledgment, surface customer impact, apply documented mitigations (circuit-breakers, throttles, short-term rate-limits).n- runtime/sre (on-call): containment actions (fallback routing, model variant switch, capacity throttles).n- runtime engineering/model onboarding: root-cause investigation for model artifact or quantization regressions.n- trust safety / security (if sensitive data exposure suspected): immediate involvement.nndetection and triggers (signals):n- quality signals (any of):n - quality_score_delta (synthetic eval score) 2x.n - automated eval alert: personalisation-eval-failure rate 5 on golden prompts.n- cost / performance signals (any of):n - per-request gpu ms p95 increases by 40 vs baseline over 30m.n - per-token compute cost (gpu-time tokens) 1.3x baseline for the same model/sequence distribution.n - unexpected spike in per-tenant charges or throttling events.n- composite trigger (requires 1 quality 1 cost signal):n - composite_regression_cascade true when both cross thresholds within same 30-minute window.nnimmediate triage (015 minutes):n1) acknowledge the alert and tag in incident channel: cust-alerts/regression-cascade, post short summary and links to dashboards.n2) l1: confirm customer impact and severity using:n - query: select count() from requests where tenant_id and last_30m and tokenization anomalies, enable prefix-caching bypass and drop aggressive auto-batching for the tenant to isolate kv-cache behavior.n4) open a short-lived incident channel and attach traces, request ids, and representative failing outputs. preserve at least 72 hours of request bodies for postmortem (encrypted at rest).nnmitigation and customer protection (60240 minutes):n1) apply model-level rollback if artifact/weight corruption is suspected. rollback checklist:n - confirm candidate model sha and compare checksums: sha256sum model-vx.tar.gzn - verify that the previous model variant (vx-1) had stable synthetic-eval metrics for the affected prompts.n - initiate canary rollback with 5 traffic for 30 minutes, monitor quality/cost deltas.n2) if cost spike is due to a serving configuration (batching/sequence-length kernel changes): revert to previous kernel selection policy via runtime config flags. example flag toggles:n - runtime.feature_flags.kernel_selector legacyn - runtime.batch.window_ms 10n3) for customer-facing protection, offer temporary quota relief or a safety-mode model with guaranteed latency and cost caps (coordinate with finance for credits).n4) customer comms: customer success drafts an initial status note (see templates below) and schedules an incident-specific sync if the customer requests.nnlonger-term analysis and qbr integration (24 hours):n- collect and store: request traces, model shas, quantization config, kernel selections, and the sequence-length distribution during the incident window.n- postmortem: standard 5-part rca (timeline, impact, root cause hypothesis, mitigation, preventive actions). owner: runtime engineering. deliverable within 72 hours.n- qbr inclusion: define actions and metrics to present to the customer (quality regression delta, unblock timeline, and planned mitigations).nnescalation matrix (summary):n- l1 support (first 15m) - runtime/sre on-call (1560m) - runtime engineering model immediate route pin fallback notify exec on-call.n- if rollback candidate fails to recover quality for canary - escalate to full rollback approval within 3 hours.nnrunbook configs and alert rules detection and automated remediation playbook, content: overviewnnpurpose: this playbook defines how redwood detects silent degradations (performance or quality regressions that do not immediately trigger customer-facing errors) and how we automatically remediate or escalate them. it centralizes detection signals, automated mitigation actions, ownership, and customer communication templates.nnscope: applies to hosted api, dedicated, and private tenants for production inference pipelines. focus areas: inference quality drift (semantic regressions), behind-the-scenes latency/cost regressions, and resource contention that degrades tail latency without complete failures.nnprinciplesnn- detect early using behavioral signals instead of waiting for incident thresholds.n- prefer automated safe remediation (circuit breakers, model fallback, synthetic rollbacks) when available.n- keep customers informed for any automated action that modifies their request routing, model variant, or cost profile.nnkey definitionsnn- silent degradation: degradation in availability, latency tail, unit cost, or model output fidelity that does not meet an immediate sla but will materially affect customer experience over time (e.g., 15 increase in 95th percentile latency sustained for 30 minutes while error rate remains soft mitigation - hard mitigation - human escalation).n- synthetic journey: end-to-end customer request simulation that verifies correctness, latency, and token cost against a baseline.nnsignals and detection rulesnn1) telemetry signals (primary):n - p95 latency increase: 20 over rolling 60-min baseline for a customer segment.n - median tokens-per-generation increase: 30 vs. expected prompt distribution.n - inference unit cost variance: 25 sustained for 30 minutes.n - model-quality drift: decrease in internal eval accuracy/qa score by 5 on control prompt-set.n - synthetic journey failure rate: 3 failed assertions in last 10 runs.nn2) composite alerts (trigger when 2 signals occur within a 30-minute window):n - example: p95 latency tokens increase - composite degradation alert.nn3) noise control and suppression:n - require minimum sample size (50 requests) in 30-minute window to avoid noisy triggers.n - apply anomaly detection smoothing: use robust median-of-means to ignore one-off spikes.nnmitigation ladder (automated-first flow)nnstage 0 observability escalation (automatic, no customer impact):n- enrich alert with correlating dimensions: region, model_variant, tenant_id, pod_id, request_path.n- run synthetic journey (fast) against the same variant and region.n- snapshot kv cache hit ratio and batch size distribution.n- notify oncall via slack channel ops-customer-alerts with prefilled context.nnstage 1 soft mitigations (safe, reversible):n1. adaptive single-tenant batching loosen: reduce max batch wait time from config (default 25 ms - 10 ms) to reduce tail latency for latency-sensitive customers.n - command: curl -x post admin_api/tenants/tenant/config -d batch_wait_ms:10n2. prefix-kv cache warmup disable/enable toggle: temporarily disable prefix cache prefetch for affected tenant to prevent thrash.n3. reduce quantization aggressiveness for the specific model_variant (if supported) to restore tail latency at expense of small cost increase.n- automation: playbook automation runs these incrementally with health checks after each change (10-minute stabilization window).nnstage 2 hard mitigations (automated but higher-impact):n1. model-fallback to higher-latency but more stable variant (e.g., redwood-model-v2.small - redwood-model-v2.base).n - route policy change: set fallbacktrue for affected tenant and route for 15 minutes.n2. cross-region failover for regional capacity anomalies (only for customers with cross-region enabled).n3. temporary request-throttling or per-tenant fairshare enforcement to protect shared capacity.n- automation: require 3 confirmation checks (composite signal persists across 3 consecutive 10-minute windows) before applying.nnstage 3 human-in-the-loop and customer-impacting actions:n- paging to sre and customer success for coordinated action.n- consider scheduled model rollback (if recent model rollout is correlated).n- initiate coordinated customer communication and qbr action items.nnescalation matrix and ownershipnn- primary owner: sre (eng-sre) responsible for automated runbook maintenance and operations targeting.n- secondary owner: customer success responsible for customer notification and follow-up.n- tertiary owner: runtime/serving team responsible for fixing systemic regressions (kernel changes, batching logic).nnseverity mapping (example):n- sev-3 (degradation): p95 latency up 20, small customer impact. action: stages 0-1 automated. notify cs.n- sev-2 (significant degradation): p95 up 50 or synthetic failures 10. action: stages 0-2 automated plus sre paging.n- sev-1 (critical): sustained degradation causing customer sla breach or data loss. action: full incident runbook immediate human response and customer-wide comms.nncustomer communication templatesnn- auto-notify (low impact): we detected increased latency affecting your tenant in region x. weve applied temporary mitigations and are monitoring. no action required on your side. status: investigating.n- escalated notification (when model-fallback or throttling applied): to prevent downstream impact we temporarily routed requests to a stable model variant. expected impact: small quality delta for 1560 minutes. we will notify when normal routing is restored.nnimplementation details and examplesnn1) synthetic journey definition (yaml example):n name: conversational-checkn frequency_minutes: 5n tenant_scope: controln steps:n - send_prompt: summarize: the market yesterday...n - assert_latency_lt_ms: 350n - assert_tokens_lt: 300n - compute_quality_score: baseline_eval.jsonnn2) example alert rule (pseudo):n- name: cs-enablement@redwood.ai., doc_id: dsid_42ffe8a8e8f54ce682b4ec0f45537c65, source_type: confluence, title: tenant capacity profiling, cost prediction, and qbr template, content: overviewnnthis document describes the standardized approach redwood customer success (cs) and sre use to: 1) profile an enterprise tenants capacity and request shape, 2) produce a 312 month cost and capacity prediction for qbrs, and 3) include a reusable qbr template that surfaces risk, recommended actions, and contractual implications for dedicated/private customers. the goal is to make capacity conversations data-driven and reproducible across accounts.nngoalsn- provide a canonical set of metrics and queries for tenant-level capacity profiling.n- define a lightweight forecasting methodology (short, medium, long horizon) that balances observed telemetry with business signals.n- produce a qbr-ready one-pager and supporting appendix for technical stakeholders and commercial owners.n- define ownership, cadence, and escalation steps when capacity risk exceeds thresholds.nnscopen- applies to: dedicated and private tenants, customers with committed capacity contracts, and any hosted customer requesting formal capacity planning.n- not covered: model training costs, third-party model hosting (unless integrated through redwood routing), or non-inference infrastructure (storage-only pipelines).nndefinitions and key metricsn- 95th/99th p90/p99 latency: token-level generation latency at the configured model route.n- token-throughput (tokens/s): measured per model pool.n- requests per second (rps): api request rate.n- concurrency: number of simultaneous in-flight requests per tenant.n- tail utilization: percent of time a tenant consumes 80 of its reserved gpu pool.n- cost-per-1k-tokens: unit-cost metric normalized for forecasting.nnprimary data sources (examples)- metrics: telemetry ingestion (prometheus) - metric names: redwood.request.count, redwood.request.latency_ms, redwood.kv_cache.hit_rate, redwood.tokens.generatedn- billing: per-tenant billing records (bigquery table: billing.tenant_usage)n- traces: sampled request traces in x-ray/jaeger for degradation analysisn- config: tenant_config table for reserved pool sizes, routing policies, model pinsnnprofiling methodology (step-by-step)n1) baseline window: collect a 14-day patterns for running slo-focused experiments and model canaries on redwoods inference fleet. it establishes a safety-first approach so teams can iterate model rollouts and runtime tuning while short-term error budget without sre sign-off.n2) observable experiments all canaries must ship with an experiment dashboard, trace sampling, and dedicated alert rules.n3) capacity-aware rollouts duration of the experiment.n- if headroom cannot be met, the rollout must use lower traffic or extended ramp with sre-approved acceptance criteria.nnalert rule examples (prometheus-style compliance foundation), content: 1. summarynretention controls productize customer-configurable data retention across core redwood inference data classes (request/response logs, prompts/completions where stored, audit logs, traces/metrics, and limited artifacts) with safe defaults per deployment tier. the feature set includes:n- a consistent retention policy model, evaluated centrally, with require:n- explicit retention periods per data class (and sometimes per region).n- clear deletion semantics (ttl vs. purge, time-to-delete, idempotency).n- legal hold / incident hold capabilities with an auditable trail.n- evidence that policies are enforced (monitoring verification signals).nntoday, retention behavior is inconsistent across stores and hard to describe during security reviews. this increases sales/cs overhead, creates compliance risk (over-retention), and increases operational risk (unbounded storage growth).nn 3. goals / non-goalsn 3.1 goalsn1) ship customer-configurable (policy surface auditability)nn2) provide auditable visibility:n- retention policy change historyn- exportable configuration (machine-readable)nn3) reduce security-review overhead:n- standardized terminology and predictable answers (ties into security faq compliance report pack work).nn 3.2 non-goals (initial release)n- full custom report builder or bring your own grc integrations beyond export formats.n- arbitrary per-field redaction policies (handled separately under logging standards).n- instant delete guarantees across all systems (we will provide bounded purge slas, not synchronous deletion).nn 4. personas and user storiesn 4.1 personasnsecurity admin (customer)n- owns compliance posture needs proof of retention configuration and enforcement.n- wants safe defaults incident exceptions to preserve debuggability with approvals.nnauditor / grc (customer redwood internal)n- needs an exported view of retention settings and a change trail (who changed what, when, why).n- needs clear mapping of data classes to storage systems and deletion mechanisms.nn 4.2 core user storiesn1) as a security admin, i can set retention for request/response logs and traces to 7 security admin, i can place a legal hold on audit logs for a defined case, with approvals and an audit trail.nn 5. definitions and data classes (v1)nretention controls applies to the following logical data classes (each maps to one or more backing stores):n- request/response logs: api gateway/service request metadata response metadata. may include prompts/completions only if logging is enabled to capture them.n- prompts/completions (where stored): content captured for debugging/analytics when a tenant enables content logging.n- audit logs: immutable event trail of control-plane and security-relevant actions (e.g., policy changes, access changes, key events).n- traces/metrics: telemetry emitted by the platform (service traces, performance metrics, error aggregates).n- artifacts (limited, where applicable): evaluation datasets or artifacts stored within redwood-managed systems (not customer-owned buckets).nnout of scope for v1 (explicitly): customer-managed exports stored in customer-controlled locations, and data stored entirely in customer-managed infrastructure in private deployments where redwood is not the data processor.nn 6. product requirementsn 6.1 functional the recommended approach for designing, running, and validating tenant-level synthetic workloads during enterprise onboarding, cutover canaries, and qbr-driven stability assessments. it targets customer-success engineers, sres, and solutions engineers who are responsible for validating that a tenants production traffic profile will meet latency, cost, and fidelity targets on redwood inference.nngoals and success criteriann- validate tenant sla / slo alignment before production cutover. typical thresholds: p99 latency lt 450ms (generation-only paths), error rate lt 0.5 for 5m window, and no more than 15 token-cost uplift vs. forecast.n- detect functional regressions introduced by model or infra changes (output fidelity checks).n- identify capacity hotspots (kv cache miss ratios, batching inefficiencies, burst throttling).n- produce artifact for qbr: run report, signal deltas, and remediation recommendations.nnwhen to runnn1. pre-cutover validation: after tenant config and telemetry hooks are provisioned, before final dns cutover.n2. canary validation: during incremental traffic ramp (1 25 100).n3. quarterly stability review (qbr): scheduled synthetic runs that mimic seasonal peak patterns.nnsynthetic workload taxonomynn- deterministic replay (traffic replayer): replay of sanitized historical requests (best-fidelity for output regression checks).n- probabilistic generator (template-based): parameterized prompt templates covering length, instruction complexity, and tool-calling patterns (best for stress and variety).n- spike/burst test: short windows of extremely high rps to exercise autoscaling and fairshare.n- long-tail test: low-qps wide-distribution of rare prompts to exercise model cache cold-starts and fallback routing.nndesign principlesnn1. safety-first: sanitize pii before replay enforce privacy and retention rules.n2. observability-driven: every synthetic request must carry tracing headers and a unique synthetic tag (tenant.synthetic_run_id).n3. signal parity: ensure synthetic requests traverse the same ingress, auth, and routing layers as real traffic (no bypasses).n4. incremental scope: start with smoke functional load spike. halt on safety or slo failures.nnrequired telemetry assertionsnn- core telemetry (required): request_id, tenant_id, model_name, route, trace_id, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_estimate_usd, kv_cache_hit (boolean), batch_size, response_status.n- slo/assertion matrix (examples):n assertion threshold action on fail n ------:---n p95 end-to-end latency (route: /v1/generate) lt 220ms pause ramp, triage n p99 token-latency generation lt 450ms escalate to runtime oncall n kv cache hit ratio (common-prefixes) gt 70 investigate cache keying / prefixing n token cost uplift lt 15 vs forecast flag for finops review n model fidelity regression (bleu/rouge or eval set drift) delta lt 2 trigger model rollback plan nnworkload construction checklistnn- obtain tenant traffic profile: average rps, peak rps, typical prompt length, usage mix (single-shot, chat, embeddings).n- prepare sanitized sample corpus (size: 1k10k requests depending on test). mask pii using redaction script.n- create templates to increase/decrease prompt complexity. examples: short-instruction (520 tokens), medium-context (50250 tokens), long-context (2504k tokens).n- define time distribution: steady-state, daily-peak window(s), burst windows.n- map templates to routing rules (hosted/dedicated/private / fallback variants).nnvalidation run procedure (step-by-step)nn1. pre-flight (owner: customer-success):n - confirm telemetry forwarding is active and dashboards ingest synthetic tags.n - ensure dedicated canaries are provisioned for isolation (if required).n - prepare stakeholder channel and incident paging list.n2. smoke test (5m):n - run 50100 requests across each route/model. verify reachability, auth, and baseline latency.n - command example (template-based):n curl -x post n -h authorization: bearer tenant_api_key n -h x-synthetic-run: tenant.synthetic_run_idrun-20260210-01 n -h content-type: application/json n -d model:rwd-small-compat,input:summarize: the quarter...,max_tokens:64nn3. functional regression checks (3060m):n - replay deterministic corpus against pinned model versions. collect evaluation metrics (bleu/rouge/embedding-similarity) against golden outputs.n - run automated diff job to compute percent of responses flagged by heuristic safety checks.nn4. load ramp (13 hours):n - ramp per agreed plan: 5 25 50 100. at each step, hold for 1030 minutes and evaluate assertions.n - observe batching behavior: watch average batch_size and token-latency.nn5. spike test (1530 minutes):n - generate multiple short bursts (10x baseline rps) for 25 minutes each to validate autoscaling and fairshare.nn6. long-tail sweep (60120 minutes):n - execute a wide variety of low-frequency prompts to assess cache cold-starts and fallback.nn7. post-run analysis and artifact generation:n - produce run report with graphs: latency percentiles, kv_cache_hit ratio over time, batch_size distribution, error traces, token cost per minute.n - attach diff-summary for functional regression and fidelity metrics.nnfailure modes, common root causes, and mitigationsnn- high p99 token-latency:n - root causes: insufficient batching due to low aggregation window, oversized model variant, kv cache misses.n - mitigations: increase batching window for non-latency-critical routes, enable smaller quantized variant, tune cache keying.n- elevated error rate during ramp:n - root causes: rate limits, quota enforcement, auth issues, misconfigured ingress acl.n - mitigations: throttle client, raise quota with cust-success approval, verify tenant api key and ip allowlist.n- token cost far above forecast:n - root causes: model switchover to larger size, repeated retries causing duplicate tokens, unexpected long-context prompts.n - mitigations: pin model version, add client-side deduplication and debounce, apply prompt-length caps at ingress.nnrunbook snippets and toolsnn- redactor (python): simple dsid_6882443aebd74b9083a0ae16337ff6b2, source_type: confluence, title: service degradation credit calculator and approval flow, content: overviewnnnpurposen-------nthis playbook defines the operational calculator, approval workflow, and customer communication templates used when redwood inference determines an eligible service credit after a verified service degradation. it is intended for customer success (cs), billing, sre, and legal to coordinate consistent, auditable credit actions for enterprise customers.nnscopen-----n- applies to hosted and dedicated customers covered by an sla or slo agreement.n- covers degradations affecting availability, tail latency slo breaches, and sustained quality regressions that meet the credit policy thresholds in the customer contract.n- does not cover discounts for product/feature requests, account disputes unrelated to service degradation, or third-party billed items.nndefinitionsn-----------n- incident period: window of time for which slo behavior is measured.n- eligible degradation: measurable breach where verified telemetry and rca show platform responsibility.n- credit cap: maximum credit allowed per billing period, defined by contract (commonly 100 of monthly usage for the impacted service or the contract-specified cap).nnwhen to use this calculatorn---------------------------n1. incident has a postmortem and owner-confirmed root cause assigning primary responsibility to redwood.n2. telemetry artifacts (traces, metrics, request logs) are available for the incident window.n3. customer has requested compensation or cs/sre recommends offering a credit based on sla terms.nncredit calculation methodologynnprinciplesn- calculation must be deterministic and reproducible from telemetry.n- prefer simple, contract-aligned formulas over ad hoc amounts.n- include throttling to enforce contract credit caps and avoid double-counting across related incidents.nnbase formula (availability slo example)n- let slo_target contractual availability percentage (e.g., 99.9).n- let actual measured availability during the incident window as a percentage.n- degradation max(0, slo_target - actual).n- rawcreditpercent (degradation / (100 - slo_target)) 100.n- appliedcreditpercent min(rawcreditpercent, contractcreditcappercent).nnexample: 99.9 slo, actual 99.6 over billing monthn- degradation 99.9 - 99.6 0.3n- rawcreditpercent (0.3 / 0.1) 100 300 - capped to contractcreditcappercent (e.g., 100)nnlatency slo (p99 example)n- define slo_target_p99 in ms (e.g., 150ms).n- compute p99_actual for incident window.n- if p99_actual no credit.n- if p99_actual slo_target_p99: latencydelta p99_actual - slo_target_p99.n- rawcreditpercent clamp((latencydelta / slo_target_p99) latencyweight, 0, contractcreditcappercent)n- latencyweight is a policy constant (default 50) to avoid overcompensating short bursts.nnquality regressions (model outputs)n- credits for quality regressions are only eligible when a regression is (a) caused by a platform rollout or model swap and (b) leads to measurable downstream failure (e.g., x increase in downstream error rates or customer-reported failure rate).n- use a metric-based threshold with an evaluative audit (example: 15 increase in failed qa checks for a validated evaluation prompt set).nncomposite incidents and aggregationn- multiple urgent escalations affecting enterprise customers (hosted, dedicated, private). it standardizes handoff from support - customer success - engineering/sre/onprem teams and ensures sla alignment, rapid mitigation, and consistent postmortem follow-through.nnscope: applies to incidents triggered by customer-facing outages, severe quality regressions, billing anomalies tied to inference, or security-sensitive events that impact an enterprise account. not intended for routine tickets or feature requests.nnaudience: support l2/l3, customer success managers (csm), solutions engineers (se), sre/runtime engineers, dedicated/private deployment owners.nnproblem statement: enterprise customers expect predictable slas and clear escalation paths. during multiteam incidents we observe delays due to missing telemetry, unclear ownership for dedicated/private handoffs, and inconsistent customer comms. this playbook remedies those gaps.nn---nnseverity definitions and sla targetsnn1) severity taxonomy (enterprise standard)n - sev1 (critical): complete or near-complete service unavailability for production traffic (e.g., 100 request failures, model serve crash, data exfiltration).n - sev2 (high): severe degradation impacting a large subset of traffic or major feature (e.g., p95 latency 5x slo, repeat hallucination producing sensitive output).n - sev3 (medium): partial loss of functionality or reduced performance affecting a minority of users workaround exists.n - sev4 (low): minor issues, documentation questions, enhancement requests.nn2) sla targets (enterprise response/acknowledge mitigation expectations)n - sev1: acknowledge within 15 minutes. initial mitigation plan within 60 minutes. customer update every 30 minutes until mitigation. target full resolution or acceptable workaround in 6 hours (unless constrained by onprem factors).n - sev2: acknowledge within 60 minutes. plan within 4 business hours. updates every 24 hours. target resolution source_type: confluence, title: customer comms templates (support cs), content: purposenuse these templates for consistent, customer-safe communication during escalations across hosted, dedicated, and private tiers. these templates are designed for:n- initial acknowledgementn- mitigation / investigation updatesn- workaround guidance (known issues)n- resolution follow-up (including next steps and optional rca workflow)nnthese templates are written to reduce back-and-forth, align to support slas, and avoid overpromising.nn tone content guidance (read before using)nbe clear, calm, and specific. latency, blocked workflow).n- ask for the minimum viable diagnostics: request ids, timestamps, region, model, sdk version, and whether streaming/non-streaming.n- provide a concrete next update time (next update by 14:30 pt).n- if a workaround exists, provide it as copy/paste steps and clearly label it as temporary.n- use we believe / were investigating / our current hypothesis when not confirmed.n- if relevant, state what is safe to share (e.g., no action needed vs please retry with).nn dont (what not to promise)n- do not promise etas unless sre/eng has provided an externally sharing.n- do not imply contractual outcomes (credits, sla breach confirmation) in-line. route to the credits process and exec escalation protocol when needed.n- do not ask for sensitive data (full prompts, customer datasets, secrets). prefer request ids and sanitized logs. if logs are needed: provide explicit redaction instructions and use approved secure channels.n- do not imply that pinned model versions or routing policies are guaranteed in all failure modesuse the documented policy language.nn consistency rulesn- use the same severity language across channels. if you use p0/p1 enterprise onboarding, dedicated cutovers, or scheduled resilience drills. the ladder gives customer success, sre, and engineering teams a safe, repeatable set of scenarios that increase in impact, from low-risk smoke tests to full-region failovers. the qa harness provides automation snippets, acceptance criteria, and a post-test report template to accelerate validation and qbr artifacts.nnscopenn- applies to hosted, dedicated, and private customers running production traffic via the redwood api or dedicated pools.n- focus areas: model serving availability, routing/fallback, kv/prefix cache behavior, telemetry continuity, and cost/safety controls.n- not within scope: changes to customer production data stores outside redwood endpoints, third-party cloud provider restoration steps (except as monitored outcomes).nndefinitionsnn- simulation ladder: ordered list of test scenarios from non-disruptive to high-impact.n- qa harness: scripts, monitors, and reporting actions: ramp canary qps from 1 - 100 over 10 minutes using load tool.n - acceptance: per-customer rate-limit webhook fires, no global degradation, slos maintained for other tenants.nn5. region on-call practicesnn---nn definitions (what we mean by priority vs severity)n- support priority (p0p4): how urgently support must respond/coordinate based on customer impact and contractual expectations, including single-customer criticality.n- incident severity (sev0sev3): engineering/sre incident classification based on service health impact, scope, and whether we should run formal incident process.nnsupport assigns p-level in jira. engineering/sre assigns sev-level when an incident is declared (or if we are operating under incident-style coordination).nn---nn quick mapping table (default)n support priority default incident severity mapping typical scope support posture n------------n p0 sev0 (or sev1 if isolated to 1 region/tier) widespread outage or critical enterprise outage with no workaround immediate paging bridge frequent customer updates consider status page qualification n p1 sev1 (sometimes sev2) major degradation, partial outage, or high-risk enterprise issue rapid escalation bridge may be required time-boxed investigation n p2 sev2 degradation affecting subset of customers/features triage quickly escalate if triggers hit publish workaround if repeatable n p3 sev3 minor issue, workaround exists, limited impact normal queue with clear next steps no paging n p4 n/a question/feature request/how-to route to docs/cs/pm no incident process nnimportant: the mapping is a default, not a rule. a single-customer issue can be p0 (support priority) without being sev0 (global incident) if the platform is healthy overall.nn---nn support priority (p0p4) definitions and examplesn p0 critical customer impact (immediate response)ndefinition: a customer cannot use a contracted core capability or is experiencing a critical security/compliance impact, and there is no viable workaround. includes single-customer stop-the-line enterprise situations.nncommon p0 examplesn- auth outage: login/token issuance failures (hosted console, api auth, sso) preventing access for many users or a key enterprise admin path.n- region hard outage: 5xx/timeout failures for core inference endpoints in a region for a meaningful portion of traffic.n- streaming disconnects at scale: widespread stream resets/truncation that break production workloads and cannot be mitigated with retries/timeouts.n- private deployment down: customers control issuendefinition: significant production impact with partial functionality remaining, or a critical enterprise issue with a plausible workaround/mitigation but ongoing risk.nncommon p1 examplesn- region degradation: elevated p95 latency or error rate affecting a large subset of requests service remains partially functional.n- dedicated autoscaling instability: latency spikes/throughput drops due to oscillation temporary config knobs can mitigate.n- quota / 429 spike after change: many customer requests failing due to rate-limit behavior may have a workaround or partial mitigation (e.g., client throttling), but impact is active.nn p2 moderate impact / subset of customers / workaround likelyndefinition: noticeable impact but limited scope, or impact that is intermittent and/or has a validated workaround.nncommon p2 examplesn- streaming disconnects limited to one sdk version with workaround (timeout/reconnect guidance).n- embeddings timeouts in one region affecting subset of tenants, improving with retry/backoff.n- audit log delivery latency beyond typical expectations but within tolerated window for most customers mitigation available.nn p3 minor issue / low urgencyndefinition: low production impact, cosmetic issues, or issues with clear workaround and no immediate risk.nnexamplesn- console dashboard missing a breakdown dimension (e.g., region view gaps) while underlying service is healthy.n- structured output validation error messaging confusing but requests succeed with minor adjustments.nn p4 informational / how-to / feature requestndefinition: no service impairment customer needs guidance or requests product changes.nn---nn incident severity (sev0sev3) definitions (engineering/sre)nsupport should understand these so that handoffs and comms are consistent.nn sev0 full outage or extremely high impact (company-level)ndefinition: core production capability is down or effectively unusable for a broad customer set or there is a severe security/compliance event requiring immediate response.nntypical indicatorsn- multi-region outage or widespread inference failuresn- global auth/token issuance outagen- a safety/security issue requiring coordinated responsenn sev1 major degradation / partial outage (high customer impact)ndefinition: material degradation impacting a significant portion of customers/traffic service is partially working.nn sev2 limited degradation / localized incidentndefinition: localized region/tier/model issue, moderate impact, or intermittent failure patterns.nn sev3 minor incident / operational issuendefinition: small impact, low urgency, often handled without full incident process.nn---nn escalation triggers (when to page / start a bridge / move to incidents)ntriggers below apply regardless confluence, title: sensitive-data-exposure-escalation-and-remediation-playbook-2026, content: overview:nthis playbook defines the end-to-end escalation, containment, remediation, and post-incident review process for confirmed or strongly suspected exposures of customer-sensitive data (pii, proprietary customer content, model prompts with sensitive inputs, or retained telemetry). it applies to hosted redwood api, redwood dedicated, and redwood private deployments. the document emphasizes fast containment, clear communication, legal and compliance coordination, and preserving evidence for forensic review.nnscope and definitions:n- sensitive data: anything classified as pii, pci, phi, proprietary trade secrets, or customer-designated restricted data.n- exposure: data confirmed to have been transmitted to an unauthorized destination (external cloud, public internet, third-party vendor without contract), or accessible to unauthorized internal actors.n- suspected exposure: credible indicators (logs, alerts, customer report) that merit immediate containment investigation but are not yet confirmed.n- affected customer: the tenant or organization whose data may be exposed.nndetection triggers (examples):n1) customer report of seeing data returned in unrelated request.n2) ids/ips or data loss prevention (dlp) alert referencing pii patterns in outbound traffic from an inference node.n3) unexpected s3/object-store public acl changes, presigned url issuance to unfamiliar ips.n4) audit log showing api key usage from an ip/geography inconsistent with customer config or dedicated/private infra.n5) telemetry or evals showing kv cache collisions or prefix leakage during rollouts.nnimmediate (first 30 minutes) checklist triage and containment (owner: oncall-sre security-oncall):n1) acknowledge the alert and start an incident in the incident tracker. record timeline, reporter, and initial evidence.n2) classify severity:n - sev-1: confirmed exposure to external party or broad public disclosure.n - sev-2: confirmed exposure limited to small set of actors (internal user or partner) or likely exposure requiring further action.n - sev-3: suspected exposure with low confidence.n3) if sev-1 or sev-2, notify security on-call (pager) and customer success lead for the account within 15 minutes.n4) preserve evidence: snapshot relevant instances, collect kernel logs, container stdout/stderr, inference node audit logs, networking flow logs, and any object-store access logs. follow forensic collection checklist below.n5) apply immediate confluence, title: status page customer escalation playbook (disputed status accuracy), content: purposenthis playbook is used by support and customer success when a customer reports that the public status page does not reflect the impact they are experiencing (status page says everything is ok, but we are failing). it provides:n- a standard intake checklist to quickly validate what the customer is seeing.n- a clear escalation path to sre/on-call and the incident comms lead.n- approved customer-facing responses and guardrails.n- a consistent way to correct status page inaccuracies without increasing on-call burden.nnthis is a customer trust workflow. our goals are (1) fast acknowledgement, (2) accurate classification to the right public component(s), and (3) avoiding speculative or customer-sensitive disclosures.nn when to use this playbooknuse this playbook when any of the following are true:n- customer claims status page indicates operational but they have errors/latency.n- customer claims wrong component/region is marked degraded.n- customer claims incident is missing (no active incident) while multiple customers are impacted.n- customer requests proof/evidence of impact or asks for a post-incident summary while the status page remains green.nndo not use this playbook for:n- single-tenant dedicated or private issues isolated to a single customer environment without broader platform impact (see dedicated/private guidance).n- pure how-to questions about interpreting the status page components (route to docs/devex guidance).nn definitions and guardrailsn what the public status page representsn- the status page reflects platform component health by product surface and region (e.g., hosted api us-east, streaming eu-west).n- it is not a guarantee that every request is successful for every customer, and it does not expose customer-specific capacity constraints.nn required guardrails (must follow)n- do not disclose: customer-specific capacity, noisy-neighbor details, account identifiers, or security-sensitive root cause.n- do not over-promise sla credits or contractual remedies in support channels.n- do not speculate on root cause. stick to that streaming responses stop emitting tokens mid-generation while the http connection remains open. the client may not receive an error or a terminal done event. this is typically described as a freeze or stall in server-sent events (sse).nn symptomsn- streaming completion stops mid-sentence.n- tcp/tls connection remains open.n- no final event (e.g., done) is observed by the client.n- client ui shows an infinite spinner or hangs waiting for more tokens.nn where weve seen itn- dedicated and hosted api traffic, primarily under higher concurrency or with intermediaries (proxies/lbs).n- internal reproduction was easiest when response compression (gzip) was applied to text/event-stream.nn primary contributing factors (current understanding)n1. buffering/backpressure in intermediaries when payload chunks are small (token-by-token).n2. gzip/compression on sse causing chunk coalescing and delayed flush.n3. client implementations that wait indefinitely without a read timeout.nn mitigations / workaroundsn customer-side recommended configurationn- set a client-side read timeout for streaming responses (do not wait indefinitely).n- implement retry with idempotency keys for safe replay of requests.n- if a proxy is involved (e.g., nginx), disable buffering for event streams:n - nginx: proxy_buffering offn- ensure the client uses curl -n or equivalent (no output buffering) during debugging.nn redwood-side mitigationsn- disable gzip/compression for content-type: text/event-stream.n- flush token chunks and send periodic heartbeats to keep the stream active.nn triage checklist (support/on-call)n1. confirm endpoint: openai-compatible streaming (streamtrue) vs redwood native streaming.n2. ask if any proxy/lb exists between client and redwood.n3. request a minimal reproduction (curl -n) and region/model.n4. check gateway config for sse compression in the customers region/tier.n5. if customer can tolerate, recommend switching region temporarily to validate hypothesis.nn linked examplesn- sup-1842 (arcadia health): fixed by disabling gzip for sse heartbeat flush.n- sup-1911 (northwind robotics): likely proxy buffering customer mitigated by disabling summaryndedicated gpu pools can occasionally enter an autoscaling oscillation pattern (rapid scale up/down or repeated rescheduling) that drives latency spikes, intermittent 5xx/timeout errors, and unstable throughput. this article describes how support/cs can identify the pattern quickly, apply safe short-term mitigations, and determine when to involve sre/capacity.nnthis is a workaround / (customer-managed cluster autoscaling similar symptoms but different knobs/ownership).nn---nn customer-visible symptomsncustomers may report one or more of:n- latency spikes (p95/p99 jumps) coincident never settles (replicas keep changing)nnsupport-side signals you may see:n- frequent capacity changing notes in internal dashboardsn- increased queueing / batching delay even when average load looks acceptablen- elevated retry rates (customer-side) amplifying loadnn---nn what oscillation looks like (pattern definitions)nwe use oscillation to describe any of these patterns over a short window (typically 1560 minutes):n1) replica thrash: replica count toggles up/down repeatedly (e.g., 6107118)n2) scale-down too aggressively: scales down quickly after a burst, then immediately scales back upn3) placement churn: replicas are recreated/restarted frequently (less common usually infrastructure/placement pressure)nnpractical rule of thumb:n- if the pool performs 3 scale actions in 30 minutes and customer latency is materially impacted, treat as oscillation.nn---nn how to confirm (dashboards key metrics)nuse the dedicated customers canonical pool dashboards (support-safe quick view links may be pinned in runbooks if you dont have them, ask sre on-call for the pools dashboard link).nn 1) confirm the customer pool regionnbefore you interpret graphs, confirm:n- customer/org namen- dedicated pool name / cluster identifiern- region (e.g., us-east, eu-west)n- affected endpoint(s): chat, completions, embeddings, reranknn 2) look for correlation between scaling and latencynin the same time range, review:n- replica count (or active workers)n- scale events (up/down)n- p95/p99 latencyn- request rate / tokens per secondn- queue depth / scheduling delaynnstrong indicator:n- p95 latency spikes align with scale-down events or repeated scale actions.nn 3) check utilization targets vs actual behaviornoscillation often occurs when the autoscaler chases a noisy signal.nreview:n- stabilizes)n- min replicas too low for the customers baseline concurrency (causes repeated warmups)n- bursty traffic short averaging window on the scaling signaln- large prompt-length variance leading replicas to the smallest value that keeps p95 latency stable during steady-state.n- if the customer has a predictable baseline load, set min replicas to cover that baseline without scaling.nnoperational guidance:n- prefer a conservative increase (e.g., 12 replicas at a time) and observe for 1015 minutes.nn mitigation b: slow down scale-down behaviorngoal: prevent rapid downscaling that forces repeated warmups and queue spikes.n- increase scale-down cooldown (or downscale stabilization window).n- if supported, increase downscale step size conservatism (scale down fewer replicas per action).nnsuggested starting point (typical):n- scale-down cooldown: 1530 minutes (depending on workload burstiness)nn mitigation c: reduce retry amplification (customer guidance)ngoal: prevent client retries from compounding load.nrecommend:n- exponential backoff with jittern- cap retries (e.g., 23 attempts)n- ensure streaming reconnect logic is idempotent where applicablennonly provide retry guidance thats consistent with the sdk/docs guidance link to the relevant troubleshooting page if available.nn mitigation d: temporary burst headroomnif the issue is triggered by predictable bursts:n- raise max replicas temporarily (if contractually permitted) or enable burst capacity (dedicated feature dependent)n- coordinate with capacity/sre for approval and scheduling constraintsnn---nn configuration knobs (what they do)nexact field names vary by pool generation and internal tooling, but the concepts map cleanly.nn knob what it controls typical symptom average search p95 latency 3x baseline for 30 minutes.n- indexer error rate 5 for 30 minutes despite retries.nnrollback procedure:n1. pause ingestion and redirect reads to snapshot-backed fallback index.n - index-cli promote --index s3://redwood-backups/tenant/ts/snapshot --as tenant_fallbackn2. restore snapshot to active environment if necessary: index-cli restore --source incidents:nn1) ephemeral port churn nat table exhaustion on stateful edge proxies, causing new connections to fail with rst or be reset after tls handshake.n2) imbalanced keepalive and health-check interactions where load balancer probes evict live backend sessions during short surges.n3) tls session cache miss patterns combined with aggressively small client tls timeouts that increase backend cpu and cause transient overload.n4) fanout amplification when a single client request fans out to multiple model variants and an upstream slow backend causes head-of-line timeouts.nnsymptoms (how customers and sres will notice this):n- short, periodic spikes of 502/503/504 errors concentrated to specific ingress proxies (not whole region).n- error rates correlated to increase in ephemeral port allocation (netstat / ss shows many time_wait).n- backend model nodes show normal cpu but elevated accept queue length or connection backlog.n- trace ids show upstream tls handshake succeeded but the first application read returns eof or econnreset.n- synthetic journey checks show success for head requests but post/generation endpoints intermittently fail.nnimmediate mitigation runbook (for
