overviewnpredictive autoscaling is an opt-in mode for redwood dedicated that biases scale decisions using forecasted demand (time-of-day patterns, scheduled events, historical request rates/latency). predictive mode does not override customer-configured min/max bounds and will fall back to reactive signals when forecasts are stale/unavailable.nnthis page lists the most common known issues observed during pilot/canary, how to recognize them, and recommended workarounds for customer success and support. this is not a full runbook for deep debugging and mitigations, use the dedicated on-call runbook linked above.nnh2. scope / when this page appliesn applies to: dedicated deployments with predictive mode enabled (feature-flagged per account/deployment).n not applicable to: hosted api autoscaling or dedicated deployments running reactive-only scaling.nnh2. quick definitions (customer-friendly)n forecast / prediction: a projected target capacity (replicas/gpu slices) for an upcoming time window.n reactive scaling: signals like queue depth, saturation, and latency that trigger scaling based on current conditions.n bounds: customer-configured min and max capacity. the autoscaler clamps desired capacity within these bounds.n bound-hit: when the autoscaler wants to go above max or below min but is prevented by bounds.nnh1. rollout caveats (read first)n1) opt-in guarded rollout: predictive mode is still rolling out. some regions/accounts may not be eligible.n2) model/workload sensitivity: highly bursty workloads with low steady-state traffic can produce noisy forecasts.n3) do not promise no queueing under max bounds: if traffic exceeds max-bound capacity and the region cannot burst, queueing/latency can occur. this is expected behavior the product surfaces it via bound-hit metrics.n4) time-to-effect: changes to predictive settings may take up to 1020 minutes to reflect in decisions (depending on caching and evaluation intervals).nnh1. known issues workaroundsnnh2. 1) false positives (over-scaling before traffic arrives)nsymptomsn capacity ramps up early customer sees increased spend/idle utilization.n forecast line is above actual demand prediction error is consistently positive.nnlikely causesn holidays/product changes make recent history unrepresentative.n scheduled-event definitions are too broad (e.g., daily job marked as high when it is moderate).n low-volume workloads where small absolute errors become large relative errors.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) reduce predictive bias (preferred): switch to predictive reactive override (if available in the customers build) or lower the predictive weight via internal config (eng-assisted).n2) use a tighter max bound to cap spend if the customers primary concern is budget.n3) if customer can tolerate brief queueing, recommend reactive-only during the window and re-enable predictive after retraining/after a week of stable traffic.nnsupport notesn collect: deployment_id, region, last 7 days of request rate, and a screenshot of desired vs bounded capacity.n if the customer is in contract negotiation over cost ceilings, steer toward bounds and recommended ranges, not predictive promises.nnh2. 2) timezone misalignment (forecast ramps at the wrong local time)nsymptomsn customer reports it scales for our ramp, but 13 hours too early/late.n recurring daily ramp shows a consistent offset.nnlikely causesn traffic exhibits local-time patterns but the forecast is effectively aligned to utc (or mis-tagged timezone).n scheduled events were provided in local time but entered/processed as utc.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) confirm the customers operational timezone and the timezone assumed for any scheduled events.n2) temporary mitigation: set a higher min bound covering the ramp window until timezone is corrected.n3) if the account uses scheduled events: update the event schedule with explicit timezone (eng-assisted if the ui/api does not expose timezone selection yet).nnescalation triggern if offset is consistent and reproducible, file an escalation to eng infra with: account_id, deployment_id, region, customer timezone, and at least two days of graphs showing the offset.nnh2. 3) insufficient history (under-scaling because the predictor lacks training data)nsymptomsn predictive mode enabled, but scaling behaves similar to reactive-only.n forecast confidence is low or not available autoscaler logs indicate fallback to reactive.nnlikely causesn new deployment or new model route without enough steady history.n major traffic shape change in the last few days.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) set a conservative min bound aligned to baseline throughput to avoid cold starts.n2) use reactive-only for the first 12 weeks of a new deployment, then re-enable predictive mode once traffic stabilizes.n3) if ramp is known and contractual, use scheduled events (if enabled for the account) as an interim signal source.nnsupport noten predictive mode is not a guarantee it is a best-effort bias that requires stable patterns.nnh2. 4) stale forecast / prediction pipeline outage (sudden behavior change)nsymptomsn predictive scaling appears to stop capacity only changes after queue depth increases.n ui shows forecast timestamp is old, or forecast unavailable.nnlikely causesn forecast provider returned stale data the autoscaler rejected it due to staleness checks.n regional data pipeline delay.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) treat as expected fail-safe: reactive scaling takes over.n2) raise min bound temporarily for the affected ramp window.n3) if customer is impacted (p95 latency regression), advise disabling predictive mode until pipeline recovers.nnescalation triggern any incident where stale forecasts correlate with user-visible latency/slo breach: escalate to sre per the dedicated autoscaler runbook.nnh2. 5) oscillation / capacity jitter (scale up/down thrash)nsymptomsn replicas/gpu count changes frequently (e.g., every few minutes).n customer sees request latency jitter autoscaler event stream shows alternating scale-up and scale-down.nnlikely causesn noisy predictions combined with aggressive cooldowns.n workload has spiky batch traffic that looks like repeated ramps.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) increase cooldown / dampening parameters (eng-assisted if not customer-configurable yet).n2) increase min step size for scale changes (avoid micro-adjustments).n3) prefer reactive signals for scale-down, predictive for scale-up (hybrid mode) where available.n4) if the customer is latency-sensitive, disable predictive temporarily and stabilize with min bound.nnsupport noten if a pilot customer reports oscillation, check whether they are on the build containing anti-oscillation guardrails. if not, coordinate an upgrade or disable predictive.nnh2. 6) null/empty prediction edge case (unsafe downscale risk)nsymptomsn a forecast response contains null/empty values desired capacity appears to drop unexpectedly.nnstatusn mitigated by a hotfix to prevent scale-to-zero when predictor returns null. some older pilot environments may not have the fix.nnrecommended workaroundsn1) if suspected: disable predictive mode immediately and set min bound to a safe baseline.n2) escalate to eng infra with urgency and include timestamps deployment_id.nnh2. 7) max-bound saturation (predictive wants more capacity than allowed)nsymptomsn queue depth increases during ramp customer sees we told it to scale, but it didnt.n metrics show frequent max-bound hit events.nnlikely causesn the customers max bound is below what the workload requires for the ramp.n region capacity shortage prevents provisioning even below max (rare but possible).nnrecommended workaroundsn1) clarify intent: if max bound is a hard budget cap, then queueing is an expected tradeoff.n2) if customer goal is sla/latency, recommend increasing max bound or using burst capacity (if contract allows).n3) for predictable ramps: raise min bound ahead of the ramp so the system is already warm.nnescalation triggern if min bound cannot be met due to region shortage, treat as a reliability event (see shortage behavior in the runbook).nnh1. what to ask the customer (minimum checklist)n1) deployment name / deployment_id and regionn2) current bounds: min, max, cooldowns (if known)n3) predictive mode state (enabled? hybrid? scheduled events?)n4) the customers local timezone and the time window of the rampn5) impact statement: spend concern vs latency/sla concernn6) screenshots or exports of: desired vs bounded capacity, queue depth, and p95 latency over the affected windownnh1. recommended customer guidance (safe, non-committal language)n predictive autoscaling helps pre-warm capacity for repeating traffic patterns, but it still respects your min/max bounds and will fall back to reactive scaling when forecasts are not available.n if the primary goal is controlling spend, set a max bound youre comfortable with and we can tune predictive behavior to avoid early ramp-ups.n if the primary goal is meeting latency slo during a known ramp, a higher baseline min (or scheduled event) is often the most reliable first step.nnh1. when to escalate (internal)nescalate to eng infra / sre if any of the following are true:n predictive mode enabled and customer reports sustained latency regression (p95/p99) during a known rampn reproducible timezone offset or consistently stale forecastsn oscillation causing user-visible impactn suspected null/empty prediction edge casen min bound cannot be met (possible region shortage)nninclude in escalation: account_id, deployment_id, region, timestamps, graphs for queue depth desired/bounded capacity, and (2) streaming cancellation behavior.nnthis page provides a support-ready explanation and recommended mitigations.nn key definitionsn- attempt: a single request admitted by the redwood api gateway (server-side).n- logical request: what the customer thinks of as one user action may map to multiple attempts if the client retries.nn what we billn retriesn- redwood usage is recorded per-attempt.n- if a client retries after a timeout or non-200 response, each admitted attempt can be billable.n- the usage dashboard lists rows by request_id (attempt identifier).nn streaming cancellationn- prompt tokens are counted once the request is admitted (even if the client cancels the stream later).n- completion tokens are counted based on tokens actually generated/streamed prior to cancellation.nn common customer symptomsn- we only sent n requests but we see n rows: retries created additional attempts.n- we timed out at 15s so we expected zero bill: prompt tokens partial completion tokens may still be counted.nn recommended mitigationsn1) avoid automatic retries on client-side timeouts for long generations.n2) increase client timeout where possible (align to max expected generation time).n3) reduce max_tokens / output length to meet latency budgets.n4) for troubleshooting, ask for a small set of request_ids the customers retry/cancel metrics.nn support playbook (quick response blurb)nwe record usage per server-admitted attempt. if your client retries after a timeout, each admitted attempt can appear separately in usage and can be billable. for streaming, prompt tokens are counted once admitted completion tokens reflect what was generated before cancellation.nn referencesn- sup-1842 (northwind ai escalation)n- int-330 (ui helper text kb link)n- slack support page helps support/cs respond to customer reports of new overload protection errors (circuit breakers load shedding) on redwood hosted api.nngoals:n- explain what the customer is seeing (stable may reject requests early and predictably rather than allowing them to time out or generate random 5xx.nncustomers may now see:n- 429 responses for admission / quota / per-tenant caps.n- 503 responses when a regional/model circuit breaker is open or the system is actively shedding load.nnthese responses:n- include stable error codes and a machine-readable json payload.n- typically include a retry-after header to indicate safe retry timing.n- include redwood request/correlation ids for tracing.nn quick triage checklist (support)n1) confirm this is an overload-protection response (see how to recognize below).n2) verify the customer is following recommended retry/backoff (or advise them to change).n3) collect required debug info (ids, time window, region/model, response headers).n4) determine if this is expected transient overload vs a bug/misconfig (missing retry-after, incorrect status mapping, fallback not triggering).n5) escalate to eng oncall when criteria are met (see when to escalate).nn how to recognize overload-protection responsesn common http statusesn- 429 too many requestsn - used for admission controls such as per-tenant concurrency caps, token buckets, or tier limits.n - usually safe to retry with backoff if retry-after is provided.nn- 503 service unavailablen - used when the platform is overloaded at the regional/model level (breaker open) or actively shedding load to protect slos.n - usually safe to retry with backoff and/or reduce load. may persist until capacity recovers.nn expected headers (may vary by route)n- retry-after: integer seconds is preferred (e.g., retry-after: 2).n- x-redwood-request-id: unique id for a single request attempt.n- x-redwood-correlation-id: groups related attempts across services (gateway routing runtime). some clients/logs only show one of these either is helpful.nnif the response is 429/503 and includes a redwood overload error code in the json body, treat it as overload protection.nn error payload: what customers seenoverload errors are additive and json-compatible with existing response parsing.nntypical shape (example):n- error.type: overload_error (or rate_limit_error in some cases)n- error.code: stable machine coden- error.message: human-readablen- error.request_id: mirrors x-redwood-request-id where availablen- error.correlation_id: mirrors x-redwood-correlation-id where availablennexample snippet (illustrative only):nn error: n type: overload_error,n code: breaker_open,n message: the service is temporarily overloaded. please retry after the specified delay.,n request_id: req_01j9...,n correlation_id: corr_01j9...n nnn canonical mapping: status meaning what we tell customersnuse this table to drive consistent customer guidance.nn http typical meaning what support should say customer action n-------------------------------------------------------------------n 429 admission control / rate limiting / tier cap hit your request was rejected to protect system stability. this is not a model failure it indicates you are sending requests faster than the current allowed rate/concurrency. respect retry-after implement exponential backoff jitter reduce concurrency consider batching if persistent, discuss tier/capacity options. n 503 regional/model breaker open or load shedding redwood is temporarily overloaded in the requested region/model. we are rejecting early to avoid timeouts and protect overall reliability. respect retry-after backoff jitter optionally route to another region/model if configured reduce max_tokens/streaming concurrency retry with bounded attempts. nnnotes:n- if the customer reports timeouts with no json error, treat as a separate issue (possible client/network or upstream timeouts) and escalate based on impact.n- if the customer gets 5xx without the overload payload, collect details it may be an unrelated incident.nn retry backoff guidance (what we should recommend)n golden rulesn- always respect retry-after when provided.n- use exponential backoff with jitter do not retry immediately.n- cap retries to avoid amplifying overload.n- reduce concurrency rather than increasing it during overload.n- prefer idempotency keys for safe retries on non-streaming requests.nn recommended algorithm (support-approved)nif retry-after is present:n- sleep retry-after seconds, then retry.nnif retry-after is missing:n- backoff schedule suggestion: 0.5s, 1s, 2s, 4s, then stop (max 4 retries), each with 2040 jitter.nnbounds:n- maximum total retry time budget: 1020 seconds for interactive apps, 60 seconds for batch jobs.n- maximum concurrent retries: keep to a small fraction of steady-state concurrency (e.g., 1020).nn streaming-specific guidancenstreaming workloads can worsen overload if clients open many concurrent streams.n- recommend lower streaming concurrency during peak periods.n- if the customer can tolerate it, recommend shorter outputs (reduce max_tokens) and/or shorter prompts.n- if a stream fails mid-response with an overload error on reconnect attempts, advise them to back off and resume with a bounded number of attempts.nn what not to recommendn- just retry in a tight loop.n- retry immediately with the same concurrency.n- spin up many parallel retries to get through.nn how to interpret and use correlation idsn which ids to ask fornask the customer for (in order of preference):n1) x-redwood-correlation-id (best for cross-service tracing)n2) x-redwood-request-id (single request attempt)n3) timestamp region model route if ids are not availablenn where customers can find themn- response headers in their http client.n- sdk exception fields (python/typescript sdks surface request ids newer versions surface correlation ids when present).n- their application logs if they log response headers.nn how support should use them internallyn- paste the id(s) into the internal log search / tracing tool.n- capture:n - the error.coden - the route (e.g., /v1/chat/completions, /v1/responses, embeddings endpoint)n - the region (requested served)n - whether retry-after was present and its valuennif support cannot access dashboards/tracing, escalate with the ids and all purposenthis page is a support/cs reference for explaining 429 responses after the hot-route capacity protection rollout. it covers:n- what customers may see (payload headers)n- how to distinguish quota vs rate-limit vs overload shedding/admission controln- recommended customer-side retry/backoff behaviorn- when and how to escalate (and what data to collect)nnthis doc is written for support and tams. for implementation details, see the platform design/adr pages linked in related pages.nn---nn what changed (customer-visible)nbeginning with the enterprise priority rollout, redwood enforces tier-aware capacity protection on a set of protected routes (commonly: /v1/chat/completions, /v1/embeddings, /v1/rerank).nncustomers may observe:n- more predictable 429s for best-effort/self-serve traffic during regional pressure.n- enterprise traffic preserved longer (priority routing per-tier budgets), but enterprise requests can still receive 429s when:n - the accounts own limits are reached, orn - the route is in sustained overload and the enterprise budget is exhausted.n- new reason codes and additional headers to explain why the request was rejected.nnimportant framing for customers:n- 429 is not a generic outage signal. it is a deliberate backpressure mechanism to protect overall fleet health and enterprise slos.n- 429 responses are safe to retry when the reason indicates transient pressure, using the guidance below.nn---nn 429 response format (what support should look for)nn common json fields (all 429s)nmost clients will receive an error payload shaped like:n- error.type: rate_limit_exceeded or quota_exceeded or overloadedn- error.code: a stable machine-readable reason code (see table below)n- error.message: human-readable summaryn- error.request_id: request identifier (also returned in response headers)nnif a customer claims the payload is missing or inconsistent, ask for:n- raw response bodyn- full response headersn- sdk version / client librarynn standard headers (may vary by route)nsupport should request and record these headers when present:n- x-redwood-request-id: request id used for internal tracingn- retry-after: seconds to wait before retry (only set for some transient reasons)n- x-redwood-retry-after-ms: millisecond retry hint (preferred when present)n- x-redwood-limit-scope: account api_key route (where enforcement applies)n- x-redwood-limit-policy: policy identifier (internal-friendly string customer can share as opaque)n- x-redwood-429-reason: short reason token (maps to reason codes below)n- x-redwood-rate-limit-limit: numeric limit (requests per window) when applicablen- x-redwood-rate-limit-remaining: remaining requests in current window (when applicable)n- x-redwood-rate-limit-reset: epoch time or seconds-until-reset (when applicable)nnnotes:n- some enterprise customers will only see a subset of limit headers depending on contract configuration and route group settings.n- absence of headers is not automatically a bug it can indicate a rejection occurred upstream of quota evaluation (e.g., admission control).nn---nn reason codes (how to interpret 429s)nuse the following table to classify the issue and advise the customer.nn a) quota- and rate-limit-driven 429s (customer-specific)nthese are expected when a customer exceeds their configured limits.nn category error.type x-redwood-429-reason (typical) meaning customer guidance n---------------n hard quota exceeded quota_exceeded quota_window_exhausted customer has consumed their quota for the current window. do not retry immediately. wait until reset. consider limit increase request. n rate limit exceeded rate_limit_exceeded rate_limit_account customer exceeded account-level request rate. retry with exponential backoff jitter. reduce concurrency / smooth bursts. n route-group rate limit rate_limit_exceeded rate_limit_route_group customer exceeded a per-route or route-group cap. same as above ask them to spread load or request a higher burst allowance. n token / compute guardrail rate_limit_exceeded token_budget_exceeded customer exceeded a token/compute budget (if enabled for contract). reduce max_tokens / request size smooth traffic discuss contract sizing. nn b) overload protection / admission control 429s (fleet pressure)nthese indicate transient capacity protection behavior.nn category error.type x-redwood-429-reason (typical) meaning customer guidance n---------------n admission control (best-effort shed) overloaded shed_best_effort fleet/route is under pressure best-effort traffic is being throttled first. retry with exponential backoff jitter. prefer queueing client-side. n admission control (enterprise budget exhausted) overloaded shed_enterprise_budget protected route is overloaded and enterprise budget is fully utilized. retry using retry-after if present reduce concurrency contact support if sustained. n regional capacity constraint overloaded region_capacity selected region is capacity constrained request rejected to prevent tail latency cascade. retry with backoff if multi-region is enabled, allow client failover. n policy evaluation deny overloaded policy_deny_overload policy engine denied admission due to active overload rule (e.g., queue depth trigger). treat as transient. retry with backoff. provide request ids for investigation if frequent. nnsupport positioning:n- for enterprise accounts: this is protective backpressure to preserve latency/availability for protected routes. it can occur during unusual bursts or regional pressure.n- for self-serve/best-effort: during peak pressure, the platform prioritizes higher-sla traffic your requests may be throttled earlier.nn---nn recommended customer retry backoff guidancenprovide the following general guidance (tailor to the customers stack):nn when to retryn- retry 429s when:n - error.type overloaded (most cases)n - error.type rate_limit_exceededn- do not aggressively retry when:n - error.type quota_exceeded and the response includes a reset hint (wait until reset)nn how to retry (recommended algorithm)n- use exponential backoff with full jitter.n- start with 250500ms base delay.n- cap max delay at 1030s.n- add client-side request queueing to avoid stampedes.n- respect retry-after and/or x-redwood-retry-after-ms when present (prefer the ms header).nnsuggested pseudocode guidance to share (language-agnostic):n1) if retry-after present sleep for that duration ( small jitter) then retryn2) else backoff random(0, min(cap, base 2attempt))n3) stop after a reasonable max attempts (typically 58) and surface a retriable error to the applicationnn concurrency guidancencustomers with high parallelism should:n- implement a per-route concurrency limiter (token bucket / semaphore)n- smooth bursty workloads (batching where possible)n- avoid synchronized retries across many workers (jitter)nn idempotency guidancen- for non-streaming requests, retries are generally safe.n- for streaming requests, see streaming semantics below.nn---nn streaming semantics during shedding (common ticket driver)nsome customers report inconsistent termination on streaming responses during load shedding.nnsupport guidance:n- if a request is rejected before streaming begins, they should receive a normal 429 with reason headers.n- if a request is accepted and customers to log the x-redwood-request-id and last event received.nnescalate if:n- customers see a successful http status but the stream ends without an explicit termination signal and without consistent client-visible error handling, orn- the customer provides multiple request ids showing premature termination correlated with new overload reasons.nn---nn what support should ask for (intake budget-aware sampling and onboarding guide, content: summaryn-------nthis playbook describes redwoods recommended approach for onboarding enterprise customers to a budget-aware telemetry sampling strategy. it focuses on balancing fidelity and observability cost by combining adaptive sampling, reservoir sampling for high-cardinality tenants, and cost-feedback loops driven by billing/ingestion signals. the guide contains architecture patterns, configuration examples, rollout steps, acceptance criteria, and an operational runbook for support teams.nngoalsn-----n- ensure observable signal quality for slos and qbr metrics while controlling telemetry ingestion cost at tenant and org levels.n- provide a reproducible onboarding checklist that customer success, solutions engineering, and platform teams can follow.n- reduce noise and storage costs without losing critical anomaly and regression signals.nnwhen to use this guiden----------------------nuse this playbook for new enterprise tenants where expected telemetry volume or cost could exceed baseline thresholds, or for existing customers whose telemetry spend triggers a cost-protection review. typical triggers:n- projected ingestion 2k/month for logs/metrics/traces (estimate)n- hosting dedicated or high-throughput agents behind heavy api trafficn- customers requesting strict cost caps or billing alertsnnhigh-level architecturen-----------------------n1) data sources: sdks, agent-side sampling, edge sidecars, ingress proxies.n2) adaptive sampling service: centralized orchestration that issues per-tenant sampling policies and receives cost/traffic telemetry.n3) store query: short-term hot store long-term cold store sampling tags preserved for deterministic rehydration.n4) cost telemetry feedback: ingestion meter emits cost estimates back to the adaptive sampling service for policy updates.nncore concepts and patternsn--------------------------n- budget-aware sampling: set a target ingestion budget and tune sampling to meet it while prioritizing high-value traces/events.n- priority buckets: classify events/traces into priority tiers (critical, high, normal, debug) using rules derived from tenant-provided signal sets.n- reservoir sampling for high-cardinality keys: maintain a fixed reservoir per key (user_id/session_id) to avoid missing rare but important patterns.n- deterministic retention tags: attach deterministic tags so downstream ingestion can rehydrate or re-evaluate samples if needed.n- grace windows: when a model rollout or canary is active, temporarily raise fidelity for affected traffic slices.nnsampling algorithms we recommendn------------------------------n- static-rate sampling: simple global rate for low-risk tenants. good as a baseline.n- adaptive latency-aware sampling: increase sampling for requests with latency p95 to keep tail behavior visible.n- budget-driven proportional sampling: compute per-minute budget deficit and multiply base sampling by budget_factor target_spend/current_spend.n- hybrid reservoirprobabilistic: reservoir for cardinality keys probabilistic sampling for generic events.nnconfiguration examplesn----------------------nbelow is a representative yaml policy that the adaptive sampling service consumes. replace variables as appropriate for the tenant.nn example: tenant sampling policyntenant_id: tenant-1234nbudget_monthly_usd: 1200npriority_buckets:n critical:n selectors:n - event.type deployment_errorn sample_rate: 1.0n high:n selectors:n - request.latency_ms 500n sample_rate: 0.75n normal:n selectors: n sample_rate: 0.2n debug:n selectors: n sample_rate: 0.02nreservoir_keys:n - user_idn - session_idnreservoir_target_per_minute: 1000nbudget_mode: proportionalnbudget_evaluation_window_minutes: 60nncli and api snippetsn--------------------n- inspect current policy: redwoodctl sampling get --tenant tenant-1234n- apply policy: redwoodctl sampling apply --file tenant-1234-sampling.yamln- force snapshot of reservoir state: redwoodctl sampling snapshot --tenant tenant-1234 --out /tmp/snap.jsonnnrollout and onboarding steps (owner assignments)n------------------------------------------------n1) pre-onboard (solutions eng)n - collect expected qps, user cardinality, peak window and cost constraints from customer. (owner: solutions eng)n - baseline: deploy instrumentation agent on staging and collect 72 hours of data. (owner: customer success se)n2) policy design (customer success eng platform)n - create initial policy yaml using templates above. (owner: eng platform)n - decide priority buckets and reservoir keys with customer. (owner: customer success)n3) staging validation (customer success customer)n - apply policy to staging, run synthetic traffic for 24-48 hours. validate that slo telemetry remains visible (p50/p95/p99). (owner: customer success) - generate cost estimate report for the month given observed ingest rates. (owner: finance-legal telemetry)n4) canary (eng sre customer)n - canary to 510 production traffic slice or to a small service subset. monitor signal fidelity and missed-anomaly rate. (owner: eng sre)n5) full rollout and tune (customer success eng sre)n - gradually increase to 100 over 2472 hours with close monitoring. tune bucket rates and reservoir targets. (owner: customer success)nnacceptance criteria and qbr signalsn----------------------------------n- telemetry cost at or below target budget 10 after first full calendar month.n- no more than 2 missed p0 anomalies during the first 30 days attributable to sampling.n- slo visibility: key sli time-series (error rate, p95 latency, tokens-per-request) retain 95 of pre-sampling alert fidelity for critical services.n- qbr metrics to track: ingestion_cost_by_tenant, sampling_rate_by_bucket, missed_anomaly_count, reservoir_fill_rationnmonitoring dashboards and alertsn------------------------------ncreate the following dashboards before canary:n- tenant overview: total ingestion per hour, cost estimate rolling 30d, sampling rate heatmap.n- bucket fidelity: large payloads and backpressure handling, content: summary:nnthis integration guide defines the contract, operational controls, and recommended implementation patterns for integrating customer endpoints that receive batched webhooks containing large payloads. it is intended for platform engineers, integration engineers on customer teams, and customer success engineers who coordinate go-lives. the goal is to minimize dropped traffic, bound memory/cpu cost at the receiver, and ensure predictable retry/backpressure behavior across redwood hosted and dedicated/private environments.nnaudience:n- customer success (cs) and solutions engineersn- integration/platform engineers at customer organizationsn- redwood sres responsible for ingress proxies and client librariesnnwhy this exists:n- customers frequently need batched delivery to reduce per-request overhead for high-throughput use cases (e.g., embedding sync, event batches, document uploads).n- large payloads (256 kb) amplify failure modes: slow receivers, head-of-line blocking, and unexpected client memory spikes.n- without an explicit contract, different clients interpret retries/backoff differently leading to cascading load and downtime.nnscope and applicability:n- applies to: webhook-style delivery (http/https) from redwood integration proxies to customer-owned endpoints used during onboarding and production flows.n- not covered: pure streaming (grpc) integrations or in-band synchronous inference responses. see streaming-webhook guide for streaming semantics.nnkey definitions (used in this guide):n- batch: a single http post containing an array of records/events/documents.n- payload size: total bytes of the request body, after compression if compression negotiation is used.n- delivery window: time period within which redwood will attempt retries before handing the message to dead-letter or escalation flows.n- backpressure token: short-lived header (x-rwbp-token) issued by the receiver to indicate temporary capacity constraints.nncontract: request and response expectationsnnrequired request headers:n- content-type: application/jsonn- x-rw-tenant: (mandatory for dedicated/private routing)n- x-rw-batch-count: (number of items in this batch)n- x-rw-batch-bytes: (uncompressed size in bytes)n- x-rw-id: (idempotency key for the batch)n- accept-encoding: gzip (supported, optional)nnrecommended (optional) headers:n- x-rw-prefetch: (used by receivers to tune prefetch/buffers)nnresponse codes and semantics:n- 200 ok: full acceptance. redwood considers batch delivered no retries. body may contain a json acknowledgment mapping ids to per-item statuses (see per-item ack format below).n- 202 accepted: receiver accepted batch for asynchronous processing. redwood treats as success (no retry).n- 429 too many requests: receiver is asking the sender to slow down. must include retry-after (seconds) header or x-rw-backoff (ms). redwood will respect retry-after and fall back to exponential backoff.n- 503 service unavailable: temporary capacity problem. must include retry-after or x-rw-backoff. redwood will attempt retry according to configured retry window and failover policies.n- 4xx (other): permanent client errors (e.g., malformed payload). redwood will surface to customer and not retry.n- 5xx: transient server error. redwood will perform retries and escalate per escalation policy if persistent.nnper-item acknowledgment format (optional body on 200):n- if receiver wants to indicate partial acceptance, return 200 with json: id_statuses: id: , status: acceptedrejectedretry, reason: optional human text n- redwood will retry only items marked retry or missing from id_statuses when configured for fine-grained retries. coarse-grained integrations should return full 200/202 and avoid partial acceptance.nnpayload sizing and batching constraints (default recommended):n threshold value notes n------:---n recommended max batch items 200 prevent large cpu/json parse spikes on receivers n recommended max batch bytes (uncompressed) 8,388,608 (8 mb) soft recommendation verify with customer during onboarding n hard max batch bytes (policy) 16,777,216 (16 mb) redwood will reject 16mb with 413 payload too large unless negotiated n preferred per-item size for stability 512kb or batches 8mb, customers should implement a two-phase handshake:n 1) receiver responds with 202 and x-rw-upload-url: pre-signed url for multipart upload (s3 or azure blob allowed).n 2) redwood will upload large blobs to the provided url and then post a trimmed batch with references (blob ids/urls) instead of inlining payloads.n- handshake failures should be returned as 4xx/5xx accordingly redwood will retry the batch flow but not the individual large-blob uploads unless the receiver accepts them.nnbackpressure and flow control mechanismn- short-term backpressure: receiver returns 429 or 503 with retry-after in seconds or x-rw-backoff in milliseconds. redwood will:n - respect retry-after and pause pushes to that endpoint for the duration plus jitter.n - gradually ramp down parallel connections (min connection limit 1, not 0) then attempt slow probe requests.n- token-based capacity signaling (recommended):n - receiver may issue an x-rwbp-token header in responses (value valid for 30s). when set, redwood reduces concurrency to the level encoded in the token metadata (opaque to redwood). tokens are advisory and used to coordinate multi-proxy setups.n- long-term flow control: if an endpoint repeatedly signals backpressure (more than n times within m minutes), redwood will move the tenant to an adaptive-fanout queue and notify the cs owner for remediation.nnretry policy (default, overridable by customer contract)n1) immediate retries: on 5xx up to 2 immediate attempts, 200ms apart.n2) exponential backoff: initial 1s, multiplier 2, max interval 60s. total retry window default 15 minutes for individual batches.n3) for ttl-sensitive messages (configurable flag in integration manifest), total retry window reduced to 90 seconds.n4) after exhausting retry window, redwood will:n - move batch to tenant-specific dead-letter queue (dlq) for inspection, andn - trigger cs escalation per the escalation matrix below.nnobservability contract: metrics and traces the receiver must expose/emit during onboardingn- required telemetry for onboarding:n - deliverysuccessrate (per tenant, per endpoint)n - avgprocessinglatency (p50/p95) measured from initial receipt to 202/200 responsen - currentqueuedepth or pendingjobs (if asynchronous processing)n- redwood will correlate traces using the x-rw-id and a trace header x-rw-trace-id (if present). customers should log/emit the trace id in request processing logs.nnintegration test checklist (onboarding preflight)n1) basic handshake: redwood posts a batch of 10 small items, endpoint returns 200.n2) partial acceptance: return per-item ack and verify redwood retries only expected items.n3) backpressure simulation: return 429 with retry-after30 and confirm redwood respects the pause.n4) large payload: send a single 1.5 mb item and verify multipart handshake path completes.n5) rate flood: simulate burst of 500 batches in 60s and confirm receiver cpu/heap remains within expected bounds.n6) observability: confirm deliverysuccessrate and avgprocessinglatency are visible in both redwood console and customer dashboards.nnoperational runbook and escalation matrixn- owners:n - redwood cs integration lead: maya chen cli.n, doc_id: dsid_e960a27631cd4a7a96b6cd5496b46842, source_type: confluence, title: gpu fragmentation, compaction, and admission control playbook, content: summarynnthis playbook describes detection, triage, automated mitigation, and long-term controls for gpu-side memory fragmentation and allocation inefficiencies that lead to sudden request admission failures or unexpected latency spikes. it defines a compact, production-safe compaction daemon design, integration points with the scheduler admission controller, telemetry and slos to monitor, and an incident response runbook for on-call engineers.nnproblem statementnn- symptom: bursts of oom/admission-rejects for otherwise-capable gpus, high allocation retry counts, or elevated tail latency for model requests despite available aggregate free memory.n- root cause class: fragmentation of device memory and inefficient allocation patterns (many short-lived small allocations, large pinned kv caches, transient cuda allocations by third-party kernels) that leave free memory fragmented into non-contiguous regions. on some gpus this prevents large contiguous allocations required by kernels or model kv caches and forces the runtime to fall back to slower execution paths or reject requests.nnwhy this mattersnn- impact on slos: admission failures and long alloc-retry loops can increase p95/p99 latency and reduce throughput. customers experience degraded responsiveness while dashboards report available_free_bytes but high allocation failures.n- cost: noisy retries and degraded kernels increase per-token gpu time and therefore cost.nnkey concepts and terminologynn- fragmentation_score: heuristic ratio of unusable free regions over total free memory (0..1). higher means worse fragmentation.n- compaction: coordinated evacuation of low-priority allocations and re-creation of large contiguous free blocks (software-level: free reallocate or runtime-level: memory defragmentation apis where available).n- admission control threshold: configured fragmentation_score and free_pct thresholds that gate new request acceptance.n- compactor_daemon: lightweight service bound to each node/gpu that performs safe compaction cycles and exposes a handshake with the scheduler.nntelemetry and signals to monitor (recommended promql / queries)nn- metrics to emit from runtime and compactor:n - runtime_gpu_free_bytes_total (gauge)n - runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes (gauge)n - runtime_gpu_allocation_retries_total (counter)n - runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score (gauge: 0..1)n - compactor_cycles_total (counter)n - compactor_last_duration_seconds (gauge)n - admission_rejects_by_reasonreason (counter)nn- example promqls:n - fragmentation score (per-gpu): avg(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score) by (gpu_id)n - allocation-failure rate: increase(runtime_gpu_allocation_retries_total5m) / increase(runtime_requests_total5m)n - usable-free-pct: runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes / total_gpu_memory_bytesnnacceptable thresholds (guidelines tune per fleet)nn metric warning critical rationale n------:---:---n runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score 0.35 0.60 above 0.35 we see elevated allocation retries 0.6 correlates with admission rejects in historical traces n runtime_gpu_largest_free_block_bytes 50 250 empirical thresholds from production baselines nndetection rules and alerting recommendationsnn1. fire a p1 if: average(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score) 0.60 on 3 gpus in a rack for 10m and admission_rejects_by_reasonreasonfragmentation increases by 50/min.n2. fire a p2 if: per-gpu runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score between 0.35 and 0.60 sustained for 30m or allocation retry rate threshold.n3. add a transient ticketed warning when usable-free-pct 30 within timeout, escalate to manual eviction sequence.n4. eviction sequence (if compaction fails)n - evict low-priority sessions and persistent kv caches according to eviction policy: first global lru small sessions, then candidate long-lived kv caches tagged as evictable.n - re-check fragmentation metrics. if still degraded, schedule node restart as last resort.n5. post-incident analysisn - correlate with recent kernel rollouts, third-party library changes, and model variants.n - create a regression/bug entry if compactor failed or if specific model access patterns consistently cause fragmentation.nnautomated compaction design (summary)nn- goals: minimize user-visible impact, preserve in-flight sessions, avoid full node restarts, and provide deterministic improvements for fragmentation_score.n- phases:n 1. negotiate: compactor queries scheduler for safe eviction candidates marks epochs for short allocation quiesce.n 2. drain-small-allocs: pause/serialize new small non-critical allocations and attempt to free short-lived buffers.n 3. move-and-realloc: for evictable objects (large kv caches with copy-on-restore semantics), copy to host memory or alternate gpu then free and reallocate to coalesce free regions.n 4. resume: restore paused allocations and release scheduler drain marks.nncompactor safety knobs and config example (yaml)nnyamlncompactor:n enabled: truen run_interval_seconds: 300n max_duration_seconds: 120n safe_eviction_percentage: 0.20 will not evict more than 20 of active sessions without manual approvaln min_fragmentation_delta: 0.25 required improvement for auto-marking successn telemetry_window_seconds: 60n backoff_multiplier: 2.0n per_gpu_parallelism: 1n eviction_tags_priority: background-lru,low-priority-kv,test-sandboxn admission_thresholds:n fragmentation_score_warning: 0.35n fragmentation_score_critical: 0.60n largest_free_block_pct_warning: 0.25n largest_free_block_pct_critical: 0.15nnnscheduler admission control contract (api sketch)nn- input: request metadata (model_id, expected_peak_alloc_bytes, priority) and current gpu stats (free_bytes, largest_free_block_bytes, fragmentation_score).n- decision logic (high level):n - if fragmentation_score critical and expected_peak_alloc_bytes largest_free_block_bytes 0.9 reject with reasonfragmentation.n - if fragmentation_score warning and priority low delay / queue with backoff token.n - otherwise accept.nncli and control endpoints (examples)nn- trigger compaction for gpu-4 on node-22 with 10m timeout:nnbashnredwoodctl compactor run --node node-22 --gpu 4 --timeout 600nnn- query per-gpu fragmentation scores over the last 15m:nnbashnredwoodctl metrics query avg_over_time(runtime_gpu_fragmentation_score15m) --gpu allnnnintegration testing and benchmarking guidancenn- synthetic benchmark: the benchmark must exercise mixed allocation patterns (many small allocations occasional large kv loads). use the synthetic mix generator in the perf-suite:n - small_alloc_rate: 400/s, size_distribution: lognormal(mu8, sigma1.1)n - large_kv_loads: every 30s load 8gb kv blockn - concurrency: 128 sessions per gpun- measure before/after compactor: fragmentation_score, p99 latency, allocation_retries, throughput.n- expected improvements: successful compaction should reduce fragmentation_score by 0.3 and reduce allocation_retries by 60 in controlled benchmarks.nnlong-term mitigations and engineering actionsnn- kernel hygiene: minimize transient device allocations in commonly used kernels reuse buffers prefer pooled allocators. instrument third-party libraries used by model runtimes.n- kv cache reshaping: provide api for proactively chunked kv cache placement that avoids huge single contiguous allocations when model variant supports sharded kv.n- scheduler heuristics: gradually prefer gpus with low fragmentation_score for large-batch or high-memory requests prefer dense placement for small-session workloads to increase contiguous free spans elsewhere.nnrollout and canary checklistnn1. unit and integration tests for compactor logic with synthetic fragmentation scenarios.n2. canary compactor enabled on 5 of nodes with telemetry reporting and auto-rollback. monitor fragmentation_score and allocation_retries for 72 hours.n3. enable admission control in passive mode (log-only) for two weeks. verify alert signal fidelity.n4. switch to active mode with conservative thresholds for an additional two weeks, verify customer slos.n5. incrementally increase compactor aggressiveness and tune safe_eviction_percentage.nnownership and contactsnn- primary owner: eng/serving-runtime (maya chen)n- secondary: eng/scheduler (diego alvarez)n- on-call rotation: serving-runtime pager team (see ops roster)nnpost-incident review and rca templatenn- summary: one-paragraph incident descriptionn- timeline: 510 minute granularity events from detection to mitigationn- detection root cause: instrumentation and signals that first indicated fragmentationn- technical root cause: codepaths/kernels or workloads responsible for fragmentationn- mitigation steps executed and effectiveness metricsn- action items: short, medium, long-term (owners and deadlines)nnappendix: troubleshooting snippets and sample promqlnn- find top 10 quota protector webhook used by redwood inference to reliably surface customer quota events and automate protective credits and throttling adjustments during anomalous billing or rate-limit events. the document explains the webhook contract, delivery guarantees, recommended reconciliation workflow for enterprise customers, on-call runbooks for mismatches, and examples for implementing a receiver and reconciliation worker in third-party billing systems.nngoalsn- reduce false-positive quota rejections for enterprise customers during bursty or partial-failure conditions.n- provide deterministic reconciliation steps to reconcile token usage vs. billing records within a 72-hour window.n- support automated protective credits (temporary credits) and safe rollback actions with auditability.nnwhen occur.n- partners who want proactive notifications and a standard reconciliation api for invoicing systems.nnprerequisitesn- customer must have a configured webhook receiver endpoint reachable from reconciliation.nnwebhook contract (delivery semantics)n1) event types (payload field event_type):n - quota.alert: short-lived alert when usage approaches a quota threshold (info).n - quota.protective_action: redwood applied a temporary protective credit or soft-throttle (action).n - quota.reconcile_request: redwood requests reconciliation for an identified discrepancy (reconcile).n - quota.reconcile_result: customer posts back reconciliation outcome (result).n2) delivery guarantees:n - redwood will attempt delivery with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours.n - events are delivered at-least-once receivers must be idempotent (see idempotency section).n - quota.reconcile_request is guaranteed to be emitted once per discrepancy case.n3) security:n - each http request includes x-redwood-timestamp and x-redwood-signature (hmac-sha256 of body timestamp with shared secret).n - request body is application/json and utf-8 encoded.nnexample payloadsn- 2026-02-18t22:00:00z,n window_start: 2026-02-18t20:00:00z,n window_end: 2026-02-18t21:00:00z,n reported_usage_tokens: 1200000,n observed_usage_tokens: 980000,n suggested_action: credit_25000_tokens_or_manual_review,n details_url: and receiver best practicesn- use event_id as the primary idempotency key. store event_id and processing result for 90 days.n- design reconciliation handlers to accept repeated reconcile_request events and only create a single case per unique correlation_id.n- return standard http codes: 200 for success, 202 for accepted (async processing), 4xx for client errors, 5xx for transient failures. redwood will retry on 5xx and network errors.nnsample receiver flow (recommended)n1) verify signature and timestamp within /- 5 minutes. reject otherwise with 401.n2) check local dedupe store by event_id if found, return 200 with existing outcome.n3) for quota.protective_action: apply temporary internal protective credit and create an internal ticket with priorityhigh if actiontemporary_credit.n4) for quota.reconcile_request: enqueue a reconciliation job that performs matching between reported_usage_tokens and your billing records for the provided window. post a quota.reconcile_result when complete.nnreconciliation worker designn- match level: ingestion-level (per request id) if available fallback to route-level aggregation by minute.n- tolerance band: accept discrepancies 2.5 and 10 escalates to human review.n- audit trail: include the redwood event_id, your reconciliation_job_id, and links to raw records.nnautomated protective credits and accounting flown1) on reconcile_request that falls into the automated band, your system should:n - create a refundable credit entry tied to the tenant and reconciliation_job_id.n - post billing exports.n3) auto-expiry: credits applied as protective must be stamped with expiry (default 30 days) and a reconciliation flag to convert to permanent credit only after human approval.nnslos 202job_id to indicate longer processing windows.n- alerting: customers should alert if more than 5 reconcile_request events are queued for 24 hours for a single tenant.nnon-call runbook: unresolved internal billing ops: create ticket with tags recon-stuck, tenant: and assign to billing-ops on-call.n2) if the reconcile_result indicates disagreement (customer refutes observed usage), run a manual audit:n a) export raw request logs from redwood for the window (console - tenants - export usage).n b) crosswalk timestamps and request ids. if discrepancies persist, open a joint investigation with redwood sre via the enterprise support channel.n3) if finance disputes remain after 7 days, follow the contractual dispute process (see related_pages billing-credit-policy).nntroubleshooting common playbook, content: overviewnnthis playbook documents proven connector integration patterns and operator runbooks for handling tenant-heavy ingest surges against redwood inference endpoints (hosted, dedicated, and private). it is intended for solutions engineers, customer success, sres, and partner integrators who build connectors or bridges that forward high-volume telemetry, batched requests, or streaming job workloads into redwood.nngoalsn- prevent noisy-tenant surges from degrading other tenants or customer slas.n- provide single-source connector configuration templates for backpressure, graceful degradation, and safe failover.n- define operational checks, monitoring signals, and an on-call escalation ladder.nnscopen- applies to connectors that: ingest text payloads for generation, embeddings, or reranking proxy tenant traffic or batch large historical backfills.n- covers both synchronous (api) and asynchronous (job/batch) ingestion patterns.n- does not cover hardware-level gpu autoscaling (see eng-infra docs).nnhigh-level patterns (when to use each)n1) client-side rate shaping (ideal for saas partners)n - best when you control the client sdk or agent.n - enforce tenant-level qps/tpu caps and token limits proactively.n2) connector-side adaptive throttling (recommended default)n - connector maintains per-tenant token counters and request queues adjusts ingress windows based on downstream latency and error rates.n3) burst cache queueing with prioritized dispatchn - for bursty workloads: short-term kv/prefix cache for repeated prompts prioritized consumer queue to dispatch high-value requests first.n4) degraded-mode fallback to lower-cost model variantsn - fall back to quantized or smaller model variants when latency slos break. useful in dedicated and private where model variants are available.n5) backfill and bulk job isolationn - run large backfills on isolated routing paths and quota pools never share production routing with real-time traffic.nnconnector architecture (text diagram)n- ingress - per-tenant ingress limiter - priority queue (hot/warm/cold) - dispatch worker pool - redwood proxy (smart routing) - redwood inference endpointsn- optional: local caching layer and metrics exporter between queue and dispatch.nnrequired preconditionsn- tenant quotas configured in redwood console or via api (min and max token caps).n- observability hooks configured: request tracing, per-tenant latency histograms, error counters, and token-metering.n- circuit-breaker library available in connector runtime (examples use circuitbreaker v1.2).nnconnector configuration examplesn1) per-tenant sliding window token limiter (pseudo-yaml)n---n tenant rate limiternwindow_seconds: 60nmax_tokens_per_window: 10000nburst_allowance: 1.5npriority_buckets:n - hot: 0.6 60 capacity reserved for high-priority routesn - warm: 0.3n - cold: 0.1n---nn2) adaptive dispatch strategy (pseudo-config)n---nautoscale:n enabled: truen target_latency_ms: 200n min_workers: 2n max_workers: 100n cooldown_seconds: 30nbackoff:n initial_ms: 100n max_ms: 5000n factor: 2.0n---nnimplementation recipesna) synchronous connector (recommended) - validate incoming request size and tokens reject with 429 when tenant quota exceeded.n- maintain a token bucket per tenant persisted in redis for cross-instance coordination.n- if downstream latency target_latency_ms for 3 consecutive windows, reduce per-tenant throughput by multiplier 0.5 and emit event to telemetry.nnb) asynchronous large-batch worker - accept job payloads, store in durable queue (sqs/kafka), run preflight estimator that calculates token estimate, and schedule against a backfill queue with dedicated capacity pools.n- mark job low-priority when it would exceed daily tenant quota schedule to off-peak windows.nnc) prioritization examplen- tags: critical (slas), interactive (real-time), background (backfills).n- dispatcher policy: always reserve 30 of capacity for critical and interactive. background only consumes spare capacity or dedicated backfill pool.nnmonitoring telemetry (what to track)n- per-tenant token consumption (tokens/min, tokens/day)n- 95th/99th latency per tenant and per routen- 429 rate and quota rejections per tenantn- queue depth by priority bucketn- dispatch worker saturation (gpu_utilization, inflight_requests)n- model fallback events and quality-regression alertsn- cost metrics: estimated tokens billed vs allowednnsuggested slos and thresholds (connector owner to adopt)n- target p95 end-to-end latency: 300ms for interactive routes, 1.5s for batch submission acceptance.n- queue depth alert: queue_depth 500 for 5m - page oncall.n- token spike alert: tenant token rate 3x baseline for 5m - create incident priority p2.n- error ratio alert: 5xx_rate 2 over 3m - page p1.nnrunbook: surge detected (step-by-step)n1) detection: alert triggered (token spike or queue_depth or p99 latency).n2) triage: oncall examines per-tenant metrics, request traces, and redwood console slo page.n3) immediate mitigation (515 minutes):n - throttle the offending tenant to safe cap (e.g., 50 of capacity) using redis token bucket override.n - if available, shift tenant to a dedicated low-priority pool or pause background jobs.n - if customer has a go-live playbook, contact cs lead to coordinate intentional throttling.n4) short-term containment (1560 minutes):n - enable degraded-mode: route tenant to smaller model variant or quantized profile.n - add temporary rule in gateway to drop non-critical requests (e.g., trace-only or sampling).n5) recovery postmortem (60 minutes):n - maintain reduced cap until token rate returns to baseline for 30m.n - open rca with customer and document actions in ticket include traces and telemetry snapshots.nnescalation communication matrixn- if mitigation fails in 30 minutes escalate to tier 2 sre and cs director.n- customer communication template (first 30 minutes): acknowledge the surge, confirm an active mitigation, and provide eta 6090 minutes.n- post-incident follow-up: share rca and recommended client-side changes (e.g., batching, retry backoff).nnquality safeguards for degraded-mode fallbacksn- if switching to smaller model variant, run a validation prompt set (20 representative prompts) and measure fidelity threshold ( 90 acceptable). if below threshold: avoid fallback and instead tighten throttling.nntesting qa checklist before enabling connector in productionn- load test with per-tenant mix: 80 interactive, 15 background, 5 critical.n- verify token metering persists across restart and multiple instances.n- chaos test: simulate network partition to redis ensure connector fails open-to-safe-mode (reject new requests with 503 rather than silently accept).n- confirm alerts and dashboards surface tenant attribution in labeling queue) ingress-gateway - telemetry-gatekeeper - telemetry-events-prod (feedback.raw) - enrichment workers - labeling-hub (labeling.inbound) - human labelers/auto-labelers - labeling-hub.outbound - model-eval-harness - eval.results - telemetry-archive / qbr-datasetnndata summary:nthis guide describes recommended architecture, configuration, testing, and operational runbooks for integrating redwood inference with a customer or partner-side priority proxy. the pattern is intended for enterprise customers that run a multipurpose ingress layer that must: (1) prioritize latencysensitive inference requests, (2) handle large-volume background/async jobs without starving realtime traffic, and (3) implement an adaptive backoff strategy when redwood responds with transient errors or capacity signals.nngoals:n- preserve 95th/99th percentile latency slos for live inference routes.n- maintain throughput for background pipelines without increasing cost to the customer.n- provide clear telemetry and escalation hooks for degraded conditions.nnintended audience:n- customer success engineers and integration engineers implementing ingress or api gateway policies.n- customer platform and sre teams responsible for on-prem or vpc deployments.nnkey concepts and terminology:n- priority proxy: an edge or ingress proxy (e.g., envoy, nginx, api gateway) that classifies and schedules requests based on route, header, or token attributes.n- live route: low-latency user-facing inference endpoints (chat, completion, synchronously user-blocking).n- background route: batch/async endpoints (embeddings indexing, bulk scoring) that can be queued or slowed to protect live slos.n- adaptive backoff: client-side or proxy-driven logic that reduces request rate to redwood when observing specific signals (429s, 503s, elevated latency, or explicit capacity hints in response headers).nnarchitecture overview:n1) classification: ingress annotates requests with x-redwood-priority: high normal background. assignment should happen as early as possible (edge auth layer or api gateway).n2) routing: priority header maps to separate internal queues/pools within the proxy. live pool configured with fast-path (short timeouts, small queue depth). background pool configured with large queue depth and longer retries.n3) rate-limiting and token buckets: define separate token buckets for high and background priorities with configurable refill rates.n4) backoff signals: redwood will send one or more of the following signals when it detects load/capacity pressure: http 429 with retry-after, 503 service unavailable, x-redwood-capacity: degraded constrained, and a latency-based heuristic (long tail latency configured threshold). proxy must translate these into adaptive backoff decisions.nnconfiguration reference (envoy / lua / nginx examples):n- example envoy route filter snippet (yaml-like):nn - name: envoy.filters. typed_config:n @type: type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters. inline_code: n function envoy_on_request(request_handle)n local priority request_handle:headers():get(x-request-priority) or normaln if priority background thenn request_handle:headers():add(x-redwood-priority, background)n elsen request_handle:headers():add(x-redwood-priority, high)n endn endnn- token-bucket policy table (recommended defaults):nn priority token refill (tokens/s) burst capacity (tokens) max queued requests n ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------n high 100 200 50 n normal 40 80 200 n background 5 50 1000 nnoperational backoff algorithm (recommended):n1) on first 429 or 503 for a specific backend instance: multiply current per-route request allowance by 0.6 and set a soft cooldown timer t 10s.n2) if retry-after present: use retry-after as initial t (capped at 60s).n3) exponential grow-back: every t interval without further 429/503 events, increase allowance by factor 1.25 until original baseline is reached.n4) high-priority routes are exempt from aggressive multiply unless consecutive failure rate 10 for 30s. in that case, failover to an alternate redwood region/model variant (see rollout failover).nnexample proxy policy (pseudo-config):nn policies:n - match: header: x-redwood-priority: highn bucket: highn backoff_strategy: conservativen - match: header: x-redwood-priority: backgroundn bucket: backgroundn backoff_strategy: aggressivennintegration-specific headers to surface to redwood and to watch for in responses:n- outbound to redwood: x-redwood-priority, x-request-id, x-customer-tenant, x-client-versionn- expected redwood response headers: retry-after, x-redwood-capacity, x-redwood-model-variantnntelemetry and dashboards (minimum required):n- per-priority request rate (rps) and error rate (4xx/5xx)n- 95th/99th latency by priority and routen- 429/503 count and retry-after distributionn- queue depth per pool and token-bucket token consumptionn- model variant fallback counts and failover reasonsnnsuggested grafana panels and alerts:n- alert: high-priority 99p latency 800ms for 5m - sev 2, notify customer sre and csm.n- alert: high-priority error rate 5 for 3m - sev 1, trigger incident process.n- alert: background queue depth 75 capacity for 10m - pager to integration owner (warn).n- alert: adaptive backoff active for 2 min and rps still 50 of baseline - ops review.nntesting and validation checklist (pre-go-live):n1) functional test: verify x-redwood-priority header set correctly for all client types.n2) failure simulation: return 429 and 503 from a redwood test backend and verify proxy reduces allowance per algorithm and that retry-after is respected.n3) load test: run mixed workload that mirrors production split (example: 70 background, 30 live) and confirm high route p95/p99 latency remains within slo at target baseline.n4) chaos test: introduce model-variant failover and confirm client receives x-redwood-model-variant header and traffic migrates per routing policy.n5) telemetry validation: ensure metrics show expected buckets and queue depth test alert firing thresholds in staging.nnrollout and fallback steps:n1) canary: enable policies for 5 of traffic (by ip range or customer id). monitor latency and error metrics for 30 minutes.n2) ramp: 20 - 50 - 100 over incremental windows no shorter than 30 minutes after no alerts.n3) on alert (see conditions above): revert to previous proxy policy snapshot and open a ticket with redwood cs with attached telemetry.n4) if redwood signals capacity degraded for single region/model variant, initiate automatic failover to configured secondary region/model variant and notify stakeholders.nnoperational runbook (play-by-play):n1) detection: alert fires for high-priority p99 latency.n2) triage: on-call runs the following checks: per-route p99, queue depth, 429/503 spike, any active adaptive-backoff windows.n3) short-term mitigation: increase high-priority token refill by 10 (if safe), drain background tokens by 30, and increase replica count for client-side frontends if autoscaling available.n4) escalation: if mitigation fails within 10 minutes and error rates remain high, escalate to redwood customer success and eng sre. include: last 15m traces, p95/p99 history, and recent model variant headers.n5) post-incident: run rca within 72 hours and update proxy policy with tuned thresholds.nnescalation contacts over-aggressive background throttling starves pipelines for hours.n mitigation: implement slow-fail queue drains with observable cutoff metrics and secondary offload to batch worker pool.n- pitfall: missing x-request-id header prevents tracing across systems.n mitigation: fail early and add generated request id at ingress if client absent.n- pitfall: relying only on latency heuristics can produce false positives under gc or networking blips.n mitigation: combine latency signal with 429/503 counts and retry-after presence.nnappendix a example curl smoke test:nn curl -i -h authorization: bearer detection and repair runbook, content: summary:nnthis runbook describes detection patterns, triage steps, containment, and repair procedures for telemetry corruption that can affect slo calculation and errorbudget decisions. telemetry corruption includes any systematic integrity failure in metrics, traces, or logs that causes slis to be inaccurate (for example, missing labels, zeroed counters, duplicate events, stale timestamps, or aggregation compiler bugs). the runbook focuses on slo correctness and making safe decisions when sli data is unreliable.nnscope:n- in scope: aggregate sli telemetry (prometheus/pushgateway metrics, preaggregated counters, trace spans ingested into the tracing pipeline, logs parsed into the metrics pipeline), the slo computation pipeline (aggregation jobs and rollup jobs), and the observability ingestion/etl (kafka topics, consumer groups, transform jobs).n- out of scope: application code correctness unrelated to telemetry (e.g., business logic bugs causing real errors).nnwhy this matters:n- incorrect telemetry can cause false slo breaches or mask real outages, leading to improper capacity scaling, costly incident responses, incorrect billing/chargeback, and bad downstream product decisions.nnowner escalation:n- primary oncall: observability sre rotation (pager: sre-observability).n- secondary: runtime sre (pager sre-runtime).n- escalation path: oncall - observability lead (ava martinez) - head of sre (nikhil verma).nndefinitions and mapping to slis/slos:n- raw event: single telemetry event (metric sample, trace span, log line).n- rollup job: scheduled aggregation that computes sli numerator/denominator windows (1m, 5m, 1h).n- corruption types: missing samples, stale timestamps, label drift, duplicate events, aggregation regressions (offbyone windows), downstream truncation.nnkey signals to watch (high level):n- sudden drop to zero across many counters (indicates producer/ingestion issue).n- large (10) divergence between raw rate and rollup rate over 5m windows.n- increased cardinality of metric labels (new unexpected label values) or missing expected labels.n- trace sampling rate collapse or identical trace ids repeated.n- log ingestion lag (consumer offset lag 10m) or spikes in dropped messages.n- sli backfill discrepancy: sli computed from recent raw data differs from raw query by 5.nndetection recipes (examples):n- promql: compare raw counter and rollup metric for a service (5m lookback):n - raw rate query: rate(service_requests_total5m)n - rollup rate: service_requests_rollup_count5m:5m or an average of the preaggregated metricn - anomaly indicator: (abs(rate - rollup) / max(rate, 1e-6)) 0.05 for 2 samples - alertnn- missing labels detection (grafana/logql):n - query counts grouped by expected label set and assert presence: sum by(region,env)(service_requests_total)n - if count for any expected envprod drops to 0 while others remain, raise investigation.nn- trace duplication check (example with jaeger/tempo api):n - curl and check for identical span ids or repeated root trace ids 100 occurrences - suspect replay/consumer dedup bug.nn- consumer lag check (kafka example):n - cli: kafka-consumer-groups --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group observation-etl grep -e observation-etln - alert threshold: partition lag 1,000,000 messages or 10 minutes backlognnintegrity matrix (reference table):n- metrics: missing samples / label drift / zeroing / duplication.n- traces: sampling collapse / duplication / missing service tag.n- logs: parse failures / truncation / timestamp munging.nnimmediate triage checklist (fast path):n1) acknowledge alert and set incident type: telemetry_corruption.n2) record initial symptoms and time window (start ts).n3) snapshot current slo dashboards and raw metrics (save gifs or dashboard snapshots).n4) check upstream producers: application metrics exporter status (service /metrics endpoints), exporter logs.n - commands: curl -ss head -n 50n5) check ingestion/etl layer: consumer group lag, transform job logs, error topics.n6) check rollup jobs: job executor logs, recent job durations, and failures.n7) decide containment action: pause slo alerts / mark slo data as unreliable for window x, or switch to an alternate sli source (fallback sli).nncontainment and immediate mitigation (safety-first):n- if telemetry corruption is confirmed and slos are used for automated throttles or billing, place slo calculations into readonly/failover mode and notify downstream consumers.n- apply temporary flagging so that automatic remediation (capacity autoscaling, circuit breakers) does not act on corrupted sli values.n- if possible, switch slo computation to a secondary pipeline that uses raw events rather than rollups (see fallback sli sources below).nnrepair recovery (detailed procedure):nstep a isolate the component:n1) identify which layer is corrupted: producer, ingestion broker, transform job, rollup job, or slo aggregator. use the detection recipes above to localize.n2) if transform job is failing, cordon the job (k8s: kubectl cordon /kubectl scale --replicas0 deployment/etl-transform) and rerun a canary instance with debug flags.nnstep b create reproducible snapshot and safe workspace:n1) capture a time-bound snapshot of raw messages from the broker for the suspect window. example (kafka):n kafka-console-consumer --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic telemetry-raw --partition 3 --offset 12345 --max-messages 1000 /tmp/snapshot-part3.jsonn2) export rollup outputs and job logs for the same window.nnstep c integrity checks and repair actions (choose applicable):n- label repair: if labels are missing due to transform bug, run idempotent label enrich job against snapshot and recompute rollups.n- duplicate suppression: if duplicate events exist, deduplicate by unique_event_id and recompute aggregates.n- timestamp repair: if timestamps truncated (e.g., second precision lost), reconstruct using broker offsets and producer time if available otherwise mark affected window as unverifiable and proceed with backfill using application logs.n- recompute rollups: run rollup job in a controlled backfill mode (dry run - validation - commit). ensure the backfill is idempotent: use deterministic windowing and versioned rollup keys.nnexample backfill sequence (bash):n- step 1: run dry run (no writes)n python etl/rollup.py --window-start2025-02-18t14:00:00z --window-end2025-02-18t14:05:00z --dry-run --source summarynnthis guide describes redwood inferences recommended approach for evolving customer telemetry contracts while preserving backward compatibility for enterprise onboarding and ongoing integrations. the target audience is customer success engineers (cse), observability engineers, and partner engineering teams responsible for telemetry ingestion and schema changes.nngoalsn- minimize customer downtime and avoid ingestion failures during schema updates.n- provide a predictable, testable migration path for producers and consumers of telemetry.n- maintain high-quality slos for telemetry ingestion and downstream dashboards.n- provide clear ownership, automation playbooks, and rollback procedures.nnwhen to use this documentn- customer is integrating redwood agent, sidecar, or direct api and requests a schema extension.n- product/engineering plans to add or deprecate telemetry fields for model-level metrics, cost-attribution labels, or tenant metadata.n- observability team detects a breakage after a schema rollout.nnkey terminologyn- telemetry contract: the json schema describing what telemetry events we accept on the ingestion api (ingest.v1.events).n- producer: the service or customer component emitting telemetry.n- consumer: redwood services (observability pipelines, billing, alerting) that depend on specific fields.n- soft-compat: new optional fields tolerated by consumers old fields continue to be honored.n- hard-compat: required fields that, if missing, will cause ingestion rejection.nncompatibility strategy (overview)n1) use semantic versioning for schema artifacts (e.g., ingest.v1 - ingest.v2).n2) strict compatibility rules:n - adding optional fields: allowed in minor version bumps (v1.1 - v1.2).n - adding required fields or changing types: requires major version bump (v1 - v2) and coordinated migration.n - deprecation: mark fields deprecated for one major-version cycle before removal.n3) dual-write and dual-read support: ingestion pipeline should accept older and newer schemas for the duration of migration window.n4) automated schema validation canary ingestion for early detection.nnversioning policy (table)n change type version bump required rollout window notes n add optional field minor (vx.y) 1 week backwards compatible consumers should ignore unknown fields n add required field / type change major (vx1.0) 812 non-goalsn- this document focuses on event-to-batch pipelines that call redwoods rest api or private connector. it does not cover one-off interactive chat integrations or client-side sdk usage.nnhigh-level architecturen1) event producer: customer service emits events into a durable queue (kafka topic, kinesis stream, or sqs).n2) batcher/connector: our recommended connector groups events by tenant/model and prepares batched requests using prefix/kv cache hints.n3) redwood frontdoor: requests are sent to redwood routed api endpoint or private connector (vpc) based on customer deployment.n4) post-processing: enrichment service applies business logic, writes results to datastore (bigquery/snowflake/s3) and triggers downstream workflows.nntext diagram (logical)nevent producer - kafka (topic: events-ingest) - connector (batcher) - redwood api/private - enricher - storagennprerequisites and requirementsn- accounts: customer must have a redwood api key with batch ingestion with models sequence length).n- retry policy: exponential backoff starting at 200ms, max 60s, 5 attempts.n- circuit breaker: open after 50 error rate over 1-minute sliding window rampdown to 10 traffic on fallback model.nnsample connector configuration (yaml)nnconnector:n type: kafka-consumern topics:n - events-ingestn batch:n max_events: 1000n max_wait_ms: 250n max_tokens: 65536n vault:kms/redwood-service-accountnnnbatch formation guidelinesn- group by tenant and model variant to maximize cache hits (same modelprompt structure yields kv cache reuse).n- preserve ordering for time-series dependent events otherwise process out-of-order to increase batching.n- attach deterministic prompt templates to avoid quality variance across batches.nncall pattern and payload examplen- connector.n - long-term: collect request_ids and open a support ticket via redwood console with timeline, sample payloads, and relevant trace ids.n2) partial batch failures (some items succeed)n - best practice: connector must implement item-level retries. mark successful items as complete enqueue failed items to retry queue with exponential backoff.n3) network flaps / dns issuesn - workaround: 2x expected peak for 30 minutes. verify token consumption, latency slos, and error behavior.n- canary rollout: start at 1 traffic for 30 minutes, 5 for 2 hours, 25 for 24 hours, then 100.n- regression tests: prompt set-based qa to compare output distributions between model variants.nnoperational runbook (step-by-step)n1) detection: alert triggers or user report indicating high errors or latency.n2) triage (5 minutes): check connector logs, batch failure rate, redwood console for downstream errors, token usage spike.n3) immediate mitigation (10 minutes): reduce connector concurrency by 50, enable fallback model at 10 traffic, increase batch window to 500ms to reduce api qps.n4) escalation (30 minutes): if errors persist, open redwood support case (include request_ids, traces, sample payloads) and notify cse and account exec.n5) post-incident (72 hours): run rca with customer and redwood team, document mitigations and follow-up actions.nnescalation contacts and slasn- on-call sre (customer): pager duty team (customer side) primary contact.n- redwood cse: cse-oncall@redwood.ai (weekday 08:0018:00 pt) response target 1 hour.n- redwood sre escalation: sre-escalations@redwood.ai response target 30 minutes for p1.n- for private deployments include vpn and account team contacts (see customer onboarding packet).nnknown limitations and recommended workaroundsn- model early throttling reduces noisy retries and downstream cost spikes.n- grace windows enable short bursts (e.g., 515s) without immediate hard rejections, improving ux for interactive product flows.n- request but increase refill delay to prevent repeated bursts.nngrace window vs. hard enforcement:n- grace window: a short period during which the server returns 200/soft-throttle but sets
