developer simulation kit telemetry bridge for preflight testing, content: summarynnthis prd proposes a developer simulation kit (devsim) and a telemetry bridge that together provide engineers with an offline, high-fidelity preflight environment for: workload simulation, latency/cost forecasting, fidelity experiments, and telemetry capture that mirrors production signals. the goal is to reduce time-to-safe-deploy for engine and product teams by catching regressions and cost surprises earlier.nncontext and motivationnn- teams repeatedly run into late-stage surprises when moving workloads from test harnesses to hosted/dedicated/private environments: unexpected tail-latency spikes, different token costs due to batching/caching behavior, and gaps in observability.n- current sandboxes either (a) are lightweight and fast but underestimate cost/latency, or (b) are production clones that are expensive and slow to provision.n- devsim telemetry bridge is a developer-focused sandbox designed to be: portable (local/ci/cloud), inexpensive to run, and representative of production runtime behaviors (batching, kv cache warm-up, quantization variants).nngoals (what success looks like)nn1. provide a reproducible simulation that approximates hosted inference latencies and token cost within /-10 for canonical workloads.n2. surface fidelity regressions via synthetic and recorded prompt sets before production rollout.n3. emit telemetry that is structurally compatible with production dashboards and alerts so preflight runs can be used in continuous gating.n4. reduce mean time to detect cost/latency regressions during release validation from days to hours.nnnon-goalsnn- not intended to replace full private deployment validation for regulated customers.n- not a replacement for long-duration soak tests or stress tests at production scale.nnuser personasnn- platform engineers: want to validate runtime kernel changes and batching policies.n- ml engineers: want to test quantization/fidelity changes against representative prompts.n- product engineers: want quick cost/latency estimates for feature experiments.nnhigh-level product conceptnndevsim consists of three components:nn1) local simulation runtime (lsr)n- lightweight containerized runtime that mimics production serving behavior: continuous batching, kv cache emulation (cold/warm cycles), quantization toggles, and failure injection.n- configurable hardware profile (e.g., v100/rtx6000 equivalent timings) with pluggable latency/cost profiles derived from production benchmarking.nn2) workload runnern- cli and sdk for running recorded or synthetic workloads with control over concurrency, sequence length distributions, prompt sets, and session stickiness.nn3) telemetry bridgen- streaming adapter that maps devsim events to the production telemetry schema and can either forward to a staging ingestion endpoint or write to a staging s3 bucket in the same format as production.nndetailed workload runner must accept a recording input (see recording format below) and replay with configurable timing and concurrency.n- fr-3: telemetry bridge must emit the following canonical event types: request_start, request_end, token_emitted, batch_formed, cache_hit, cache_miss, fallback_invoked, model_variant_selected.n- fr-4: devsim must provide a cost model that estimates per-request token cost given batch size, quantization variant, and sequence length.n- fr-5: devsim must be runnable in ci (docker image 20 vs baseline and absolute p95 400ms (over 1h window).n- alert: cost-estimate-driftn - trigger: mean estimated cost deviation 15 vs last production 7d rolling baseline.nnquality acceptance criteriann- qc-1: run three canonical recordings (chat-short, chat-long, embeddings-bulk). each run must meet nfr-1 accuracy target.n- qc-2: telemetry events from devsim replay ingested into staging must be queryable with the same saved queries as production (no schema adaptation).n- qc-3: developer onboarding: a new engineer can run the default replay and inspect the preflight dashboard within 20 minutes following readme.nnrollout plannn1. alpha (4 weeks): internal platform and ml teams. manual sign-up for staging telemetry forwarding.n2. beta (8 weeks): expand to product teams add ci integration templates for github actions and gitlab.n3. ga (12 weeks): public documentation, console integration to surface preflight reports in the deployment flow, optimize integration for cost-optimization suggestions.nnrollout checklistnn- lsr docker images built and published to staging registry and versioned.n- telemetry bridge endpoint deployed to staging and covered by rbac.n- three canonical recordings validated and checked into recordings repo.n- preflight dashboards (staging) and alert rules created.n- ci integration templates added to docs.nndependencies integrationsnn- telemetry ingestion pipeline (observability team) must accept staging forwarding with identical schema.n- cost model calibration dataset from runtime benchmarking (runtime team).n- console engineering to surface preflight run summaries and attach to rollout approvals.nnrisks and mitigationsnn- risk: simulation diverges from production over time as runtime kernels evolve.n - mitigation: enforce image/version parity run an automated weekly calibration job that compares baseline recordings run in devsim vs a small production cluster and produces calibration deltas.n- risk: telemetry forwarding misused and pollutes production metrics.n - mitigation: rbac tagging require explicit approval for forwarding to any non-staging ingestion endpoint.nnownership and contactsnn- product owner: maya chen (product)n- tech lead: aaron li (platform engineering)n- runtime interface: priya nair (serving designs, operational controls, and a runbook for websocket-based ingestion integrations with redwood inference. it is intended for partner integrators, sdk teams, and customer success engineers onboarding customers that prefer persistent connection models (websocket, bidirectional http/2, or similar). the guidance focuses on: graceful backpressure handling, reconnect and resume semantics, observable signals, and actionable escalation steps when connections degrade.nnwhen to use this playbooknn- customers sending stream-oriented events with low per-message latency requirements (telemetry, conversational tokens, streaming embeddings ingestion).n- integrations where long-lived client connections reduce overhead and improve responsiveness compared to polling or webhooks.n- scenarios that must tolerate transient network issues and resume without duplicate processing.nngoals and success criteriann- maintain end-to-end ingestion availability 99.9 (slo) for customer traffic under normal network conditions.n- avoid unbounded memory growth in brokers/ingest frontends when downstream is congested.n- provide deterministic client behavior on reconnect: at-most-once delivery where required, or exactly-once semantics where customers implement idempotency keys.nnarchitecture patterns (recommended)nn1) terminate websocket at a lightweight edge proxyn- edge (layer 7) terminates tls and authenticates the initial request. use a proxy (envoy/nginx) that can do connection-level limits and graceful drain.nn2) forward to an ingestion front-end with internal queuingn- the front-end should accept frames and append to a bounded in-memory queue per-tenant. when limits are reached it applies backpressure by signaling clients (close frame or application-level flow-control message).nn3) decouple consuming workers from the front-endn- worker pool processes queued messages and writes to durable storage or message bus (kafka/rabbit/cloud pub/sub) with independent scaling.nnclient best practicesnn- authenticate once with a short-lived token and include a tenant id in the opening handshake.n- support a small receive buffer and cooperative flow control: stop sending if the server sends a pause control frame, resume on resume.n- implement exponential backoff with jitter for reconnect attempts and cap to a reasonable ceiling (e.g., 30s).n- preserve in-flight message ids and provide idempotency keys for operations that must be exactly-once.n- segment large payloads into smaller frames and apply client-side rate limiting.nnserver / redwood-internal best practicesnn- per-connection quotas: configure per-tenant and per-connection message and byte rate limits. default: 200 messages/min and 2 mb/min per connection (tunable).n- bounded queues: use per-tenant ring buffers with a configurable max (default 10k messages). when full, apply backpressure rather than unbounded allocation.n- control frames: implement a minimal control protocol on top of websocket (control type: pause resume ack nack) to signal clients.nnreconnect and resume semanticsnn- lightweight resume: clients include a resume_token assigned by the front-end in the opening handshake. the front-end keeps a short-lived in-memory window mapping tokens - last-ack position (recommended ttl: 90s).n- durable resume (for higher guarantees): instruct clients to checkpoint offsets into a durable store (e.g., tenant-state api) after receiving server acks.nnbackpressure strategies (ordered preference)nn1) cooperative flow-control (preferred)n- server sends pause - client throttles send rate. server sends periodic resume to allow more data.nn2) token bucket token exchangen- server grants credits to client client can send up to credits. when depleted, client must stop until new credits arrive.nn3) explicit close with retry hintn- if a tenant exceeds absolute safety limits, close connection with a close code and a retry-after in the close payload. example: close(4001, retry-after15).nn4) drop oldest (safest for memory control)n- as a last resort, drop oldest messages in the per-tenant ring buffer and emit a metric and audit event. documenting dropped events is required for customers.nnobservable signals and metrics (recommended prometheus names)nn- websocket_connections_totaltenant (gauge)n- disable immediate retry for 3060 seconds.nn3) mitigation (3090 minutes)n- apply throttles or rate-limits at the edge for the tenant to prevent system-wide destabilization.n- if queue is full and safe, throttle.n- deterministic fallback: a predictable and auditable mapping (e.g., primary-fallback-quantized-fallback-llm2) so rollbacks and billing attribution are safe.nnpre-integration checklist (customer-side):n1) identify primary request classes and slos (latency p95, availability target, max per-request cost).n2) ensure model compatibility: prompt schemas, function-calling contracts, and tokenization behaviors.n3) provision redwood api keys and endpoint mapping for the primary and fallback model endpoints record model versions.n4) define telemetry tags that will be used by the proxy to annotate requests (tenant_id, route_id, fallback_reason, model_variant).n5) agree on billing attribution policy with finance (how fallback calls are charged when triggered by the platform).nnarchitecture patterns (3 recommended):na) thin router with deterministic failover (low complexity)n- behavior: proxy routes single request to primary upon configurable error/timeout/failure policy, sequentially retries to fallback variants.n- use when: small latency overhead budget, deterministic cost expectations.n- pros: predictable billing, simple tracing.n- cons: potential delay on failover path.nnb) concurrent fanout with race policy (parallel first-success wins)n- behavior: proxy issues parallel requests to primary and one or more fallback variants first successful response is returned.n- use when: ultra-low tail-latency is critical and extra cost is acceptable for cold starts.n- pros: best p99 latency in many failure modes.n- cons: higher token cost and complexity in deduplication.nnc) shadowing sampling for quality regression detectionn- behavior: primary responses are returned to users the same request is sent asynchronously (shadowed) to fallback/experimental variants for offline evaluation.n- use when: deploying new quantized models or tuned prompt sets requires acceptance testing.n- pros: safe production testing collects eval signals.n- cons: requires storage for shadow traces and eval pipeline.nnconfiguration examplesn- example router decision yaml (thin router):nnrouter:n default_policy: sequential_failovern timeout_ms: nnnhttp status mapping and recommendationsnn- 200 / 2xx: success redwood marks delivery succeeded and stops retries.n- 429: throttle treat as transient. retry using exponential backoff with jitter.n- 5xx: transient server error retry using exponential backoff with capped max interval.n- 408 / 499 / network errors: transient retry.n- 4xx (400, 401, 403): permanent failure (client code issue or auth). do not retry automatically surface to integrations team and customer.nnrecommended retry schedule (example)nn- immediate retry policy with exponential backoff jitter. conservative schedule used attempt before expirynn- default expiry window: 6 hours for non-critical events 2472 hours for business-critical events (negotiated in contract).n- note: customers may configure shorter windows in their destination configuration.nnidempotency and deduplication guidancenn1) idempotency key content: preferred: stable event_id (uuid v4) or sha256(event_id tenant_id).n2) deduplication window: set store more metadata use ttl attribute and conditional put.n - postgres: use unique constraint on (event_id, tenant_id) with background cleanup better if you already have transactional db.n4) accept-late-arrival semantic: if a duplicate arrives outside ttl, treat as new event or log as late duplicate per customer policy.nnexample dedup pseudocode (redis)nn// pseudo-codenif setnx(dedupe:, backoff guide, content: overviewnnpurposenthis guide describes recommended patterns, configuration defaults, and operational playbooks for adaptive batching and error backoff on inbound inference requests. it is intended for customer integration engineers, solutions architects, and sres who implement or validate connectors that send traffic to redwood inference (hosted, dedicated, or private).nnscope and assumptionsn- applies to both streaming (chunked / websocket) and synchronous http/rest ingest paths.n- assumes a proxy or sidecar exists in the customer environment which can buffer, batch, and retry (e.g., envoy, custom sidecar, or managed connector).n- focus on reducing tail latency, preventing overload, and preserving slos during transient errors and capacity surges.nnwhen to apply adaptive batchingn- high request parallelism with many short requests (avg tokens ingress proxy/sidecar (batcher) - rate limiter / circuit breaker - redwood edge - serving runtimennkey components and responsibilitiesn- batcher: groups small requests into a single request payload when beneficial. responsible for configurable max batch size, max waiting time, and priority queues.n- retry controller: applies retry policy with exponential backoff jitter, respects server-provided retry-after headers and throttle signals.n- circuit breaker: trips under elevated error rates or increased p99 serve latency to fail fast and avoid queue buildup.n- metrics tracer: emits per-batch and per-request metrics (see metrics section) and attaches trace ids for correlation.nnconfiguration recommended defaults (table)nparameter default rationalen------------------------nmax_batch_size 16 fits typical gpu parallelism for small requests tune upward for long-context modelsnmax_batch_latency_ms 30 limits additional wait introduced by batching to keep interactive latency under 200ms p95nmin_batch_size 1 allows passthrough for single request when latency-critical or when queue is emptynbatch_priority_threshold_tokens 120 requests longer than this are sent in dedicated batches to avoid head-of-line blockingnqueue_capacity 200 prevents unbounded memory growth choose based on sidecar memory profilencircuit_breaker_error_pct 20 trip if 20 of calls in sliding window fail (adjust per tenant sla)ncb_window_seconds 60 sliding evaluation windownretry_policy exponential_jitter backoff base 200ms, multiplier 2, max 5 attemptsnretry_on 429, 503, 502, network_errors only retry transient errors 4xx otherwise returned to guidelines for office plants and low-effort decor in redwood inference offices. the goal is to maintain a safe, healthy workplace, reduce allergens and pest risk, and ensure plants support wellbeing and culture without creating maintenance burden.nnscope:n- applies to all shared indoor office spaces, meeting rooms, and communal areas in redwood-managed offices.n- does not cover employee personal standing water, or pests.n2) watering: follow the plant-specific schedule (see table below) avoid overwatering. use saucers to prevent leaks.n3) clean leaves monthly: wipe dust buildup to keep plants healthy and improve air quality.n4) report issues: log major problems in facilities with a photo and location.nnwatering schedule by plant type (general guidance):n- snake plant (sansevieria): water every 46 weeks. low light tolerant.n- zz plant (zamioculcas zamiifolia): water every 46 weeks. very low maintenance.n- pothos/devils ivy: water every 1014 days trim vines if they encroach on walkways.n- spider plant: water every 1014 days prefers bright, indirect light.n- peace lily: water every 710 days avoid placement where pollen may bother coworkers.n- succulents/cacti: water every 36 weeks depending on season.nnplacement and safety guidelines:n- do not place plants where they block egress, fire extinguishers, electrical panels, or sensors.n- avoid hanging plants directly over desks where drips could occur.n- ensure pots have trays mopping and carpet damage incidents have previously come from unchecked overflow.n- do not place heavily-shedding plants in meeting rooms or near shared keyboards and equipment.n- plants with known mild-to-high toxicity (e.g., philodendron, oleander) are not allowed in common areas.nnpersonal desk plants (employee-owned):n- allowed but must be maintained by the owner. if a plant becomes a nuisance (pests, mold, water damage) facilities may request removal.n- use a waterproof tray and keep a small saucer under the pot.n- notify facilities in case of spider/ant/pest sightings so coordinated treatment can occur.nnprocurement and requests:n- to request a new plant or replacement, file a request in the facilities request form (link in sidebar) with: proposed location, desired plant type (if known), and any accessibility concerns.n- facilities maintains a small budget for replacements. for larger decorative refreshes, submit a ticket to people ops with proposed spend and rationale.n- preferred vendors: local nurseries and the approved vendor list (see facilities vendor doc).nndecor guidelines (small items accompanying plants):n- pots and stands should be neutral (matte blacks, grays, natural wood) unless coordinated as part of a themed refresh.n- no scented candles or oil diffusers in shared areas.n- avoid porous pots that retain moisture directly against furniture use trays and felt pads under stands.nnmaintenance cadence and ownership:n- facilities: weekly checklists, monthly leaf-clean, quarterly plant health review.n- people ops: budget approvals, large refresh planning, and accommodation handling for allergies/sensitivities.n- teams may volunteer to sponsor plants in their area (signup through people ops) volunteer teams are responsible for basic watering on a shared rota.nnpest and allergy procedures:n- if pests (aphids, spider mites) are detected, quarantine the plant and notify facilities immediately. do not attempt over-the-counter pesticide sprays without coordination.n- for allergy complaints, people ops will identify nearby plants and offer relocation/removal options. we prioritize non-confrontational resolutions and temporary workarounds (e.g., moving desks).nnexceptions and accommodations:n- if an individual requires a scent-free or plant-free workspace for medical reasons, people ops will provide reasonable accommodation, including relocation or desk shields if needed.nnappendix: quick reference (contact links)n- facilities channel: facilities purposenthis standard defines the minimum engineering requirements for implementing data retention (ttl) and deletion across redwood inference systems.nnit exists to ensure:n- retention controls are enforceable (not just configurable).n- purge mechanisms are safe, idempotent, and observable.n- we can provide credible evidence for internal audits and customer security reviews (soc 2/iso-style).nnthis is a must-follow standard for any store or service that holds customer-affecting data classes subject to retention.nn scopenapplies to:n- control-plane and data-plane stores that persist any of the following (examples):n - request/response logs (where enabled)n - prompts/completions stored at rest (where enabled)n - audit logsn - traces/metrics/log aggregatesn - artifacts (eval datasets, report packages, exported evidence bundles)nndoes not replace:n- data classification and logging standards (redaction, pii controls).n- legal hold / exceptions policy (see security compliance pages).nn definitionsn- ttl (time-to-live): maximum time data is allowed to exist after its relevant timestamp (usually created_at / ingested_at).n- retention policy: tenant data-class specific configuration describing ttl, residency constraints, and exception behavior.n- purge job: automated deletion process that enforces ttl by deleting records/objects past their expiry.n- idempotent deletion: a purge job can run multiple times (retries, replays) and yields the same end state without causing incorrect deletions or operational harm.n- deletion verification: a set of metrics and checks proving that expired data is actually removed within an allowed lag window.n- ttl lag: now - max(deleted_cutoff_applied) for a given store/tenant/data class. in other words, how far behind deletion is from the intended ttl boundary.nn design principlesn1. policy is evaluated centrally enforcement is local.n - policy evaluation source of truth is the control plane (see adr-017).n - each store/feature must implement enforcement in the component that owns the data.nn2. delete is a production operation.n - purge paths must be designed for predictable load, backpressure, and safe retries.nn3. verification is mandatory.n - if you cant measure deletion, we treat it as not implemented.nn4. prefer deterministic, incremental deletion over big sweeps.n - use primary-key ordered pagination and bounded batch sizes.nn5. respect legal hold and documented exceptions.n - holds must be enforced consistently and be auditable.nn required implementation checklist (all stores)nthe following are minimum requirements for any ttl enforcement implementation.nn 1) data model requirementsnrequired fields (or equivalent):n- tenant_id (or org/project/workspace id)n- data_class (explicit or implied by table/bucket)n- created_at or ingested_at timestamp (source-of-truth clock described below)n- optional but strongly recommended:n - region (if multi-region)n - policy_version_applied (or last-evaluated policy reference)n - hold_status / hold_reason (if holds apply at record/object granularity)nntime source standard:n- use database/server-side timestamps for expiry decisions when possible (e.g., now() in sql) to avoid clock skew.nn 2) deletion semanticsnyou must document (in the owning system doc):n- whether deletion is hard delete (required for retention enforcement unless explicitly approved otherwise).n- if soft-delete/tombstones exist for product needs, define:n - when tombstones are permanently removedn - whether tombstones are themselves subject to ttln - how exports/reporting treat tombstoned recordsnnnot allowed as the only enforcement mechanism:n- we filter expired rows at read time. (this is not deletion.)nn 3) purge job requirementsnall purge jobs must be:n- idempotent (safe to re-run deletes are repeatable).n- bounded (limits per run to prevent db/storage pressure).n- retryable with exponential backoff.n- observable (metrics structured logs run identifiers).n- multi-tenant safe (no cross-tenant deletion).n- hold-aware (legal hold / incident hold must prevent deletion when applicable).nn 4) verification requirementsnyou must implement:n- ttl lag metric(s)n- deletion success/failure metricsn- backlog size estimates (where meaningful)n- alerts (see below)n- a dashboard panel set (see dashboards)nn 5) runbook and ownershipnbefore ga:n- create/extend a runbook describing how to monitor, throttle, re-run, and validate the purge.n- explicitly assign an owning team and on-call escalation.nn standard purge job patternn recommended algorithm (sql-backed stores)nkey idea: delete in small, ordered batches using an index that supports the filter.nnrequired indexes (example):n- (tenant_id, created_at, id) or equivalent.nnbatch delete pattern:n1. compute cutoff: cutoff_ts now() - ttl_duration (from policy).n2. select candidate ids using deterministic ordering and a strict upper bound.n3. delete by id list (or range) with safeguards.n4. emit metrics for deleted rows, runtime, and errors.nnexample (illustrative):n- select: select id from request_logs where tenant_id 1 and created_at 24h lagn - dedicated: page at 12h lagn - private: page at 24h lag (or as contractually required)nn2. purge job error burstn- condition: purge_failures_total rate above threshold for 15 minutes and purge_rows_deleted_total not increasing.n- guidance: threshold depends on schedule for hourly jobs, any consistent failure across 2 consecutive runs should page.nn ticket alerts (p2)n3. backlog growingn- condition: purge_backlog_estimate increasing for 6 hours.nn4. job not runningn- condition: missing purge_job_duration_seconds and purge_rows_deleted_total activity for 2x expected schedule interval.nn dashboards (required panels)ncreate a dashboard (or extend the standard retention dashboard) with:n- ttl lag over time (ttl_lag_seconds) by region/storen- rows deleted per run / per hour (purge_rows_deleted_total rate)n- failure rate (purge_failures_total rate) with top failure_typen- job duration (purge_job_duration_seconds p50/p95)n- backlog estimate (if available)n- overlay of deploy markers for the purge component (when supported)nn performance and safety guardrailsn database pressure controlsn- hard limit deletes per batch (e.g., 1k10k rows) and per minute (environment dependent).n- prefer primary-key pagination avoid large offset scans.n- use read replicas for candidate selection only if correctness is preserved.n- use statement timeouts and cancellation do not allow long-running delete transactions.nn schedulingn- jobs should be scheduled at a cadence that matches ttl granularity and expected write volume.n- stagger schedules by region to reduce peak load.nn backfills and migrationsnif adding ttl to an existing store:n- provide a backfill plan for legacy rows without timestamps or without tenant attribution.n- plan for initial backlog deletion (ramp slowly).n- define success criteria (e.g., ttl_lag_seconds soft limits - hard limits) with human-in-the-loop gates.n3. ensure mitigations are cost-aware and reversible with clear rollback primitives.n4. provide dashboards and playbooks so oncall and sres can quickly evaluate cause, customer impact, and remediation.nnscope and non-goalsn-------------------n- scope: realtime and 10m/1h aggregated signals affecting hosted and dedicated clusters. applies to inference request routing, prefetched caches, and tenant-level autoscaling.n- non-goal: tenant credit/billing dispute resolution (handled by billing workflows).nndefinitionsn-----------n- tenant: account or api key group that owns requests and billing.n- tss: tenant safety scorecard, normalized 0.0 - 100.0 (higher higher risk).n- soft mitigation: non-blocking action (rate-limited responses, lower-priority queue).n- hard mitigation: blocking action (temporary rate limit, model downgrade, or eviction).nnscorecard components and rationalen---------------------------------nwe combine telemetry into compact sub-scores, each mapped to 0-100. the final tss is a weighted sum, clipped to 100. sub-scores:nn1) token burst score (weight 30)n- measures percentile of short-window token rate vs. tenant baseline. detects token storms.n- signal sources: request_token_count, request_rate_1m, historical_7d_baseline.nn2) gpu interference score (weight 20)n- derived from gpu metrics: shared_p99_latency_increase, gpu_util_spikes, memory_swap_events. correlates with tenant placement on noisy nodes.nn3) kv cache pressure score (weight 15)n- tracks cache miss rate, prefix eviction rate, and hot-key skew. high score indicates evictions harming other tenants.nn4) quality-stability score (weight 15)n- model-level errors: repeated malformed requests, function-calling misuses, and saturation of streaming channel errors.nn5) slo burn score (weight 20)n- direct slo impact: latency_p50/p95 increases attributable to tenant-weighted requests and error budget burn.nnscoring table (example weights)n-------------------------------n component weight nominal threshold high-risk threshold notes dsid_b55949676c6c4bae970c47e57ed4000c, source_type: confluence, title: multitenant replay oracle and scheduler debug playbook, content: overviewnnthis playbook describes a deterministic replay and investigation workflow (the replay oracle) for diagnosing multitenant scheduler and kernel interactions that cause slo violations or throughput regressions. it unifies capture, deterministic reconstruction, scheduler decision replay, and hypothesis-driven kernel perturbation to root cause hardtoreproduce latency and fidelity issues.nnaudiencenn- oncall sres and runtime engineers performing postincident forensics.n- runtime scheduler and kernel maintainers executing regressions or perf experiments.n- applied ml/evals engineers validating quality regressions caused by scheduling/economic changes.nnscope and when to use this playbooknnuse the replay oracle when any of the following are true:n1) tail latency spikes ( p99.9) recur without a clear origin in ingress or model change.n2) multitenant interference suspected (queueing patterns match but treatment varies by cohort).n3) kernel or preemption regressions are suspected and local instrumentation is insufficient to reproduce.nnsignal model (what we capture)nnwe capture a minimal, reconstructable set of signals that allow deterministic replay across layers:nn- ingress event envelope: request id, route, client token, timestamp, raw prompt hash.n- scheduler trace: policy decisions, priority, admission slot id, kernel assignment hint, preemption markers.n- kernel execution trace: kernel id, launch parameters, input lengths, occupancy estimate, gpu memory deltas.n- kv cache delta log: keys read/written, cache hit/miss per request.n- system telemetry: gpu utilization, nvlink errors, host nic drops, and node thermal events.nncapture format and storage contractnn- capture format: newline-delimited json (ndjson) with one top-level envelope per request. schema example: nnn request_id: abc123, route: /v1/generate, timestamp: 2026-02-02t15:22:11z, scheduler: decision_id: d-99, priority: interactive, assigned_kernel: kv-sharded-v2 , kernel_trace: phase: forward, launch_ms: 123, occupancy_pct: 78 , kvcache_deltas: k1,k2, sys: gpu_util: 56, nvlink_err: 0 nnn- retention: store captures for 90 days in the incident archive s3 bucket. for highseverity incidents, persist a 365day snapshot.n- access controls: captures are confidential set confidentiality: restricted for customersensitive incidents.nnquick triage checklist (first 10 minutes)nn1. confirm incident scope: which routes/tenants are affected, timeframe, and slo signal.n2. check whether a capture already exists for sample request_ids if not, trigger capture on the active nodes using the ephemeral-replay-capture flag.n3. retrieve host/system telemetry (gpu thermal, nic, cpu steal) for the timeframe.n4. run a fast differential: compare scheduler decision distributions (priority mix, admission latency) between healthy and unhealthy windows.nndetailed investigation procedure (ordered)nn1) capture colocated and crosstenant samplesnn- use the capture coordinator cli to atomically snapshot n requests across all affected pods. example: nnnredwood-capture --time-window2026-02-02t15:20:00z/2026-02-02t15:25:00z --routes/v1/generate --output/tmp/capture.ndjsonnnn2) reconstruct scheduler decisions locallynn- replay the scheduler decision stream against a sandboxed scheduler that uses the same policy version and kernel mapper. the sandbox should be configured with deterministic pseudorandom seeds and identical token accounting quotas.n- tooling: scheduler-replay (see example below).nn3) deterministic kernel replay and microperturbationsnn- use the kernelreplayer to feed kernel launches in the original launch order into an isolated node (or simulator) to observe perkernel timing and preemption behavior.n- run perturbation experiments: add controlled delays at preemption points, adjust kernel preemption granularity, and toggle small occupancy caps.nn4) kv cache reconstruction and warmup assessmentnn- rebuild perrequest kv cache state using the delta log and reexecute to measure delta hit/miss timings. poor warmup sequences often manifest as long tails when many requests require sequential kv loads.nn5) hypothesis-driven kernel variationnn- if the replay shows repeated long tail during kernel phase x, try the following:n a) swap to a fallback kernel with lower occupancy but better preemption responsiveness.n b) introduce batch slicing at the scheduler shim to reduce singlekernel execution times.n c) temporarily mark the tenant for priority isolation and compare outcomes.nninstrumentation and sampling guidancenn- sampling rates: default capture sampling is 0.1 of requests incidents should increase to 520 for the affected routes.n- recommended additional spans to enable for incidents:n - scheduler.decision_id (tag)n - kernel.launch_id and kernel.phasen - kvcache.key_hints (truncated)n - host.gpu_thermal_tripnn- cost guidance: enable highfidelity capture only on a small set of nodes to limit telemetry volumes. use the capture coordinator to shard samples across host pools.nnconfig and required knobs (table)nn- the following table lists the runtime config keys, recommended incident defaults, and owner.nn config_key default incident default operational runbook for enabling/disabling sampling policies, validating sample health, and performing trace-driven experiments.nnminimum trace contract (required fields in a sampled trace)n---------------------------------------------------------n1) request_id (global uuid)n2) ingest_timestamp and ingest_node idn3) scheduler-arrival scheduler-dispatch spans with kernel_hint attributen4) kernel-execution span(s) with kernel_name, kernel_version, and gpu_affinity tagsn5) kvcache/kv-prefetch spans (if used) with hit/miss indicatorn6) response_timestamp and final_status coden7) cost_estimate.tokens and sequence_length metadatannsampling strategies (policy catalog)n----------------------------------n- time-bound uniform (tb-uniform): keep 1 in n requests uniformly across wall-clock time per route. good for baseline telemetry.n- probabilistic priority-weighted (ppw): sample with probability p(route, priority) where priority is derived from token-count or customer tier. useful to bias toward expensive or high-value requests.n- burst-capture window (bcw): on detection of a latency spike for a cohort, enable 100 sampling for x minutes for that cohort. use for rapid root-cause windows.n- horizon-shot correlated sampling (hscs): sample one request per session-length bucket per user/session to preserve sequence continuity for long-running dialogues.n- deterministic replay anchor (dra): tag a small stable fraction of requests (e.g., 0.1) with a persistent seed so they are consistently captured across both prod and bench replay pipelines.nnrecommended default policy (production)n--------------------------------------n- per-route tb-uniform base rate: 1/500 (0.2) for low-traffic routes, 1/200 for medium, 1/50 for high-latency or high-cost routes.n- ppw multiplier: 3x for requests with token_count 512 or from enterprise-tier customers.n- bcw: automatically enabled for 10 minutes when 99th latency for a route exceeds 2x expected baseline.n- dra: persistent seed with 0.1 global capture rate for deterministic replay.nninstrumentation checklistn------------------------n- sdks must annotate traces with the minimum trace contract keys above.n- all scheduler nodes must propagate kernel_hint and kernel_version to the downstream kernel agent.n- kernel agents must emit precise start/end timestamps with gpu cardinality (e.g., gpu_index, nvlink hops).n- a lightweight per-request summary (json) should be emitted to a short-lived sampling buffer before full trace ingestion to power fast validation. example summary: nn request_id:uuid,route:/generate,tokens:124,sequence_len:256,kernel:sharded-attn-v2,latency_ms:123.4,sample_flag:dra-1nnstorage and retention guidelinesn-------------------------------n- full traces: retain for 30 days in hot store (for on-call and triage). after 30 days, move to cold archive for 12 months if flagged by dra or enterprise customer.n- summaries: retain for 90 days in time-series store for quick dashboards and sampling health metrics.n- replay corpus: extracted deterministic seeds (dra) persist indefinitely until retired by experiment owners.nnquality and acceptance criteria for a sampling runn------------------------------------------------n- coverage: sampled traces must collectively cover at least 95 of kernel variants observed in a 24-hour window for the route under test.n- freshness: median time from trace emission to availability in the triage ui must be 98 of sampled traces must contain all spans in the minimum trace contract.n- replayability: at least 90 of dra-tagged traces must be usable in the replay harness (i.e., no missing session context or input truncation).nnmetrics and dashboards to buildn-----------------------------n- sampling health dashboard (per-route): sample_rate, sample_coverage (kernel variant coverage), missing_fields_pct, ingest_delay_p50/p95/p99.n- bcw incident dashboard: recent windows, top contributing kernels, request surface heatmap.n- replay readiness: dra integrity, replay-success-rate, input-normalization-delta.nnrunbook: enabling a bcw capture after an incidentn------------------------------------------------n1) detect spike: alert triggers when 99th latency 2x baseline for 5m.n2) triage owner confirms cohort and scope via the incident channel.n3) from sampling control ui or cli, enable bcw for the affected route with duration 10m and collect full traces. cli example:nn redwood-samplectl enable --route /generate --policy bcw --duration 10m --reason post-incident triage --owner oncall-teamnn4) validate: ensure summaries appear in sampling buffer and full traces start arriving in triage ui within 2 minutes.n5) collect candidate traces (tag as incident-yyyymmdd) and export to bench replay: nn redwood-replay export --tags incident-20250109 --format ndjson --output s3://redwood-labs/incident-replays/2025-01-09nn6) after window expires, automatically revert sampling rates to base policy. confirm revert with: nn redwood-samplectl status --route /generatennoperational safety and cost controlsn----------------------------------n- global safety cap: no more than 5 of aggregate traffic may be sampled with full traces at any time without explicit approval.n- per-tenant override must be gated to enterprise-ops and logged in the audit trail.n- sampling control operations require two-person approval for changes that increase global sampled traffic above 1.nnexperiment checklist dashboard.n5) export corpus to bench and run replay capture microbenchmarks for kernel candidates.n6) document findings and if required, open a kernel regression ticket (include dra seeds and representative traces).nncommon pitfalls and mitigationsn------------------------------n- pitfall: skewed sampling where only low-latency requests are captured (usually due to client-side propensity).n mitigation: enforce server-side sampling decision paired with a short deterministic hash of request_id to avoid client bias.n- pitfall: missing kernel_version tag in legacy agents.n mitigation: deploy lightweight agent shim that backfills version from environment metadata and mark shimged traces for review.n- pitfall: replay failures caused by truncated session context.n title: runtime experiment lab protocols and kernel fuzz suite 2026, content: summaryn-------nthis page documents the runtime experiment lab protocols and the kernel fuzz suite (kfs): a repeatable, auditable set of experiments and tooling we use to exercise scheduling, kernel selection, and execution edge cases in the redwood serving runtime. the goal is to find latent correctness bugs and fidelity regressions, validate mitigation strategies, and produce reproducible artifacts for profiling and remediation teams.nnscopen-----n- applies to all internal runtime kernel builds and scheduler releases before a canary rollout.n- targets gpu and accelerator execution layers, batch slicing, kv-cache prefetch pathways, and scheduler handoff code paths.n- not intended for customer-facing load testing or production-scale benchmarking (see the benchmarking catalog).nnowning team and contactsn-----------------------n- primary owner: eng - serving runtime (runtime-experiments@redwood.example.com)n- experiment custodian (lab ops): aisha pateln- observability liaison: marco nguyenn- security reviewer: lin chenn- slack channel: runtime-labnnmotivation and success criterian-------------------------------nwhy we run a fuzzing/testbed program:n- many kernel regressions are non-deterministic and appear only under complex interleavings of scheduling and batching.n- automated fuzzing can expose correctness issues (bad memory accesses, kernel crashes), api contract regressions (inference fidelity changes), and performance cliffs.n- success criteria for a release candidate: zero reproducible kernel crashes, fidelity drift within defined bounds, and no unexplained tail-latency increases after exercising the kfs and protocol suite.nnhigh-level testbed architecturen-------------------------------ncomponents and their roles:n- lab controller: lightweight service that orchestrates experiments, collects artifacts, and uploads to the experiment bucket (s3://redwood-runtime-lab).n- isolated runner cluster: ephemeral fleet of instances with representative accelerator types (a100/rtx/custom). each runner is instrumented with the profiler agent and secure collector.n- kernel harness: small shim that loads the runtime binary, injects test inputs, and toggles kernel-selection flags.n- fuzzer engine: mutated input generator workload orchestrator (see kfs modules).n- observability stack: traces (x-ray/jaeger), perf kernels, gpu telemetry (sm utilization, memory histograms), aggregated into the runtime-lab dashboard.nnkernel fuzz suite (kfs) componentsn----------------------------------n- input mutation engine (im): generates permutations of sequence lengths, prompt/prefix shapes, and kv-cache states.n- scheduling combinator (sc): composes concurrency shapes and priority mixes (e.g., 80 background low-priority long seq, 20 high-priority short seq bursts).n- kernel toggler (kt): flips kernel selection heuristics and quantization code paths at runtime to test fallback logic.n- state snapshotter (ss): captures kernel inputs, memory maps, and kv cache deltas for deterministic replay.n- crash triage agent (cta): automatic symbolication and core extraction posts to lab bug queue with attachments.nnrepresentative kfs testcases (examples)n--------------------------------------n1) mixed-fidelity handoff: 500 low-priority requests with sequence512 interleaved with high-priority requests sequence64 every 30ms. kernel toggles to half-precision for background path.n2) kv-cache eviction race: two tenants share a shard induce eviction threshold crossing while prefetcher runs.n3) preemption batch-slice race: synthetic workloads that induce cooperative preemption, followed by load spike to trigger slice reassembly logic.n4) cross-kernel migration: on-the-fly switch from optimized attention kernel a to fallback kernel b with kv merge.nnexperiment protocol (must be followed no immediate crashes. labctl run-suite --suitekfs-quick --rcrc-1234n5. run targeted fuzz campaigns (per schedule): labctl run-fuzz --campaignkv-eviction-race --duration2h --seed42n6. after each end-to-end-latency-attribution-using-shadow-channels-2024, content: summarynnthis playbook describes our shadow channel methodology for attributing end-to-end latency to internal components (kernel dispatch, nvlink latency, kv-cache misses, prefix-serialization, enqueue/dequeue overhead) without impacting production slos. it documents design, instrumentation, sampling, cost constraints, and an on-call runbook for triage.nnscopenn- applies to all hosted and dedicated model-serving clusters running the redwood runtime.n- focus: high-p99 tail and intermittent spikes that are not explained by request size or known deployments.n- out of scope: offline microbenchmarks, model-level correctness regressions.nnwhy shadow channels?nntraditional profiling (heavy tracing on live requests) risks increased latency and cost. shadow channels replicate a small fraction of live requests and route them through alternative, instrumented execution paths that capture per-stage timestamps and kernel-level markers, while ensuring no user-facing effects. shadow runs are asynchronous and do not block the original request flow.nndesign overviewnn1) sampling and routingn- global sample rate: default 0.5 of eligible requests. adjustable per-tenant via token metadata.n- eligibility: production requests with sequence_length 8 and not marked internal_test or contain pii flags.n- routing: the live request continues on the low-latency path the shadow copy is forked and sent to an instrumented runtime instance pool (shadow pool) with lower priority scheduling and strict cpu/gpu time quotas.nn2) shadow pool characteristicsn- separate node label: node-roleshadow-instrumented.n- scheduler policy: preemptible, batch slicing disabled, per-request kernel trace hooks enabled.n- capacity: sized to handle worst-case sample burst for 30s at configured sample rate. autoscaling disabled use fixed pools to minimize side effects.nn3) instrumentation surfacen- per-stage timestamps (monotonic): request_received, prefix_deserialize_start/end, kvcache_lookup_start/end, kernel_dispatch_start/end (per kernel), nvlink_wait_start/end, response_serialize_start/end.n- kernel markers: kernel_id, kernel_variant, quantization_path, custream id.n- hardware telemetry: gpu occupancy, sm utilization, memory allocation delta, nvlink per-transfer latency (where available).n- correlation ids: original_request_id, shadow_request_id, sample_seed, tenant_id.nn4) data retention and privacyn- shadow payloads are hashed payloads with detectable pii are dropped from storage. raw request text is never stored in long-term telemetry buckets.n- shadow logs retained 30 days in hot storage and 365 days in compressed cold storage for regression analysis.nnattribution algorithm (high level)nn- preprocess: discard shadow samples with error codes or model-variant mismatches. normalize for request size and token counts.n- stage delta calculation: compute t_stage end - start for each instrumented stage. produce per-sample vector t_prefix, t_kv, t_kernels_total, t_nvlink, t_serialize.n- noise filtering: apply median absolute deviation (mad) filter to remove outliers caused by background maintenance (oom kills, node reboots).n- attribution score: for each sample compute fraction f_stage t_stage / t_total. aggregate by time window (1m, 5m) and compute p90/p95/p99 of f_stage per kernel_id.n- cross-correlation: time-shifted cross-correlation between gpu occupancy and t_kernels_total to detect resource contention patterns.nndashboards and alertsnnminimum dashboards to entropy-aware-tail-sampling-and-replay-playbook, content: summaryn-------nthis playbook describes an entropy-aware sampling and replay pipeline used to capture and investigate rare, high-cost tail latency events in the serving runtime. the goal is to produce a small, high-value corpus of end-to-end requests (inputcontextresponseruntime-trace) for offline replay, debugging, and kernel-level root-cause analysis without overwhelming storage or incurring excessive cost.nnmotivationn----------ntraditional frequency-based samplers either oversample common fast requests or miss low-frequency pathological requests that drive p99p999 latency. entropy-aware sampling combines statistical rarity in the request surface (input entropy), deviation from expected latency signatures (residual latency), and scheduler/kernel signals (unexpected kernel hops, cache misses) to prioritize traces for capture.nnwhen to usen-----------n- investigating unexplained p99 spikes.n- prioritizing data for quantization/regression testing when corpus budget is limited.n- building reproducer sets for kernel or nvlink anomalies.nndefinitions and signals consideredn--------------------------------n- request_entropy: shannon estimate on token distribution or prompt template fingerprint.n- residual_latency: observed_latency - expected_latency(model, seq_len, tenant_profile).n- kernel_hop_count: times request switched gpu kernels or was preempted.n- kv_cache_miss_rate: fraction of kv lookups that missed warm caches.n- cross_tenant_noise_index: normalized measure of concurrent slot contention.nnsampling algorithm (high level)n-------------------------------n1. for each request, compute a sampling_score w1 normalized(request_entropy) w2 normalized(residual_latency) w3 normalized(kernel_hop_count) w4 normalized(kv_cache_miss_rate).n2. apply a minimum threshold t_min and a dynamic reservoir budget per epoch (1h window).n3. apply adaptive decay so that repeated requests from the same request_fingerprint are downweighted within the same epoch to protect diversity.n4. enrich sampled items with a short runtime-trace (per-request timeline), kernel telemetry (kernel id, duration, preemption flags), and a small snapshot of kv cache state (fingerprints only, not raw content).nnweights and tuning recommendationsn--------------------------------n- default weights: w10.25, w20.45, w30.2, w40.1. these were empirically validated on mixed-production workloads (search-like chat).n- increase w2 if investigating latency regressions increase w1 when investigating model/prompt edge cases.n- reservoir sizing: aim for 210k captures per hour for large fleets reduce by 10x in restricted-cost environments.nnoperational implementation (components)n--------------------------------------n- sampler-service: in-line low-latency component that receives lightweight telemetry and returns sample decisions. must attach a sample_id header for later reassembly.n- capture-proxy: short-circuit store for sampled request bodies and enriched traces writes to compressed object store and indexes to telemetry db.n- replay-harness: isolated runner that can replay captured requests against staging kernels and collect deterministic kernel traces.n- retention-controller: policy engine that ages captures by priority and storage pressure.nnexample sampling config (yaml)n----------------------------nsampling:n epoch_window: 1hn reservoir_target_per_hour: 5000n threshold_min: 0.6n weights:n entropy: 0.25n residual_latency: 0.45n kernel_hops: 0.2n kv_miss: 0.1n dedupe_decay_seconds: 600n fingerprint_fields: prompt_template_id, user_agent, tenant_idnntelemetry and metrics to emit (required)n--------------------------------------n- runtime.sampler.score (gauge, labeled by sample_id, tenant_id, model)n- runtime.sampler.decision (counter: sampledrejected)n- runtime.capture.size_bytes (histogram)n- runtime.capture.latency_ms (time for capture proxy roundtrip)n- runtime.replay.success (counter)n- kernel.hop.count (counter per request)n- kvcache.fingerprint.count (gauge)nnreplay harness contractn-----------------------n1. replay must accept a compressed tarball containing: metadata.json, request.json, small_trace.pb, kernel_hints.json.n2. replay must run in an isolated namespace with pinned kernel images matching the original kernel id or best-effort compatible variant.n3. replay should produce a canonical result bundle: stdout json, kernel-trace.pb, telemetry-snapshot.json, and a fidelity-report comparing runtime signatures against the captured baseline.nnrunbook: investigating a p99 spike with entropy samplesn-----------------------------------------------------n1. identify spike window and query telemetry: p50/p90/p99, sampler.decision ratio, reservoir usage.n2. pull top n samples by score (n200 by default) and surface the distribution by fingerprint, model, and tenant.n3. triage by category: input-entropy dominant, kernel-hop dominant, kv-miss dominant, or mixed.n4. for kernel-hop cases: run replay-harness on the top 5 captures, compare kernel-trace.pb to stored baseline, and check for kernel version skew or nvlink remapping.n5. for kv-miss dominant: check kvcache hit rates across the cluster and warmup patterns consult the kvcache-prefetch logs.n6. draft incident note with root cause hypotheses and remedial actions (kernel patch, scheduler-rule, cache policy change).nnslos and thresholds for sampling pipeline healthn------------------------------------------------n- sampler.decision_latency: p95 99 for declared samples.n- replay.harness.repeatability: 95 for deterministic kernels (document exceptions).nnstorage, retention, and backfill guidancen----------------------------------------n- target compressed capture size: median 3kb, 95th percentile 0.95) keep 90 days general captures keep 714 days depending on storage tier.n- backfill: if replays require additional context we do not capture inline (e.g., larger kv snapshots) we store hooks to request ephemeral backfill runs against a temporary snapshot of tenant state under approved compliance process.nnprivacy and compliance notesn---------------------------n- do not capture full pii or customer content unless an explicit approved data-retention exception exists. sampler must filter or redact fields defined in the global pii filter config.n- all captures are tagged with confidentiality: internal and logged in the audit service.nnoperational checks and dashboards (recommended)n---------------------------------------------n- dashboard: sampler overview (decisions/hour, avg score, reservoir fill).n- dashboard: capture quality (size distribution, replay success over time, median time-to-replay).n- alert: capture.success_rate 5ms.nnappendix: cli examplesn----------------------n- create a replay bundle from capture store (example):n rcli capture fetch --id sample-2026-09-11-0001 --out ./bundle.tgznn- run replay against staging:n rcli replay run --bundle ./bundle.tgz --target staging --collect kernel-trace,telemetry --timeout 10mnnfaqn---nq: how do we avoid capturing test traffic or repeated plg samples?na: use fingerprint_fields to identify onboarding/test flows and set an explicit exclude policy.nnq: does sampling add latency to production calls?na: the in-line sampler must be asynchronous in critical-path if score calculation exceeds low-latency budget prefer a fast-path estimate and deferred final capture.nnowners and contactsn-------------------nprimary: eng-serving-runtime/profiling (team alias).nescalation: aisha patel (aisha.patel@redwood.ai), marco ruiz summarynthis playbook describes the developer-local runtime sandbox and associated benchmarking profiling workflows used to reproduce key production behaviors without requiring full cluster access. the sandbox is intentionally lightweight and deterministic: it models the runtime dispatch, a kv cache shim, a kernel-proxy for scheduling experiments, and easy-to-run microbenchmarks. use this guide to iterate on kernel scheduler patches, evaluate batching strategies, and validate optimization hypotheses before graduating changes to the full perf suite.nnscopen- reproduce request lifecycle: api - dispatcher - kernel-proxy - model executor (mock or quantized engine).n- run microbenchmarks that mimic production prompt shapes (short, medium, long) and multi-turn chat traces.n- exercise scheduling policies (fair-share, priority-driven, cooperative preemption) in a reproducible environment.n- capture perf traces (cpu/gpu timelines), kernel occupancy, and per-token cost estimates.n- limitations: does not emulate multi-tenant noisy neighbors at scale, and gpu topology is single-node only. see known differences section.nnprerequisitesn1) linux workstation with docker 20.10 or a macos machine with docker desktop and a supported gpu passthrough (optional).n2) tools/runtime-sandbox repo checked out (internal): git clone git@repo.internal:redwood/tools/runtime-sandbox.gitn3) python 3.10, pipenv or virtualenv for running harness scripts.nnsandbox components (what runs locally)n- runtime-dispatcher-lite: lightweight http front-end that accepts redwood api-style requests and translates compute work into a scheduling request.n- kvcached-shim: in-memory kv cache with controllable hit-rate to simulate warm/cold sessions.n- kernel-proxy: process that implements a subset of production kernel selection queuing logic pluggable policies: simple_fifo, fair_share, priority_shepherd.n- model-mock: tunable latency stub or a real local quantized engine (ggml/onnxruntime path) for feedback loop protocol, content: overview:nthis page defines the experiment feedback loop protocol used by the serving runtime team to design, run, and act on profiling and kernel scheduling experiments that change runtime behavior. the protocol standardizes hypothesis framing, telemetry instrumentation, safety gates, analysis artifacts, and rollout rules. it is intended for engineers running microbenchmarks, shadow traffic experiments, and online canaries that touch the kernel scheduler, kv cache, batching heuristics, and model variant routing.nnwhy we have a formal protocol:n- reduce noisy experiments and ensure reproducible results.n- protect slos and customer traffic during investigations.n- provide clear handoffs from experimenters to runtime operators and release engineers.nnscope:napplies to experiments that: 1) modify kernel scheduler configuration or code paths, 2) alter request shaping / admission, 3) introduce new telemetry or sampling, or 4) change runtime fallback/degradation modes. not intended for purely offline model evaluation.nnroles and ownership:n- experiment owner: engineer who proposes and executes the experiment (primary contact).n- runtime oncall: sre responsible for live traffic safety gates (will have emergency rollback authority).n- observability owner: platform engineer who validates instrumentation and dashboards.n- release captain: release engineer who approves any rollout to dedicated or hosted clusters.nnhigh-level workflow (5 phases):n1) hypothesis safety plann - write a short hypothesis: changing kernel x threshold will reduce p99 latency by 10 for short sequences without increasing p99 for long sequences.n - identify safety slos (see table below) and define abort thresholds.n - pre-validate on playground or shadow cluster.n2) instrumentation baselinen - add required metrics and trace points.n - run baseline collection for at least 3 steady-state runs (48h recommended for production-like signals).n3) controlled rollout (shadow - canary - ramp)n - start with offline shadowing, then small canary (1 traffic) with strict abort gates, then staged ramps.n4) analysis and signal extractionn - produce an experiment report (templated). include causal attribution, raw traces, and kernel-level timeline.n5) action: revert, iterate, or promoten - if passing gates, schedule full rollout and add config to runtime feature flags.nnsafety slos and abort thresholds (default values):n signal baseline window metric abort threshold (quick abort) notes n------:---:---:n p50 latency (inferred) baseline median 25 detects immediate regressions for short ops n p95 latency baseline p95 15 sensitive to medium tail widening n p99 latency baseline p99 10 critical immediate abort if exceeded repeatedly n error rate (5xx/transport) baseline error rate 100 relative or absolute 0.5 transport / kernel faults n kernel watchdog restarts 0 in baseline window any occurrence immediate abort and system investigation nninstrumentation checklist:n- metrics: per-route p50/p95/p99, token-throughput, queue-depth per scheduler slot, kernel-run-time distributions (ms), kvcache-hit-rate, model-variant-fallback-count.n- tracing: attach request-id, kernel-id, scheduling-decision-id, tenant-id, model-version.n- logs: structured json with kernel signals (fields: timestamp, kernel_phase, gpu_id, free_mem_mb, queue_len).n- sampling policy: pid-based stratified sampling entropy-aware tail amplification.nnexperiment runbook (step-by-step):n1) fill experiment form (template attached) with hypothesis, owner, safety slos, and rollback plan.n2) create feature-flagged branch for runtime config changes include toggle defaultoff.n3) deploy to dev-lab and run benchmark harness (use: tools/bench/run_local.sh --profileshadow --duration60m).n4) validate telemetry: ensure the new metrics appear in /observability/metric-registry and traces include kernel_id.n5) start offline shadowing for 2448h using replay tool (tools/traffic/replay --targetshadow --corpusprod-corpus-2025).n6) if shadow looks stable, coordinate with runtime oncall to start canary: target 1 traffic for 30 minutes. watch slos.n7) if canary passes, ramp to 5 for 2 hours, then 20 for 6 hours, then 100 with staged rollouts per region.n8) after any rollout step, produce a short update in the experiment thread and update the experiment report.nnexperiment report template (required fields):n- titlen- ownern- hypothesisn- timeline (start/stop times)n- baseline statistics (p50/p95/p99, error rates)n- experiment statistics (same metrics, per-stage)n- traces: 3 representative traces for each failure moden- kernel trace heatmap (attach image)n- root cause analysis / attribution statementn- decision and next steps (promote / iterate / rollback)nnquick cli snippets and examples:n- start local shadow run:n ./tools/traffic/replay --targetshadow --datasetplayground-corpus --duration3600n- collect a kernel timeline for a outside experiment.n3) use quantile-based comparison (not mean) for latency signals.n4) for kernel-level attribution, align request traces by kernel_start timestamp and compute occupancy vs. wait-time correlation matrix.nnfallout and rollback patterns:n- immediate rollback: triggered by kernel watchdog restarts, large p99 increases, or 0.5 absolute error increase. runtime oncall will flip feature flag and open an incident if needed.n- graceful rollback: if subtle regressions appear, pause ramp and revert config changes from the feature-flagged branch, then follow up with a targeted fix and re-proposal.nnpostmortem and knowledge capture:n- for any abort or noticeable impact, the experiment owner must open an experiment-pm doc within 72 hours summarizing what happened and the reproduction steps.n- attach kernel traces, metrics dashboards, and the final experiment report.nnsafety guard examples (preset safe profiles):n- safe-lite: suitable for dev-lab and internal load tests. slos relaxed, fast rollback.n- safe-canary: default for canary on hosted clusters enforce p99 abort and error rate gates.n- safe-strict: used before dedicated rollout requires 7d baseline and extended handbook: from incident forensics to capacity slo remediation, content: summarynthis handbook defines a prescriptive, auditable pipeline for converting incident evidence and post-incident findings into concrete slo, error-budget, capacity, and tooling actions. the goal is to shorten the time from discovery - evidence - decision - remediation while preserving blamelessness and traceability.nnaudiencen- sre oncall and rotation leadsn- service owners and service reliability stewardsn- product managers responsible for tiered slasn- capacity and forecasting teamsnnwhy this existsn- we frequently collect high-quality forensic evidence in incident reviews but lack a standardized path that guarantees remediation (capacity, slos, tooling changes) is implemented and validated.n- this doc codifies who decides, how we prioritize, how we measure remediation success, and how evidence is stored and linked.nnkey principlesn- evidence-first: every action must be linked to evidence items (logs, replays, synthetic canaries, graphs, sample tokens).n- minimal viable remediation: prefer fast, reversible mitigations (traffic shaping, temporary headroom) while planning permanent fixes.n- ownership and deadlines: each remediation item has an owner, eta, verification steps, and a quality gate.n- playbookable: run the same steps for incidents of similar class (latency spike, oom cascade, model regression, capacity saturation).nnhigh-level pipeline (4 stages)n1) capture (during incident)n - assign an evidence recorder (oncall sre) to collect: dashboards snapshot, p50/p95/p99 latency slices, error counts by tenant, representative request/response pairs, kernel/oom logs, kubernetes pod events, heap/gc traces, kv cache usage, model cache hit/miss rates.n - use the incident evidence collector script: n curl -ss -h authorization: bearer evid_token evidence_bundle.jsonn2) triage (post-incident 0-72 hours)n - run an evidence triage meeting within 72 hours source_type: confluence, title: kernel hint propagation profiling pipeline, content: summary:nnthis document specifies the kernel hint propagation profiling pipeline (khppp) an end-to-end process used by the serving runtime team to capture, synthesize, and propagate lightweight kernel hints from production traces to the kernel selection and scheduler subsystems. the pipeline is optimized for low-overhead sampling, deterministic replay for hypothesis testing, and safe automated rollout of hint-driven kernel recommendations to the runtime.nngoals:n- reduce unexpected kernel regressions by surfacing causal correlations between request shape and kernel latency.n- provide repeatable profiling artifacts usable by scheduler and kernel teams for autotune jobs.n- automate a canary rollout path for kernel hint changes with observable safety gates.nnscope and non-goals:n- scope: inference request-level sampling - trace enrichment - hint extraction - validation replay - recommendation artifact - canary rollout.n- non-goals: full-model-level retraining or kernel code changes (those are handled by kernel engineering rfcs).nnowner and runbook contact:n- primary owner: eng-serving-runtime / kernel signals team (oncall: @kernel-signals).n- secondary: eng-platform / scheduler (oncall: @scheduler-op).n- on-call escalation ladder: pager - lead kernel engineer - runtime sre.nnarchitecture overview:n1) in-proxy lightweight sampler (service: trace-sampler): attaches to request ingress and emits a sampled event with the following fields: request_id, model_id, route, token_len, prefix_hash, routing_decision, upstream_kernel_hint (if present). sampling rate is configurable per-service (default 0.1).nn2) enrichment correlation (service: hint-enricher): enriches sampled events with kernel telemetry pulled from kernel-telemetry-store (per-gpu kernel latency percentiles, occupancy, kernel version). correlation computes the candidate hint map for (model_id, sequence_bucket, route).nn3) hint extractor (service: hint-extractor): runs a lightweight causal check (granger-inspired) to output a candidate hint: hint_id, model_family, sequence_bucket, suggested_kernel_profile, confidence_score, sample_count, top_covariates. output written to artifact-store as a jsonl stream with ttl 90 days.nn4) replay validation (service: hint-replay): replays a bounded subset of the original sampled traces in the internal replay lab (sandbox runtime) to validate latency delta, regression rate, and resource delta. replay uses the same scheduler and kernel loader versions as production canary.nn5) recommendation and canary (service: hint-orchestrator): packages validated hints into a signed recommendation manifest and drives a staged canary rollout through the runtime configuration service (route-level config).nnslos and thresholds (applies to the pipeline):n- end-to-end artifact availability: 99 within 15 minutes of sample capture.n- false-positive detection: target false-positive rate for deployed hints 3 or absolute 40ms must auto-abort.n- resource delta: kernel profile must not increase gpu memory usage by 6 without manual signoff.nnsampling configuration table (example):nn service default-sampling max-sampling notes n---------------------------:-------------:-------n public-api 0.1 1 route override by sla tier n internal-batch 0.05 0.5 high-throughput, low-latency sensitivity n dedicated-gpu 0.2 2 more signal for deterministic workloads nndata retention and pii notes:n- sampled traces omit prompt payloads by default. the pipeline stores prompt hashes and token counts only. full payload capture is gated behind an explicit customer opt-in and legal review.nntrace enrichment schema (sample line):nnn traces per candidate hint (or all if sample_count 4 and resource delta 0.75.n- tentative if: p99 improves 14 and resource delta schedule extended evaluation (72h).n- reject if: p99 regresses 0 or error_rate increases 0.1 or resource delta 10.nncanary rollout procedure (operational checklist):n1) create signed manifest via hint-orchestrator, include: hint_id, target_routes, advisory_notes, rollback_conditions.n2) deploy to 1 of traffic in canary region (region: us-west2 by default).n3) monitor canary dashboard for 30 minutes baseline, then 6-hour extended observation window.n4) protocolnnoverviewnthis document defines the lab protocol, tooling, and interpretation guide for interactive kernel latency surface mapping a repeatable experiment to discover how scheduler decisions, kernel selection, and request shapes interact to produce the observed latency surface across our gpu fleet. the goal is to produce a compact, actionable artifact (the latency surface) for: triage, kernel hinting, scheduler tuning, and ci gating for kernel rollouts.nnwhy we need this playbookn- compliments static microbenchmarks by exposing cross-layer effects (scheduling, batching, kv cache warmup, and transport).n- produces a 2d/3d surface (example axes: concurrency x sequence length x kernel variant) that helps quantify non-linear tail behavior.n- provides reproducible artifacts to attach to incident reviews and perf regression prs.nnscope and assumptionsn- scope: production-like runtime and staging clusters only. not intended for developer sandbox machines.n- assumes trace-captured workload shapes (sequence length distribution, token rate, concurrency histogram).n- requires telemetry stack: tracing enabled, kernel-hint annotations (k_hint), scheduler decisions logged, and kv cache hit-rate metrics.nnownership and contactsn- primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/perf (on-call: michael chen)n- kernel scheduling lead: lena ortizn- sre contact for fleet experiments: tomás riveranndefinitionsn- latency surface: a vectorized map of p50/p90/p99 generation latency over discretized axes (concurrency, sequence length, kernel variant, model shard count).n- kernel variant: a named execution path (e.g., fast-attn-v2-fp16, sharded-kv-quant-8b).nnhigh-level experiment stepsn1) select workload corpusn - use recent 7-day trace that matches the target customer profile. export as request-surface.json following the format in appendix a.n2) provision experiment clustern - create an isolated staging fleet subset (min size 8 gpus, matching target hardware generation). ensure same networking path as prod (vpc peering).n3) apply instrumentation and deterministic seedn - enable full tracing (trace-leveldebug), kernel hinting annotations, and set kvcache-deterministictrue for warmup runs.n4) define axis gridn - concurrency: 1, 4, 8, 16, 32n - sequence length: 8, 32, 128, 512n - kernel variants: select 34 candidates under testn - for heterogeneous pools, include shard counts 1, 2, 4n5) run warmup phase (10 minutes per grid point)n6) execute measurement phase (310 minutes per grid point depending on noise)n7) aggregate and synthesize the latency surfacen8) produce findings and suggested action items (kernel hints, scheduler policy changes, rollout gates)nndetailed commands and examplesn- provisioning (example using infra-tool):n infra-tool create-experiment --name latency-surface-2027-11 --region us-west2 --gpus 8 --image runtime-experiment:v2027.03nn- trace replay command (local runner):n trace-runner --input request-surface.json --concurrency 8 --sequence-length 128 --interval 0.01 --target --annotations k_hintonnn- kernel probe invocation (on-node):n sudo /opt/runtime/bin/kernel-probe --pid runtime_pid --duration 120 --out /tmp/kprobe.jsonnn- telemetry collection snippets (yaml):n telemetry_capture: n capture: truen metrics: latency_ms.p50,latency_ms.p90,latency_ms.p99,kvcache.hit_rate,kernel.exec_nsn trace: truennmeasurement considerations and guardrailsn- warmup is mandatory: discard first 120s of samples per grid point to avoid startup noise.n- target request-rate should be bounded to avoid saturation outside interest range. use rate limiter parameter to shape inputs.n- if node-level cpu steals or ooms are observed, mark grid point as invalid and rerun after fixing interference.n- use p99 over sliding window of 60s as primary tail metric.nndata model and artifact formatn- latency surface artifact is a newline-delimited json (ndjson) file where each record has flat fields only:n - timestamp, axis_concurrency, axis_sequence_length, kernel_variant, p50_ms, p90_ms, p99_ms, sample_count, kvcache_hit_rate, scheduler_decisionn- attach raw traces (zip) and kernel-probe outputs to the artifact bundle for deep dive.nninterpreting the surface: quick heuristicsn- sharp upward slope in p99 when going from concurrency 8 - 16 suggests scheduler admission/backpressure tuning required.n- diverging p90 vs p99 for the same kernel variant indicates tail amplification (likely inter-batch interference).n- if a kernel variant shows better p50 but worse p99 consistently, consider local hedging or slot reservation policies for latency-sensitive tenants.nnrecommended actions matrixn symptom likely cause recommended quick action longer-term remediation owner n---------------n p99 spike at medium concurrency kernel blocking on nvlink or serialization enable per-request kernel timeout / hedge patch kernel to reduce global locks add preemption hints kernel team n p50 improves but p99 worsens inter-batch head-of-line contention add burst isolation for small sequences scheduler crediting by sequence-length class scheduler team n p99 increases with shard count kv cache warmup inefficiency increase prefetch window for multi-shard requests rework kv prefetch algorithm to prioritize hot prefixes runtime team nnci gates and rollout criterian- attach latency-surface artifact and p99 delta plots to every kernel rollout pr.n- mandatory pass criteria for major kernel releases: p99 delta 10 increase.n- for canary: run abbreviated surface (concurrency 1,8,32, sequence lengths 8,128,512) in canary fleet with 48h observation window.nndashboarding and visualizationn- visualize as a 3d surface (concurrency x seq-length x p99) in grafana using the latency-surface ndjson - timeseries transformer. provide a linked panel to sample traces for any selected grid point.n- store artifacts in object-store prefix: s3://redwood-runtime-experiments/latency-surfaces/yyyy/experiment-id/artifact.ndjsonnnknown limitationsn- lab results are sensitive to cross-tenant noise and scheduler tuning annotate experiments with cluster packing details.n- results for highly heterogeneous models (different layer shapes) might not be comparable restrict comparisons to similar model classes.nnreporting template (to attach to prs/incidents)n- experiment id: n- date run: n- cluster: //n- workload corpus id: (link)n- key findings (bulleted)n- action items and ownersn- attached
