content: summaryn-------nthis playbook documents our approach to energy- and power-aware kernel scheduling for the redwood serving runtime, and prescribes a repeatable profiling and benchmarking workflow for validating energy-related optimizations. the goal is to reduce total energy per inference (joules/token) while preserving latency slos and model-quality constraints.nnscopen-----napplies to: the serving runtime (scheduler, kernel mapper, and dispatch layers) and the gpu-hotpath kernel implementations. covers: telemetry, local and cluster-level scheduling policies, profiling methodology, benchmark scenarios, rollout recipes, and incident runbook steps for energy regressions. does not replace thermal/firmware actions performed by cloud providers.nnmotivationn----------n- our customer demand and operational costs require optimizing energy consumption for sustained workloads (e.g., embeddings, high-qps chat).n- naive throughput maximization can increase energy per token due to inefficient kernel choices and poor batching alignment.n- we need a documented, repeatable way to measure energy impact of runtime changes, and safe rollout patterns that respect latency slos.nngoals and success criterian-------------------------n1. reduce median joules/token for production embedding workloads by 15 in targeted fleets without increasing p99 latency by 5.n2. establish an energy-profiling pipeline that provides reproducible per-kernel and per-request energy attribution within 10 measurement error.n3. add automated benchmark scenarios to ci that flag 10 regression in energy-per-token relative to baseline.nndesign overviewn---------------nat a high level we extend the runtime with three cooperating components:nn1) energy estimator (lightweight):n- runs per-device and per-kernel cost models built from microbenchmarks (see benchmark suite section).n- inputs: kernel name, sequence length, batch size, quantization profile, gpu model and power cap.n- output: estimated joules for the predicted execution path.nn2) power-aware scheduler layer (policy hooks):n- policy types: power-capped admission, energy-windowing, and cost-weighted-priority.n- scheduler consults estimator to compute cost delta when selecting kernel variant or slotting across gpus.n- policies can be per-tenant, per-model, or global.nn3) telemetry attribution:n- fine-grained telemetry emitted for each request: kernel sequence, execution time, energy_estimate, actual_energy_reading (when available), and decision_reason.n- telemetry schema additions are in the team wiki (see related pages).nnscheduling policies (examples)n----------------------------n- power-capped admission: refuse or re-route requests when aggregate expected power cluster cap threshold. use for burst isolation on constrained fleets.n- energy-windowing: prefer kernel variants with lower energy for long-running batched requests even at slight latency cost.n- cost-weighted priority: score each candidate placement by (priority_score / estimated_joules) to maximize useful work per joule.nnpolicy configuration tablen-------------------------nkey parameter description typical valuen-----------------------------------------npower_cap_pct percent of device sustained power that scheduler will target 80nenergy_margin allowed increase in jain-style cost to trade energy for latency 1.10nsample_interval_s how often to sample device power sensors for calibration 30nwindow_ms energy-windowing decision horizon 2000nnprofiling methodologyn---------------------nobjective: capture both model-level and kernel-level energy signals with reproducible noise bounds.nn1) environment requirements:n- isolated host or pinned node to avoid cross-tenant noise.n- node-level power telemetry enabled (nvml/amduprof/etc) with sampling frequency 10hz.n- soldered measurement (external pdus) for fleet-level validation when available.nn2) signals to collect:n- per-request: request_id, model, kernel_variant, batch_size, seq_len, start_ts, end_ts, gpu_power_series, gpu_temp_series, inferred_joules_estimate, actual_joules_measurement (if sampling available).n- per-device: sku, firmware version, driver version, cuda/cudnn/cufft versions (if applicable), clock settings, power-limit.nn3) sampling strategy and noise control:n- run each microbenchmark 50 times and report median and 95 ci.n- for end-to-end workload runs, replay production traces with at least 10 minutes sustained windows for steady-state measurement.n- use a/b paired tests across identical hardware to factor out ambient variation.nn4) attribution technique:n- when device-level power is coarse, perform causal attribution by: (a) collect per-kernel execution intervals (b) integrate power trace over intervals (c) normalize by background idle baseline measured in the same experimental window.nnbenchmark suite additionsn------------------------nwe extend the existing perf suite with energy-focused artifacts:n- microbench-energy-generator: microbenchmarks per kernel and per-sequence-length that emit time and power traces.n- steady-state-replay: component that replays production qps traces with controllable slotting and power caps.n- energy-ci-checker: ci task that runs selected profiles and fails on 10 energy regression.nnsample cli commandsn-------------------n run a microbenchmark for a kernel variant and record powern tools/bench/microbench-energy --model gpt-3.5-small --kernel relu-fused --batch 8 --seq 512 --iters 100 --output /tmp/bench.jsonnn run steady-state replay for 10 minutes under 80 power capn tools/bench/steady-replay --trace traces/embeddings_jan.bt --duration 600 --power-cap 80 --out /tmp/replay.jsonnnexpected baseline table occupancy and concurrency audit playbook for serving runtime, content: overview:nnthis playbook describes a repeatable audit process to assess and remediate gpu occupancy and request concurrency issues in the redwood serving runtime. it is intended for on-call engineers, performance engineers, and sres responsible for multi-tenant inference pools and kernel scheduler tuning. the goal is to detect pathological occupancy/concurrency patterns early, quantify their impact on latency/cost, and prescribe targeted mitigations.nnwhy this matters:nn- low gpu occupancy (sm utilization) or poor warp efficiency increases per-token cost and can drastically raise tail latency for short requests.n- excessive concurrency without appropriate kernel crediting can cause kernel contention, eviction churn, and kv-cache thrash.n- multi-tenant pools and dynamic batching increase the surface area for occupancy anomalies automated audits help prevent regressions when we change kernel mappers, quantization profiles, or shard placement rules.nnscope and audience:nn- scope: gpus used by redwood-hosted runtime (heterogeneous pools), dedicated clusters on rdw, and private deployment models where we operate the inference stack.n- audience: runtime performance team, serving runtime owners, sre, release engineers.nnkey concepts and metrics (short primer):nn- sm occupancy: fraction of streaming multiprocessor compute capacity active. monitored with nvidia-smi dmon/ dcgm metric: gpu_sm_active and nvprof metrics like sm_efficiency.n- warp efficiency: fraction of executed threads performing useful work (warp_execution_efficiency).n- gpu active time / kernel time: total kernel execution time versus idle/wait time.n- cuda stream utilization: concurrency of cuda streams per process (useful for kernel overlap).n- kernel queue length: number of enqueued kernels waiting execution per gpu.n- token-per-second per-gpu and per-request token latency: application-visible metrics correlated with kernel metrics.nnacceptance thresholds (operational guidance):nn- avg sm occupancy: target 3080 depending on model size. small models (45 with batching large models (70b) may be 2040 due to register pressure.n- warp efficiency: target 70 investigate below 60.n- kernel queue length (p95): 16, treat as congestion.n- kernel preemption events: zero preferred any spike should be investigated.nnaudit cadence and triggers:nn- scheduled audit: weekly automated run across production pools.n- release-triggered audit: run after kernel mapper, quantization, or scheduler changes.n- incident-triggered audit: triggered by sustained slo degradation (p95 latency increase 20 or error spike).nnautomated data collection (what to gather):nn1) dcgm / prometheus exporter snapshots for each gpu: sm_efficiency, sm_active, gpu_util, mem_used, sm_clock, power.n2) kernel-level traces (perfetto / cupti) sampled for 60s across representative nodes.n3) per-request runtime traces (trace-id keyed) including batch size, sequence length, model variant, and scheduling priority.n4) kernel queue metrics and kernel metadata (kernel name, duration, per-kernel average latency).n5) kv-cache hit/miss rates and warmup time per request shard.n6) system-level metrics: numa statistics, pcie throughput, nvlink/ nvlink errors.nnhow to run an audit (step-by-step):nn1. kick off collection:n - run the automated collector job (prod-audit-collector) for the target pool. cli: nn bashn ./tools/profiler/run-audit --pool gpu-pool-2 --duration 60s --out /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.jsonn nn - ensure collector captures dcgm metrics at 250ms granularity and samples 1 cupti trace per physical gpu.nn2. baseline correlation (automated):n - run the baseline comparator tool to correlate p95 latency and per-gpu sm_efficiency. example: nn bashn ./tools/perf/compare-baseline --current /tmp/audit-gpu-pool-2.json --baseline s3://perf-baselines/gpu-pool-2/2026-01-01.jsonn nn - output: csv with columns (metric, current_p50, current_p95, baseline_p95, relative_change).nn3. high-level triage (manual):n - open the generated dashboard link from the collector output. inspect: sm occupancy heatmap, kernel queue length timeseries, per-model aggregated warp efficiency.n - if p95 latency correlates with occupancy drop (sm_efficiency falls while kernel queue increases), flag as kernel contention.nn4. deep dive: kernel-level analysis:n - identify top 5 kernels by total time in the trace. use the kernel map to attribute kernels to model layers (attention, mlp, softmax).n - for each kernel, inspect duration distribution, occupancy-dependent latency (plot duration vs active warps).n - look for kernels with large variance or heavy tail (p99 4x median). those are primary candidates for micro-optimization or fallback tuning.nn5. concurrency accounting check:n - verify kernel-credit accounting logs to ensure per-request credit consumption matches runtime expectations. query: nn promqln sum by (pool) (increase(kernel_credit_consumed_total5m))n nn - if observed concurrency configured_max_concurrency by 20, investigate admission control or credit leak bugs.nn6. kv-cache correlation:n - join per-request latency with kv-cache hit rate. a simultaneous drop in hit-rate and sm occupancy often indicates aggressive eviction policies during high concurrency.nn7. numa/pcie check:n - if occupancy low but gpu util high and kernel times are fragmented, inspect numa binding and transfer stalls. use numactl --hardware and perf record to validate.nnautomated remediation recommendations (ordered):nn1) apply immediate throttling: reduce admission concurrency for the affected model/pool by 20 (fast rollback).n2) switch to a compatible lower-parallel kernel variant (runtime supports alternative kernel variants labeled fast-path, conservative).n3) increase batching window for short-sequence workloads for 30s to evaluate impact.n4) adjust kernel mapper hints to prefer fewer concurrent small kernels on the same gpu (see kernel mapper tuning snippet below).nnkernel mapper tuning example (config snippet):nn- purpose: prefer sequential execution for kernels with low occupancy and high variancen- config keys (yaml):nn kernel_mapper:n prioritize_small_kernel_serialization: truen small_kernel_threshold_ms: 1.5n concurrency_grouping_window_ms: 12n p95(request_latency) with 1 - avg(sm_efficiency) (both normalized) to surface inverse relationships.nnincident play examples (short):nn- symptom: sudden p95 spike for short-text generation where edge-case-kernel-flake-hunting-and-bisect-playbook, content: overview:nnthis playbook documents a pragmatic, reproducible process for identifying, diagnosing, and safely remediating intermittent (flake) regressions originating in the serving runtime kernel or scheduler layers. it emphasizes low-risk bisecting, deterministic trace capture, and guarded rollouts with automated rollback hooks. this is intended for runtime oncall, kernel engineers, and performance sres.nnwhy this is necessary:n- flaky kernel behavior (slow kernels that sometimes spike, rare preemption races, transient memory corruption, or sporadic nvlink stalls) is one of the highest-impact sources of nondeterministic tail latency and customer-facing errors.n- these issues are often subtle and require a structured approach: isolate scope, reproduce at scale, collect causal telemetry, and perform a controlled binary/config bisect.nnscope and ownership:n- applies to: kernel modules, kernel-level scheduler correlated spikes in kernel-duration, kernel-restarts, and gpu-queue-depth metrics.n2) apply quick filters to rule out environmental noise:n - node-level thermal throttling (node.thermal.throttle 0).n - cloud spot eviction or host reboots in the same time window.n3) if signal persists, declare a flake investigation and assign a lead.nnreproduction checklist (ordered):n1) narrow to a small reproducible workload. prefer a request-corpus of 10100 requests that historically triggered spikes.n2) create a dedicated test cohort on a shadow fleet segment with identical runtime flags.n3) use baseline.nnsteps:n1) create a minimal experiment matrix with these axes: kernel binary (n revisions), scheduler config (35 knob permutations), quantization/precision path (fp16/int8/quantized fallback).n2) start with binary-only bisect: if recent kernel commits exist in the window, perform a binary bisection across commits using the harness.n - use git-bisect-style automation integrated per iteration (batch slicing, preemption-window-ms, async-handoff-enable).n4) for nondeterministic outcomes, apply statistical stopping rules: stop when 95 confidence that candidate is different from baseline (binomial test with alpha0.05).nntelemetry to collect for each candidate run (minimum):n- kernel.duration_ms (p50/p95/p99)n- kernel.context-switches (per-shard)n- kernel.preempt-mismatch-countn- gpu.dispatch-latency_msn- kvcache.hit-raten- node.thermal.throttlen- process.core-dumps (if present)nntrace artifact cataloging (naming and meta):n- use standardized for prognosing potential runtime failures and running targeted, controlled failureinjection experiments against the serving runtime. it combines profiling and benchmark signals, scheduler/kernels heuristics, and a strict safety checklist to reduce operator risk and improve our ability to catch regressions before customer impact.nngoalsnn- validate that new kernels, scheduling changes, or quantization patches do not introduce cascading failure modes.n- surface latent failure signatures using lowblast synthetic probes rather than largescale chaos.n- produce deterministic, debuggable traffic may be shadowed to target without affecting live responses.n - blast radius limit: no more than 5 of total capacity in a controlled canary cluster (default).n - autoabort slo thresholds: 99th percentile increase 2x baseline or error rate delta 0.5 triggers immediate abort.n - observability guards: tracing, kernel telemetry, kvcache epoch counters, perslot memory, scheduler credit logs, and gpu thermal metrics must be active.nnexperiment design checklistnn1. hypothesis: one sentence describing expected outcome and failure signal (e.g., a race in eviction will increase kv cache miss rate and cause tail latency spikes in slot 3).n2. data prerequisites: baseline profiling snapshot and synthetic replay corpus representing target workload.n3. safety gates: identify abort thresholds and responsible oncall.n4. trace anchors: list of trace ids/tags to capture (e.g., experiment_id, slot_id, kernel_variant).n5. artifact plan: roll forward plan (how to collect traces and artifacts) and rollback plan (revert flag, restart plan).nnconcrete injection primitives and examplesnn- controlled kernel delay: inject a deterministic 550ms kernel execution delay for a specific kernel_id on a single test shard.n- kv cache miss flood: artificially invalidate prefix cache for a cohort to simulate warmstart pressure.n- scheduler token drain: reduce admission tokens by x for a tenant cohort to simulate quota starvation.n- synthetic memory pressure: allocate transient pinned memory on cuda for a test container to emulate fragmentation.nnexample: kernel delay injection (cli)nnbashn create title: adaptive load-aware tracing playbook, content: summary:na pragmatic playbook for diagnosing latency and fidelity regressions using adaptive, load-aware tracing across the serving runtime. covers when to enable high-fidelity traces, how to combine kernel scheduling signals with request-level traces, benchmark validation patterns, and safe remediation steps for production rollouts.nncontent:npurpose and scope:nnthis playbook prescribes an adaptive, load-aware approach to tracing and profiling the serving runtime when investigating latency regressions, kernel scheduling anomalies, or workload-driven performance variance. it explains how to converge signals from: runtime spans, per-request kernel hints, gpu kernel/stream telemetry, and synthetic benchmark cohorts to identify root causes and validate fixes.nnkey principles:n- start broad, then increase fidelity: use sampling shadow channels to limit overhead, escalate to full-flame traces only when necessary.n- correlate across layers: always tie kernel telemetry to request ids and shard placement to avoid false attributions.n- be load-aware: certain regressions only surface at specific concurrency shapes or sequence-length distributions. reproduce using shaped synthetic traffic.n- safe-by-default: tracing safeguards (rate limits, timeboxed captures) must be used for production captures.nnwhen to use this playbook:n1) sustained shift in p95/p99 latency that cannot be explained by infra changes in the last 24 hours.n2) intermittent tail spikes that correlate with specific model variants or tenant groups.n3) new kernel rollout or scheduler change where we see unexplained cost increases.n4) regression alerts from rl-based batching/autotune showing degradation in unit economics or quality.nnprerequisites and quick checks:n- confirm slo and the exact metric(s) impacted with product owner.n- gather recent release-notes and kernel rollouts in the last 72 hours.n- ensure tracing-collector has at least 5gb/day spare ingestion budget for escalation captures.n- recreate baseline by running the canonical microbenchmark for the implicated model variant (see benchmark section).nninstrumentation checklist (pre-capture):n- ensure request ids are propagated through all layers (client - gateway - dispatcher - kernel). check header x-req-id presence.n- tag spans with model_variant, kernel_profile_hint, tenant_id, and shard_id.n- verify gpu kernel telemetry (latency, occupancy, sm utilization, memory ops) is enabled on candidate nodes.n- ensure kvcache prefetch logs and eviction metrics are being emitted for warmup windows.n- confirm sampling rules exist: 0.5 baseline, 5 on degraded routes, 100 for targeted tenant during a 10-minute window if authorized.nnstep-by-step investigation (ordered):n1) high-level triage (515 minutes)n 1.1 pull timeline: overlay p50/p95/p99, qps, error rate, and recent deploys.n 1.2 identify affected routes: run runtime-sre., doc_id: dsid_332ff13df79f4e6ea24d0a38534dec68, source_type: confluence, title: shadow-channel experimentation framework and telemetry contract, content: summarynnthis document defines redwoods shadow-channel experimentation framework (sef) and the accompanying telemetry contract used to run non-invasive experiments across the serving runtime. sef lets engineers validate scheduler and kernel changes, batching strategies, and caching heuristics by mirroring live requests into an isolated execution path (the shadow channel) without affecting production responses.nngoalsn- enable high-confidence performance and correctness experiments using live traffic.n- standardize telemetry so experiment results are comparable across kernels, schedulers, and topologies.n- provide an operator-safe runbook for starting, observing, and rolling back experiments.nnnon-goalsn- sef is not a canary rollout mechanism for user-facing traffic (use the rollout service for canaries).n- sef does not modify customer-facing outputs quality validation must use offline evals or compare-only decoders.nnwhen to use sefn1. kernel-level performance patches that require realistic traffic shaping.n2. scheduler policy changes impacting admission, preemption, or slot assignment.n3. kv cache prefetch/hint algorithms where hit/miss patterns are critical.n4. new batching heuristics or continuous-batching changes.nnarchitecture overviewnnsef has three main logical components: mirror, shadow executor, and aggregation/verifier.n- mirror (mirror-proxy): intercepts an incoming request and clones a deterministic copy of the request context and tokens. mirrors run in the request ingress plane and annotate requests with a correlation_id.n- shadow executor (shadow-exec): a sandboxed runtime instance (container-level isolation) that consumes mirrored traffic. shadow-exec may load alternative kernels, scheduler flags, or quantization profiles. it returns telemetry only outputs are discarded or stored in a private experiment index.n- aggregation/verifier (exp-agg): aggregates shadow telemetry, computes experiment metrics (latency delta, kernel time, queue time, kvcache hit breakdown, token throughput), and performs quality checks. exp-agg produces a report stored in the experiments index and notifies slack/confluence hooks.nnkey propertiesn- non-intrusive: shadow paths must not alter production responses or resource quotas used for live serving.n- budgeted: experiments must be assigned a budget (tokens/sec or of cluster capacity). if the shadow budget is exceeded, the mirror-proxy drops mirrored traffic for that experiment.n- deterministic correlation: all mirrored requests share a correlation_id prefix to link production and shadow telemetry.nntelemetry contract (required fields)nevery shadow-exec must emit the following fields for each mirrored request (json lines to exp-agg):n- correlation_id: string (prefix links to production request)n- experiment_id: stringn- timestamp_utc: iso8601 stringn- stage_durations_ms: list (ingress, queue, kernel_dispatch, kernel_exec, decoder, kvcache_lookup) encoded as csv of numbersn- kernel_signature: string (kernel name variant commit)n- scheduler_profile: string (policy name profile hash)n- kvcache_stats: csv (hits, misses, prefetches, eviction_count)n- cpu_usec: integern- gpu_usec: integern- memory_bytes: integern- status: ok exec_error resource_throttled timed_outn- sampled_trace_id: optional string (links to full trace in tracing system)nnmetric definitions (computed by exp-agg)n- shadow_p95_latency_ms: 95th percentile of end-to-end shadow latencyn- delta_p95_ms: shadow_p95 - prod_p95 (linked by correlation_id)n- kernel_time_ratio: kernel_exec / end_to_endn- kv_hit_rate: hits / (hits misses)n- resource_overhead_percent: (gpu_usec cpu_usec equivalent) / prod_resource_usagennslo and safety thresholds for experimentsn- max allowed delta_p95_ms: 5ms for latency-sensitive tiers, 20ms for best-effort experiments. exceeding triggers automatic suspension.n- max resource overhead percent: 25 (across aggregate traffic).n- error budget for exec_error: 0.2 of mirrored requests per hour.nnexperiment lifecycle (operator steps)n1. create experiment metadata in experiments-service with experiment_id, owner, target clusters, budget (tokens/sec or ), and risk classification (low/medium/high).n2. push experiment config to mirror-proxy: rdinfer-mirrorctl create --id --budget 50rps --target shadow-cluster:shadow-v2 --policy sample:1/1000n3. validate mirror can deliver minimal load by enabling a 0.1 sample on a low-traffic route.n4. start shadow-exec job: k8s apply -f shadow-exec-.yaml. shadow-exec must run with nodeselectorisolated-exec and resource limits set to toolkit, operational patterns, and safe procedures used by runtime engineers to perform rapid sleuthing (hypothesis-driven triage) and non-disruptive probing of the serving runtime in production and pre-production environments. the guidance balances signal fidelity with cost and safety constraints and provides concrete probe recipes, a sampling governor configuration, escalation paths, and ownership.nnsummary / intentn- goal: reduce mean-time-to-detect and mean-time-to-resolve for latency, fidelity, and kernel-related regressions while containing overhead to a safe telemetry budget.n- ops-first playbook for production-safe investigation.nnsignal taxonomy (quick reference)n1) traces: end-to-end request streams with kernel handoffs annotated. use for causal chain reconstruction and tail-latency attribution.n2) microprobes: high-frequency short-duration kernel timings (gpu dispatch, memcpy, kernel enqueue latency). use for kernel regressions and scheduler jitter.n3) counters gauges: queue lengths, admission tokens, kv-cache hit rates, busy gpu percent, slot credits. use for capacity and trend analysis.n4) synthetic samples: replayed request surface (shadow) to reproduce behavior without impacting live traffic.nnsleuthing checklist (initial 10-minute triage)n1. confirm symptom and scope: aggregate error/latency dashboards, which tenants/routes affected, and start time.n2. correlate with deployments and config changes (canary rollouts, kernel changes, model swaps) using the deployment timeline.n3. check kernel and scheduler health streams: kernel-failure-rate, kernel-queueing-latency, enqueue-to-start gap.n4. validate resource thermal indicators: gpu utilization, power capping events, pcie/nvlink errors.n5. if the above are inconclusive, enable targeted microprobes (see probe recipes).nnsafe probing principlesn- principle 1: budget first. probes must respect the tracing budget (default 0.05 of total request cpu and 10 or error rates double in the probed cohort, automatically disable the probing flag.nnprobe recipes (practical, copy-paste)n1) microprobe: kernel enqueue-to-start distribution - purpose: detect scheduling stalls and handoff jitter - target: one node in the affected pod group or a dedicated canary - steps:n 1. create feature flag microprobe.enq_start with cohort 0.5.n 2. configure runtime to emit microprobe events with 200ns timestamp resolution for each kernel enqueue and dispatch.n 3. sampling: 1-in-n request sampling with n 250 by default (adjust down to 50 for an active canary).n 4. collect for 30 minutes and generate a heatmap of enqueue-start latency by kernel type.n 5. if enqueue-start p99 3x baseline, escalate and increase sampling to 1-in-25 for one node for 10 minutes.nn2) trace enrichment: correlated trace kv-cache delta - purpose: connect cache warmup/fidelity issues to end-to-end latency - steps:n 1. enable trace-enrichment flag for the affected route.n 2. for sampled traces, attach kv-cache hit/miss sequence and cache size at request start.n 3. use the trace-joiner job to merge microprobe events with trace spans post-collection.n 4. run the synthesized trace analysis to find patterns where cache miss bursts precede tail latency.nn3) shadow replay burst: safe synthetic stress - purpose: reproduce a peaky failure surface without saturating live capacity - steps:n 1. mirror 0.5 of production traffic to a shadow cluster with strict admission caps (20 of node cpu/gpu used by shadow).n 2. run the same request ordering but pause prefixes at the scheduler to test pre-emption and kernel churn.n 3. capture both runtime-level telemetry and kernel microprobes.nnsampling governor and config (copy into config manifest)n key default unit meaning safe bounds n sampling.global_rate 0.0005 fraction fraction of total requests traced 1e-6 .. 0.01 n sampling.microprobe_strategy periodic string selection approach: periodic periodicadaptivefingerprint n sampling.max_additional_cpu_pct 0.05 fraction extra cpu budget for probes 0.0 .. 0.1 n sampling.node_quota 100 items/s per-node microprobe quota 10 .. 1000 nnexample yaml snippetnnsampling:n global_rate: 0.0005 0.05 of requestsn microprobe_strategy: adaptiven max_additional_cpu_pct: 0.05n node_quota: 100nntelemetry retention cost controlsn- keep high-resolution microprobe traces for 7 days by default. aggregate rollups (histograms, heatmaps) are preserved for 90 days.n- if monthly trace ingestion exceeds 120 of budget, automatic downsampling triggers: reduce global_rate by 2x and notify owners.nninvestigation kernel-change list.n3. execute targeted probes: enable microprobe.enq_start at cohort 0.5 and trace-enrich for the route.n4. collect: wait 3060 minutes or until 510k sampled events.n5. analyze: run routes - p0 incident page and cross-team warroom.n - reproducible regression localized to kernel variant - open kernel team ticket and link telemetry snapshots.nnoperational safety automations (what pragmatic, operationally focused observability sla for the serving runtime kernel layer and specifies a profiling cadence and playbook for keeping kernel regressions visible and remediable. the goal is to ensure kernel-level performance signals (latency, dispatch/backpressure, memory pressure, and kernel success rates) are actionable by oncall and engineering, tied to benchmarking experiments, and budgeted within profiling cost constraints.nnwhy this mattersnn- kernel regressions are the root cause of the majority of hard-to-diagnose tail-latency incidents.n- observability at the kernel boundary is expensive we need a cost-aware sampling strategy and a clear schedule so telemetry budgets are predictable.n- tying profiling to the benchmarking suite and release gates reduces the chance of regressing a deployment unnoticed.nnscopennthis document covers the manifest, slos, sampling tracing cadence, profiling runbook, integration points with the benchmarking suite and release process, and known limitations. it applies to:nn- the inference runtime kernel components (dispatcher, scheduler, kernel executor, kv cache interface).n- host-level telemetry produced by kernel shim and gpu-side counters that we ingest via the kernel agent.nnkey definitionsnn- kernel sample: a single end-to-end kernel execution record (dispatch - kernel launch - completion) including timestamps, kernel variant id, request classification, memory footprint, and outcome code.n- observability sla: the target for alertable metrics derived from kernel samples (e.g., kernel_p99_duration, kernel_error_rate).n- profiling window: an intentional time-bounded full-capture session used for deep analysis (trace-level).nnobservability sla (metrics and thresholds)nntable: metric alert threshold target (slo) runbook severityn- kernel_p95_execution_ms 80ms sustained 5m slo: p95 200ms sustained 5m slo: p99 0.5 over 10m slo: 200 for 1m slo: median 1/min slo: 30 minutes due to cost.nnprofiling playbook (step-by-step)nnpreconditions: you are oncall or the owner of a flagged release. have access to the profiling orchestration tool (profilingctl) and the benchmark runner.nn1) validate the alert: confirm prometheus/grafana alert and cross-check with product-level slos.n2) correlate: use the request-tagged rollups to identify cohorts (model variant, seq_length_bucket, priority_class).n3) if tail signals are present, promote a profiling window targeting the affected shard(s) for 15 minutes (profilingctl start-window --shard --duration 15m --cohort ).n4) collect kernel samples and gpu-side counters. verify the sample set exceeds the minimum capture size ( 200 kernel samples for statistical validity).n5) run the local analysis pipeline (profile-analyze) to generate: hotspot table, costly-kernel-variants, and cross-correlation with dispatcher queue depth.nn- hotspot table: top 10 kernel variants by p99 increase vs baseline.n- costly-kernel-variants: kernel ids with a 2x increase in per-invocation gpu time.nn6) triage: if a single kernel variant explains 40 of the p99 shift, open an rfc and page the kernel owner. if no single variant emerges, escalate to sysinfra and kernel scheduling owners to look for admission/queueing interactions.nn7) mitigation options (short-term):n - rollback kernel patch orn - switch offending cohort to a fallback model variant orn - temporarily increase admission control for the priority class to shed non-critical traffic.nn8) postmortem: capture the artifact id of the profiling capture and link it to the incident ticket. run a follow-up benchmark against the microbench suite to validate proposed fixes.nnintegration with benchmarking suitenn- the profiling orchestration integrates with the benchmarking suite via a shared experiment manifest. each profiling window can be replayed against the benchmark harness to produce a reproducible microbench against the exact kernel variants observed.n- benchmark experiments to run after a profiling session:n - sequence-length-scaling scenario at 4 concurrency pointsn - kv-cache-warmup profile to emulate long-session trafficn - scheduler-priority-noise injection to validate admission controlsnnrelease gating and automationnn- any release that touches: kernel code, scheduler, admission controller, or the dispatcher must include a profiling gate. the ci pipeline will schedule a canary profiling window automatically and fail the gate if:n - kernel_p99_execution_ms increases by 10 vs canary baseline orn - kernel_error_rate increases by 0.05 percentage points.nnrunbooks (high level)nn- sev1: (p99 spike or error rate)n 1) page runtime-oncall and kernel-owner.n 2) run profiling window (15m) targeted at canary shard(s).n 3) if profiling confirms a single kernel variant: apply emergency rollback and re-run profiling.n 4) if not, invoke admission-control escalation to shed traffic and restore slos.nn- sev2: (p95 or queue depth)n 1) perform correlation and schedule a 15m profiling window.n 2) tune admission control thresholds for the affected priority class.n 3) schedule a follow-up benchmark to validate tuning.nnknown limitations and gotchasnn- sampling bias: deterministic sampling of top cohorts improves reproducibility but can miss rare degradations in low-volume tenants. use on-demand deep captures for those.n- gpu counters missing on legacy accelerator drivers: in those cases we fallback to host-side timing and increase sampling rate for statistical confidence.n- profiling cost: full-trace windows are expensive long captures require leadership sign-off. abuse of on-demand windows has previously consumed 30 of monthly profiling budget we now require ticketing and attach artifact ids.nnoperational changes, or cost optimizations (batching, quantization, caching). the goal is repeatable, low-noise profiling that produces actionable signal for rollouts and release gates.nnscope and level):n1) most requests emit lightweight sketches (per-minute histograms of request latency, queue wait, kernel execution) tagged by model_variant and route.n2) a small fraction of requests produce full traces with per-kernel timings and gpu occupancy snapshots.n3) attribution uses samples to estimate distribution of per-kernel latencies within each sketch bucket using importance weighting.nnattribution algorithm (procedural):n1) select window: choose the incident window (t0..t1) and the route/model to analyze.n2) compute sketch deltas: obtain histogram of request latency and queue wait from sketches for the window.n3) retrieve sampled traces: pull all sampled traces matching the same route/model and time window.n4) for each sampled trace, compute kernel fractions: f_k kernel_k_time / total_gpu_time.n5) use importance weights w (count_histogram_bin / sample_count_bin) adjustment_factor to scale sample fractions to the full histogram bins.n6) estimate per-kernel latency contribution per bin: est_k_bin f_k median_latency_bin w.n7) aggregate across bins to produce: total_est_k, percent_contrib_k, and confidence intervals (bootstrap samples on the traces).nnexample: if 95th requests have median latency 420ms and sampled traces show 60 time in attention kernels and 30 in kv cache sync, attribution reports attention approximately 252ms (60), kv sync approximately 126ms (30), remainder in queueing and overhead.nnpractical investigation playbook (step-by-step):n1) identify the symptom: route x, 95th latency 2x slo, time window 13:02-13:22 utc.n2) pull three artifacts: sketches (1s resolution), sampled traces (all), node-level gpu metrics (occupancy, mem_bw).n3) run attribution algorithm to produce per-kernel contributions and confidence bands.n4) if attention kernels are dominant: run quick kernel heatmap query and check recent kernel parameter changes or new model variants rolled out in that window.n5) if queue/warmup dominates: inspect autoscaling and pre-warm logs check request arrival patterns and burst rates.n6) if kv cache sync shows up: correlate with cache miss rate and backend store latency.n7) generate an incident hypothesis and log in the incident tracker, attaching top three contributing factors and suggested mitigations.nnautomatable checks and quick queries (examples):n- promql: 5m rate of requests incident ticket with event ids of representative traces.nnquick mitigations (common):n- increase per-route concurrency cap by 20 for 2 min via routing console (when admission controller is too restrictive).n- temporarily pin route to a lower-fidelity model-variant to avoid kernel stalls.n- evict cold kvcache on a small percentage of nodes to re-balance warm cache.n- throttle low-priority background workloads on nodes reporting thermal or memory pressure.nnexample kql/sql queries (schematic):n1) minute rollup for route: select ts_minute, shard_id, kernel_variant, q50, q95, q99, dsid_29313788890d45e0bf291ea321e8c5cd, source_type: confluence, title: kv cache compaction profiling playbook, content: purposenthis page documents how to profile kv cache fragmentation and compaction behavior in the serving runtime. it focuses on:n- capturing allocator state snapshots (fragmentation, freelists, per-sequence residency)n- correlating compaction/eviction activity with tail latency you are actively mitigating a production incident, follow the runtime operational runbook and use this page for deeper diagnosis.nn when to use this playbooknuse these steps when you see one or more of the following:n- p95/p99 decode latency spikes during burst traffic, especially with mixed prompt lengthsn- increased allocator overhead (alloc/free/defrag) or copy activity, without throughput gainsn- unexpected evictions or opportunistic shedding correlated with kv memory pressuren- intermittent ooms in high-churn chat workloads even when average utilization looks safenn prerequisites / accessn- access to the runtime host (hosted canary or staging pool) via standard sre ssh / debug workflown- a trace viewer for redwood distributed traces (console tracing) and access to the serving runtime servicen- permission to use runtime debug endpoints (these are internal-only and may be disabled in some dedicated/private environments)nnrecommended tooling (internal):n- rwdctl (runtime debug cli) or equivalent admin rpc clientn- rwtrace (trace export helper) or console trace exportn- pprof (cpu profiling) where enablednn safety and performance notesn- allocator snapshots are designed to be low overhead, but they still walk allocator structures. do not take snapshots at very high frequency in production.n- if you enable compaction debug logging, it can increase overhead and may distort latency measurements.n- never capture request payloads or raw prompts in artifacts. store only allocator state, counters, and trace ids.nn---nn key concepts / what to look forn fragmentation vs utilizationnhigh kv utilization is not necessarily bad. the key risk factor is fragmentation (free memory exists but cannot satisfy contiguous page/block needs without relocation).nnsymptoms of pathological fragmentation:n- fragmentation ratio stays high or increases over time even after load stabilizesn- allocation failures/slow-path allocations rise while total free bytes are non-trivialn- compaction bytes moved spikes repeatedly but fragmentation does not improven- eviction rate increases during bursts in a way that correlates with latency spikesnn scheduler phasesnmost deployments budget compaction around scheduler boundaries:n- prefill decode transitionn- decode loop time-slicesn- background compaction worker (if enabled)nnwhen correlating to tail latency, the question is: did compaction work happen on the critical path of decode?nn---nn metrics to pull (minimum set)nuse these metric names/definitions as standardized in the metrics (counter)n- kv_cache_compaction_budget_exhausted_total (counter)n- kv_cache_evictions_total (counter with labels for reason/tier)n- runtime_decode_latency_ms (histogram p50/p95/p99)nnhelpful kv.compaction.copy_kernelsn- kv.eviction.select_candidaten- kv.eviction.evict_sequencen- scheduler.decode_tickn- scheduler.prefillnnwhat you want to determine:n- whether compaction steps overlap limits)?n- does fragmentation ratio improve after bytes moved, or stay flat?n- are evictions rising (especially for higher tiers or pinned sessions)?n- do traces show compaction spans on the critical path of decode?nnif traces show compaction on the decode critical path, confirm whether compaction is being triggered in the wrong scheduler phase or whether budgeting is too aggressive.nn---nn procedure c: diagnose pathological fragmentation patternsnthis section provides common patterns and how to validate them.nn pattern 1: mixed-length churn causes swiss cheese freelistsnindicators:n- free bytes are moderate/highn- largest contiguous free run is smalln- free-list histogram is heavily skewed to small run sizesn- slow-path allocations rise during burstsnnvalidation steps:n- compare baseline vs burst snapshot: free-run histogram should shift toward smaller runsn- check if compaction runs increase but largest run does not recovernnlikely root causes:n- block/page sizes mismatch common sequence length distributionn- compaction trigger threshold too high (reactive instead of proactive)n- compaction budget too low to catch up during churnnnnext actions:n- try lowering fragmentation trigger (canary only)n- increase compaction budget slightly and confirm compaction stays off decode critical pathn- confirm scheduler hook placement (prefill/decode boundary vs continuous background)nn pattern 2: long-lived pinned sessions block compactionnindicators:n- many sequences marked pinnedn- high fragmentation ratio localized to specific arenasn- compaction repeatedly skips large pinned regionsnnvalidation steps:n- snapshot: verify pinned counts and pinned-byte totalsn- trace: evictions may spike for non-pinned sequences while pinned remain residentnnnext actions:n- confirm pinned semantics are correct (e.g., tool-calling sessions, dedicated enterprise settings)n- evaluate whether pinned sessions should be moved to separate arena/pool configurationn- confirm eviction policy is tier-aware and respects pinned sequencesnn pattern 3: compaction thrash (bytes moved high, no benefit)nindicators:n- bytes_moved_total grows quicklyn- fragmentation ratio does not improve (or improves briefly then regresses)n- copy kernels show up frequently in tracesnnvalidation steps:n- compare snapshots across 3 points (before/during/after): does largest run increase and stay increased?n- check if eviction events immediately re-fragment the arena (churn after compaction)nnlikely root causes:n- workload churn rate is higher than compactions steady-state ability to maintain contiguityn- compaction trigger oscillation (no hysteresis)nnnext actions:n- add/adjust hysteresis between start compaction and stop compaction thresholdsn- reduce compaction aggressiveness and rely more on eviction under overload, or vice versa, depending on tier goalsnn pattern 4: budgeting misplacement causes decode stallsnindicators:n- traces show compaction spans nested under decode critical spansn- p99 spikes align with kv.compaction.step durationsn- budget_exhausted_total may be low (we are doing work, but at the wrong time)nnvalidation steps:n- inspect scheduler phase annotations in tracen- check whether compaction is being called at every decode tick instead of at safe boundariesnnnext actions:n- move budget enforcement to safe scheduler boundariesn- cap step duration more aggressively (time-based budget) rather than bytes-onlynn---nn procedure d: minimal reproducible benchmark in perf labnwhen you need a reliable repro outside source_type: confluence, title: workload portrait sampler playbook, content: overviewnnthis playbook prescribes a compact, reproducible method for building workload portraits and converting those portraits into sampler policies used by the runtime. the goal is simple: capture the most diagnostically valuable traces given constrained storage and ingestion budgets, prioritize slo-sensitive cohorts, and validate sampling choices via shadow replay before production rollout.nnaudiencennruntime engineers, sres, performance researchers, and platform product engineers who are responsible for profiling, kernel scheduling validation, and observability.nngoalsnn- produce workload portraits: histograms, canonical traces, and impact statements per route/cohort.n- generate versioned sampler policies that map cohorts to sample rates, triggers, and retention tiers.n- validate sampling and capture fidelity through mirrored collection and shadow replay.nncore concepts (short)nn- workload portrait: short json/yaml summary containing p50/p95/p99 of sequence length, tokens, kv cache hit rate, and 3 canonical traces.n- cohort: predicate for sampling (route, model, customer_tier, seq_bucket).n- sampler policy: control-plane artifact (yaml) mapping cohorts - sample_rate triggers.n- shadow replay: deterministic replay of captured traces against baseline and candidate kernels.nnprinciplesnn1) discover before capturing: use cheap histograms (5m granularity) for discovery escalate to full traces only where needed.n2) keep policies limited and auditable: small set of cohort predicates that are easy to reason about and versioned in git.n3) validate in staging: mirror, replay, and run explicit hypothesis tests before any policy changes go wide.n4) privacy-first: redact/pseudonymize textual content by default keep provenance metadata for debugging.nnprocess (step-by-step)nn1) discovery (7-14 days)n- select anchor routes: 8-12 routes covering 75 of token volume or sla-bound endpoints. include a mix of plg and enterprise.n- deploy histogram exporter (5m buckets) to collect seq_len, tokens_per_request, kv_cache_hit_pct, and response_size. collect 14 days.n- perform brief owner interviews (15-30m) to capture slos, fidelity tolerances, and known hotspots.nndeliverables: portrait.csv (route, p50/p95/p99 seq_len, tokens, owner, sla_flag), owner-notes.md.nn2) portrait synthesis (2-4 days)n- cluster histogram vectors and business attributes into 3-6 portraits (examples: interactive-short, streaming-multi-turn, batch-embeddings).n- for each portrait produce: one-line impact statement, primary slo metric, cost-sensitivity score (1-5), and sample density recommendation.nn3) sampler policy design (2-3 days)n- baseline discovery rate: 0.05 to 0.5 depending on token volume.n- portrait-driven rules: prioritize slo-bound cohorts with higher baseline rates and escalation triggers.n- retention tiers: full traces (14d default), escalated retention (up to 90d with approvals), aggregated histograms (365d).nnexample sampler yaml (human readable)nnsampler_version: 4ndefault_sample_rate: 0.0005 0.05ncohorts:n - id: interactive_shortn match: route chat: and seq_len 50 in 30 minutes.n- sampler errors: sampler_error_rate 0.2.n- config drift: policy_sync_lag 2 minutes on 10 of nodes.nnoncall triage steps:n1) check control-plane rollout logs and policy versions.n2) query node sampler health: curl if coverage loss confirmed: enable emergency_full_capture for affected cohorts (ttl: 6h) and page runtime team.n4) collect trace ids, attach to incident ticket, and escalate to runtime-observability.nncli snippetsnn- emergency full capture via control-plane: n rctl sampler trigger --policy emergency_full --cohort interactive_short --ttl 360nn- list sampled traces for route: n rctl traces list --route chat:widget --since 24h --limit 500nn- check node policy version: n curl jq .versionnndashboards (recommended panels)nn- coverage matrix: cohort x hour showing sample_rate and total_traces.n- sampler health: policy_sync_lag, sampler_errors_per_min, sample_loss_rate.n- portrait regression panel: p95/p99 deltas by portrait.n- cost vs visibility: daily storage cost for traces vs number of portraits captured.nnconfiguration cost guideline (summary)nnitem default rationalendefault discovery sample rate 0.05 low-cost discovery for high-volume routesnfull-trace retention 14 days enough for incident triage and replaynhistogram retention 365 days useful for trend/seasonality analysisnestimate storage 90/day per 10k full traces varies with compression and redactionnnprivacy and securitynn- redact full prompt text fields and store only hashed identifiers for join operations.n- restricted customers: capture only aggregated telemetry diagnostics and remediation playbook, content: summary:nthis playbook defines a concrete, repeatable process for diagnosing and remediating gpu memory fragmentation observed in redwood serving hosts. it consolidates telemetry to capture, commands and tooling to run during a live incident, thresholds we consider actionable, short-term mitigations to restore capacity, and long-term fixes to avoid recurrence.nnwhy this matters:n- fragmentation can cause apparent out-of-memory (oom) or allocation failures even when aggregate free memory looks sufficient.n- for inference workloads with persistent kv caches, allocator metadata, and mixed allocation sizes (small tensors, large kv pages), fragmentation reduces usable contiguous memory and increases tail latency / request rejection.n- fast triage reduces customer impact and avoids unnecessary instance reprovisioning.nnscope / audience:n- applies to redwood dedicated and private runtime nodes running cuda-based inference backends (pytorch/tvm/rust cuda runtime).n- intended for oncall sres, runtime engineers, and platform-hosting engineers.nnsymptoms that point to fragmentation (not just peak usage):n1) allocation failures or repeated cudamalloc retries while nvidia-smi reports 20 free memory.n2) rapid oscillation of free memory without matching process exit/creation events.n3) frequent small free segments reported by allocator introspection (see telemetry to collect).n4) successful large allocations after contiguous-space freeing (restart/evict/cache-trim).nntelemetry to collect (must be available on all runtime nodes):n- nvml / nvidia-smi samples (1s granularity if possible): memory.total, memory.used, memory.free, utilization.gpu, process pids and memory per process.n - command: nvidia-smi --query-gpumemory.total,memory.used,memory.free,utilization.gpu --formatcsv -l 1n- cuda allocator metrics (if enabled via runtime): per-process: allocated_bytes, reserved_bytes, allocation_failures, peak_reserved.n - for pytorch: torch_cuda_alloc_confenabled_stattrue or custom allocator hooks.n- cuda malloc-async / mempool stats: free_count, reserved_count, largest_free_block_size (if runtime exposes).n- host-level memory churn and oom events: dmesg for oom-killer, system journal for process sigkill.n- gpu per-process mmap-style allocations: nv-hostengine / nsight info or driver logs.n- runtime-level kv cache metrics: shard_reserved_bytes, shard_active_bytes, eviction_count.n- traces / flamegraphs around allocation calls during suspect windows.nnderived metrics and dashboard panels we recommend:n- fragmentation ratio 1 - (largest_contiguous_free_block / memory.free). (if largest_contiguous is unavailable, approximate using max single free chunk observed via allocator telemetry.)n- allocation failure rate / minute per process.n- average and p95 contiguous_free_block_size over 5m windows.n- of memory held by long-lived allocations ( 10m).n- eviction frequency and time-to-evict for kv cache.n- requests rejected due to mem budget exceeded.nnactionable thresholds (initial defaults, tune per fleet):n- fragmentation ratio 0.6 for more than 2 minutes investigate.n- allocation failure rate 3/min for any process immediate mitigation.n- largest_contiguous_free_block urgent.nnimmediate triage steps (ordered, meant for live incidents):n1) confirm symptom: correlate api error logs (cuda oom, allocation failed) with gpu telemetry timestamps.n2) capture snapshot (do not reboot until snapshot taken):n - sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-appspid,process_name,used_memory --formatcsv -f /tmp/gpu-proc-snapshot.csvn - sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpumemory.total,memory.used,memory.free --formatcsv -f /tmp/gpu-snapshot.csvn - collect runtime allocator stats (endpoint /debug/alloc-stats or environment hooks).n - if possible, run nsight systems quick snapshot: nsys profile --samplenone --tracecuda --output/tmp/nsys-snapshotn3) identify long-lived owners: sort per-process used_memory and cross-reference process start times. if a single process holds a lot of small allocations, open a ticket for that service to examine pooling settings.n4) apply safe short-term mitigations (pick in descending order of non-disruptiveness):n - trigger runtime cache trimming api for the affected shard(s). example: curl -x post - if allocator supports trimming (cudamallocasync pools), call the pool release function (approx: cuda api cudamempooltrim).n - reduce per-request cache prefetch length or per-request tensor pre-allocation via feature flags.n - as last resort for single-host recovery: gracefully restart the offending process (preferred) rather than full host reboot. use graceful drain/replica failover steps documented in the services runbook.n5) if mitigations restore contiguous memory, keep the node in investigational mode: increase logging, take several post-mitigation snapshots.nnif live mitigations fail (escalation path):n- if multiple nodes show fragmentation simultaneously, escalate to runtimeinfra owners immediately.n- reprovision with hot-swap of capacity: put node into drain in autoscaler, migrate traffic, then reboot host to reclaim whole gpu state. reboot is last resort and requires labeling for postmortem.nnroot cause analysis checklist (post-incident):n- which allocator was in use (cudamalloc, cudamallocasync, cub::devicememorypool, pytorch caching allocator)?n- were there mixed allocation sizes or a burst of very small allocations (tens to hundreds of kb)?n- were there pinned host allocations interfering with dma?n- is there a mismatch between tensor pooling parameters (max_split_size_mb) and typical tensor sizes for this workload?n- did kernel scheduling (concurrent kernels) leave many small allocations resident?n- was quantization or model shard fragmentation causing many small mapping allocations (memcpy/backing pages)?nnlong-term remediation patterns and engineering changes:n1) enable allocator-level stats by default in canary fleets and add fragment metrics to runtime telemetry.n2) switch heavy-allocation workloads to cudamallocasync explicit mempool trimming where supported.n3) tune torch_cuda_alloc_conf settings for services with many small tensors. example: export torch_cuda_alloc_confmax_split_size_mb:32,garbage_collection_threshold:0.7n4) introduce periodic background consolidation: low-priority background job that releases cached pools when utilization is low.n5) add a shard-aware allocator: prefer coalesced large allocations for kv cache pages and compact small per-request allocations into batch arenas.n6) add preflight allocation check: ensure largest_contiguous_free_block model_peak_allocation before scheduling a heavy request (fail fast/route to fallback).n7) improve admission control: route requests that need large contiguous allocation to nodes with verified contiguous capacity.nnrecommended config snippets and examples:n- pytorch allocator stats enable (env):n export torch_cuda_alloc_confenable_stattrue,max_split_size_mb:32nn- example pool trim via cuda (pseudocode):n // runtime exposes admin endpoint calling into cuda mempool apin cudamempooltrim(mempool, bytestotrim)nn- grafana / prometheus query examples (promql-like pseudo):n - frag_ratio 1 - (gpu_largest_contig_free_bytes / gpu_free_bytes)n - allocation_failures_per_min increase(cuda_allocation_failures_total1m)n - p95_largest_free histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (gpu_largest_free_block_size_bytes_bucket))nnownership and slas for mitigations:n- first responder: runtime oncall (sre) initial triage and snapshot collection within 5 minutes of alert.n- runtime engineering: implement short-term mitigations and coordinate safe process restarts within 30 minutes.n- platform infra: if host reboot required, schedule and annotate, and complete within 60 minutes with approval.n- post-incident rca: assigned to runtime engineering, deliverable within 7 business days with action items.nnplaybook for reproducibility tests (qa / dev):n1) create a synthetic workload that alternates many small allocations with sporadic large allocations to mimic kv request tensors.n2) run on a canary node with allocator statistics enabled and measure fragmentation growth.n3) test mitigations: trimming, adjusting max_split_size_mb, and using cudamallocasync. measure time to recover and allocation failure counts.n4) record results and add to the regression test harness (link in related pages).nnpostmortem template fields to fill if fragmentation caused production impact:n- incident start/end timestampsn- symptoms observed and evidence (logs, snapshots)n- short-term mitigations applied and timestampsn- root cause hypothesis and evidence supporting itn- long-term actions planned and ownersnnappendix: quick commands and notesn- snapshot gpu processes: sudo nvidia-smi --query-compute-appspid,process_name,used_memory --formatcsvn- continuous nvml sampling: nvidia-smi --query-gpumemory.used,memory.free --formatcsv -l 1 /tmp/gpu-sample.csv n- nsight quick trace: nsys profile --tracecuda --output/tmp/trace -t 10s n- pytorch: print(torch.cuda.memory_stats()) and torch.cuda.memory_reserved()/memory_allocated() endpoints.nnnotes and tradeoffs:n- reboots clear fragmentation but hide underlying leaks/anti-patterns. prefer tracing and allocator changes over reboot as the primary fix.n- enabling allocator stats has a small perf overhead start with a 1 canary population before fleet-wide rollout.n- some hardware/driver combos expose more allocator metadata (e.g., newer cuda runtimes). maintain a compatibility matrix in the runtime wiki.nncontacts and escalation list:n- runtime-oncall@redwood.internal (primary)n- eng-serving-runtime@redwood.internal dsid_bcb3aaffdc814cca8743392c5275119f, source_type: confluence, title: kernel interaction correlation lab and investigation checklist, content: overviewnnpurpose: this document defines a repeatable lab and step-by-step investigation checklist for diagnosing subtle kernel-level interaction issues in the serving runtime (contention, preemption races, kv cache coherence artifacts, and cross-kernel priority inversion). the intent is to provide a reproducible experimental harness, required telemetry fields, and a prioritized checklist on-call and sre engineers can follow.nnaudience: runtime sres, performance engineers, kernel engineers, and on-call rotation members.nnscope and when to use this guiden- use this playbook when: tail latency spikes (99th percentile increases by 2x), unexplained gpu scheduler stalls, intermittent model-switch oscillations, or when a regression appears only under mixed-concurrency workloads.n- out of scope: hardware-level power faults (use hardware incident runbook), application-level correctness bugs in the model code.nnbackground and rationalen- modern inference workloads combine continuous batching, kv cache, and multiple kernel variants. subtle interactions (e.g., a long-running kernel holding a tensor memory lock while preemption is attempted) can manifest as short-lived but high-impact latency spikes. these interactions are difficult to identify from high-level traces causal correlation across runtime, kernel scheduler, and gpu dispatch telemetry is required.nntelemetry and signal catalog (required)n- request-level signals:n - request_id (string)n - route/model (string)n - timestamp_queued_ms (int)n - timestamp_kernel_enqueue_ms (int)n - timestamp_kernel_start_ms (int)n - timestamp_kernel_end_ms (int)n - cpu_thread (string)n - kernel_variant (string)n - batch_id (string)n - kv_cache_hit_ratio (float)n - tokens_generated (int)nn- kernel/dispatcher signals:n - gpu_dispatch_time_msn - gpu_complete_time_msn - kernel_preempt_attempts (int)n - kernel_preempt_duration_msn - occupancy_percentn - tensor_memory_alloc_bytesn - kernel_wait_queue_lennn- system signals:n - node_cpu_load_1mn - node_gpu_temp_celsiusn - nvlink_retry_countn - iommu_faultsn - cgroup_preempt_eventsnnquick reference thresholds (operational defaults)n- 99th percentile latency increase: alert if 2x baseline for 5m window.n- kernel preempt attempts: alert if 10 attempts/min on a node.n- gpu occupancy: alert if 95 for sustained 2m while tail latency increases.nninvestigation checklist (ordered, prescriptive)n1) triage and collect artifacts (first 10 minutes)n - capture high-level traces: request traces for the afflicted timeframe (trace id or request_id).n - export kernel-level telemetry: gpu_dispatch_time_ms, kernel_variant per batch, preempt counters.n - snapshot node-level metrics: top process gpu memory, nvtop snapshot, nvidia-smi dmon 1s for 30s.n - preserve scheduler logs and admission controller decision logs for the period.nn2) fast correlation (1030 minutes)n - correlate request trace timestamps with kernel start/end timestamps. look for requests with long gap between kernel_enqueue and kernel_start (queueing at cpu/dispatcher).n - identify whether affected requests share model/version or batch shape. if yes, candidate a model-specific kernel variant.n - query: prometheus examplen - promql: n increase(kernel_preempt_attempts_total5m)n n - quick grep on dispatcher logs for spike patterns: grep -e preempthandoffwait_queue /var/log/runtime/dispatcher.log sed -n 1,200pnn3) kernel-level deep-dive (30120 minutes) - reconstruct kernel timeline using kernel_trace_id map to request_ids.n - if preemption attempts are present, examine preempt_duration_ms distribution. long durations indicate stalled preempt handlers or unexpected gpu stall.n - run a focused microbenchmark: replay a small synthetic trace containing the same batch sizes and sequence lengths. use the lab harness described below.nn4) hypothesis-driven fault injection (13 hours)n - hypothesis examples:n - h1: a kernel variant with large scratch memory occasionally triggers a slow tensor allocation path causing long preempt durations.n - h2: kv cache hot-skip path causes serialization on a shared mutex while kernel handoff waits, causing queue buildup.n - for h1: deploy a canary variant with reduced scratch growth (quantized variant) and run shadow traffic. observe preempt and tail latency.n - for h2: run mutex contention stress test: deliberately increase concurrent kv hits on same keyspace and observe kernel_wait_queue_len.nn5) mitigation and rollback (if confirmed)n - immediate mitigations:n - route affected traffic to fallback kernel variant or smaller model variant.n - temporarily reduce max_concurrency for the node to shed potential long-running kernels.n - rollback checklist:n - validate fallback route maintains 95th/99th latency slos for a 10-minute observation window.n - if dsid_603b5d5581004b3189093ee80c45f5ca, source_type: confluence, title: profiling mixed prefill/decode contention (mixed-workload tail latency), content: purposenthis playbook documents how to reproduce and diagnose mixed prefill/decode contention that produces user-visible p95 tail latency regressions under mixed prompt-length distributions (e.g., short chat prompts interleaved with long-context prompts).nnin steady-state homogeneous traffic, continuous batching tends to be stable. under mixed workloads, we commonly see:n- head-of-line blocking: long-prefill requests dominate gpu time and batch selection.n- scheduler instability: rapid shifts between prefill-heavy and decode-heavy work.n- kernel selection thrash: frequent switching of attention kernels/profiles as sequence lengths vary.n- kv cache pressure: eviction/compaction spikes that amplify decode latency.nnthis doc is written to be usable by serving runtime kernel teams and as a reference during canary triage.nn---nn when to use this playbooknuse this playbook when you observe one or more of the following in hosted or dedicated pools:n- ttft (time-to-first-token) p95 increases primarily during spikes of long-context traffic.n- decode token latency looks fine in isolation, but p95 end-to-end increases due to queueing and/or prefill blocking.n- per-gpu throughput remains similar, but p95 and p99 drift upward under mixed mixes.n- increased variance in per-iteration batch composition and/or sequence-length distribution.nnnot a good fit if the issue is clearly:n- network or upstream api latency.n- model-level regressions unrelated to serving (e.g., prompt changes, tool calling loops).n- gpu health / ecc / throttling incidents.nn---nn definitions (quick)n- prefill: processing the prompt/context to initialize kv cache.n- decode: iterative next-token generation using kv cache.n- mixed-workload contention: prefill workload stealing scheduling budget from decode (or vice versa), creating tail amplification.n- kernel thrash: repeated switching between kernels/profiles (often due to sequence-length variability) that reduces effective gpu utilization.nn---nn prerequisites and accessnenvironmentsn- prefer a controlled staging pool or perf canary environment first.n- if profiling prod canary, coordinate with sre (see operational safety).nntoolsn- grafana dashboards for runtime scheduler class metrics.n- tracing (tempo) and logs (loki) access.n- nsight systems (nsys) and optionally nsight compute (ncu).n- triton debug/autotune controls (if relevant for the deployed iteration budget.nn2) decode starvationn- decode iteration p95 increases even when per-token compute is stable.n- queue time dominates but gpu utilization stays high (gpu is busy, just on the wrong work).nn3) kv cache eviction spikesn- evictions/compactions spike during long-context bursts.n- decode iteration latency increases shortly after eviction spikes.nn4) kernel thrashn- kernel selection prefill/decode contentionn what healthy looks liken- prefill bursts are present but bounded.n- decode iterations are regular with limited jitter.n- minimal gaps between kernel launches.n- batch composition does not oscillate dramatically iteration-to-iteration.nn red flagsn1) prefill runs dominate long continuous windowsn- timeline shows long unbroken sequences of prefill kernels.n- short requests ttft increases due to waiting behind long-prefill work.nn2) kernel launch gaps / synchronization stallsn- gaps appear when switching between prefill and decode phases.n- often coincides with memory pressure, cache management, or host-side batching logic.nn3) kernel profile oscillation (thrash)n- attention kernel variants switch frequently.n- increased cpu overhead for kernel selection/autotune or code paths that depend on shape buckets.nn4) memory bandwidth saturation during cache eventsn- spikes in memory throughput correlate with kv cache compaction/eviction.n- decode iterations immediately after eviction show higher latency.nn---nn triton kernel selection debugging tips (when kernel thrash is suspected)n common causesn- sequence lengths cross internal bucket boundaries frequently (short/long mixed in same batch).n- autotuner evaluates multiple configs due to varied shapes.n- runtime alternates between different attention implementations based on (seq_len, batch_size, head_dim, dtype, quant profile).nn what to enable (non-prod first)nif using triton-based kernels or autotuned paths in your build:n- enable autotune logging for a single run window.n- pin (indicating cache eviction or non-reuse).n- shape drift causing many unique compiled variants.nnmitigation patterns (to validate during experiments):n- increase shape bucketing stability (larger buckets, fewer boundaries).n- avoid mixing extreme seq lengths in a single batch when it forces worst-case kernel choice.n- pin kernel profiles per sku/model where supported.nn---nn kv cache eviction/compaction debugging (cache pressure spikes)n symptomsn- kv_cache_evictions_total spikes during long-context bursts.n- kv_cache_hit_ratio drops and does not recover quickly.n- decode iteration latency becomes noisy (high variance) after evictions.nn what to checkn- is the cache sized appropriately for the concurrency and max context length?n- are long-context requests dominating concurrency in a way the pool wasnt sized for?n- is cache compaction running too frequently (small free segments, fragmentation)?nn practical diagnosticsn- correlate eviction spikes with request mix changes and batch size changes.n- confirm whether cache events align with prefill-heavy windows.n- check if a new scheduling policy increased the number of active sequences in-flight and raised cache residency requirements.nn---nn common failure modes and how to confirm themn 1) kernel thrash due to sequence-length variabilitynconfirmn- kernel selection changes increase behavior only appears when nsight is attachedn- latency shifts significantly with profiler on/offnnnext stepsn- shorten capture reduce trace categoriesn- prefer nsys over ncu avoid excessive loggingnn---nn triage checklist (copy/paste into incident threads)n1) workload: mix ratio, arrival pattern, concurrency, prompt token distribution, output token distribution.n2) versions: runtime, doc_id: dsid_c6c3f0dc1de74bf98f4284c3230b495a, source_type: confluence, title: sequence runway sampling and batch fidelity playbook, content: summarynnthis playbook defines the sequence runway sampling method and operational guidance for measuring the interaction between request sequence-length distributions and batching fidelity. sequence runway is a structured sampling technique intended to produce representative micro-batches for performance profiling, kernel-sensitivity analysis, and fidelity regression detection across production-shaped traffic.nnwhy we built thisnn- traditional uniform sampling under-represents transitions between short and long prefix lengths that trigger kernel path changes (attention tiling, kv cache hotness, quantized kernels).n- ad-hoc sampling can miss edge cases where batch packing semantics significantly change per-token latency and model quality.n- sequence runway makes those transitions first-class, enabling repeatable benchmarking, better kernel hinting, and targeted mitigations (prefetching, backpressure tuning, or model-variant routing).nngoalsnn1. provide a repeatable protocol for generating micro-batches that exercise kernel breakpoints and batching boundary cases.n2. surface fidelity regressions introduced by batching or quantized-variant fallbacks.n3. produce telemetry artifacts (trace kernel tags per-token latencies) consumable by the profiling pipeline and the benchmarking suite.nnscope and non-goalsnn- in scope: sampling and experiment protocol for online traffic replay, local synthetic corpus generation, expected telemetry schema, runbook for interpreting results.n- out of scope: model architecture changes, kernel implementation guidance beyond suggested mitigations, client-side prompt engineering.nnownership and contactsnn- primary owner: eng-serving-runtime profiling teamn- runbook contact: aisha kapoor (author) pager: runtime-profilingn- secondary reviewers/experts: mikhail petrov (kernel), samira chen (benchmarks)nndefinitionsnn- sequence runway: an ordered set of request samples grouped by prefix length bands that intentionally create boundary transitions inside a micro-batch.n- band: a contiguous interval of sequence lengths (e.g., 1-8, 9-64, 65-256).n- micro-batch: a single server batch observed by the runtime containing multiple requests.n- fidelity regression: measurable drop in model output quality attributable to batching, kernel-variant fallback, or quantization.nnsampling design (high level)nn1) traffic characterizationnn- collect 2472 hours of request metadata (sequence_length, model_variant, route, client_tier) sampled at 0.51 to create a baseline histogram.n- produce an empirical cdf and identify elbow points and kernel breakpoints (see reference: sequence-length-scaling-and-kernel-breakpoints).nn2) band selectionnn- choose 46 bands covering the observed distribution: very-short, short, medium, long, xlong. example bands: 1-8, 9-64, 65-256, 257-1024.n- for each band, compute target sample counts proportional to traffic volume but inject additional samples at band boundaries (10 of total samples) to stress transitions.nn3) runway constructionnn- a runway is an ordered list: b1 - b1 - b2 - b2 - b3 - b3 - b2 - b4, where each bx represents a sample drawn from band x. orders should be designed to:n - create short-long and long-short transitions.n - trigger kv cache cold/warm boundaries (e.g., repeated prefixes then sudden long continuation).nn4) micro-batch packingnn- pack samples into micro-batches using the same runtime packing policy used in production (e.g., sequence-length-first packing or round-robin across routes).n- ensure some micro-batches intentionally violate ideal packing to exercise admission controllers and preemption.nnconfig example (yaml)nn---nexperiment_name: sequence-runway-q2-2026nbands:n - name: very_shortn range: 1, 8n weight: 0.30n - name: shortn range: 9, 64n weight: 0.45n - name: mediumn range: 65, 256n weight: 0.20n - name: longn range: 257, 1024n weight: 0.05nboundary_injection: 0.10nrunways_per_round: 200nmicro_batch_size_target: 8nlines_of_workload_per_run: 5000n---nncli example to generate runways (profiling toolkit v0.7):nn ri-profile generate-runway --config ./runway-config.yaml --out ./runways/seq-runway-2026.ndjsonnnformat notesnn- output is ndjson where each record contains: sample_id, prompt_hash, sequence_length, band, model_hint, expected_kernel_variant.n- telemetry pipeline expects trace_id and batch_id populated per request to correlate server-side traces.nntelemetry and traces to collectnn- per-request: client_route, token_count, sequence_length, model_variant, kernel_hint, packing_slot, admission_decision, queue_time_ms, start_time, end_time, per_token_latencies (list), top_kernel_tags.n- per-batch: batch_id, batch_size, slot_shape (vector of sequence lengths), packing_policy, aggregate_queue_time_ms, kernel_variant_distribution.nnbenchmarks and evaluation matrixnn- run each runway against the following matrix:n - model variants: fp16, 8-bit-quant, dynamic-bf16-fallbackn - scheduler policies: sequence-first, fairness-governor, priority-decoden - admission thresholds: 90th percentile latency slo target breakers (e.g., 200ms, 500ms)nnevaluation metrics (primary)nn- per-token p90 and p99 latency shift relative to shadow baseline.n- kernel-sensitivity-index: proportion of tokens that executed on a non-primary kernel path.n- fidelity delta: bleu/rouge/embedding-distance on deterministic prompts where applicable.n- batch packing inefficiency: wasted slot ratio (empty tokens inside batch).nnoperational runbook: when you get anomalous resultsnn1) symptom: p99 per-token latency increased by 15 vs baseline and coincides with an increased kernel-sensitivity-index.n2) quick triage:n - check batch_id rollups to see if specific micro-batch shapes are correlated.n - inspect kernel tags in traces for slow kernels or unexpected fallbacks.n - query admission logs for increased preemption or queue spikes.nn3) mitigations (iterative):n - short-term: reduce micro_batch_size_target by 25 on a canary pool enable conservative admission for affected routes.n - medium-term: enable kv prefetching for runways that show cold-cache stalls.n - long-term: work with kernel team to fuse or optimize frequently hit kernel paths consider model-variant routing to a lower-latency kernel for latency-sensitive customers.nn4) recovery checklist:n - roll back any runtime admission tuning if it increases error rates.n - re-run a focused runway that isolates the offending band to validate a fix.n - open a postmortem if fix required 1 hour of mitigation or customer impact occurred.nnrollout matrix and experiment safetynn- start with lab-only runs using recorded traffic in the sandbox cluster.n- canary on a non-customer-delta production shard (10 of traffic) with elevated tracing enabled.n- if canary passes for 24 hours with no 5 p99 drift and no fidelity delta 0.5 relative units, expand to 50 then 100.n- always include automatic circuit-breaker to abort experiments on: error-rate increase 0.5pp, p99 drift 20, or kernel ooms.nnexample query snippetsnn- identify boundary-heavy micro-batches:n select batch_id, count() as batch_size, array_agg(sequence_length order by sequence_length desc)
