--dump-effective-config excerpt., doc_id: dsid_8271993eae994b89beed2760c2d4e090, source_type: confluence, title: model-aware request shaper design and operations, content: overviewnnthis document defines the design, operational procedures, and observability requirements for the model-aware request shaper (mars): a cross-layer runtime component that adapts admission, batching, and kernel hints based on the target model variant, request class, and active fidelity constraints.nnmars is intended to reduce sla violations and improve unit cost by making shaping decisions informed by model characteristics (sequence length distribution, kv cache friendliness, quantization profile) rather than treating all requests uniformly. this page covers: design goals, architecture diagrams, scheduler interactions, telemetry and profiling playbook, benchmark procedure, rollout checklist, runbook for common incidents, configuration reference, and ownership.nngoals and non-goalsnngoals:n- reduce 95th/99th token-latency slo violations for multi-model fleets by coordinating batching and kernel selection per model variant.n- preserve strict fairness across tenants while enabling cost-aware prioritization for reserved/dedicated pools.n- provide actionable telemetry and knobs for on-call and sre to react to model-specific regressions quickly.n- allow per-customer/model feature flags (prefetching, aggressive batching, relaxed latency window) and safe fallbacks.nnnon-goals:n- mars does not replace global admission controllers that enforce account-level rate limits it augments them with model-aware signals.n- mars does not attempt to change model weights or quantization at runtime it surfaces suggestions to the optimize team only.nnhigh-level architecturenn(ascii diagram)nnclient - api gateway - router - mars - admission controller - scheduler - kernel executornncomponents:n- model hint registry: stores per-model metadata (expected token distribution, hot prefix likelihood, kv-cache sensitivity, preferred kernel families). populated from model-onboarding pipeline and updated by profiling jobs.n- request classifier: lightweight classifier that attaches a request signature (model_id, prompt-length-bucket, customer-tier, op_type) to each request. runs in the front-line router.n- shaping policy engine (mars core): evaluates policies to decide shaping actions: permit/queue/reject, batch slicing keys, kernel hints, kv-prefetch directives, and expected tail-fallthrough rules. uses declarative policy profiles authored by scheduler team.n- telemetry enricher: adds model-aware fields to traces and metrics (model.variant, hint_version, predicted_sequence_bucket, chosen_kernel_hint).n- feedback loop: periodic job that reconcilies actual latency/cost vs predicted and updates model hint registry (signal back to profiling playbooks).nnpolicy model and examplesnnpolicies are expressed in our scheduler policy dsl (see scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles) and are composed of conditions and actions. example policies (pseudo-dsl):nn1) low-latency small prompt policy:nwhen model.family redwood-compat-tiny and prompt_bucket in 0-64:n - set kernel_hint fast-small-ctxn - max_batch_size 16n - admission_priority interactivenn2) cost-sensitive long-seq policy for batch windows:nwhen model.quant_profile int4 and median_length 256:n - enable_kv_prefetch(true)n - set_kernel_hint concat-friendlyn - target_batch_latency_ms 120n - admission_priority best-effortnnscheduler interactions and kernel handshakennmars communicates intent to the scheduler and kernel executor via:n- kernel hint header: structured token the scheduler maps to kernel families (sharded vs fused attention, prepacked weights).n- batch-slice key: chosen to optimize packing (e.g., same prompt_bucket kv-cache affinity).n- preferred prefetch directive: instruct kernel to pre-issue kv cache lookups or to use lazy prefetch.nnthe scheduler must validate kernel hints against the current kernel compatibility matrix. if a hint is incompatible with the node (e.g., missing kernel plugin), the scheduler will either map to a nearest compatible hint or follow the mars-declared fallback priority list.nnkv cache coordinationnnmars can request coordinated kv prefetch windows for long-running sessions. coordination rules:n- prefetch is gated by per-node memory watermarks (see config table below).n- prefetch concurrent limit default: 4 per-gpu.n- when prefetch window is enabled, mars will mark the request as heavy admission priority may be lowered unless the customer tier is reserved.nntelemetry and profiling playbook (operational)nnpurpose: ensure model-aware shaping decisions are observable and profile memory.watermark_eviction_count 0 in window. critical alert.n- batch-slice starvation: fraction of requests assigned to native batch 1 - 5 - 20 - 100 with 1h holds and automated rollback if p95 slo1.1.n- post-rollout validation: run benchmark protocol for 60m.nnownership and contactsnn- mars core owner: maya patel (eng-serving-runtime).n- scheduler integration: daniel chen dsid_39c44edd323f4c51974d2500f0333b77, source_type: confluence, title: kernel sandboxing, bandwidth controls, and cooperative shepherding manual, content: overview:nnthis document defines the design, operational controls, and incident procedures for the kernel sandboxing and cooperative shepherding subsystem (kscs). kscs is the combination of: the sandbox controller that constrains per-cohort resource bandwidth, an admission/governor layer that enforces soft and hard limits, and a cooperative shepherding protocol between the scheduler and kernel plugins to enable graceful handoff, preemption-friendly slices, and prioritized progress for latencysensitive requests.nnscope and intent:n- scope: applies to the runtime kernel and scheduler integrations used by redwoods hosted and dedicated inference clusters.n- intent: reduce noisy-neighbor and runaway kernel behavior while preserving tail latency for high-priority tiers and enabling safe experimental kernel rollouts.nndesign goals:n1) safety: prevent single tenant/cohort from starving others avoid node ooms and gpu hangs.n2) latency preservation: keep high-priority request p99 within slos where possible.n3) observability: expose deterministic telemetry for allocation and handoff decisions.n4) replayability: allow deterministic replay of scheduling decisions for investigation.nnarchitecture overview:n- components:n - sandbox controller (sandboxd): central agent per node that negotiates quota windows, issues bandwidth tokens, and exposes an rpc for kernel plugin sync.n - kernel plugin interface (kpi): light-weight abi inside each kernel that accepts token credits, preemption hints, and cooperative-shepherding callbacks.n - bandwidth governor: admission service in the scheduler that translates request characteristics into bandwidth profiles (tokens/sec, max-slice-ms, priority).n - shepherd agent: cross-node coordinator for multi-stage requests (e.g., multi-shard kv cache warmups) that requests temporary credits and releases them on completion.nnhow it works (high level):n1) request classified by admission - bandwidth profile assigned (e.g., interactive-high, batch-background).n2) scheduler requests token allocation from sandboxd for the chosen cohort. sandboxd enforces cohort global windows using a leaky-bucket model.n3) kernel receives tokens and can run a slice up to configured max-slice-ms. if a higher priority request arrives, kernel uses cooperative callback to yield at a safe boundary.n4) shepherd agent mediates long-running handoffs (for example, model swap or large kv prefetch) to avoid long blocking of interactive slots.nnterminology:n- token: smallest unit of bandwidth credit (represents a short amount of gpu work permissable).n- cohort: a classification of traffic (customer-tier workload-class).n- slice: contiguous execution window inside a kernel invocation (bounded by max-slice-ms).n- shepherding: cooperative handoff process where a running kernel segment coordinates with scheduler to release or re-acquire credits gracefully.nnmodeled policies and examples:n- leaky-bucket parameters (default):n - bucket_size_tokens: 10_000n - refill_rate_tokens_per_sec: 5_000n - max_burst_tokens: 15_000n- priority mapping (example):n - interactive-high: tokens/sec 5_000, max-slice-ms 6, preemption-grace-ms 2n - interactive-low: tokens/sec telemetry and metrics (exposed via /metrics and traces):n- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_totalcohort, node (counter)n- sandboxd_cohort_tokens_availablecohort, node (gauge)n- kernel_slice_duration_mscohort, confluence, title: tenant-aware kernel ladder: architecture, profiling, and runbook, content: summary:nthis handbook documents the tenant-aware kernel ladder: a runtime subsystem that adaptively promotes and demotes kernel configurations per-tenant to meet latency slos while optimizing gpu utilization and cost. it combines architecture rationale, kernel scheduling rules, profiling playbook, benchmarking plan, rollout checklist, and an incident runbook.nnpurpose and scope:n- audience: serving runtime engineers, sres, on-call, and performance engineers.n- scope: design and operational scheduler hints (batch slice size, preemption score, qcache warmup).n- per-tenant control plane maps tenant - ladder policy. policy attributes: base_profile, min_profile, max_profile, promotion_cooldown_s, demotion_cooldown_s, telemetry_weights.n- runtime components:n - ladder controller (per-node): watches incoming telemetry and per-tenant session state, emits profile-change intents.n - kernel activation agent (per-gpu): applies profile bundles and issues kernel handshake ensures safe rollback if activation fails.n - quota crediter: ensures profile changes respect slot accounting and kernel credits.n - telemetry exporter: publishes promotion/demotion events and rationale to metrics and traces.nnarchitecture diagram (text):n- request - request-classifier - tenant possible, move only new allocations to the higher profile and let existing sessions finish (soft promotion).n- hard promotion: if tail latency promotion_threshold for 3 consecutive 1-min windows, force immediate kernel swap for hot sessions with warm-up prefetch.n- demotion: only demote when sustained over a 10-minute window and gpu utilization headroom 25.n- safety: at most 20 of a nodes decisions that trade off latency, cost, and fairness across tenants and routes. the design combines kernel-cost estimates from the profiler, per-route slas, and configurable economic policies to updated release checklist.n, doc_id: dsid_9679c59278ba4bc9afd09f4b2dc03d83, source_type: confluence, title: slot-abort contract and graceful recovery protocol, content: summarynnthis document specifies the slot-abort contract and graceful recovery protocol used by the serving runtime scheduler and kernel plugins. it formalizes the signals, invariants, telemetry, operator runbook, and verification tests required for safe slot abortion, state preservation, and deterministic recovery paths. the goal is to minimize user-visible slo impact during kernel-level preemption, eviction, or forced termination while keeping the runtime auditable and testable.nnintended audiencen- runtime kernel and scheduler engineersn- oncall and sre teamsn- release engineers validating scheduler behaviorn- performance and profiling teamsnngoals and non-goalsngoals:n- define a single contract for how a running request slot may be aborted or suspended.n- ensure deterministic state handoff for recoverable requests (kv cache, partial logits, decoding state).n- provide telemetry and traces needed to map aborted slots to user-level tail latency/regressions.n- standardize operator recovery steps and automated remediation.nnnon-goals:n- this is not a doc for admission control or long-term placement policies (see scheduler-policy-language-declarative-profiles).n- does not change model-serving api semantics for clients all changes are internal to runtime.nnbackgroundnredwoods serving runtime supports preemptive slot reclamation to maintain capacity and qos. historically, ad-hoc slot killing led to state loss, user-visible 5xxs, and noisy post-incident debugging. the slot-abort contract aims to normalize this behavior across kernel variants (synchronous kernels, async handoff kernels, multi-gpu shards).nnterminologyn- slot: a runtime-execution reservation associated with a request pipeline (may span kvcache token generation).n- abort: an intentional termination of a slot prior to natural completion (categories below).n- suspend: a low-latency serialization of in-flight state to persistent or shared memory for later resume.n- handshake: the two-phase protocol between scheduler and kernel for safe slot transition.nnabort categories (with examples)n1) planned abort (managed): graceful eviction intended for maintenance or preemption windows. example: drained node for upgrade.n2) priority preemptive abort (policy): scheduler reclaims slot to satisfy a higher-priority request (e.g., enterprise dedicated pool overrides best-effort).n3) forced abort (emergency): kernel or host signals unrecoverable state (oom, nvlink fatal) and cannot complete handshake.n4) latency-offload abort: scheduler chooses to cut low-value tail requests to preserve p50/p95 for paying customers.nnsignaling and contractn- outgoing abort request from scheduler to kernel: an rpc call abortslot(slot_id, reason_code, deadline_ms).n- kernel must reply within handshake_deadline_ms with one of: ack_suspend, ack_terminate, nak_retry.n- if ack_suspend: kernel emits a resume_token and writes minimal state to the shared suspension store (s3-like or in-cluster memstore).n- if ack_terminate: kernel attempts a best-effort flush of outputs (streamed partials) then perform local cleanup.n- if no reply before handshake_deadline_ms: scheduler marks slot as forcekilled and increments forcekill counter for telemetry.nndefault timeouts (configurable):n config key default notes n ---------- ------- ----- n handshake_deadline_ms 250 time allotted for kernel to respond to abortslot.n suspend_write_ms 100 time allowed to persist suspend state.n resume_call_timeout_ms 350 timeout for resume rpc when restoring a suspended slot.nnstate model and persistence contractn- minimal resume_token payload (string) must include: slot_schema_version, kernel_variant, kvcache_keys_hash, partial_decode_cursor, bytes_written_checksum.n- suspension store contract: put(resume_token, binary_snapshot) must be idempotent and versioned. failure modes must return explicit error codes (store_ewrite, storefull).n- on resume, kernel must validate token schema_version and kvcache_hash mismatch - fail_resume and surface as recoverable shim error.nntelemetry trace signals (required)nemit standardized tracing annotations and metrics for every abort flow:n- trace/span tags: slot.id, abort.reason, abort.initiator (scheduler/kernel/host), kernel.variant, resume.token.present (true/false).n- counters: slot.abort.total, slot.abort.forcekill, slot.suspend.success, slot.resume.success, slot.resume.fail.n- histograms: suspend_write_latency_ms, resume_latency_ms, abort_handshake_latency_ms.nnslo impact alerting thresholdsnuse these as initial operational thresholds (tunable per pool):n- if slot.abort.forcekill / slot.abort.total 0.05 for 1h - sev2.n- if slot.resume.fail rate 0.01 over 30m - sev2 and rollback any enabling rollout.n- if suspend_write_latency_ms p95 200ms - investigate storage layer create sev3.n- tail-latency correlation: if p99_request_latency increases by 15 coincident with increased slot.aborts - open incident.nnoperator runbook (investigation and remediation)n1) detect: receive alert (e.g., slot.resume.fail 1).n2) gather context:n - kubectl logs of kernel pod(s) with slot.id retrieve trace span from tracing ui.n - query suspension store for resume_token existence: curl -x get - check node gpu health: nvidia-smi -q verify ecc/warnings.n3) triaging steps (ordered):n a) if forcekill counter increased across many slots - suspect handshake_deadline tuning or kernel blocking. temporarily increase handshake_deadline_ms in canary to 500ms and observe.n b) if store errors (store_ewrite / storefull) - free space or fail fast to ensure kernel falls back to ack_terminate path.n c) if resume validation fails (schema mismatch) - mark resume_token as invalid schedule automated metric to failback to full retry path and roll back kernel variant that introduced schema change.n4) remediation:n - for storage latency: route suspend writes to fallback in-cluster memstore and flag for storage team.n - for kernel stalls: trigger runtime profiling (see profile: gstack capture command below) and scale up auxiliary worker threads.n - for node-level failures: cordon node and migrate slots via scheduler handoff policy.n5) communication: create incident with slot.id examples, attach traces and last 50 lines of kernel logs, and tag oncall team.nnexample commands and snippetsn- abortslot rpc pseudo-call (go):n client.abortslot(ctx, pb.abortrequestslotid: slot-12345, reason: pb.abortreason_preempt, deadlinems: 250)nn- inspect suspend store:n curl -s -h authorization: bearer suspend_store_token jq .nn- quick local debug: capture the last 2mb of kernel logs and upload to s3:n kubectl logs -n runtime kernel-pod-abc --tail10000 /tmp/kernel-logs.txt aws s3 cp /tmp/kernel-logs.txt s3://redwood-debug/(hostname)-kernel-logs.txtnntest suite and benchmarksnwe require a set of unit and integration checks for any change to scheduler or kernel:n- unit tests: verify resume_token schema round-trip, idempotency of store operations, and handshake timeouts.n- integration tests (ci): simulate planned abort, preemptive abort, forced abort under mixed load and assert percent of forcekills 99.5, slot.resume.success 99.9 for canary.n- confirm no increase in customer-facing 5xxs or p99 latency beyond 5 baseline.n- approve by runtime lead and sre reviewer.nnimplementation notes for kernel authorsn- keep suspend payload minimal avoid serializing entire kvcache instead persist key hashes and rely on shared kvcache invalidation/refresh on scheduler resource tagging and precedence manifest, content: overviewnnpurpose: this document specifies the resource-tagging and precedence manifest used by redwoods scheduler to make deterministic decisions about kernel assignment, admission control, and graceful degradation. resource tags let higher layers add lightweight metadata to requests (workload characteristics, cost-sensitivity, fidelity budget, retry semantics) that the scheduler uses together with telemetry to make per-request placement and preemption choices.nngoalsn- make scheduling decisions predictable and auditable by standardizing tags and precedence rules.n- expose controllable levers to product and platform teams to express cost vs fidelity tradeoffs.n- ensure backward compatibility: untagged requests follow current best-effort policies.n- provide operator runbooks and profiling guidance for tag-driven regressions.nnscope and non-goalsn- scope: runtime admission controller, scheduler policy layer, kernel hinting, and observability fields.n- non-goals: model selection logic, api surface changes for customers (tags are internal to redwood and derived from routing policies or per-tenant config).nnkey concepts and terminologyn- resource tag: structured label attached to a request at the service boundary. tags are short key:value tokens.n- precedence manifest: ordered rule set that maps tag combinations to scheduling actions (admit, queue-with-sla, degrade-mode, preemptible).n- degradation mode: a policy action that reduces fidelity (quantized model variant, prefix cache usage, early cutoff).n- kernel hint: annotation passed to kernel mapper that influences kernel selection (e.g., preferred kernel family or tight latency bound).nndesign principlesn1) keep tags small and typed: allow exactly the tag keys documented in the manifest.n2) deterministic precedence: rules are evaluated top-to-bottom earlier rule wins.n3) least-privilege impact: tags can only reduce resource footprint or request priority, never increase allocation.n4) observability-first: every evaluation emits a traceable event containing the matched rule id and rationale.nnresource tag schema (canonical keys)n- fidelity: high, standard, economical fidelity budget for the requestn- cost_sensitivity: low, medium, high willingness to use expensive kernels or cpu fallbackn- latency_class: interactive, best_effort, batch latency tolerancen- preemptible: true, false candidate for preemption under pressuren- cache_hint: kv_prefetch, prefix_cache_ok, no_cache cache preferencesn- isolation: tenant_dedicated, tenant_shared tenancy isolation impacts shard placementnnexample tagging table (ascii)n tag key purpose default notes n fidelity fidelity budget standard highuse highest-quality model variant if latency allows n cost_sensitivity operator cost tolerance medium lowprefer quantized kernels and batching n latency_class scheduling latency target interactive impacts admission timeout n preemptible preemption candidacy false true allows background eviction under pressure nnprecedence manifest (human-readable sample)n1) rule_id: p-01-critical-interactiven match: fidelityhigh and latency_classinteractive and isolationtenant_dedicatedn action: admit_prefetch, kernel_hintlow-latency, preemptiblefalsen rationale: sla-backed dedicated tenant traffic must be prioritized kernel hint prefers kernels tuned for short sequencesnn2) rule_id: p-02-econ-backgroundn match: fidelityeconomical or cost_sensitivityhigh or preemptibletruen action: queue-with-sla(200ms), kernel_hintquantized-prefer, allow_batched_executiontruen rationale: background tasks should use cost-optimized paths and accept higher latencynn3) rule_id: p-03-standard-sharedn match: summary:nnthis playbook defines the sla-aware admission controller and backpressure strategy for redwoods serving runtime. it describes the design, configuration, operational runbook, and recommended testing/benchmarking steps to ensure tenant-level slos are respected under mixed workloads and overload scenarios. the playbook targets runtime-admission (service), kernel-scheduler (service), and dispatcher components and is intended for on-call, runtime engineers, and sres.nngoals and scope:nn- ensure per-tenant and per-route latency slos are prioritized when system capacity is constrained.n- provide deterministic admission behavior that is auditable and testable.n- define backpressure signals exposed to clients and internal services.n- offer a practical operational runbook for detecting, mitigating, and rolling back admission policy changes.nnout of scope:nn- model-level quality regressions (handled by optimize/evals).n- long-term capacity provisioning (handled by capacity-planning team).nnbackground and motivation:nnas traffic patterns diversify and multi-tenant traffic mixes (short-chat, long-generation, embeddings), the runtime must protect defined slos (p95/p99 for latency) for high-priority tenants. simple fifo queues allow noisy tenants to consume disproportionate kernel slots and drive slo violations. an admission controller that incorporates sla buckets, dynamic scoring, and token budgets prevents this while enabling graceful degradation for best-effort traffic.nndesign overview (high level):nn1) componentsn- runtime-admission: front-line http/grpc gateway that accepts requests, validates routing, and evaluates admission score.n- kernel-scheduler: allocates kernel slots and issues low-level backpressure when gpu resources are saturated.n- dispatcher: routes admitted requests to worker shards and observes queueing metrics.nn2) signals and inputs to admission decisionn- tenant sla tier (platinum/gold/silver/best-effort).n- real-time queue depth and queue wait time (per-tenant).n- recent kernel eviction/timeout rates and per-shard utilization.n- token budget consumption (per-tenant per-window).n- experiment/canary overrides (for rollout testing).nn3) outcome actionsn- admit immediately and assign priority metadata.n- defer (hold in bounded waiting queue with estimated wait).n- reject with structured payload (429 with retry-after and fallback model suggestion).n- route to best-effort fallback pool (quantized/low-cost variant).nnadmission algorithm (practical rules):nn- each tenant has a configured sla bucket: tier, p95_ms_target, burst_tokens_per_minute, steady_tokens_per_minute. example tiers: platinum (p95 120ms), gold (p95 200ms), silver (p95 500ms), best-effort (no p95 slo).nn- score calculation (simplified):n score (tier_weight / (1 queue_wait_ratio)) available_token_ratio - penalty(kernel_eviction_rate)n where values are normalized to 0,1. the admission threshold is configurable per-service.nn- token budgets are refilled on a leaky-bucket requests consume budget proportional to estimated token cost (sequence length model_cost_factor).nnbackpressure signals and api:nn- kernel-scheduler exposes grpc stream /v1/backpressure with messages: shard_id, congestion_level, suggested_drain_ms, affected_models.n- runtime-admission subscribes and translates congestion_level to per-tenant queue caps and admission thresholds.n- http response header additions for observability and client behavior: x-redwood-admission: admitteddeferredrejected, x-redwood-estimated-wait: , x-redwood-policy-id: .nnslos and thresholds (examples):nn- default per-tenant p95 targets (example): platinum 120ms, gold 200ms, silver 500ms.n- maximum admission queue depth per shard: 512 requests.n- defer-to-reject pivot: if average estimated wait 2 p95_target for tier and kernel_eviction_rate 0.05, switch to reject for best-effort.nnconfiguration examples (yaml):nn admission-policy.yamlnpolicy:n name: sla-aware-defaultn burst_tokens_per_minute: 10n steady_tokens_per_minute: 2nn kernel backpressure thresholdsnkernel:n congestion_levels:n - level: 0n util_pct: 0-70n - level: 1n util_pct: 71-85n - level: 2n util_pct: 86-95n - level: 3n util_pct: 96-100n level_actions:n 0: no_actionn 1: tighten_admission_by: 10n 2: tighten_admission_by: 25n 3: reject_non_critical: truennoperational runbook (oncall) - overload detection:nn1) detect: alerts to pager when aggregated kernel_utilization 92 for 60s or p95 per-tenant latency configured p95_target for two consecutive 30s windows.n2) triage: use dashboards: runtime dsid_2fdb77f4ee0f41f8bcfe3681c657f968, source_type: confluence, title: per-request kernel hedging and lazy activation guide, content: overviewn-------nthis guide documents the design, operator configuration, and runbook for the per-request kernel hedging and lazy activation mechanisms implemented in the redwood inference runtime. these features are targeted at reducing tail latency caused by kernel cold-starts, kernel contention, and cross-tenant kernel churn without sacrificing average throughput or fair resource sharing.nngoals and non-goalsn-------------------n- goals:n - reduce 99th and 99.9th percentile latency for short and medium-length generation requests by enabling hedged fallbacks and lazy kernel activation.n - limit additional cost and kernel churn by constraining hedging concurrency and using heuristics to trigger lazy activation only when beneficial.n - provide clear telemetry and operator controls to tune behavior per-tenant, per-model, and per-runtime-pool.n- non-goals:n - replace the scheduler or admission control these features are orthogonal and intentionally conservative.n - change core cost accounting semantics hedged requests are tracked for chargeback and forecasting but billed according to existing token accounting.nnarchitecture and high-level flown-------------------------------n1. request classification: incoming rpcs are annotated with request hints (sequence_length_estimate, priority_class, model_variant_hint). the classifier runs in the front-end (service: router-proxy) and tags requests that are hedge-eligible.n2. kernel lookup probe: the runtime consults the kernel catalog for the requested model_variant. if the preferred kernel instance is unavailable or in a cold state, the runtime triggers lazy activation and marks a soft deadline (hedge_deadline_ms).n3. hedged probe: at hedge_deadline_ms, the scheduler may launch a hedged request to an alternative kernel variant or a pre-warmed lightweight kernel shim (see kernel variants below).n4. fast-path response: whichever path returns first wins the other hedged request is cancelled and its metrics are recorded for hedging efficiency calculations.nnkey components and servicesn---------------------------n- router-proxy: tags requests with hints and enforces per-route hedging policy (config in /etc/redwood/router/hedge-policy.yaml).n- kernel-manager: maintains kernel lifecycle (active, warming, idle) and exposes activation apis.n- scheduler-core: decision engine that evaluates hedging eligibility against slot quotas and queue length signals.n- telemetry-collector: emits hedging metrics and traces (see observability section).nnkernel variants and fallbacksn----------------------------nwe recommend a small hierarchy of kernel variants to hedge against:n- optimized-kernel: fastest path, may require quantized kernels and certain hardware features.n- lite-kernel-shim: reduced feature set (no kv cache) but very fast to activate used as the first hedged fallback for short requests.n- cpu-emulation: last-resort fallback for durability, used only when gpu options are saturated.nnconfiguration examplesn----------------------ndefault per-tenant configuration (router/hedge-policy.yaml):nn---n hedge policy tokens per-tenantntenant_id: nhedge_enabled: truenhedge_deadline_ms: 40nmax_hedge_concurrency_per_tenant: 4nlite_kernel_activation_timeout_ms: 120nallow_cpu_fallback: falsen---nnscheduler policy snippet (scheduler/policy.d):nnpolicy hedge-lazy-activation n when request.is_short_sequence and kernel.state in idle, coldn and tenant.hedge_quota.available 0n then schedule.lazy_activate(kernel) set.deadline(40ms) allow.hedge(alternative lite-kernel-shim)nnobservability and metricsn-------------------------nrequired metrics (emitted by kernel-manager and scheduler-core):n- hedging.attempts (counter)n- hedging.successes (counter, hedged request returned first)n- hedging.failures (counter)n- hedging.cancellation_overhead_ms (histogram)n- kernel.activation.latency_ms (histogram) by kernel_variantn- kernel.usage.active_slots (gauge)n- tenant.hedge_quota.available (gauge)nnrecommended tracing spans:n- router-proxy.classify - kernel-manager.lookup - scheduler-core.decision - kernel..executenndashboards and alertsn---------------------ncreate a dashboard with the following panels:n- hedge hit rate: hedging.successes / hedging.attempts (target 0.6 for short sequences)n- hedge cost ratio: tokens_consumed_by_hedged_requests / tokens_consumed_total (warn if 0.15)n- kernel activation p95/p99 per-variant (warn if p99 250ms for lite-kernel-shim)nnalerts (examples):n- hedging.error-rate 5 sustained for 5m - page oncall (pagerduty: runtime-core)n- hedging.cost-ratio 20 for 10m - notify runtime-costs slack channelnnoperational runbook (tail-latency incident)n------------------------------------------n1. pager fires for high 99th latency.n2. open runtime dashboard, filter by route and tenant. check hedging.attempts and kernel.activation.latency_ms.n3. if hedging.attempts are high but hedging.successes are low:n a. reduce hedge_deadline_ms by 10ms increments to avoid launching costly hedges.n b. consider increasing the limit on lite-kernel pre-warmers for the affected pool (see pre-warm section).n4. if hedging.cost-ratio is high (15):n a. temporarily disable hedging for low-value tenants via router-proxy config.n b. schedule capacity bump for the affected kernel_variant.n5. if kernel.activation.latency_ms p99 spikes:n a. inspect kernel-manager logs for ooms or driver errors.n b. roll back recent kernel or driver rollouts (see rollout and compatibility).nnpre-warm and capacity controlsn-----------------------------n- pre-warm clusters: dedicated lightweight pools of lite-kernel-shim instances. use prewarm.policy.yaml to define min_ready_count per-pool.n- adaptive pre-warm heuristic: if short_sequence_rate 60 and prewarm_utilization 70 then scale pre-warm by 20.nntable: example pre-warm title: scheduler policy baseline (q1 2026 perf suite), content: purposenthis page defines the scheduler configuration baseline used for the q1 2026 perf baseline representative workload suite runs.nnthe baseline is the set of scheduler knobs (and guardrails) that are considered default-correct for benchmarking and regression detection across:n- regions: us-east, eu-westn- gpu skus: h100 / a100 / l40s (where applicable)n- workloads: chat streaming, tool/function calling, long-context prefill, embeddings high-qpsnnthe intent is to:n1) make perf results comparable over time (reproducible, attributable).n2) represent production behavior (no benchmark-only shortcuts that hide real latency sources).n3) keep the scheduler explainable under tail latency (p95/p99) investigations.nnthis baseline is referenced by the run manifest schema (see adr-0172) and is expected to be applied verbatim in baseline sweeps unless explicitly noted in the manifest.nn---nn non-goalsn- this is not a design doc for new scheduling algorithms.n- this does not define kernel selection (see kernel selection matrix (q1 2026)).n- this does not prescribe customer-specific tiering policies. it defines a stable benchmark policy that is compatible with production semantics.nn---nn glossary (scheduler-adjacent)n- ttft: time-to-first-token (server-side, first token committed to the streaming transport / response body).n- tpot: time per output token (server-side excludes client read/backpressure unless explicitly testing client pacing).n- prefill: prompt processing phase.n- decode: token generation phase.n- continuous batching: dynamic batch assembly across time while tokens are being decoded.n- queue wait: time request spends waiting in scheduler prior to admission into a batch.nnmetric boundaries for perf suite runs must follow the definitions in adr-0172 and the metrics dictionary. this page only specifies the scheduler inputs that influence those metrics.nn---nn baseline versioningnbaseline name: sched-baseline-q1-2026-v1nnbaseline anchor runtime tag (for baseline sweep signoff): runtime-q1-2026-baselinen- the exact runtime commit sha and container digest are captured in each run manifest.nnpolicy on changes: any change to baseline defaults requires:n- updating this page (and bumping baseline name suffix),n- a short rationale in the change log section, andn- a perf-suite re-calibration run if the change is expected to affect p95/p99.nn---nn scheduler architecture assumptions (as exercised by the perf suite)nthe baseline assumes a standard redwood serving topology:n- ingress admission control per-endpoint queues batch assembler gpu dispatchn- requests are categorized by route/workload mode (chat streaming vs non-streaming embeddings) and by model.n- the batch assembler supports:n - separate prefill and decode micro-batches,n - overlap of prefill/compute with decode where supported,n - kv cache accounting and guardrails.nnthis baseline uses deterministic policy choices where possible, to minimize scheduler randomness as a variance source.nn---nn baseline policy principlesn1) tail latency protection first, then throughputn - baseline aims to keep p99 ttft stable under representative traffic shapes.n - throughput optimizations must not introduce unbounded queue growth.nn2) fairness without starvationn - under mixed concurrency, smaller requests should not be permanently blocked behind long-prefill requests.nn3) explicit overload behaviorn - when capacity is insufficient, the scheduler should degrade predictably via backpressure and load-shed rules, not via timeouts.nn4) no hidden warm cache only assumptionsn - baseline supports both cold and warm cache scenarios the scheduler policies must behave safely in both.nn---nn baseline increments until the watermark is below threshold or until min_decode_microbatch_size is reached.nnrationale:n- prefill caps are set to avoid long-prefill p99 ttft cliffs caused by over-aggregation.n- decode caps constrain per-step latency spikes that disproportionately affect streaming ttfttpot tails.nn---nn queue discipline and fairness policyn selected discipline: wfq_cost_awarenwe use a cost-aware weighted fair queuing approximation over (tenant, model) flows.nnwhy wfq-like behavior vs fifo?n- fifo amplifies tail latency under heterogeneous request sizes (especially long-prefill mixed with short chat prompts).n- cost-aware selection improves mean throughput while preventing elephant requests from blocking mice requests indefinitely.nn fairness scope: per_tenant_per_modelneach (tenant, model) is treated as a fairness group. this matches our production need to prevent a single tenants workload mix from monopolizing one models capacity while still allowing different models to saturate different pools.nn anti-starvation: age boostneach queued request receives an age-based multiplier to its effective priority score.n- half-life: 2000msn- max boost: 3xnnthis is specifically to keep multi-turn tool calling and long-prefill workloads from starving behind high-qps short chats in mixed mixes.nn---nn backpressure and admission controlnadmission control is enabled and must be treated as part of the baseline (not an optional optimization).nn key thresholdsn- soft bound: max_queue_time_ms 800n - requests predicted to exceed this are rejected early with 429 scheduler_overload.n- hard bound: shed_after_queue_time_ms 1000n - if the queue contains requests older than this threshold (e.g., burst beyond expected mix), the scheduler begins load shedding by policy.nn why early reject (429) is the baseline behaviorn- prevents silent ttft blowups that turn into ambiguous client timeouts.n- keeps benchmark results interpretable: once saturation occurs, the system expresses overload explicitly.n- aligns with sre guidance that overload should page/alert based on rate of rejects rather than tail latency explosions.nn queue depth boundnmax_queue_depth_multiplier 2.0 relative to the workloads declared concurrency target.nnrationale:n- deep queues may make throughput look stable while ttft becomes non-representative.n- bounding queue depth makes saturation visible in both dashboards and manifests.nn---nn overload behaviornwhen overloaded (queue and/or kv watermark), the scheduler transitions through these stages:nn1) backpressure via admission controln - reject new requests once queue-time prediction exceeds bounds.nn2) adaptive batching reductionn - reduce effective batch size to control ttft tails (especially for long-prefill).nn3) load sheddingn - policy: drop_oldest_in_queuen - rationale: if a request has already waited long enough to violate the ttft budget, completing it is less valuable than keeping the system responsive for newly arriving short requests.nn4) hard stop / safetyn - if kv hard limit is reached: kv_hard_limit_action shed (never oom the worker during baseline runs).nnnote: the perf suite must tag overload events in results (reject rates, shed counts). any baseline run where overload dominates the sample must be marked invalid for baseline comparison unless the workload explicitly tests overload behavior.nn---nn streaming-specific behaviornstreaming adds two common sources of measurement confusion: server flush policy and client-read backpressure. the baseline defines server behavior to reduce variability:nn- server_push_only: truen - the server emits tokens on its own schedule it does not attempt to synchronize with a benchmark clients read cadence.n- stream_flush_interval_ms: 20n - chosen to approximate production streaming smoothness while limiting flush overhead.nnguidance for the perf harness:n- client must read continuously and avoid introducing backpressure.n- ttft is measured at first token committed on server side, per adr-0172.nn---nn instrumentation requirements (baseline runs)nfor q1 2026 baseline runs, instrumentation is considered mandatory (sampling 1.0). the goal is attribution, not lowest overhead.nnthe scheduler must emit at minimum:n- queue wait time histogram (per workload model)n- batch assembly time histogramn- batch size distributions (prefill and decode)n- counters: rejects, sheds, kv watermark excursionsn- correlation ids that link:n - workload generator request scheduler queue event batch event model execution tracennthis is required to support triage playbooks (see perf suite profiling playbook).nn---nn known trade-offs and rationale notesn- cost model simplicity: the token-based cost model is intentionally simple to reduce drift. it will not perfectly predict runtime cost across model families, but it substantially improves fairness vs fifo.n- aggressive queue-time bounds: we prefer explicit overload signals. this can reduce apparent throughput in extreme bursts, but makes tails interpretable and matches production expectations.n- overlap enabled: prefill/decode overlap is enabled to reflect real runtime behavior. if overlap changes between releases, that should be treated as a first-class perf change and investigated (not papered over by policy tweaks).nn---nn dsid_8d9d9c0c0e1f4ded8b83c086cef1bd0b, source_type: confluence, title: traffic mirroring end-to-end benchmark protocol, content: summarynnthis document defines the canonical end-to-end (e2e) benchmark protocol for measuring runtime performance using traffic mirroring. traffic mirroring benchmarks run real production traffic in read-only mode against candidate runtime builds, model variants, or kernel scheduling configurations. the goals are to:nn- obtain representative latency and correctness signals with minimal production risk.n- compare candidate changes to a baseline across cost and tail-latency envelopes.n- produce reproducible artifacts suitable for release gating and perf regression detection.nnscopennapplies to: eng-serving-runtime teams running hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. this protocol is intended for:n- new kernel scheduling releasesn- runtime build changes that touch request routing or batchingn- model-variant rollout validation (e.g., quantized vs float variants)n- autoscaling/slotting policy experimentsnnexcludes: experiments that mutate customer-visible state or alter traffic semantics (see safety checklist).nnkey conceptsnn- mirrored traffic: a copy of production requests sent concurrently to the candidate system without forwarding responses back to the user.n- shadow target: an isolated cluster or pool that processes mirrored traffic for measurement and logging.n- replay-safe: traffic transformed to remove sensitive pii and non-idempotent operations.nnroles and ownershipnn- benchmark owner: person who schedules and signs off the run (example: priya shah).n- runtime owner: service-level owner of the candidate runtime build.n- observability owner: responsible for ensuring required dashboards and traces are available.n- sre approval: sre must sign off for any run that exceeds baseline resource consumption thresholds.nnslos and acceptance criteriannbaseline: production cluster a (stable). candidate: cluster b (mirrored). acceptance requires:n- p50 latency delta 98. for non-deterministic outputs, use embed-similarity thresholds (cosine 0.985).nnsafety checklist (must be completed before any mirror run)nn1) sanitize inputs: remove authorization headers and any customer pii using the request-sanitizer pipeline.n2) ensure the candidate is strictly read-only: no upstream writes, no metrics emitted to billing systems.n3) mirror traffic rate scaling: start at 1 of production qps and increase only after sre approval.n4) resource isolation: shadow target must have separate autoscaling group / node-pool and no shared persistent storage with prod.n5) alerting: create temporary alert suppressions to avoid noisy page storms and ensure critical alerts still page.nnprocedure: run plannn1) prepare candidate build and environment:n - deploy candidate runtime to shadow cluster b with identical network topology and model pins.n - ensure kv cache behavior is reset unless intentionally testing cache warmup.n - tag build with bench-run// for trace correlation.nn2) configure mirroring:n - use the traffic-mirror service (internal) to configure rule: mirror-rule:--.n - example rule config (yaml):nn mirror_rule: n name: chat-completions-shadow-2027-01n source: prod-gatewayn match: path_prefix: /v1/chat/completionsn sampler: fixed_raten rate: 0.01n sanitizer: request-sanitizer-v2n targets: shadow-cluster-bnn - cli to apply (internal):n traffic-mirror apply --from prod-gateway --to shadow-cluster-b --path-prefix /v1/chat/completions --rate 0.01 --sanitizer request-sanitizer-v2 --name chat-completions-shadow-nn3) warmup and ramping:n - start with 0.1 mirror rate for 10 minutes to validate pipeline. confirm no errors and resource headroom.n - ramp to target mirror rate (commonly 1 or 5 depending on risk classification) in exponentially increasing steps (0.5, 1, 2). each step: hold for 515 minutes and observe metrics.nn4) data collection windows:n - short-run benchmarking: 3060 minutes. use when kernel or kernel-parameter changes are small.n - long-run benchmarking: 624 hours. use for model-variant comparisons or autoscaling policy changes.n - capture request/response timeline traces, kernel metrics, gpu utilization, per-token latency histograms, kv cache hit rates, and queue length series.nn5) instrumentation and required telemetrynnrequired traces/metrics (minimum):n- request.timeline: trace spans for gateway-router-runtime-kernel-executorn- runtime.latency_ms: p50/p95/p99 histograms by route and modeln- kernel.queue_length: 1s resolution time-series per gpu slotn- kernel.dispatch_time_ms: per-request quantilesn- gpu.utilization_pct: per-gpun- kvcache.hit_rate: rolling 1m and 5mn- embed-similarity: sample of 200 request pairs comparing baseline vs candidate outputsnntagging: all metrics must include bench.run_id and bench.build_tag dimensions.nnartifacts to persistnn- raw traces: stored in obs.test-bench/traces/ (retention 90d)n- aggregated histograms: obs.test-bench/histograms/.jsonn- representative sample of requests and candidate responses (sanitized): s3://bench-artifacts//samples.jsonl.gzn- perf report: s3://bench-artifacts//report.html (generated by bench-reporting tool)nnanalysis and reportingnn1) automated report generation:n - after the run finishes the bench-orchestrator will produce a summary report containing latency deltas, resource deltas (gpu-hours used), and semantic similarity.n - the report includes waterfall diagnostics for slow tail requests and a heatmap of queue growth over time.nn2) manual triage checklist:n - if p99 delta acceptance, run failure mode triage: inspect kernel dispatch traces, check for blocking allocations, and examine kernel-runloop starvation.n - compare kvcache.hit_rate trends: a sudden drop suggests cache population mismatch or differing shard keys.n - check for dispatcher backpressure events and kernel preemption counts.nn3) release gating:n - candidate passes if all acceptance criteria are met and no new critical incidents were generated during the run.n - for marginal cases, run a focused replay of suspect requests with increased sampling (100500x) to amplify differences for debugging.nntroubleshooting and common failure modesnn- symptom: elevated p95 with normal gpu utilizationn action: inspect kernel.queue_length and dispatch_time_ms for contention verify batch-slicing thresholds and preemption windows.nn- symptom: higher error rate on candidaten action: check sanitizer pipeline for malformed transformed requests validate model version pins look for ooms in runtime logs.nn- symptom: semantic drift (embed-similarity drop)n action: confirm identical tokenizer and model quantization parameters check for off-by-one sequence padding differences.nn- symptom: large cost delta with similar latencyn action: analyze per-token gpu cycles using kernel-cycle counters check for degenerate scheduling producing small, inefficient kernels (e.g., repeated tiny-attention launches).nnoperational controls and cost limitsnn- default mirror rate cap for non-critical patches: 1 of prod qps.n- for kernel/platform team experiments that intentionally stress resources, a waiver must be obtained from sre and finance for temporary increased cloud spend (submit bench-cost-waiver/).nnautomation recipes and scriptsnn- artifact retentionnn- all run artifacts are retained for 90 days by default. stakeholders must archive essential artifacts to the release retro bucket for multi-year retention if used for compliance.n- any unexpected production-facing incident correlated to a mirroring run triggers a full incident review and possible rollback of mirror permissions.nnnotes on privacy and compliancenn- traceable kernel affinity guide, content: overviewnnthis document describes a pragmatic design and operational playbook for co-scheduling mixed-size llm inference requests (small models, medium backbone models, and large-context llms) on heterogeneous gpu pools while preserving predictable latency slos and providing traceable kernel-to-request affinity for incident investigation. it complements the scheduler language profiles and heterogeneous-pool guidance its aim is prescriptive: how to set affinity, observe it end-to-end, and run safe rollouts.nnscopenn- applies to hosted and dedicated clusters that share the same scheduler control plane.n- covers inference-only workloads (token-generation and chat) and does not cover training jobs.n- targets co-location of models with different memory/compute footprints on the same compute nodes and multi-model pipelines where a single request touches more than one model.nnmotivationnnco-scheduling increases gpu utilization but introduces contention that impacts tail latency and quality (eviction of kv cache, kernel serialization). engineering teams need:nn1. a predictable model for assigning kernel affinity so traces map to requests.n2. runtime choices (slotting, preemption policy) that preserve latency budgets.n3. a rollout/runbook for experiments and regressions.nnkey concepts and definitionsnn- model size class: small (13b or long-context variants).n- kernel affinity: declarative hint that binds a requests kernel selection to a set of kernel implementations and gpu slot properties (tensor cores, persistent kernel lanes, quantized fast-paths).n- slot reservation: transient gpu resource reservation for latency-sensitive requests (duration measured in ms/tokens).n- traceable affinity token (aft): a unique trace id propagated from api gateway through the scheduler to kernel telemetry so all runtime artifacts can be correlated to the originating request.nndesign overviewnn1) affinity-first routingnn- in the routing layer, requests declare the expected model-size-class and latency tier (critical / best-effort). the routes configuration converts these into scheduler affinity tags: model_classsmall/medium/large, latency_tiercriticalstandardbackground.n- the scheduler maps affinity tags to kernel profiles and slot classes. example mapping:nn model_class latency_tier kernel_profile slot_class preemption_allowed n---------------------------------------------------------------------------n large critical large-opt-v2 reserved_hq false n medium standard medium-quant shared_mid true n small background small-fastpath opportunistic true nn2) kernel profile hintsnn- kernel_profile is a scheduler-side label that selects an ordered list of kernel implementations (e.g., tensorcore-fused, int8-quantized, fallback-generic). the runtime evaluates the list, preferring earlier entries but falling back safely.n- kernel profiles are versioned (kernel_profile: name@vn) to allow safe rollouts and telemetry rollbacks.nn3) traceable affinity propagationnn- the api gateway assigns an aft (traceable affinity token) to each request: aft format: r___. this token is:nn - logged at ingress (gateway)n - attached to rpc metadata to scheduler and runtimen - emitted in kernel telemetry as kernel.affinity_tokennn- example (pseudo-http header):nn x-affinity-token: batch slicing: spec and operational playbook, content: summary:nthis document defines the design and operational guidance for preemption-aware batch slicing a kernel-scheduler-adjacent feature that slices large inference batches into smaller execution windows aligned to expected preemption boundaries and gpu occupancy windows. the goal is to reduce tail-latency spikes caused by mid-kernel preemption, long-running kernels blocking higher-priority work, and kv-cache warmup penalties while preserving throughput and unit-cost efficiency.nnintroduction:nlarge requests and long-sequence generation can produce kernel executions that exceed preemption windows on shared gpu pools. when preemption occurs mid-kernel, it can cause: lost progress for kv cache priming, long tail latencies for higher-priority requests, and noisy gpu utilization signals that complicate autoscaling. preemption-aware batch slicing inserts low-overhead slice boundaries and scheduling hints so the kernel mapper and dispatcher can make better trade-offs between latency and efficiency.nnscope:n- applies to: runtime dispatcher kernel mapper per-shard executor on heterogeneous gpu fleets (hosted and dedicated modes).n- not in scope: model-architecture-level sequence truncation, offline compilation changes, or business-layer client batching policies.nnmotivation_and_goals:n- reduce 95th/99th percentile latency regressions caused by preemption during long kernels.n- minimize kv-cache thrash from repeated long preemptions.n- preserve (or gracefully trade) throughput for improved latency predictability.n- provide knobs for operations to tune behavior per service / customer tier.nncore_design_principles:n- non-invasive: default behavior should be conservative (opt-in per route or model bundle).n- scheduler hints: expose slice boundary hints to kernel mapper and gpu dispatcher rather than forcing a single global policy.n- cheap slicing: slices add minimal overhead ( slice_threshold_ms, candidate for slicing.n2. slice generation: generate a sequence of slice descriptors. each slice descriptor contains: slice_token_budget, expected_execution_ms, priority_hint, and cache_warmup (boolean).n3. execution model: slices are enqueued to shard executors. the kernel mapper may coalesce slices from different requests if compatibility and priority allow, subject to slice size upper bounds.n4. preemption and recovery: if a slice is preempted mid-execution, runtime records a preempted_slice event and restarts the slice respecting cache_warmup. recovery strategy prefers resuming from last kv checkpoint if supported otherwise slice is retried and warmup penalty is recorded.n5. completion semantics: final response is reassembled from slice outputs. the runtime ensures deterministic ordering and idempotency of slice execution.nninteractions_with_existing_systems:n- kv cache: slices should be sized to preserve meaningful kv reuse. the runtime tags warmup slices to avoid evicting critical entries.n- adaptive kernel mapper: uses slice.expected_execution_ms to choose different kernel implementations (fast-preemptible kernels vs high-throughput kernels).n- priority and credit accounting: slice_priority is charged against the original request budget and interacts with kernel-credit-accounting and fairness systems.n- autoscaler: emits slice-level throughput and preemption rates to autoscaler to help scaling decisions (see metrics section).nnconfiguration_reference_table:nparameter default descriptionnslice.enabled false master kill-switch. must be enabled per route or model via config blob.nslice.threshold_ms 120 estimate threshold above which requests become slicing candidates (ms).nslice.max_tokens 2048 maximum token budget for a single slice influences kernel execution time.nslice.min_tokens 16 minimum slice token size to avoid excessive overhead on tiny requests.nslice.timeout_ms 200 wall-clock timeout to cut a running slice for fairness and preemption sensitivity.nslice.priority_policy inherit inherit explicit-priority preemptible-first how a slice chooses priority.nslice.warmup_policy sticky sticky fresh whether slices assume prior kv warmup is valid.nslice.coalesce_window_ms 10 micro-window where compatible slices can be coalesced by the dispatcher.nslice.metrics_sampling 1.0 fraction of slices for detailed telemetry (0.01.0).nnsample_yaml_route_level_configuration:nroute: /v1/generate-heavynmodel: redwood/turbo-large-8knslice:n enabled: truen threshold_ms: 120n max_tokens: 1024n min_tokens: 32n timeout_ms: 250n describes the kernel handshake pattern we use to safely coordinate request routing with per-gpu kernel schedulers and how the runtime performs adaptive fallback when preferred kernels are unavailable or failing. the goal is to make fallbacks deterministic, explainable, and observable while minimizing latency and preserving slos.nnaudiencenn- runtime engineers implementing or modifying schedulers and routing policiesn- oncall and sre teams who need runbook steps for kernel-induced degradationn- product engineers who require guarantees about fallback behavior for slasnngoals and non-goalsnn- goals:n - define a lightweight, versioned handshake protocol between the router and kernel scheduler that captures capability, health, and cost signals.n - standardize adaptive fallback policies and preemption semantics across gpu pools.n - provide observability and rollout guidance to minimize regression risk.n- non-goals:n - replace the global scheduler language (dsl) this pattern plugs into the existing policy layer.n - solve long-term capacity planning it is an operational/runtime contract for request handling.nndesign principlesnn1. idempotent negotiation: handshake messages can be retried safely without side-effects.n2. backward compatibility: support protocol version negotiation to allow staggered kernel rollouts.n3. fast-path first: attempt the low-latency preferred kernel if not possible, fall back quickly to an alternative.n4. signal-driven decisions: prefer decisions based on current kernel health, queue depth, and observed tail latency.n5. observability by design: generate events for handshake start/complete/fail and fallback decisions with contextual metadata.nnhigh-level flow (text diagram)nn1) ingress router receives request with routing policy / model variant preference.n2) router issues a kernelhandshakerequest to the selected gpu shards scheduler.n3) scheduler evaluates capabilities, availability, and local constraints and replies with kernelhandshakeresponse.n4) if response accept and slot_id assigned, request proceeds.n5) if response defer or reject, router evaluates fallback policies (fast fallback, queued retry, or alternative model variant).nnkernelhandshakerequest / response schema (json examples)nn- request (router - scheduler):nnn protocol_version: 2026-01,n request_id: req-1234-abcd,n model_variant: redwood-v2-8k-quant,n sequence_length: 512,n latency_budget_ms: 80,n priority: standard,n trace_context: trace-..,n client_tier: hosted,n features: kvcache-enabled,temperature:0.2nnn- response (scheduler - router):nnn protocol_version: 2026-01,n request_id: req-1234-abcd,n status: acceptdeferrejectneeds_fallback,n slot_id: slot-5,n expected_queue_ms: 12,n reason: gpu_busykernel_mismatchmemory_pressure,n kernel_hint: q4b_hybrid_kernel_v3,n telemetry_tokens: khs-evt-5432nnnstatus semanticsnn- accept: scheduler has reserved compute slot router should forward the request immediately.n- defer: scheduler suggests retry after expected_queue_ms router may either wait up to latency_budget_ms or perform a fast fallback depending on policy.n- reject: scheduler cannot serve (capacity, incompatible kernel, or critical error). router must select fallback immediately.n- needs_fallback: scheduler can serve a compatible but lower-cost/quality kernel variant (explicit kernel_hint provided).nnstate machine (router perspective)nn1. try_preferred - (accept) - sent_to_kernel - completedn2. try_preferred - (defer) - wait_or_fallback - (retry handshake) or (fallback_decision)n3. try_preferred - (reject/needs_fallback) - fallback_select - handshake_fallbacknnadaptive fallback policies (recommended presets)nn- fast fallback (default for latency-sensitive keys): on defer 10ms or reject, immediately select the next compatible kernel variant and attempt handshake. max two fallback hops.n- quality-preserving fallback (for high-quality routes): allow one deferred retry with exponential backoff (10ms - 25ms), then fallback.n- budget-aware fallback: factor in per-token cost budget prefer cheaper kernel_hint when cost remaining scheduler roundtrip)n- fallback_rate and fallback_hops distributionn- deferred_retry_success_raten- preemption_count and forced_eviction_countnnrollout checklist for changes to handshake/scheduler logicnn1. unit integration tests validating backward and forward protocol version negotiation.n2. canary rollout to single region and non-critical tenant pool for 48 hours.n3. observe handshake latency and fallback_rate require fallback_rate delta sla threshold)n 1. identify whether router-scheduler rtt or scheduler decision time is root cause. use trace_id from kernel_handshake.start/result pairs.n 2. if router network rtt high, verify cross-az connectivity and dns resolution.n 3. if scheduler decision path slow, capture a scheduler profile sample (see profiling section below) and annotate change.nnprofiling guidance message. schedulers must support at least the last two major protocol versions.n- routers vend protocol_version header set to their implementation version schedulers may reply with negotiated_version verification manual, content: summarynnthis document specifies the deterministic scheduler simulation and verification manual used to assert functional and latency determinism for the runtime scheduler. it defines the simulation harness, reproducible test vectors, verification metrics, and an operational rollout plan for scheduler changes that must preserve determinism guarantees when enabled.nngoalsnn- provide a repeatable simulation harness that deterministically replays request surfaces, resource events, and kernel execution ordering.n- define acceptance tests and metrics for determinism regressions (bit-level or behavioral).n- give a practical verification and rollout procedure for scheduler code changes, including fuzzing, shadow validation, and staged canaries.n- document common sources of non-determinism and mitigations.nnscope and audiencennintended for runtime engineers, scheduler maintainers, test-infra owners, and oncall. this applies to core scheduler components: admission controller, slot allocator, preemption/cooperative handoff, kernel mapper, and the admission backpressure loop. it does not replace performance benchmarking (see benchmarking-and-perf-suite).nnbackground and rationalennthe scheduler influences tail latency and correctness of prefix/kv cache warmup, eviction decisions, and kernel assignment. small non-deterministic changes can produce variable slo regressions that are hard to triage in production. enforcing deterministic behavior in simulation lets us:nn- isolate regressions to code diffs quickly.n- reproduce field incidents in a lab without noisy environmental factors.n- provide stronger invariants for rollback gates.nnkey definitionsnn- deterministic run: a simulation run that, given the same seed and input trace, produces the same discrete decision sequence (admit/reject/slot-id/kernel-id/preempt events), and the same timeline of observable scheduling events.n- pseudo-deterministic run: same high-level sequence but differing low-level timings within acceptable epsilon (used for gpu kernel jitter tolerant checks).nndesign overviewnn1) deterministic scheduler mode: a test-only compilation flag that enforces ordered processing in places where production uses best-effort parallelism. when enabled:n - single-threaded logical decision loop with explicit event queue ordering.n - rng seeded from test vector header.n - kernel hinting decisions resolved using stable tie-breaker rules (e.g., sort by tenant-id then request-id).nn2) simulation harness (scheduler-sim):n - accepts input corpus: request traces, hardware event streams (thermal/power/capacity changes), and injected noise profiles.n - produces deterministic traces, event logs, and a decision diff artifact for golden comparison.nn3) trace format and seed model:n - each trace file is a newline-delimited json (ndjson) where each record includes: timestamp_ns, request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, sequence_length, token_count, client_priority, and optional kernel_hint. a header line includes a 64-bit seed and metadata.nnsimulation harness architecturenn- injector: replays request events into the scheduler sim at virtual timestamps.n- virtualclock: drives timers deterministically (no reliance on host os clock).n- kernelsimulator: models kernel execution duration deterministically from kernel profile lookup table (see profiling corpus).n- schedulercore: the deterministic decision engine (admission, slot allocation, preemption resolution).n- snapshotter: records deterministic state checkpoints (admission queues, slot maps, kvcache indexes) at configured intervals.nntest corpora and sourcesnn- production traces: anonymized and sampled workload traces from shadow-mirroring (sanitized).n- synthetic fuzz corpus: generated request shapes stressing edge cases: bulk-preempt, microbursts, long-seq streaming, 50/50 tinylong tokens.n- kernel latency profiles: extracted from profiling-playbook lab runs stored as stable fixture and used to compute kernelsimulator durations.nnverification metricsnn metric type pass threshold notes n------:---:---n decision sequence equality binary exact match byte-for-byte sequence of decision events vs golden n event timeline delta numeric (ns) 5000ms for long traces where first divergence occurs higher is better n stateful snapshot hash equality binary exact match hash of serialized scheduler snapshot at checkpoints n non-deterministic source counter numeric 0 new sources number of code paths flagged as non-deterministic since last accepted run nnprocedure: local verification (developer flow)nn1) run unit-level deterministic scheduler mode: builddeterministic make scheduler-simn2) pick a canonical trace: tools/sim/select_trace --namecanary-compact-2025.ndjsonn3) execute: ./bin/scheduler-sim --tracecanary-compact-2025.ndjson --seed0x5a3f1c9b --snapshot-interval500ms --outputout/n4) validate range.nnprocedure: ci verification gatesnn1) on pull request that touches scheduler code, ci triggers deterministic-sim job with 3 canonical traces (fast, mixed, long-tail).n2) ci compares decision sequence equality and snapshot-hash equality.n3) if ci fails: require explicit reviewer signoff and an exemption note in the pr if the change is expected to be non-deterministic (rare).nnfuzzing and stress verificationnn- differential fuzzing harness: runs the same trace under deterministic and production-parallel modes and compares high-level invariants (no deadlock, admission fairness, memory usage bounds).n- randomized seed sweep: run n256 seeds for each fuzz-input and record any divergence. seeds that cause divergence must be captured and promoted as a reproducible minimal test case.n- adversarial microbursts: synthetic traces with 100x baseline concurrency spikes to test slot starvation and preemption fairness.nnsources of non-determinism and mitigationsnn1) parallel reduction order (gpu-side): enforce canonical ordering by adding an ordering step in kernel mapper during verification builds.n2) network io arrival jitter: use virtualclock and deterministic injector instead of wall-time in sim.n3) thread scheduling in c worker pools: deterministic mode uses a single logical decision thread production differences caught by differential fuzz harness.n4) rng without seed: all rng usage must accept an explicit seeded rng from harness. add linter rule: no std::random_device without injection.n5) external system calls that return ordered-but-non-deterministic values: wrap and stub in sim.nnsimulation configuration reference (yaml example)nnsim-config.yaml:n seed: 0x5a3f1c9bn traces:n - name: canary-compact-2025n file: traces/canary-compact-2025.ndjsonn title: kernel benchmarking methodology (top hosted models): fp8/int8 vs baseline, content: purposenthis page defines the benchmark methodology we use to compare kernel paths (baseline fp16/bf16 vs fp8 and int8 variants) for redwoods top hosted models. the intent is to produce results that are:n- reproducible across clusters and over timen- representative of production traffic (prompt generation distributions concurrency prefill/decode mix)n- actionable for runtime decisions (kernel auto-selection, scheduler tuning, quantization profile policy)nnthis methodology is mandatory for results that will be used to:n- change kernel dispatch/auto-selection defaultsn- gate rollouts via perf canary thresholdsn- update internal/external performance narrativesnn---nn key definitions (what we measure)nwe distinguish kernel-level results from end-to-end serving results.nn kernel-level (microbench)nmeasures isolated kernel performance and/or tight operator sequences (e.g., attention, matmul) under controlled shapes.n- pros: low noise shape-specific insight faster iterationn- cons: does not capture scheduler interaction, request arrival patterns, kv-cache behavior under loadnn end-to-end (serving bench)nmeasures the runtime in a realistic serving loop with batching, kv cache, scheduler behavior, and realistic request mix.n- pros: what customers feel (ttft/tpot/throughput) captures interaction effectsn- cons: higher noise more confounders (thermals, clocks, contention)nn primary metrics (serving)n- ttft (time to first token): from request enqueue to first generated token (includes prefill scheduling delays)n- tpot (time per output token): average per-token latency during decode (reported as ms/token)n- tokens/s (throughput): aggregate output tokens per second at a given loadn- error rate: non-2xx / model errors / correctness fallbacks engagednn primary metrics (microbench)n- kernel latency (us / call) and derived tflop/s where applicablen- achieved memory bandwidth (gb/s) where applicablen- occupancy / launch configuration (for diagnosis, not for win criteria)nn---nn workload taxonomy (prefill vs decode)nwe always report at least these workloads per prompt-length distribution (see below)n- output: 0 generated tokens (or minimal fixed output 1 token) to isolate prefilln- report: ttft proxy (prefill time) and prefill tokens/snn w2: decode-only (kv-cache heavy)ngoal: measure steady-state decode performance and kv-cache behavior.n- input: fixed prompt (small, e.g., 3264 tokens) to establish kv cachen- output: generation length sampled from distribution (see below)n- report: tpot and decode tokens/snn w3: mixed prefill decode (representative)ngoal: capture the production-like interaction where prefill and decode compete for gpu time, and alignment edge cases).n- input prompts at the 9599th percentile prompt lengths (bounded by model context)n- report: same as w1/w3 plus error/fallback countersnn---nn representative sequence-length warmup).nnrationale:n- stabilizes clocks/thermals, jit/compile paths (if any), allocator state, and cache behavior.nn measurement windown- minimum: 10 minutes of measurements for end-to-end serving confluence, title: sequencing fence and slot coordination manual, content: summary:nthis manual describes the sequencing fence and slot coordination model used by the execution coordinator and kernel scheduler to preserve slos under mixed workloads. it combines the admission (rate-fence) model, slot reservation semantics, and reactive backpressure with practical tuning steps, diagnostics, and a short benchmarking protocol for validating changes.nnscope and goals:n- define semantics: what a sequencing fence is, how slots are reserved/released, and guarantees provided to callers.n- provide configuration table of key knobs with safe default ranges.n- give step-by-step tuning recipes for common workload classes (conversational, batch embeddings, long-completion document generation).n- runbook for operational incidents involving slot exhaustion, priority inversion, and noisy-tenant interference.n- benchmark and profiling procedure to validate changes to marshaling and coordination paths.nnaudience:n- runtime engineers (primary), sres oncall, platform pms, and solutions engineers who operate dedicated/private deployments.nnbackground and motivation:nredwoods serving runtime multiplexes heterogeneous requests across a pool of kernels. without coordinated sequencing and slot fencing, high-concurrency short requests can starve long-running kernels (priority inversion) or fragment gpu resources causing kv-cache churn. the sequencing fence enforces a deterministic execution order for critical request classes and exposes quota/slot accounting so higher layers can make routing/fallback decisions.nnconcepts and definitions:n1) slot: an opaque capacity unit representing a kernel execution entitlement (not a single gpu thread). slots have attributes: affinity (gpu type), duration_hint (ms), priority, and cohort_id (cohort for routing).n2) sequencing fence: a lightweight barrier injected by the execution coordinator that serializes the order of token-emit critical sections across slots in a shard. fences are soft (preemption allowed) or hard (no preemption while holding).n3) rate-fence (admission): policy layer that rejects/queues requests based on token cost projection and current active_slots. it is evaluated pre-scheduling and periodically recomputed from telemetry.n4) reservation lease: ephemeral lease recorded in slot ledger auto-renewed by the kernel operator or released on heartbeat loss.nnarchitecture (text diagram):n- frontend api - admission layer (rate-fence) - execution coordinator - slot ledger - scheduler - kernel dispatcher - gpu kernelsn- observability hooks: admission.decisions, slot.ledger.delta, fence.events, kernel.handoff.tracennkey metrics and slo guardrails:n- slot_utilization_pct (slo: 60 and 0 over 15m for dedicated clusters)nnconfiguration table (knobs and safe defaults):n- admission.window_seconds: 1 - 60 (default 5) sliding window used to project token cost.n- slot.max_concurrent_per_gpu: 8 - 256 (default 64) soft cap, tuned per-gpu family.n- fence.type: soft hard hybrid (default hybrid) hybrid uses soft by default, switches to hard for long duration ops.n- reservation.lease_ms: 2000 - 30000 (default 8000)n- priority.boost_threshold_ms: 50 - 200 (default 100) if a request waits longer than this, it receives temporary priority boost.nntuning recipes (high-level):n1) conversational (many short requests, strict p95 latency):n - reduce admission.window_seconds to 2s.n - enable fence.hybrid with soft locked for inference emission.n - lower slot.max_concurrent_per_gpu for the cohort serving chat to 32 to reduce kernel contention.n - observe fence_hold_time_p95 if 20ms, increase per-cohort isolation (dedicated slots).nn2) embeddings batch (large batch throughput):n - increase admission.window_seconds to 10s to allow batching.n - set reservation.lease_ms to 12000 to reduce churn.n - use hard fences for batch completion steps to ensure kv-cache coherency.nn3) long-document generation (high duration, medium concurrency):n - use hybrid fences that escalate to hard when duration_hint 2000ms.n - pre-reserve slots at admission time (reservation.preallocatetrue).n - enable priority_boost_threshold_ms for tail mitigation.nnoperational runbook: slot exhaustion incidentn1) detection: alert if slot_utilization_pct 95 or admission_reject_rate 10 sustained for 5m.n2) immediate mitigation actions (oncall):n - identify noisy cohort: query slot.ledger.delta for top 5 cohort_id by delta_slots over last 5m.n - if noisy tenant is non-critical, apply temporary quota reduction: curl -xpost coordinator/admin/quota -d cohort_id:x,max_slots:nn - if widespread, enable emergency shedding: admission.modereject-nonpremiumn3) root-cause steps:n - pull kernel traces: use ingest tool: ./tools/collect-trace --trace-type kernel-handoff --since 15m /tmp/handoff.tracen - inspect fence.events for hard fence hold durations: query metrics.fence_hold_time_p95n - check slot lease churn: count heartbeat timeouts in slot.ledger events.n4) post-incident: run traffic-simulation to reproduce the spike and iterate tuning (see benchmarking section).nnpriority inversion detection mitigationn- detection signal: priority_inversion_incidents 0 or slow_p99 among high-priority cohort increases 3x baseline.n- fast mitigation: enable short preemption window (fence.preempt_window_ms 25) and run a micro-eviction for low-priority ephemeral slots.n- longer remediation: adjust scheduler.policy_weights to favor latency-sensitive cohorts and schedule gradual
