load-shedding, content: overviewnnthis playbook documents a pragmatic, bounded-degradation approach to handling short-duration traffic spikes and sustained peaky traffic in the redwood inference runtime. it defines: roles and ownership, observable triggers, a prioritised set of degradation modes, safe limits (bounds), automated and manual escalation paths, and rollback/validation steps. the intent is to preserve customer-facing availability while protecting core slos and preventing systemic instability.nnwhy a bounded approach?n- keep sla-preserving behavior predictable: avoid uncontrolled, global model fallbacks.n- preserve fairness: ensure high-priority tenants retain minimum guarantees.n- limit blast radius: degrade in defined steps with clear metrics and automated rollback.nnscope and assumptionsn- applies to redwood hosted runtime and dedicated pools where runtime controls are available.n- assumes per-tenant request classification, priority labels, and token-level billing metadata are present.n- assumes observability: request rate, accepted concurrency, queue depth, kernel utilization, gpu memory pressure, kv cache hit rate, and per-model latency percentiles.nnowners and contactsn- primary oncall: eng-sre/runtime-oncall (pager duty)n- runtime product owner: priya shahn- escalation: runtime lead (ethan morales), serving runtime sre (sofia liu)nnkey slos referencedn- 99th-percentile completion latency (stable tier): 500msn- availability (requests returning non-5xx): 99.9 monthlyn- per-tenant reserved throughput (dedicated): honoured to 95 during degraded modenndegradation modes (ordered, bounded)n1) soft shaping at ingress (non-blocking)n - intent: reduce burstiness while avoiding immediate request rejectionn - mechanism: token bucket smoothing at edge with per-tenant burst credits and circuit windowing.n - bound: max 30s queuing per request drop to next mode if queue depth 1,000 or average queue wait 20ms for 30s.nn2) priority-aware admission control (graceful rejection)n - intent: protect high-priority tenants by shedding lowest priority requests firstn - mechanism: runtime admission controller applies per-priority thresholds (see table below).n - bound: no more than 40 rejection rate for best-effort class sustained over a 5m window without human approval.nn3) model fidelity stepdown (compute-sparing variants)n - intent: lower per-token gpu work while maintaining semantic usefulnessn - mechanism: route to lower-precision / quantized variant or smaller model family per policy.n - bound: maximum 2 fidelity steps (e.g., 16-bit - 8-bit quantized - opt-small) avoid more than one model-family reduction for paid sla customers.nn4) kv-cache prefilling and prefix aggregationn - intent: reduce repeated compute for conversational sessions by prefetching kv caches for hot prefixes and collapsing repeated prefixes server-side.n - mechanism: adaptive cache prefetch hints and short-term prefix coalescing.n - bound: additional memory reserved for prefetching capped at 10 of node gpu memory disable if memory pressure 65.nn5) graceful stub responses soft-fail hooksn - intent: avoid errors when even step 3 cannot meet latency slos by returning deterministic, labelled low-fidelity responses or partial tokens with fallback metadata.n - mechanism: system injects a gpu saturation incidents using incident bot v2 saturation cards and standard redwood dashboards. it maps bot-reported signals (gpu utilization, queue depth, kv cache pressure, scheduler/backpressure time: waiting requests before admission to gpu execution. high queue is the most actionable saturation indicator.n- scheduler backpressure / admission control: runtime is refusing or delaying work to protect latency or memory.n- kv cache pressure: cache memory nearing limit evictions/thrash increase decode latency and can trigger oom safety behavior.n- prefill vs decode: prefill (prompt pinned to region/model? 1) shift traffic to other region/pool (routing/fallback) 2) temporarily tighten per-tenant limits 3) add capacity / raise autoscale ceiling n gpu util 95100, queue rising, latency, and eventual gpu ooms due to keycache index inconsistency after journal compaction.nnthis page supersedes the emergency notes in eng-424242 by consolidating the confirmed root cause, the runtime-2.4.x hotfix behavior, and operational procedures for hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.nn summary (what happened)nover multiple escalations (hosted dedicated), customers reported affected cases, stale index entries prevented proper eviction. under fragmentation, the gpu allocator entered a stall pattern (increased reserve/retry loops), leading to runaway reservation for a subset of sessions and eventual oom.nn confirmed root cause (updated)nthe initial hypothesis (dangling pointers in the merge path) was partially correct but incomplete.nnconfirmed cause (runtime-2.4.0 through runtime-2.4.1):na race condition in the keycache journal compaction snapshot merge path where concurrent eviction and a compaction commit could publish a partially-updated index view. the index version could advance while a subset of segments still referenced pre-compaction offsets, producing a mixed-generation index.nnwhy it showed up cross-environment:nhosted, dedicated, and private deployments manifested at different thresholds because:n- workload mixes differed (long-tail autoregressive vs. short requests)n- memory pressure differed (fragmentation tolerance varies by gpu sku and co-tenant load)n- some environments had higher compaction frequency due to key churnnnsecondary amplifiers:n- long-tail autoregressive requests with large kv footprints avoid typical short-circuit evictions.n- fragmentation increases allocator compaction overhead once stalls begin, handle cleanup lags, increasing pressure further.nn blast radius / customer impactn- high severity when it triggers: request failures due to oom, degraded throughput, and sometimes traffic migration.n- hosted: multi-tenant transient throttles and elevated retries.n- dedicated/private: prolonged degradation possible if nodes are not restarted or upgraded.nn when to use this runbooknuse this runbook when you observe any combination of:n1) rapidly increasing gpu memory (allocated or reserved) without matching throughputn2) keycache index resync loops and/or elevated compaction latencyn3) gpu allocator stall metrics increasing (reserve failures, retry loops)n4) ooms on long-running sessions that do not reproduce on fresh podsnn signals and dashboardsnprimary dashboards:n- memory fragmentation / arena metrics: gpu oom heatmap: metrics to watch (names may differ slightly by cluster):n- runtime.gpu.memory_reserved_bytes vs runtime.gpu.memory_allocated_bytes (gap indicates fragmentation/reservation pressure)n- runtime.session.handle_leaks (if available)nn triage checklist (15 allocator stall metrics.n - check for index resync spikes and compaction spikes.nn3. identify runtime versionn - versions at highest risk: runtime-2.4.0, runtime-2.4.1.n - hotfix versions: runtime-2.4.2-hotfix (preferred) and runtime-2.4.1-hotfix (intermediate, if already deployed).nn4. decide immediate mitigationn - if active ooms: apply emergency mitigations first (below), then proceed to rollout/upgrade.nn immediate mitigations (no code change)n mitigation a: reduce long-lived session pressuren- temporarily lower max session ttl (if supported by the serving config) and/or reduce max context length for affected endpoints.n- preferably target only the affected model deployment(s) to minimize customer impact.nn mitigation b: force safe eviction mode (runtime flag)nif the runtime guide, content: overviewnnthis document defines the adaptive request shaper and priority synthesis subsystem: a runtime-layer component that shapes incoming inference traffic, synthesizes per-request priority scores, and coordinates with kernel scheduling and batching to meet latency slos while minimizing cost. it covers high-level architecture, scheduling interactions, telemetry and profiling guidance, integration with the benchmarking suite, release and rollout checklist, and an operational runbook.nnwhy this existsnn- problem: production llm workloads exhibit widely varying sequence lengths, cold prefixes, and priority semantics (interactive vs background). static admission controls either waste gpu cycles or violate latency slos.n- goal: provide a predictable, transparent shaping layer that maps business intents (user-facing vs background, deadline, cost-sensitivity) to runtime actions (admit, delay, throttle, reroute) and exposes deterministic knobs for sre/product to tune.nnscope and non-goalsnn- in-scope: admission control, token-budget-aware shaping, deadline-aware batching hints, priority score synthesis and annotation, integration points to kernel scheduler and batcher, relevant telemetry and dashboards.n- out-of-scope: model optimizer internals, kv cache replication, network-level routing across regions (handled by smart routing).nndesign overviewnn1) request api annotationsn- new optional fields the api accepts (internal header or sdk metadata):n - priority_hint: interactivestandardbackgroundn - deadline_ms: integer (soft deadline relative to request arrival)n - cost_sensitivity: lowmediumhigh (guides quantization/cache preference)n - work_token_budget: integer (max tokens allowed for request)nn2) priority synthesizern- consumes api annotations, historical per-identity tail-latency distribution, and a local cost estimator to compute a normalized priority_score in 0.0, 1.0.n- score semantics: closer to 1.0 higher admission and preference for low-latency kernels and smaller batches. scores are deterministic given inputs for reproducibility in benchmarking.nn3) adaptive shaper / admission controllern- core responsibilities:n - admit immediately to active queue (fast-path)n - place in delay queue with per-client backoff (soft-hold)n - reject with structured error or reroute to cheaper model variant (fallback mapper)n - annotate requests with batch hints (min_batch_size, max_wait_ms) for the batchern- local policy uses dynamic thresholds computed from target slo utilization and observed kernel queue lengths.nn4) scheduler interaction pointsn- kernel scheduler accepts requests annotated with priority_score and batch hints. the scheduler maps high priority requests onto preemptible gpu lanes or hot-shard contexts lower priority requests are eligible for cooperative preemption.nn5) cost estimatorn- lightweight model that provides per-request expected token-cost given current quantization profile and kv cache hit probability. used in priority synthesis when cost_sensitivity is set.nnconfiguration (defaults and critical knobs)nnconfiguration table (values represent recommended defaults for hosted tier):nn parameter default description operational range unit n----------------------------------------------------------n global_target_p99_ms 200 target p99 latency for interactive route 50-1000 ms n fastpath_queue_depth 256 max parallel requests admitted to fast-path 64-2048 requests n delay_queue_base_ms 30 base delay for soft-hold queue 10-200 ms n priority_decay_half_life_s 120 half-life for historical tail influence 30-600 s n min_batch_hint 1 minimum suggested batch size to batcher 1-16 tokens/requests n max_batch_wait_ms 30 maximum batch wait the shaper suggests 5-200 ms n cost_weight 0.3 weight on cost_sensitivity in score calc 0.0-1.0 fractional nnexample runtime config (yaml fragment):nnshaper:n enabled: truen global_target_p99_ms: 200n fastpath_queue_depth: 256n procedures for the redwood serving runtime to preserve customer latency slos while maximizing gpu utilization. it consolidates scheduler signals, kernel boundary preemption, and kv/prefix cache warm-start techniques into an operationally safe procedure that on-call and platform engineers can follow during scale events, upgrades, and transient overloads.nnscope:n- applies to gpu-backed serving nodes running the redwood inference runtime (all major variants: hosted, dedicated, private).n- focused on interactive text-generation and chat endpoints with strict p50/p95 latency slos ( 95 for 5s) and incoming request priority background reject with 429/backoff header background work should not destabilize interactive slos n node overloaded and incoming request priority standard try cooperative preemption: identify background lanes to evict preserves mid-tier throughput while protecting high-priority clients n node overload rolling upgrade drain graceful preempt with warm-start enabled avoids cold-cache penalties at the cost of short quiesce windows nnoperational parameters (recommended defaults):n- kernel preemption check interval: 1-3 kernel boundaries per request (every 8-16 transformer layers or 50-200ms for long decodes).n- preemption fencing timeout: 200ms (must be 60s.n- max concurrent warm-start restores: 4 per node to limit ssd contention.nnrunbook: normal-scale preemption flow (engineer-facing)n1) detect: alert fires when cluster-wide overload fraction 10 and observed p95 target for 2 minutes.n2) evaluate: check agent dashboard: preemptible-lanes metric, current kernel preemption events, and ssd write queue depth.n3) trigger soft-throttle: increase rejection probability for background priority by 20 via gateway feature flag.n4) if slos do not recover in 2 minutes, enable cooperative eviction on suspect nodes: set scheduler flag enable_coop_preempttrue for affected pool.n5) monitor: watch metrics (listed below). if eviction errors or excessive cold-starts occur, roll back the flag immediately and open an incident.nnemergency eviction flow (when nodes must be drained for hardware or security patch):n1) set graceful-drain60s for maintenance windows, enable warm-start checkpoints.n2) scheduler marks node as draining new high-priority requests are migrated immediately, background lanes are queued for eviction.n3) runtime performs ordered checkpointing of kv caches for active sessions and flushes ephemeral artifacts to local ssd with immediate replication to a standby within the az.n4) after checkpoint success or fencing timeout, scheduler migrates in-flight sessions to target nodes and resumes traffic.nnkv cache warm-start details:n- what we save: minimal per-session kv ranges (start/end positions), per-segment attention state, and a 64-byte session manifest. avoid saving full activations.n- format: lz4-compressed protobuf manifest per-shard segment files. example path: signals:n - kernel_slowdown_ratio (fraction of kernels reporting latency_baseline): 15 sustained 3m - stage-2n- memory and paging signals:n - gpu_memory_free_ratio 1000/min - stage-2n- kvcache miss storms:n - kvcache_miss_rate 0.4 for active sessions and kv_prefetch_rate stage-1n- backpressure and queueing:n - dispatcher_queue_length / max_slots 0.6 - stage-1 0.9 - stage-2nndecision matrix escalate to oncall owner): perform kernel binary rollback, scale cluster capacity beyond autoscaler limits, initiate customer-facing incident comms.nndecision matrix (table)n triggering signal dsid_124ebf7f3dfc461480f8989d610a79b7, source_type: confluence, title: kvcache epoch synchronization and repair procedures, content: overviewn--------nthis page documents the operational contract, detection signals, and step-by-step repair procedures for kv cache (kvcache) epoch divergence across runtime shards and kernels. the document is intended for oncall sres, runtime engineers, and release engineers executing maintenance or incident mitigation related to kvcache epoch drift, partial corruption, or replay divergence.nnintro and intentn- the kvcache is a soft-state prefix/kv cache used by the serving runtime to avoid recomputing early key/value activations for long-context workloads.n- an epoch is an integer monotonic marker stamped into shard-local kvcache state at the time of checkpoint or warmstart. epochs must be aligned for a shard group to accept replayed prefix tokens and to safely resume session continuation across host failovers.n- this runbook covers: detection signals, triage, safe repair patterns (resync, targeted purge, rehydrate), verification checks, and automated mitigation best practices.nnfast summary (tldr)n1) if the alert kvcache_epoch_mismatch fires, do not mass-purge immediately. run the inspection steps below to determine divergence scope (single shard, cohort, or cluster).n2) for single-shard epoch mismatch with low error rate: attempt soft resync (admin api epoch bump passive replay) - verify hashes - promote.n3) for cohort-level drift or corruption: perform coordinated epoch rotate with drain and staged rehydrate (detailed below).n4) if disk-backed checkpoint is corrupted, engage oncall runtime-owner and disable cross-shard routing until fixed.nnobservability signals and thresholdsn- alerts (prometheus/alertmanager):n - kvcache_epoch_mismatch (firing when 0.5 shard request failures referencing mismatched epoch over 5m)n - kvcache_rehydrate_failure_rate (1 failed rehydrates per shard over 5m)n - kvcache_hash_divergence (binary alert when checksum mismatch detected during meta-replay verification)n - kvcache_eviction_surge (when eviction rate increases 5x baseline for a shard cohort)nn- key metrics to inspect (promql examples):n - rate of epoch mismatch: sum(rate(kvcache_epoch_mismatch_events5m)) by (shard)n - hash divergence ratio: sum(kvcache_hash_mismatch_total) / sum(kvcache_hash_checks_total)n - rehydrate latency p95: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(kvcache_rehydrate_latency_bucket5m)) by (le))nntelemetry artifacts to collect before repairn1) kvcache meta dump (http api): curl -ss meta-shard-shard.jsonn2) kvcache local checksum: rwi kvcache inspect --shard shard --checksum checksum-shard.txtn3) short trace covering a mismatched request: trace id from logs and link to tracing uin4) node runtime logs (last 1h) and kernel handshake logsnntriage flow (detailed)n1) scope detection (3 quick checks)n a) is the mismatch limited to a single shard? query meta for epoch values across the shard group:n - admin api: /kvcache/meta?cohortcohort_idn - if only one shard shows a different epoch, proceed with single-shard repair.n b) does the hash divergence alert also fire? if no, consider epoch misstamp (clock skew or delayed checkpoint) rather than corruption.n c) check shard health: rehydrate errors, oom logs, kernel panic, disk io errors. if hardware symptoms present, escalate to infra sre.nn2) impact assessmentn - compute affected request percentage (use kvcache_epoch_mismatch events correlated with request counts). if 5 or critical customer routes affected, escalate to incident severity and use coordinated rotate.nnrepair proceduresn-----------------na. safe soft resync (preferred when divergence is minor and single-shard)n1) preconditions:n - divergence confirmed on single shard only.n - no disk corruption indicated.n - rehydrate latency within normal bounds.n2) steps:n 1. put shard into passive mode: curl -x post 2. bump epoch via admin api (this triggers a soft checkpoint boundary):n - curl -x post 3. allow the shard to receive passive replay traffic for 30s to 2m to rehydrate prefixes from normal request flow.n 4. run checksum verification: rwi kvcache inspect --shard shard --verifyn 5. if checksums match cohort leader, set mode back to active: curl -x post post-verify steps:n - monitor kvcache_epoch_mismatch and kvcache_hash_divergence for 10m. if no recurrence, close incident.nnb. targeted purge and rehydrate (use when some prefixes are corrupted)n1) preconditions:n - hash divergence localized to identifiable prefix ranges or key patternsn - customer request impact moderaten2) steps:n 1. identify offending prefix hash set from meta dump.n 2. use targeted purge api: curl -x post --data prefixes:hk:abc...,hk:xyz...n 3. wait for background rehydrate to repopulate from canonical model execution or forward the next n matching requests through bypass path to rebuild state.n 4. verify each purged prefix checksum after rehydration.nnc. coordinated epoch rotate (cohort-level)n1) preconditions:n - multi-shard or cohort-level epoch mismatch or corruptionn - rolling soft options failed or not applicablen2) safety checklist (pre-rotate)n - notify customers via incident channel if 5 request impactn - confirm backups of disk checkpoints available and validatedn - verify automated rollback playbooks present and tested in labn3) coordination steps (sequence)n 1. set cohort to read-only routing (no new sessions anchored to this cohort).n 2. for each shard in cohort, in parallel: mark passive - drain existing requests - snapshot meta - force epoch bump - restart kvcache process if necessary. use the orchestration tool: rwi kvcache rotate-cohort --cohort cohort_id --mode coordinatedn 3. wait for rehydration and cross-shard checksum convergence. allow at least 5m for warm paths and up to 30m for long-prefix workloads.n 4. re-enter cohort into active routing and ramp traffic using a 5-step circuit: 5 - 20 - 50 - 80 - 100 with 35 minute observation windows.nnd. disk checkpoint repair (when checkpoint file corrupted)n1) preconditions:n - checkpoint verification fails, file-level corruption detectedn - theres a recent healthy checkpoint on another replica or in object storen2) stepsn 1. pause cross-shard routing for cohort.n 2. copy healthy checkpoint from s3://redwood-kvcache-checkpoints/cohort/shard/latest to node (use signed url).n 3. verify file checksum locally: sha256sum checkpoint.bin grep expected_hashn 4. replace corrupted file atomically: mv checkpoint.bin checkpoint.bin.bak mv checkpoint.bin.new checkpoint.binn 5. restart kvcache service: sudo systemctl restart rw-kvcache monitor startup logs.nnverification and tests (post repair)n- functional checks (runbook)n 1) run kvcache meta diff across cohort: rwi kvcache meta-diff --cohort cohort_id meta-diff.txtn 2) run sample replay test suite (contains 50 canonical prefix scenarios): ./tools/replay-suite/run.sh --shard shard --cases sample-50n 3) hash agreement test: rwi kvcache verify-hash --cohort cohort_idn- performance checksn - ensure rehydrate latency p95 back within 10 of baseline within 30 minutes.n- safety observation windown - maintain elevated monitoring for 60 minutes. if any of the following recur, escalate to runtime incident:n kvcache_epoch_mismatch firing againn kvcache_rehydrate_failure_rate 1n kvcache_hash_divergence reappearsnnautomation and tooling notesn- rwi (runtime ops cli) has commands used above. see rwi help for subcommands and flags. example: rwi kvcache rotate-cohort --helpn- the orchestration job uses a preflight check that validates checkpoint availability and verifies storage iops before starting coordinated rotate.n- a small lambda/cron job performs nightly checksum sampling and records a digest manifest to object storage. this is used for fast verification during repairs.nnrollout and release considerationsn- changes to the kvcache serialization format or epoch semantics must be accompanied by:n 1) a compatibility test in the benchmark suite that performs cross-version meta-diff using shadow cohorts.n 2) a staged rollout: dev - canary (5) - regional canary (20) - global (100) with the kvcache epoch rotate orchestration able to abort mid-rotation.n- release note template snippet:n - component: runtime.kvcachen - change: bump epoch marker to 64-bit and add robust checkpoint crcn - safety: automated coordinated rotate orchestration and nightly checksum manifestsn - rollback: restore previous checkpoint from s3 and rotate cohort back.nnknown issues and caveatsn- clock skew can cause false-positive epoch mismatch alerts if leader shard epoch bumps while follower is slightly behind always check ntp health and kernel clock offset before repair.n- very long prefix workloads may require up to 30m for full rehydrate convergence do not prematurely escalate if inspection shows slow but steady convergence.n- partial serialization changes without back-compatibility will cause cross-version epoch mismatch ensure model-serving and kvcache serialization version are co-deployed.nnescalation matrix and dsid_dd39119b676d49f5bb7fcbce615caa92, source_type: confluence, title: scheduler inspection and repro lab manual, content: summarynnthis runbook describes a reproducible lab process for inspecting scheduler-related anomalies in the serving runtime. it is intended for oncall engineers, sres, and runtime devs who need to: detect a regression, reproduce the failure in a controlled environment, collect deterministic traces and kernel-level telemetry, and run targeted benchmarks to validate fixes.nnscopenn- components covered: dispatch, slot-manager, kernel-coordinator, prefetch-orchestrator, source_type: confluence, title: allocator bump and soft-oom simulation report, content: summary:nnthis document describes a reproducible simulation and postmortem of a class of incidents we call allocator bump leading to soft-oom symptoms in mixed tenant gpu nodes. the goal is to provide:n- a concise defect description and root-cause hypothesis.n- a repeatable test harness and config used for simulations.n- observable signatures (metrics, traces, kernel logs) for fast detection.n- mitigations, short-term runbook steps, and long-term remediation options.nnbackground and impact:nnwe observed intermittent increases in per-request allocator reservation (an allocator bump) during mixed workloads involving long-context chat and short-shot embed requests. the bump causes cross-tenant eviction churn and transient soft-oom: allocation failures that do not immediately kill processes but trigger repeated kernel preemption and degraded latency for 310 minutes. impacted customers experienced increased tokenization latency, higher error rates (502/504) on heavy tails, and elevated cost due to repeated kv-cache warmups.nnkey symptoms observed in production:n- sudden rise in node-level reserved_bytes (20 above baseline) without corresponding increase in active sessions.n- rapid eviction events across shards: eviction_rate increase by 515x.n- gpu cuda oom-type warnings followed by an uncommon sequence pattern (many concurrent short-lived requests interleaved with a few long-context generations) causes the allocator to allocate larger contiguous blocks for attention state than expected. the allocator fragmentation / rounding policy then prevents efficient compaction, bumping the effective reserved footprint and triggering eviction cascades. regression window: kernel runtime is hit, then compaction does not free those blocks immediately (compaction gated by idle window), producing the bump.nndetection signatures (for alerting):n- metric alert: node.reserved_bytes summaryncustomers may receive http 429 too many requests while their dashboard (or internal estimates) suggest they are under quota. in most cases, this is expected behavior caused by short-window rate limits (requests/minute, tokens/minute, concurrent requests) rather than plan quota (daily/monthly token or embedding allotment). in a smaller set of cases, the confusion is due to:n- misinterpreting response headers (rate limit vs quota signals)n- sdk retry behavior causing unintentional traffic amplificationn- header inconsistencies that were addressed in an engineering fix (see status / ongoing fix)nnthis article provides customer-safe troubleshooting steps, common misconfigurations, and support validation steps.nn---nn what a 429 means at redwoodna 429 indicates the request was blocked by an enforcement policy. the most common categories are:n1) rate limit exceeded (short window)n - per api key / workspace limits such as requests per minute (rpm), tokens per minute (tpm), or concurrent in-flight requests.n2) quota / budget exceeded (longer window)n - monthly/daily allotments, contract caps, or account-level safety caps.n3) protective throttling (rare)n - temporary throttles during partial degradation to protect overall availability.nnimportant: a customer can be under quota for the month and still hit 429 due to short-window limits.nn---nn symptomsncustomers typically report one or more of:n- increased 429s after an sdk upgrade (without intentional traffic increase)n- 429s occurring in bursts (e.g., at the top of the minute, after job fan-out, or during batch processing)n- dashboard shows quota remaining but requests failn- rate limit headers appear inconsistent across endpoints or responsesnn---nn how to interpret rate limit / quota headersn headers you should look forndepending on endpoint and deployment tier, responses may include some combination of:n- retry guidancen - retry-after (seconds) when the server can provide a safe retry windown- rate limit signals (short window)n - x-redwood-ratelimit-limit-requestsn - x-redwood-ratelimit-remaining-requestsn - x-redwood-ratelimit-reset-msn - (in some cases) token-based variants such as x-redwood-ratelimit-limit-tokensn- quota / budget signals (long window)n - x-redwood-quota-remaining-tokens (or similar account budget indicators when enabled)nn practical rule of thumbn- if the response includes rate limit remaining/reset headers, treat the 429 as a rate limit event.n- if the response indicates quota remaining 0 (or an explicit quota exceeded classification in the error body), treat it as a quota/budget event.n- if headers are missing or unclear, rely on:n - the structured error body classification (if present)n - retry-aftern - support-side telemetry confirmation using request idsnn why headers can look confusingn- different endpoints may enforce different limit dimensions (e.g., chat completion vs embeddings).n- concurrent usage across environments (prod staging) with the same api key can deplete short-window limits unexpectedly.n- client retries can multiply request volume, making the limit appear too low.nn---nn common customer-side causes (and fixes)n 1) concurrency spikes / fan-out jobsnpattern: a batch job or queue consumer increases parallelism (threads/processes) and triggers 429.nnfix (recommended):n- add client-side throttling:n - cap concurrent in-flight requestsn - use a token bucket limiter at the application edgen- stagger job starts (avoid synchronized bursts)n- for batch workloads, prefer larger batches where supported (and avoid micro-batches that increase rpm)nn 2) auto-retry amplifying trafficnpattern: after an sdk upgrade, 429 increases because the client retries aggressively and creates a feedback loop.nnfix (recommended):n- ensure 429 retries respect retry-after when present.n- use exponential backoff with jitter.n- cap retries (do not retry indefinitely).n- ensure retries are not happening at multiple layers (sdk gateway application).nnguidance:n- for non-idempotent operations, retries must be handled carefully. for chat/text generation, retries are generally safe if you:n - include an idempotency key (if supported by your integration)n - or ensure the request is safe to re-run from your business logic perspectivenn 3) mis-scoped api keys (shared across teams/environments)npattern: one api key used across prod/staging and multiple services.nnfix (recommended):n- use separate api keys per environment and per workload class.n- if you must share a key, implement per-service client-side rate limiting.nn 4) using streaming reconnect logic as retry without backoffnpattern: client reconnects repeatedly and quickly after a failure and unintentionally drives rpm/tpm.nnfix (recommended):n- treat reconnect as a retry: backoff jitter max attempts.n- log and surface request ids for support.nn---nn customer-safe troubleshooting checklistnask the customer to provide the following (copy/paste into an email or ticket):n1) time range of the issue (with timezone)n2) region (e.g., us-east, eu-west)n3) endpoint (chat/completions/embeddings/rerank)n4) model model version pin (if applicable)n5) sdk name version (or raw http)n6) 23 request ids from failed 429 responsesn7) the full response headers for a 429 (redact auth)n8) current client concurrency and any recent deploys/config changesnn recommended customer actionn- reduce concurrency by 50 for 15 minutes and observe whether 429s drop.n- enable logging of request ids and retry-after values.n- confirm whether multiple environments share the same api key.nn---nn workaround patterns we recommendn a) implement standard 429 handlingn- if retry-after is present: wait that duration, then retry.n- else: exponential backoff starting at 250500ms with jitter cap at 1030s.n- stop retrying after a small number of attempts (e.g., 35) and surface an error to the caller.nn b) add a client-side limitern- concurrency limiter (max in-flight)n- request-rate limiter (rpm)n- for token-heavy workloads: throttle by estimated tokens per requestnn c) upgrade to latest sdk / apply patch guidancenif the customer is on an older sdk version and seeing confusing 429/header behavior, recommend upgrading to the latest redwood sdk release. if they cannot upgrade immediately, advise:n- disable aggressive automatic retriesn- log headers and request ids for support verificationnn---nn support validation steps (internal)nuse these steps to mixed-workload scheduler prototype: known issues and edge cases, content: overviewnthis page tracks known issues, edge cases, and operational pitfalls for the mixed-workload scheduler prototype (short/long classification two-queue dispatch token budget guardrails). it is intended for runtime engineers and sres during benchmarking and canary.nnscope: scheduler behavior under mixed prompt-length distributions, interactions with the prefill/decode pipeline, kv cache pressure, and hardware/runtime-specific anomalies.nnnon-goal: this is not a full qos/tenancy policy document. for intended behavior and configuration semantics, see the design doc.nn quick triage checklist (when something looks wrong)n1. confirm the issue is actually mixed-workload related:n - compare metrics on a homogeneous workload run (all short or all long) vs mixed (e.g., 80/20).n2. check scheduler health metrics:n - per-class queue depthn - per-class time-in-queue p50/p95n - dispatch share per classn - starvation/aging countersn3. check prefill/decode split metrics:n - ttft (time-to-first-token)n - prefill latency p50/p95n - decode iteration duration and tokens/itern4. check kv cache pressure signals:n - kv cache utilizationn - cache eviction/compaction eventsn - prefill recompute rates (if available)n5. rule out kernel auto-selection instability:n - sudden changes in selected kernel paths across iterationsn - increased kernel compile/cuda graph recapture eventsnnif the issue reproduces only in a specific gpu sku or driver/cuda version, jump to hardware-specific anomalies.nn known issues and edge casesnn 1) long queue starvation under sustained short traffic (parameter-dependent)nsummary: with aggressive bias toward the short queue, long requests can make insufficient progress when short traffic is continuous. this was the primary starvation corner case found in load tests and is largely mitigated by the current aging function and minimum long-share guardrail, but it remains possible with extreme tuning.nntypical trigger conditionsn- short traffic at or above saturation (queue never drains)n- long requests classified correctly but token budgets for long set too lown- aging half-life too slow (long requests do not gain priority fast enough)nnsymptomsn- long time-in-queue p95 steadily increases and does not stabilizen- starvation counter increments for long queue (or aging override activates continuously)n- customer-visible p95 latency improves for short while long p99 becomes unboundednnmitigations / operational guidancen- ensure a hard minimum dispatch share for long (even during short bursts). avoid setting it below a low single-digit percentage in production unless the pool is dedicated to short traffic.n- enable/validate aging overrides (do not disable them for benchmarks).n- if canary: rollback if long-queue time-in-queue p95 exceeds the guardrail in the hosted tail latency slo doc.nnreferencesn- fix/adjustment: github://redwood/pr-24905-fix-long-queue-starvation-edge-casen- runbook rollback section: confluence://eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/mixed-workload-scheduler-rollout-runbooknn---nn 2) classification boundary thrash (requests oscillate around short/long threshold)nsummary: requests near the short/long threshold can be sensitive to minor estimation differences (tokenization variance, prompt formatting, system prompt changes). this can lead to unstable queue composition across time, producing oscillatory behavior in queue depths and dispatch share.nntypical trigger conditionsn- short/long threshold defined purely by raw prompt tokens, close to a common prompt size in productionn- heavy use of templates where small changes push prompts across the boundaryn- retries/continuations where same logical request ends up classified differentlynnsymptomsn- queue depth for short and long alternates with a regular period (sawtooth)n- dispatch share oscillates per-class p95 variance increases run-to-runn- kernel selection instability can appear second-order (see issue 6)nnmitigations / recommendationsn- prefer a predicted prefill-cost classifier (when available) over a strict token threshold.n- add hysteresis (two thresholds) if you observe boundary effects in a specific deployment:n - e.g., classify as short under threshold a, classify as long over threshold b, keep prior class in-between.n- re-evaluate threshold candidates using the latest prompt-length distribution sheet before production ramps.nn---nn 3) long-prefill bursts cause head-of-line blocking despite two-queue policy (prefill dominates)nsummary: two-queue scheduling reduces head-of-line blocking at the request level, but prefill can still monopolize gpu time if dispatch repeatedly selects long-prefill work (especially when long requests arrive in bursts). this is an interaction between request dispatch and the prefill/decode split.nntypical trigger conditionsn- long-spike scenario (sudden influx of long-context requests)n- prefill and decode not sufficiently separated in the scheduler decision loopn- token budgets configured per-request but not per-iterationnnsymptomsn- ttft regresses for short requests during long-prefill burstsn- gpu utilization stays high but short throughput/latency worsensn- prefill latency p95 dominates the end-to-end p95 movementnnmitigationsn- ensure prefill/decode separation hooks are enabled for the pool (if controlled by feature flag).n- use per-iteration token budgets (prefill and/or class-based) to cap worst-case amplification.n- for canary, monitor ttft specifically ttft regressions are often the earliest signal.nnreferencesn- prefill/decode separation: github://redwood/pr-24857-prefill-decode-separation-hooksn- token budgets: github://redwood/pr-24872-scheduler-token-budget-guardrailsnn---nn 4) kv cache compaction / eviction spikes under mixed workloadsnsummary: mixed workloads increase variance in kv cache residency and can amplify compaction/eviction churn. when the scheduler biases toward short requests, long requests may wait longer before decode, which can increase cache pressure depending on how the runtime accounts for reserved kv blocks and compaction windows.nntypical trigger conditionsn- high long-context share (even at 20) combined with high concurrencyn- pools running near kv capacity limits or with small per-request kv reservationsn- frequent model switching or batch fragmentation (reduces cache locality)nnsymptomsn- spiky prefill latency correlated with cache compaction/eviction eventsn- unexpected increase in prefill recompute or similar proxy metricsn- p95 improves for short, but overall throughput drops due to churnnnmitigations / tuning guidancen- avoid enabling the prototype in pools already kv-constrained without first validating cache headroom.n- if available in the runtime config, increase kv cache target headroom (lower target utilization) to reduce eviction/compaction frequency.n- prefer stable batching/route pinning during canary to reduce batch fragmentation.nnnotesn- this is frequently misattributed as scheduler regression when the underlying cause is cache churn that the new policy makes more visible (by changing interleaving patterns).nn---nn 5) fairness regressions across request classes (not multi-tenant safe)nsummary: the prototype is designed for internal short/long class bias, not customer-configurable multi-tenant qos. if traffic includes heterogeneous tenants (or endpoints) with different prompt-length distributions, the policy can inadvertently reallocate capacity across tenants.nntypical trigger conditionsn- mixed traffic from multiple routes/endpoints in the same pooln- one route predominantly short, another predominantly longn- a/b tests or canaries share a pool with production trafficnnsymptomsn- one endpoints p95 improves while another degrades more than expectedn- support tickets reference only one route got worsennmitigationsn- canary in isolated pools where possible.n- monitor by route/model where dashboards allow do not rely solely on global p95.n- if isolation isnt possible, set conservative bias and minimum long share.nn---nn 6) kernel auto-selection instability under rapid sequence length variation (hardware/runtime dependent)nsummary: when the sequence length distribution changes quickly (common in mixed short/long interleaving), the runtime may thrash between kernel variants or execution paths. this can show up as increased overhead (kernel selection, compilation, cuda graph recapture) and may negate p95 gains.nntypical trigger conditionsn- very mixed lengths within the same short time window (not just a stable 80/20 mix)n- small batch sizes combined with frequent class switchingn- deployments with stricter kernel eligibility constraints (driver/cuda combinations)nnsymptomsn- increased variance in iteration timen- spikes in graph recapture/compile/kernel selection counters (names vary by runtime build)n- throughput regression with minimal changes in average tokens/secnnmitigations / recommendationsn- if kernel thrash is suspected, run the profiling playbook to confirm selection path churn.n- consider widening the kernel eligibility window (if safe) or pinning to a stable kernel in canary for the affected sku.n- prefer dispatch policies that reduce rapid alternation (avoid overly strict round-robin between classes at very small batch sizes).nnreferencesn- profiling guidance: confluence://eng-serving-runtime/profiling-playbook/profiling-mixed-prefill-decode-contentionnn---nn 7) token budget guardrails can reduce throughput more than expected (misconfiguration)nsummary: per-iteration token budgets are a primary safety mechanism for tail latency, but overly tight budgets can fragment work, reduce effective batching, and cause avoidable throughput loss.nntypical trigger conditionsn- token budget set below what is needed to amortize prefill overhead on the given skun- budget enforced per-class without considering actual arrival ratesn- aggressive caps combined with low max batch sizennsymptomsn- p95 improves but tokens/sec drops materially beyond benchmark expectationsn- high frequency of budget overrun prevented dispatch debug logsn- short queue depth stays low, but gpu utilization dips intermittentlynnmitigationsn- use sku-specific defaults from the results summary rather than copying settings across a100/h100/l4.n- during canary, ramp budgets in small steps and watch throughput deltas alongside p95.nn---nn 8) pathological mixes that are not representative but break assumptionsnsummary: certain synthetic mixes (or adversarial customer behavior) can defeat the expected p95 improvements or create misleading results.nnexamplesn- alternating extremes: one 16-token prompt followed by one 16k-token prompt, repeating at steady state.n- long-only bursts every n seconds: causes periodic prefill cliffs.n- short requests with huge generation: prompt is short, but max_new_tokens is extremely large classification by prompt length alone is insufficient.nnmitigationsn- include max generation length (or predicted total work) in classification for environments where this is common.n- add benchmark scenarios beyond simple 80/20 mixes (long-spike, alternating extremes).nn hardware-specific anomalies (observed / reported)nthis section is intentionally operational: it lists issues we have seen at least once in benchmarking or canary.nn a) h100: higher sensitivity to kernel selection churn in mixed micro-batchesn- what we see: iteration time variance increases when dispatch alternates classes at small batch sizes.n- why it matters: p95 tail improvements can disappear even though average throughput is fine.n- what to do: bias toward fewer class switches per second (slightly larger effective batches), or pin stable kernels during canary if approved by kernels team.nn b) a100 (older driver/cuda combinations): increased cuda graph recapture eventsn- what we see: more frequent graph recapture when sequence lengths vary widely.n- what to do: verify driver/cuda compatibility matrix used by the pool consider disabling graphs for the canary window only if the trade-off is acceptable.nn c) l4 / smaller memory skus: kv cache pressure dominates scheduler improvementsn- what we see: cache eviction/compaction drives p95 more than dispatch policy changes.n- what to do: validate kv headroom first do not interpret a no improvement result as evidence the policy doesnt work.nn observability gaps and footgunsn- metric cardinality risk: per-class per-route per-model labeling can explode cardinality if enabled indiscriminately. prefer per-pool and per-model first only add per-route during focused debugging.n- dashboards lag reality during config ramps: short ramp intervals can outpace dashboard refresh and lead to misreads. use raw timeseries queries for the ramp window.n- sampling artifacts in traces: a low trace sampling rate can hide queue time variance. for canary triage, temporarily increase sampling for the canary pool only.nn canary guardrails (known-bad signals)ntreat the following as stop the line signals unless you have a clear, validated alternative explanation:n- long-queue time-in-queue p95 trending up without bound for 1015 minutes at steady trafficn- ttft p95 regression that exceeds the sre guardrail during the ramp windown- starvation counters continuously incrementing (not just occasional)n- kv eviction/compaction spikes tightly correlated with latency cliffs after enabling the flagn- kernel selection/graph recapture counters spike immediately after enablement and do not stabilizennfor explicit thresholds and rollback triggers, use: confluence://eng-sre/slo-and-error-budgets/hosted-api-tail-latency-slo-guardrailsnn open items / follow-upsn- in-flight requests to complete (or fail fast), then restart/replace.n- safe abort: controlled failure path for stuck tp steps that returns an actionable error and drains the replica (preferred over waiting indefinitely).nn---nn symptoms (what youll see)n customer-facingn- elevated request timeouts (especially streaming) and rising p99/p999 latency.n- hanging streaming responses (connection open, no tokens).n- bursty error patterns as autoscaling adds replicas but load remains concentrated on wedged ones.nn platform signalsnlook for correlated signals on the tp dashboard:n- tp rank heartbeat gaps for one or more ranks on a replica.n- in-flight collective counters stuck (no increments over time).n- scheduler queue depth rising while gpu utilization is inconsistent (some ranks busy, some idle).n- nccl errors may be absent (silent stall cases are common).nn---nn preconditions / accessnyou should have:n- access to the affected cluster (hosted or the dedicated customer cluster).n- dsid_ebf98d1a9c364a56a6b733a061b0dbdc, source_type: confluence, title: gpu watchdog: intermittent node hang investigation and mitigation, content: summaryn-------nthis document captures the investigative findings, short-term mitigations, and long-term remediation plan for a class of intermittent gpu node hangs observed in the production serving fleet during q4 2025. the pattern is characterized by a kernel-space watchdog firing followed by an immediate kubelet restart and a multi-minute node unavailable window. this page is intended for sre and runtime engineers who perform triage and for release owners planning a preventative rollout.nnscopen-----n- affects: a subset of dedicated and private pools running nvidia a100 and a10x nodes with gpu driver versions 535.x and specific firmware revisions.n- services impacted: runtime-gateway, shard-manager, schedulerd, model-evictor customer-visible effect: elevated 99th-percentile latency and transient 5xx errors while node is flapping.n- not affected: small cpu-only pools and older driver versions 520.x (no incidents observed).nnobserved impact and slo implicationsn----------------------------------n- symptom window: node enters notready for 90420s after watchdog trigger.n- typical customer impact: short-lived burst of 504/502 for in-flight sessions streaming connections drop and must reconnect.n- slos affected: request-level latency (p99) and success rate (error budget burn correlated with pool size). example: a single a100 node hang in a 16-node pool caused a 0.9 availability regression for the pool over 8 minutes during a production rollout.nnsymptoms / how this shows up in toolingn--------------------------------------n- kubernetes: repeated kubelet restarts on the node pod re-scheduling patterns look like a flock of pods moving simultaneously.n- node logs: dmesg entries with lines similar to: nvrm: xid (pci:0000:xx:00): 79, gpu has fallen off the bus followed by kernel watchdog stack traces.n- driver logs: /var/log/nvidia-installer.log often contains firmware timeout entries prior to the hang.n- metrics: sudden drop in node_gpu_utilization, spike in node_restarts_total, and increased request queueing on shard-manager.nnfirst-response checklist (for oncall)n-------------------------------------n1. identify affected node(s): kubectl get nodes --selectorpool -o wide and check for notready / kubelet age.n2. collect kernel and driver logs: scp or run remote tail of /var/log/messages, dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log.n3. capture gpu metrics snapshot: grafana - gpu pool - export time range covering the event (5m before to 10m after).n4. evacuate traffic from the node (if still reachable): kubectl cordon kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force .n5. if the node is unresponsive at ssh level and remains in notready 10m, escalate to infra for host power-cycle.n6. add an incident note with affected customer ids and the pool name.nnquick mitigation options (short-term)n------------------------------------n- automatic circuit-breaker: enable node-level automatic failing of scheduling for nodes with kubelet_restart_count 1 within 10m. this prevents repeated placement on unstable nodes.n- scheduler policy tweak: reduce concurrent long-lived streaming sessions per node by 20 to lower surface area during known risk windows (e.g., during driver upgrades).n- runtime fallback: configure shard-manager to keep a warm standby routing for hot sessions to avoid full reconnects when a node goes notready.nndetection queries and alerts (examples)n--------------------------------------n- promql to detect surges of kubelet restarts across a pool:n sum by (pool) (increase(node_kubelet_restart_totaljobnode-exporter15m)) 2n- promql to flag gpu firmware errors in driver metrics (if exposed):n increase(nvidia_driver_errors_totaltypefirmware_timeout10m) 0n- alert rule guidance: fire p1 if 2 nodes in a dedicated pool restart within 30m fire p2 if a single node restart correlates with 10 p99 latency regression for the pool.nnrepro steps (safest non-prod reproduction)n-----------------------------------------n1. create a staging pool matching production node image, driver, and firmware (tagged staging-a100-watchdog).n2. deploy a synthetic workload that pins the gpu: run a continuous 75 utilization workload for 30 minutes (the benchmark-runner container is available in images/runtime/synthetic-gpu-burner:stable).n3. run a targeted firmware stress test by toggling ecc on/off and running memory-fill patterns (do not run on prod).n4. monitor dmesg and nvidia-smi -q for early signs of timeouts. if reproduced, collect full system trace using sosreport and nv-hostengine debug toggles.nnroot cause analysis (summary)n----------------------------nafter correlating multiple incidents we determined two contributing factors:n- a race condition in the kernel-level gpu driver interaction when heavy sustained sm utilization coincided with an asynchronous firmware housekeeping task. this occasionally produced a gpu fall off bus (xid 79) and subsequent watchdog path triggering.n- the host kernel watchdog configuration and kubelet restart policy resulted in an aggressive and non-idempotent restart behavior that extended the outage window. specifically, the kubelet triggered a systemd restart of the node agent rather than isolating the gpu device and allowing a graceful driver reset.nnpermanent remediation plan (high level)n--------------------------------------n1. driver and firmware upgrade: collaborate with nvidia to obtain a driver build that fixes the observed race (target window: q1 2026). test on staging pool.n2. kubelet and systemd policy changes: modify kubelet restart thresholds and add a device-level isolation handler that attempts a driver reset (nvidia-smi --reset) before full kubelet restart.n3. runtime-level safeguards: extend shard-managers warm-standby and session-mirroring so customer sessions can continue on alternate nodes without full reconnect requirements.n4. automated canaries: add continuous canaries exercising firmware housekeeping with health checks that simulate long-lived streaming connections.n5. fleet rollout plan: phased kernel/driver rollout with canary pools (5 - 20 - 60 - 100) and a two-hour observation window per phase. abort criteria: any increase in node_restarts_total or xid-related driver errors.nnsuggested kernel and kubelet config snippet (for change pr)n----------------------------------------------------------n- eviction inconsistency, content: summaryn-------nthis page documents a reproducible, intermittent heap growth and kv-cache eviction inconsistency observed when tensorcore fusion is enabled for certain transformer kernels on our heterogeneous gpu pool. the issue appears when fused kernels are scheduled across co-located model shards and when intra-request kv prefetch overlaps with eviction windows.nnimpactn------n- scope: affects a subset (2-3) of heavy-generation requests on dedicated and private clusters using a100/nvidia ampere families with tensorcore fusion enabled.n- user-visible: transient increase in 95th-99.9th percentile latency, occasional ooms on worker processes, and increased eviction churn leading to degraded per-token cost (up to 18 for affected requests).n- business: risk to slos (p95 latency slo breaches when load spikes coincide with the bug).nnobserved signalsn----------------n- gradual heap growth on the worker process over a 530 minute window (process rss increases in steps coincident with fused-kernel dispatch).n- kv cache eviction rate spike (evictions/sec) with correlated increase in cold-start ratio for sessions.n- kernel execution traces show fused-kernel handoffs where a kernel fusion path returns before its allocated temporary buffer is reclaimed by the allocator.n- gpu-side telemetry: extended sm busy durations, repeated kernel launches for identical shapes with slightly different scheduling metadata.nnreproduction steps (conservative, reproducible in lab)n-----------------------------------------------------n1. environment: a100 (80gb) instance or equivalent ampere gpu runtime build rtf-2026.02.n2. config: enable tensor_fusiontrue, kernel_prefetchadaptive, kv_cache_async_prefetchtrue. use multi-shard model variant (shard_count 2) with batch sizes that produce interleaved attention (sequence length 1k).n3. traffic: replay a synthetic workload with a mix of long-generation and short completion requests increase concurrency to saturate a single gpu slot (utilization 7080).n4. monitor: capture process rss, allocator free-list sizes, kv eviction counters, and per-kernel timestamps via the runtimes compact trace.n5. expected: after 520 minutes, worker process rss climbs in discrete steps and eviction/sec rises sporadic ooms may be visible in stress runs.nnroot-cause hypothesisn---------------------n- the tensorcore fusion path introduces a small temporary buffer per fused dispatch that the cpu-side allocator treats as ephemeral. under certain scheduling interleavings the fused dispatch completes on the gpu but the runtimes completion callback is deferred (due to priority-driven scheduling and backpressure). while the callback is delayed the temporary buffer remains referenced by the dispatch record and is not returned to the free list. repeated interleavings create a slow leak until a gc/eviction cycle recovers memory but the recovery timing interacts badly with kv-cache eviction heuristics causing eviction storms and cold-hot thrash.n- binder: the issue manifests only when (a) fusion is enabled, (b) adaptive prefetch is used, and (c) priority inversion creates callback deferral windows.nndetection and alerting (recommended signals)n-------------------------------------------ncreate alerts that combine process-level, runtime, and kernel telemetry:nn- alert: worker-heap-growth-sustainedn - condition: process_rss growth 150mib in 10m and heap_allocated_by_runtime/free_list_shrink_ratio 0.15n - severity: p2nn- alert: kv-eviction-churn-spiken - condition: evictions_per_sec 20 for 5m and cold_start_ratio 0.12n - severity: p2nn- alert: fused-kernel-complete-defern - condition: fused_kernel_dispatch_time - completion_callback_time 200ms for 100 samples in 5mn - severity: p3nndiagnostic trace snippet (compact trace json example)n------------------------------------------------------nuse the compact-trace capture to correlate kernel launches and completion callbacks. example snippet (sanitized):nnkernel_launches: id: k1, start_ns: 1000000, end_ns: 1005000, fusion: true, temp_bytes: 8388608, id: k2, start_ns: 1007000, end_ns: 1012000, fusion: true, temp_bytes: 8388608, callbacks: id: cb1, time_ns: 1005200, kernel_id: k1, id: cb2, time_ns: 1014000, kernel_id: k2nnmitigations and workarounds (short-term)n----------------------------------------nif you observe the signals above in production, apply the following mitigations in order of increasing impact:nn1) toggle runtime flags (non-disruptive to sessions):n - disabled: tensor_fusionfalsen - if disabling fusion resolves the heap growth immediately, escalate to the runtime team for root-cause tracking.nn2) soften prefetch: set kv_cache_async_prefetchfalse or lower prefetch window from 128 tokens to 32 tokens.nn3) reduce scheduling concurrency: temporarily lower per-gpu slot concurrency to reduce interleavings (slot_concurrency - max(1, slot_concurrency - 1)).nn4) eviction smoothing: increase the eviction hysteresis window to 60s to avoid cascade eviction. dsid_a3665225878647d7a90c9f0cb59d66ca, source_type: confluence, title: adaptive observability and deferred profiling playbook, content: summarynnthis playbook defines the process, configuration, and operational runbook for adaptive observability (ao): a low-overhead, signal-driven approach to enabling deferred and targeted profiling of the serving runtime in production. ao is designed to reduce continuous profiling overhead by collecting detailed traces only when specific signals indicate increased risk to slos or suspected regressions.nngoalsnn- minimize steady-state telemetry and cpu/gpu overhead (target 95th/99th slo breach) lasting 1 minute.n- regressions detected by continuous fidelity checks (quality or token-cost anomalies).n- reproducible but infrequent workload spikes that require transient sampling.n- pre-rollout canaries when testing new kernel or scheduler patches.nnsignal taxonomy and thresholdsnnwe use three classes of signals to decide whether to activate deferred profiling:nn1) slo signalsn - 95th latency configured slo 1.3 for 60s (configurable).n - error rate 0.5 sustained for 30s.nn2) resource signalsn - gpu occupancy deviation 20 relative to baseline for 2 minutes.n - host-level thermal or watchdog interrupts (nvml alert).nn3) heuristic / anomaly signalsn - sudden unexplained spike in kernel dispatch times (per-kernel p99 grows 2x).n - evaluation harness signals: batch mismatch or kv cache miss-rate climb.nndefault thresholds are set in ao controller config. operators can tune per-cluster or per-scheduler profile.nnsafety and compatibility requirementsnn- profiling artifacts must be writeable to a detached artifact store (s3-compatible) under /ao-traces///. this avoids i/o contention on local ssds.n- kernel-level instrumentation must be gated behind an compatibility matrix: only enable kernel-level event types listed in the current nodes kernel-compat bundle.n- sampling collectors run in user-space sidecars (service name: telemetry-bridge) and must be limited to 256 mb rss and 10 cpu by cgroup.n- any automatic activation must include an automated grace period of 30s manual override available.nnimplementation componentsnn- ao controller (service: ao-controller)n - receives aggregated signals from telemetry-bridge and slo-aggregator.n - applies policy rules (selectors, thresholds, cooldowns).n - issues activation requests to node-sidecar agents via grpc.nn- node-sidecar (service: telemetry-bridge)n - runs on every runtime node as a daemonset.n - accepts activation token, spawns sampling process (perf/tracepoint/proxy-hooks), streams compressed trace to artifact store.n - publishes activation metadata to tracing-index (for later correlated queries).nn- tracing index (service: trace-index)n - stores metadata records (json) for each trace: node, kernel-version, model-variant, request-filter, reason, associated alert id.n - indexes by time, node, and correlation-id.nnpolicy examplesnndefault kernel.dispatch.p99n threshold: 2.0n window_seconds: 120n sampling:n duration_seconds: 300n sampling_mode: stratifiedn max_parallel_traces: 4n safeguards:n cooldown_seconds: 900n max_activation_per_node_per_day: 6nnsampling modesnn- ad-hoc: capture a single full trace for a specific request (highest fidelity).n- stratified: capture n traces covering short/long sequences and small/large batches.n- statistical: lower-fidelity counters micro-profiles (lower overhead).nnrunbook: immediate incident response (ao-driven capture)nn1) alerting and triagen - noc or oncall receives p95/p99 alert from slo-aggregator with alert id.n - if alert matches ao policy (controller decision), ao-controller will auto-request a capture and post the activation to the incident channel.nn2) tag).n - if traces indicate sensitive customer data in payloads, immediately escalate to security and mark trace artifacts as restricted.nn4) if no traces arriven - verify agent health: kubectl -n runtime get pods -l apptelemetry-bridge -o widen - inspect controller logs: kubectl -n runtime logs deployment/ao-controller -c controller tail -n 200n - if agents are crashed or oom-killed, follow node remediation runbook (see related pages).nn5) de-escalationn - if activation captured sufficient traces and slos recover, allow sampling to stop automatically or trigger manual stop via ao-controller.n - if activation causes instability (rare), use the ao-controller emergency-disable flag to stop further activations globally.nnpost-incident analysis checklistnn- export trace bundle workload signature. note any divergence in scheduling decisions.n- if a kernel or scheduler bug is suspected, create a repo ticket with: trace-id, node image, kernel-version, scheduler revision, and a and runtime decision guide, content: overviewn--------nthis playbook defines a repeatable approach to map service-level objectives (slos) and business economics into runtime routing and scaling decisions for redwoods inference platform. it provides concrete matrices, alert thresholds, dashboard templates, and an operational runbook so platform engineers and product owners can translate latency and cost targets into deterministic behavior at the edge, routing layer, and scheduler.nnintended audiencen- platform engineers (routing, scheduler, runtime)n- product owners and sres owning decision matrix for routing (fast-path vs. bulk-path), fallback, and quantization/compact model downgrade policiesn- standardize alerts and dashboards to expose actionable signals for automated rollback and operator handoffsn- include an operator runbook for emergent cost/latency tradeoffsnnwhy this mattersn- customers expect predictable latency but also want control over cost. platform decisions that are opaque create surprising bills or unexpected degradation. this playbook ensures reproducible, observable translation from slos - runtime policy - billing impact.nnglossary (short)n- fast-path: low-latency gpu/cpu pool optimized for latency-sensitive tokens (higher cost).n- bulk-path: higher-throughput, lower-cost pool with relaxed latency (batching, longer queuing).n- fallback policy: automatic downgrade to compatible model variant or queued execution when fast-path slos cannot be met.n- token-unit: billing unit (single generated token).nnslo economics baseline tablen slo profile p95 latency target cost priority default routing notes n------:---------n interactive (chat) 300ms high fast-path (1x dedicated gpu slice) use prefix kv cache and prefix routing never route to bulk-path by default n worker (email digest, offline) 3s low bulk-path (batched, cpu-friendly) favor quantized models, aggressive batching n mixed (webhooks, user-initiated longer responses) 800ms medium fast-path primary, bulk-path fallback use grace-period queue of 200ms before fallback nnunit economics example assumptions (internal)n- fast-path cost baseline: 0.00035 per token (includes gpu amortization, infra, sre overhead)n- bulk-path cost baseline: 0.00007 per tokenn- average tokens per request: 120n- 1 p99 tail reduction via kv cache saves 0.3 tokens per request on averagenndecision matrix: routing and runtime actionsn1) admission control (edge):n - metric: in-flight requests / fast-path capacity if 0.85, divert new requests to queuing or apply headroom throttling.n - action: if p95 fast-path latency target for 2 consecutive 60s windows - enable 200ms grace queue and allow up to 10 of new requests to be routed to bulk-path.n2) model downgrade (quality-preserving fallback):n - when budget burn-rate configured budget_saturation threshold (see config table) and p95 violation persists, switch interactive tenants to 8-bit quantized variant with a/b monitoring for quality drift.n3) autoscaling signal selection:n - prefer throughput-weighted schedule (tokens/sec) for bulk-path, latency-based for fast-path.nnruntime configuration schema (reference)n field type example description n------------n priority_profile string interactive maps to slo profile above n fast_path_capacity_pct integer 70 percent of tenant quota reserved on fast-path n fallback_grace_ms integer 200 how long to wait before fallback routing n budget_saturation_pct integer 85 percent of monthly committed budget consumed where aggressive cost controls apply n quantized_variant string gptx-8q compatible fallback model id nnalert and dashboard patternsn- primary slo dashboard (per-tenant): p50/p95/p99 latency heatmap, tokens/sec, cost-per-1000-requests, dropped/queued rate.n- cost-signal confluence, title: paged attention memory spikes (oom) allocator block manager tuning guide, content: overviewnthis page documents a recurring production failure mode for paged-attention model shards: gpu memory spikes and occasional ooms under high concurrency and long kv cache lifetimes. the issue typically manifests as allocation storms (cudamalloc/cudafree) triggered by frequent block-manager compaction sweeps, leading to fragmentation and latency tail regressions.nnthis guide consolidates what we learned from the initial canary regressions (runtime rollout around commit f3a9b2c) and subsequent fixes shipped in later runtime releases.nn symptomsn what youll seen- sudden gpu memory spikes on specific shards (often correlated with high qps and long-running sessions).n- latency tail regression (p99/p999) coincident with allocator activity.n- ooms shortly after a series of compaction events.nn representative log snippetnnw blockmgr: compacting 24 blocks - moved 18, freed 6, compaction_cost_ms42ni kvcache: reserve_block(0x7f8c) - size256kne allocator: cudamalloc failed after 3.1s, retryingnoom on device 0, requested 1.2gbnnn root causes (most common)n1. fragmentation small allocation churnn - default allocator path issues many device allocations when compaction moves blocks and temporary attention buffers are not reused.n2. allocator arena/pool too small for workloadn - a small arena leads to frequent device allocations under sustained load.n3. aggressive compaction behaviorn - compaction that attempts to move too many blocks in a single sweep can create a cascading allocation burst.nn immediate mitigations (recommended order)n 1) enable cuda async pool allocator (cudamallocasync)nwhen to use: any paged-attention deployment where compaction frequency is non-trivial (most high-qps clusters).nnwhy it helps: reduces cudamalloc/cudafree storms by routing allocations through a pool.nncaveats:n- cudamallocasync changes lifetime semantics. buffers must be returned promptly to avoid pool bloat.n- pool fragmentation is still possible when block sizes are highly variable.nn 2) increase allocator arena sizenempirically, increasing the per-gpu arena/pool reserve reduces allocation hot-path noise.nncurrent guidance (2026-02):n- start at 256mb per gpu for mid-size models (e.g., opt 27b class).n- use 512mb per gpu for very high concurrency or long session lifetimes.nnnote: our runtime defaults were raised after the initial incident confirm your deployed version before overriding.nn 3) tune paged-attention block sizenblock size is a tradeoff:n- smaller blocks more blocks more compaction activity and allocation churn.n- larger blocks fewer compactions and fewer allocations, but more internal slack (wasted memory in partially filled blocks).nncurrent recommendation:n- prefer 512kb blocks for most production workloads.n- avoid 1mb unless allocation call counts dominate and you have headroom for internal slack.nn tuning results (reference)nthe following benchmark matrix (originally reproduced on redwood/opt-2.7b, seq_len2048, steady qps 1200 on prod-ish canary) shows typical trends:nnnresults:n- block256k default alloc: p99120ms, mem_peak18.1gb, alloc_calls1780n- block256k async pool: p9990ms, mem_peak15.9gb, alloc_calls320n- block512k async pool: p9968ms, mem_peak16.8gb, alloc_calls210n- block1mb async pool: p9972ms, mem_peak18.9gb, alloc_calls140nnninterpretation:n- async pool produces the biggest win by reducing allocation call volume.n- 512kb blocks typically minimize latency tail with acceptable memory footprint.n- 1mb blocks may reduce alloc calls further but can increase wasted memory.nn standard configuration (recommended starting point)n runtime config (json)nnn allocator: cuda_async_pool,n arena_size_bytes: 268435456,n enable_workspace_reserve: true,n paged_attn_block_size_bytes: 524288,n compaction_max_relocate_fraction: 0.60nnnnnotes:n- arena_size_bytes: start at 256mb increase to 512mb if pool high-water repeatedly hits the cap during sustained traffic.n- paged_attn_block_size_bytes: 512kb default is recommended unless a model has extreme kv sparsity.n- compaction_max_relocate_fraction: safety guard to prevent compaction from attempting a massive sweep. earlier experiments used 0.75 production experience showed 0.60 is safer under bursty loads.nn shard skew and quantization interaction: investigation, mitigation, and runbook, content: summary:nthis document captures an investigation into a recurring class of production incidents where uneven kv-cache (prefix/kv) distribution across shard workers combined with aggressive post-training quantization (8-bit asymmetric) produced high tail latency and occasional ooms. it includes root-cause evidence, detection queries, a short-term mitigation runbook, recommended scheduler and quantization configuration changes, and a checklist for long-term fixes and testing.nnscope and impact:n- concentrated during synthetic-batched workloads and long-context chat sessions ( 2048 tokens).n- frequency: 3 incidents between 2025-09 and 2025-11 in us-east-1 gpu pools reproduction locally with shard skew simulator.n- business impact: api error rate increased 1.42.3x during events customers on dedicated saw throughput degradation prompting support escalations.nnkey findings (short form):n1) shard assignment heuristic allowed up to 2.5x more active kv-entries on certain workers for common long-prefix prompts, causing memory pressure and slower kv lookups.n2) quantized kernels (8-bit asymmetric) for recent model variants introduce nonuniform per-layer memory layout that increases temporary workspace allocation variance per token. when combined with prefetching, this exacerbated peak memory use.n3) kernel scheduler prioritized throughput over memory headroom during steady-state autoscaling under high skew this led to transient oom kills and a cascade of request retries that amplified tail latencies.nnrelevant metrics and alerting thresholds:n- kv_cache_local_entries_per_shard (gauge) alert if max_shard / median_shard 1.6 for 5mn- kv_cache_hit_rate (percent) warn if avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_memory_total_bytes1m)))nninvestigation artifacts (evidence):n- kernel traces showing repeated cudamalloc failure - fallback path for q8 kernels (attached as trace ids: trc-20251004-42, trc-20251021-08).n- heap dumps from affected workers demonstrating 6080 of incremental allocations were temporary layer workspaces tied to the quantized fused-kernel (dump ids: heap-20251004-a, heap-20251102-b).n- repro script: scripts/kv-skew-sim/runner.py (internal repo: infra/sim) reproduces p99 spike by driving long-prefix variety and forcing unbalanced shard assignment.nnimmediate mitigation (short-term runbook) use during incidents:n1) detect: confirm shard_skew_ratio promql 1.6 and gpu_mem_headroom_pct any device baseline2.n2) quarantine affected model a class of hard-to-reproduce memory-safety failures that we observed in production during sustained mixed workloads: a combination of interleaved (asynchronous synchronous) batching, aggressive kv-cache soft garbage collection (soft-gc), and fast slot recycling can produce illegal memory accesses and occasional kernel crashes. the net result is transient instance instability, sporadic ooms on gpus, and elevated tail latency as affected shards restart.nnbackground: why this class appearsnn- our runtime performs continuous batching with two execution paths: synchronous (hotpath) and asynchronous (background coalesced batches).n- a soft-gc subsystem attempts to reclaim kv-cache memory opportunistically when host- or device-memory pressure grows it marks entries stale and reclaims in the background without global synchronization to avoid latency cliffs.n- worker slot recycling reclaims cpu/gpu slot metadata aggressively to maximize throughput. when these three systems interleave at the wrong time, reclaimed gpu-side buffers or stream handles can be referenced by an in-flight kernel, leading to illegal memory access and cuda driver errors.nnobserved symptoms (production signals)nn- sporadic gpu kernel failures (cuda errors logged: unknown or illegal memory access) without obvious memory growth prior to failure.n- increase in tail latency and 5xx error spike in model-serving routes that use long kv cache lifetimes (chat sessions).n- short-lived pod restarts on a small percentage (0.31) of nodes restart reason crashloop at the gpu driver layer.n- traces show kernel launch times overlapped with cache-evict markers and slot-reuse timestamps.nnknown reproducibility steps (local repro)nn1. use a synthetic client that alternates short synchronous requests (prompt length 1632) with long-generation asynchronous requests (prompt length 512) to force mixed batching paths.n2. configure a small device-memory headroom to trigger soft-gc: set kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold 0.78 and kv_cache_eviction_batch_size 16.n3. reduce slot_reuse_delay_ms to a small value (10ms) to emulate aggressive recycling.n4. run the workload with a high concurrency driver until you observe intermittent cuda errors.nntelemetry and detection rulesnn- important signals to capture (add to node-level dashboards):n - cuda_error_count (per gpu): alerts when 0 in 5m windown - kv_cache_eviction_rate and kv_cache_reclaim_time_p50/p95n - slot_reuse_rate and slot_reuse_delay_ms distributionn - kernel_launch_overlap_ratio: fraction of launches that overlap with a cache-reclaim marker (sampled)nn- detection rule (recommended):n - alert if cuda_error_count 0 or kernel_launch_overlap_ratio 0.1 for a given shard and kv_cache_eviction_rate_p95 baseline 3 sigma.nnimmediate mitigations (for oncall)nn1. throttle soft-gc: admin apinn curl -x post -h authorization: bearer admin -d kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold: 0.92, kv_cache_eviction_batch_size: 4 effect: reduces background reclaim aggressiveness and gives in-flight kernels more time to complete.nn2. increase slot reuse delay to force explicit fencing:nn curl -x post -h authorization: bearer admin -d slot_reuse_delay_ms: 250 effect: prevents immediate reuse of cpu/gpu slot structs while kernels or stream callbacks may still hold references.nn3. if alerting indicates a specific node / shard: cordon the node and redeploy the runtime with the mitigations above optionally drain and restart the affected pod to clear dangling state.nnlong-term fixes (engineering roadmap)nn- short-term (sprint-scale):n 1) add explicit device-side fencing and reference counting for kv cache buffers. before reclaiming, ensure all stream callbacks have executed and kernel completion fences are observed.n 2) make soft-gc cooperative: transition from blind background reclamation to a token-based protocol where a limited number of concurrent reclaims can happen per-shard.n 3) add stronger sanitizers in the dev profiling harness to catch races (e.g., asan-like host checks and cuda memcheck in staging).nn- mid-term (quarter-scale):n 1) introduce a kernel-scheduling handshake that timestamps reclaim windows and prevents kernel launches that would reference recently reclaimed buffers.n 2) improve batch planner to prefer contiguous execution (avoid interleaving synchronous launches with async coalesced batches when soft-gc is active).n 3) add automated tests in the benchmarking suite that run mixed-workload tortures for 8 hours and report divergence metrics.nnimpact to release rollout notesnn- releases that change kv cache layout, soft-gc heuristics, or slot metadata must include:n - benchmark matrix results for mixed-sync/async workloads (see mixed-workload stress matrix).n - profiling traces demonstrating zero kernel-reclaim overlap for p99 windows.n - new canary policy requiring 48h of shadow traffic with injected gc pressure.nnbenchmarking profiling barrier token that prevents certain asynchronous batch types from starting while a reclaim token is held.n - track per-shard outstanding device-side references and decrement at kernel callback completion disallow reclaim until zero.nnminimal config reference (table)nn key suggested safe default description n------------------------------------------n kv_cache_soft_gc_threshold 0.90 fraction
