tail-latency increase.n- effect: runtime falls back to built-in baseline defaults.n- notes: use per-pool override first avoid global unless impact is broad.nn b) force a specific profile mode (e.g., h100 balanced)n- use when: throughput-first mode causes tail latency or streaming instability.n- effect: keeps profile benefits while restoring fairness/backpressure.nn c) reduce batching / tighten queue limitsn- use when: tail latency spikes, request queue growth, streaming stutter.n- effect: reduces queueing delay at the cost of throughput.nn d) constrain kv cache budgetn- use when: ooms, frequent restarts, memory fragmentation, long-context workloads.n- effect: caps memory reserved for kv cache may reduce max concurrency for long contexts.nn e) disable experimental b200 profilen- use when: any regression in b200 pools if driver/cuda mismatch suspected.n- effect: revert to h100-like baseline or generic safe config.nn(exact flag/env/helm key names vary by deployment mode see the blocked connection.n- health-aware routing: extend the smart routing policy to avoid using worker connections with elevated stall signals prefer routing new streams to underutilized connections.nnconfig knobs and recommended safe rangesnn config_key default recommended emergency tradeoffs n--------------------------------------------------------n grpc.max_concurrent_streams 100 pcie/nvlink topologies (common in our dedicated and private deployments when mixes of a100, h100, and earlier generation cards are used).n- observed when node-level device allocation policies route lead to pod memory exhaustion and partial request loss. the doc covers: detection signals, short-term mitigations, permanent fixes planned, rollout steps, post-incident verification, and ownership.nncontext and scopen------------------n- affected service: dispatcher-service (grpc frontend connection multiplexer)n- secondary impact: kernel-manager and grpc-proxy pods observed elevated summary: under sustained backpressure (long kv cache fetches / slow kernel warmstarts), the dispatcher accumulates connection windows and request buffers that are not compacted, causing memory pressure and eventual oom/kube eviction.nnwhy this mattersn------------------n- slo impact: incidents breached the 99.9 availability slo for several customer routes for 417 minutes in observed incidents.n- cost/operational: repeated restarts mask the underlying problem and create downstream load spikes (thundering herd) when services recover.nndetection and restart. this limits per-client window growth.n3) ttl/compaction: reduce dispatcher.window_idle_ttl from 10m to 90s to force faster window tear-down.n4) controlled rolling restart: restart the pods documents the behavior of automatic fallback in the redwood serving runtime for the hosted api. this policy is used during normal operations and is often enabled during model rollouts to reduce customer-visible errors during capacity or instability events.nn what fallback doesnwhen fallback is enabled on a route, the router may send requests to a fallback model instead of the primary model based on defined triggers. the request remains a standard hosted api request the router modifies the upstream target only.nn fallback triggersnfallback can activate for these reasons (not exhaustive):n- capacity pressure: primary pool is saturated (queue time above threshold).n- elevated error rate: primary 5xx above threshold over a short window.n- cold start or rollout warmup: primary replicas not ready or still ramping.n- regional impairment: a subset of instances in a region failing health checks.nn default rollout-time trigger thresholds (recommended)nfor fallback-enabled rollouts, recommended initial thresholds are:n- queue time (primary) 250 ms p95 over 3 minutesn- primary 5xx 0.8 over 5 minutesn- primary timeout rate 0.3 over 5 minutesnnteams may tune these thresholds, but must record the change in the release ticket and return to defaults after the rollout window unless there is an explicit follow-up task.nn compatibility requirementsnfallback is safe only when primary and fallback are compatible for the routes expected client behavior. in particular:n- the api surface must match: tool calling enabled/disabled should be consistent, and structured output constraints must be compatible.n- tokenization changes can affect downstream parsing and should be validated with smoke tests.n- context length and max output token limits should not be materially lower on the fallback model for high-traffic routes.nn observabilitynwhen fallback is active, metrics include:n- router.fallback_activated_count (tagged by reason)n- router.fallback_share (percentage of requests served by fallback)n- inference.latency_ms by model_version (primary vs fallback)nnlogs: routing decisions are annotated with fallback_reason and selected_model_version.nn known sharp edgesn- fallback can mask quality regressions: if the primary produces degraded outputs, overall error rates might stay low while user experience becomes inconsistent. rollback is still required.n- tool-calling: if the fallback model has different function-call style, clients may see inconsistent tool selection.n- streaming: fallback can increase time-to-first-token if the fallback pool is colder than primary.nn operational guidancen- during model rollouts, keep fallback enabled at least through the canary and the first 24 hours at 100 unless there is a known incompatibility.n- if fallback share exceeds 20 for more than 10 minutes during a rollout, treat it as a signal to pause the ramp and investigate capacity or error spikes., doc_id: title: adaptive scheduler 1.0 - launch notes and operational guide, content: overview:nnthis page documents the 1.0 launch of the adaptive scheduler, a runtime-level scheduling engine that replaces the legacy static slot allocator for production workloads. the adaptive scheduler is intended to improve tail latency, reduce per-token cost via smarter slot consolidation, and provide fine-grained slo-aware admission controls. this document summarizes architecture changes, kernel scheduling behavior, profiling and benchmark results, rollout and validation steps, operational runbooks, known issues discovered during canary, and rollback criteria.nnaudience:n- serving runtime engineersn- sres and oncall defendersn- runtime qa and benchmarking teamsn- product owners for dedicated/private customers with scheduler tunablesnnexecutive summary (tldr):n- what: adaptive scheduler 1.0 introduces: predictive slot consolidation, per-request credit accounting, and slo-driven admission policies.n- why: reduce tail 95/99 latency by 2040 on mixed workloads and reduce unit gpu time for low-latency small requests by 8 in our benchmarks.n- risk: medium changes to admission and kernel handoff behavior can influence eviction patterns and kv cache locality.n- rollout: canary - graduated regional rollout - global by-service rollout. follow the validation checklist below.nnkey changes (high level):n1) scheduler behaviorn - predictive consolidation: uses a short lookback of sequence-length histograms model variant hints to coalesce compatible requests into shared slots where latency slos permit.n - credit accounting: per-tenant credit buckets to reduce noisy-neighbor effects credits replenish at configurable rates.n - priority synthesis: combines customer route priority, inferred latency sensitivity, and experiment flags to produce an execution priority score used during contention.nn2) kernel handoff and prefetchn - lazy kernel hedging when predicted queueing 120ms (config flag). this triggers speculative kernel activation for long sequences to avoid warmstart hit.n - prefetch hints are emitted to the kv cache manager for requests expected to exceed 64 tokens.nn3) observability and control surfacen - new telemetry metrics: scheduler.priority_score, scheduler.slot_coalesce_ratio, scheduler.credit_usage, scheduler.speculative_kernels.n - new control knobs (runtime-config api): consolidation_enabled (bool), credit_window_ms (int), speculative_hedge_threshold_ms (int), coalesce_allowed_models (list).nnruntime architecture impact (detailed):n- placement: the scheduler acts as a thin service in the request path prior to the kernel dispatcher. it remains colocated on dispatcher nodes to preserve per-request provenance.n- stateful components: lightweight time-series lookback buffer (per-node, in-memory, ring-buffer) credit buckets persisted to the local faststore with periodic snapshots to the control plane for global accounting.n- failure modes: if the scheduler process crashes we fall back to the static allocator (fallback_adapter). the fallback path is implemented with the same admission checks but without consolidation.nnkernel scheduling and compatibility notes:n- kernel hinting: the scheduler may select a kernel variant with lower memory overhead but slightly higher compute latency if coalescing yields a net latency improvement for the cohort.n- eviction interplay: speculative hedging increases temporary kv cache churn the eviction policy has been retuned to raise kvcache.eviction_threshold from 0.65 - 0.72 during canary. monitor kvcache.hit_rate and pagefaults.nnprofiling playbook updates (what to run and where to look):n- baseline captures: run a 60-minute shadow capture of representative mixed traffic (small chat long generation embedding spikes) using the profiling harness.n- traces to collect: full span traces with scheduler.priority_score tag, kernel variant ids, kvcache.hint tags, and per-token timing.n- sampling guidance: during canary set sample_rate_inbound_traces to 100 for canary cohort and 15 for background traffic.n- diagnostic checklist:n 1. confirm scheduler.slot_coalesce_ratio 0.35 for mixed workloads lower values indicate consolidation not firing.n 2. validate tail latency delta: p95/p99 latency should not regress by 5 on non-canary tenants.n 3. observe speculative_kernels count ephemeral spikes are expected but sustained high rates (5 of total requests) require throttle.nnbenchmarking suite results (summary):n- setup: tests run on heterogeneous pool (a100-80gb and h100-80gb) with mixed load profiles derived from production traces.n- representative results:n - mixed-production trace: p95 improved from 210ms - 170ms (-19), p99 improved 480ms - 320ms (-33).n - small chat-only: avg token cost -8, tail unchanged within noise.n - long-sequence throughput: negligible change full-batch kernels still preferred.n- cost implication: model-nightly simulations indicate estimated gpu-hour savings of 612 for workloads with 40 small requests.nnrelease and rollout plan (operational steps):n1. pre-canary validation (lab):n - run unit tests and scheduler integration tests from kernel-mock harness.n - local stress test: 2x peak synthetic traffic for 30 minutes with consolidation_enabledtrue.nn2. canary phase (2 hours initial, extend to 48h):n - target cohort: dedicated pools in us-west-2 running non-critical traffic by default.n - metrics to gate: p95 latency (service-level), kvcache.hit_rate, scheduler.credit_usage trends, error rate, gpu utilization differential.n - validation gates: pass if no metric breaches defined thresholds (listed below).nn3. regional rollouts: 2472h per region, observe for systemic regressions.nn4. full global rollout: once regional rollouts are green for 7 days.nnvalidation thresholds (gates):n- p95 latency: no 5 regression for non-canary tenants over a 1-hour moving window.n- error rate: increase 15 relative increase.nnrunbook: incidents and mitigation stepsn- symptom a: sudden p99 spike with scheduler.slot_coalesce_ratio falling to 0.n 1. check scheduler process health on dispatcher nodes: systemctl status adaptive-scheduler.n 2. if unstable, flip runtime-config consolidation_enabledfalse for affected pools (api: post /runtime/config with pool filter).n 3. if spike persists, rollback scheduler to fallback_adapter by setting scheduler_modefallback for node group escalate to oncall.n 4. collect traces: attach scheduler. metrics and full-trace exports for 30 minutes prior to incident.nn- symptom b: elevated kv cache misses and cold starts after rolloutn 1. reduce speculative_hedge_threshold_ms by 50 (temporary) to reduce prefetching pressure.n 2. increase kvcache.capacity_soft_limit by 10 via node-profile manifest.n 3. if still high, set consolidation_allowed_models to an explicit denylist containing high-kvcache models.nn- symptom c: credit exhaustion for a tenant (errors indicating admission failure)n 1. inspect scheduler.credit_usage for tenant_id.n 2. temporarily bump credit_window_ms for the tenant to allow refill.n 3. investigate the tenants traffic shape coordinate with customer success if a production surge occurred.nnknown issues observed in canary and mitigations:n- issue 1: transient double-charge of credit bucket on dispatcher restart (race). mitigation: patch lower speculative_hedge_threshold_ms.n- issue 3: small percentage of canary requests show increased variance in per-token latency due to coalescing fragmentation on certain tensor-core kernels. runtime 1.22 release notes: workload-aware batching defaults (fast / standard / cost-efficient tiers), content: overviewnruntime v1.22 introduces workload-aware batching defaults: three customer-facing batching profiles aligned to latency slo tiers (fast, standard, cost-efficient). the runtime now selects and enforces tier-appropriate scheduler knobs using workload signals (prompt-length buckets, streaming vs non-streaming, and concurrency) to improve throughput and /token while preserving predictable tail latency.nnthis release includes:n- new tiered default profiles and a selection/override hierarchyn- tail-latency protections for fast tier and guardrails for cost-efficient tiern- telemetry reason codes to explain why this profilen- tier-labeled metrics with cardinality controlsn- rollout controls: feature flag, staged enablement, and kill switchnn whats newn 1) three batching tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient)nthe runtime now supports the following tiers:n- fast: minimizes tail latency via tighter wait budgets, stricter admission control, and anti-starvation rules.n- standard: balanced defaults for typical product traffic moderate batching with stable streaming performance.n- cost-efficient: maximizes throughput via more aggressive batching, with safeguards to prevent queue blowups during bursts.nntier defaults are defined per model family and (when required) hardware class. if a model/hardware combination cannot safely support a tiers default knob set, the runtime will fall back to a compatible profile and emit a reason code.nn 2) workload-aware selection signalsnscheduler heuristics now incorporate:n- prompt length bucket (prefill cost proxy)n- streaming flag (streaming-first latency constraints)n- observed concurrency / queue pressure (to prevent overload instability)nnthese signals influence batch formation and admission/backpressure behavior while respecting the chosen tier.nn 3) safety mechanismsn- fast tier tail-latency protection:n - tighter max-wait budgetn - admission control under queue growthn - anti-starvation for long-prefill requests in mixed workloadsn- cost-efficient guardrails:n - max batch token capsn - queue depth clamps early backpressuren - overload mode behavior standardized (see known limitations)nn 4) tier selection reason codesnthe runtime emits structured reason codes for effective profile selection, including:n- tier_default_appliedn- route_policy_overriden- customer_override_appliedn- model_constraint_fallbackn- hardware_constraint_fallbackn- overload_mode_adjustmentn- kill_switch_disablednnthese reason codes are intended to support console explanations and to accelerate regression triage.nn configuration changesn new config surfacenruntime 1.22 adds a tier-aware schema for batching defaults.nnprimary configuration locations (naming shown as currently implemented in control plane configs):n- route/model policy: batching.tier faststandardcost_efficientn- cluster/tenant override (dedicated): overrides.batching.tier and/or knob-level overridesnnoverride precedence (highest wins):n1. customer override (dedicated tenant/cluster)n2. route policy (api route/model policy)n3. tier default (runtime-recommended profile)n4. runtime safe fallback (constraints / overload)nn example: route policynyamln example: hosted api route policynroute: /v1/chat/completionsnmodel: redwood/llama-3.1-70bnbatching:n tier: fastnnn example: dedicated overridenyamln example: dedicated tenant overridentenant: acme-prodnoverrides:n batching:n tier: standardn (optional) knob overrides remain supported for enterprise casesn max_wait_ms: 1.5nnn backwards compatibilityn- existing knob-level configurations (manual batching settings) continue to be accepted.n- if both tier and manual knobs are set, the system follows the documented precedence (customer overrides first within an override scope, explicit knobs take precedence over tier defaults).nn migration notesn who needs to do something?n- hosted api customers: no action required. tier defaults are rolled out progressively behind a flag.n- dedicated customers:n - if you currently rely on manual knob tuning, you can keep it.n - if you want the new defaults, opt in by setting batching.tier at the route policy or tenant override level.n- private (vpc/on-prem):n - defaults ship with runtime 1.22, but are disabled by default unless your deployment config enables the tiered defaults flag.nn recommended migration pathn1. start with standard tier on representative routes.n2. move latency-critical streaming endpoints to fast.n3. move high-throughput async workloads (non-streaming) to cost-efficient.n4. validate using tier dashboards (p95/p99, queue depth, batch tokens) and reason-code distribution.nn deprecationsnno deprecations in 1.22. tier awareness to key latency/cost telemetry:n- tier label (effective tier) on latency histograms and cost attributionn- batch size distribution (tokens and requests)n- queue depth and time-in-queuen- release notes: kernel auto-selection v2, content: summarynruntime 1.21 introduces kernel auto-selection v2 (selector v2) for gpu inference kernels. the selector chooses the best available kernel per request using a deterministic, explainable rule-based policy keyed on:n- model family / architecture (e.g., llama-like vs mistral-like vs qwen-like)n- sequence-length regime (prefill-heavy, decode-heavy, mixed plus long-context buckets)n- gpu sku (e.g., a100 vs h100 vs l40s including normalization of common cloud instance naming)nnthis release is focused on reducing p95/p99 latency and improving throughput stability across heterogeneous fleets without correctness regressions.nnselector v2 is shipped behind feature gates and includes fast rollback, per-model allow/deny controls, and guardrails for known-unstable driver/cuda combinations.nn---nn whats new in 1.21n 1) kernel auto-selection v2 (gated)n- expanded feature extraction: model-family tags seq-length buckets gpu sku normalization.n- explicit fallback hierarchy when a preferred kernel is unavailable or denied on a sku.n- deterministic decision logic and replay tests (same inputs same kernel choice).nn 2) selection telemetry (sampled)nnew per-request telemetry is available (sampling-controlled) to support debugging and rollout monitoring:n- chosen kerneln- candidate set (capped)n- feature vector (model family, seq bucket, gpu sku)n- fallback reason (if applicable)nn 3) operator controls debuggingn- force kernel selection for reproductions and customer escalations.n- dump selection traces locally (or in canary pods) for triage.n- hot-reloadable allow/deny rules (control plane) for fast mitigation.nn---nn configuration / flagsnselector v2 is off by default in runtime 1.21 unless enabled by the control plane gate or local runtime config (dedicated/private).nn feature gates (hosted / dedicated via control plane)ngate key:n- kernel_selection.v2.enablednnscoped overrides supported:n- by model (exact model id)n- by model family (architecture tag)n- by regionn- by gpu skunn runtime config (dedicated / private)nthe following keys are supported in runtime.yaml (or equivalent env var mapping).nncore togglesn- kernel_selection.mode: v1 v2 auto (default: auto)n- kernel_selection.v2.enabled: true false (default: false)nnallow/deny lists (hot reload where supported)n- kernel_selection.v2.model_allowlist: comma-separated model idsn- kernel_selection.v2.model_denylist: comma-separated model idsn- kernel_selection.v2.gpu_sku_denylist: comma-separated normalized skus (e.g., a100-80gb, h100-sxm, l40s)n- kernel_selection.v2.driver_denylist: comma-separated driver/cuda tuples (example: 535.104.05cuda12.2)nntelemetryn- kernel_selection.telemetry.enabled: true false (default: true)n- kernel_selection.telemetry.sample_rate: float 0.01.0 (default: 0.01)n- kernel_selection.telemetry.max_candidates: integer (default: 6)nn runtime cli flags (debug / reproduction)navailable in redwood-runtime binaries starting 1.21:n- --kernel-selectionv1v2auton- --force-kernel (disables auto-selection)n- --dump-kernel-selection (writes per-request selection traces)n- --kernel-selection-telemetry-sample-ratennnotes:n- forcing a kernel is intended for debugging and should not be used as a steady-state configuration unless directed by the runbook.n- telemetry sampling does not affect selection behavior and does not introduce nondeterminism into decisions.nn---nn expected performance impactnobserved improvements vary by model family, gpu sku, and workload mix.nnin internal benchmark coverage (a100/h100/l40s) with representative prompt/decode distributions:n- p95 latency: typically 312 improvement on mixed workloads larger wins on sku/model pairs where v1 frequently fell back to conservative kernels.n- p99 latency: typically 210 improvement when the workload is correctly bucketed long-context workloads are the most sensitive (see known limitations).n- throughput stability: fewer oscillations under bursty mixed prefill/decode traffic due to better regime bucketing.n- selector overhead: bounded and low microbench indicates selector evaluation cost is in the single-digit microseconds range, and sampling-controlled telemetry overhead is negligible at default settings.nnperformance regressions should be treated as a p0 if they increase p99 tail latency beyond rollout budgets (see slo gates / dashboards).nn---nn compatibility notesn- supported gpu families in rollout scope: a100, h100, l40s.n- mig: supported, but sku normalization is strict ensure the runtime reports a normalized gpu_sku consistent with the control plane rules.n- private deployments pinned to constrained gpu types should validate with the benchmark matrix before enabling v2 globally.nn---nn known limitations / risksn1) long-context misclassification risk (prefill-heavy)n - very long prefill requests (e.g., summarization with large context windows) are sensitive to incorrect bucketing.n - if you observe tail spikes concentrated in long-context routes, disable v2 for the affected model(s) and region, then collect selection traces.nn2) driver/cuda guardrailsn - selector v2 is automatically disabled on specific driver/cuda combinations that have not completed validation.n - if you are running a nonstandard driver stack (common in some on-prem installs), confirm you are not implicitly falling back to v1.nn3) telemetry cardinalityn - new fields can increase metric cardinality if dashboards are queried without the recommended grouping limits.n - follow the dashboard spec for safe group-bys (model family / sku / seq bucket) and avoid raw model-id group-bys unless sampled and capped.nn4) kernel availability differences by skun - some optimized kernels are sku-specific. v2s fallback rules are explicit, but you may see different kernel distributions between a100 and h100 under identical traffic.nn---nn release notes: format and taxonomy (slower-change channel), content: purposenthis page defines the required format and taxonomy for runtime lts (long term support) release notes. lts release notes are intentionally slower-change: they optimize for stability, auditability, and upgrade safety for dedicated and private customers.nnthis standard is used by:n- runtime release engineering when cutting lts patch releasesn- sre during release readiness review and patch rollout monitoringn- support/cs when advising customers on whether to upgrade and how to mitigate known issuesn- product/docs when linking release notes from console and customer-facing docsnn design principles (what slower-change means)n1) every change is categorized and justified (why its safe / why it matters).n2) performance is treated as first-class: include benchmark summary and any expected tradeoffs.n3) upgrades are operationally actionable: clear sequencing, rollback notes, and compatibility.n4) audit-ready: tie artifacts to git commit(s), include provenance/checksums, and document cves in a consistent format.n5) no surprises: include no user-visible change explicitly when appropriate.nn scopenapplies to:n- all releases on runtime lts branches (e.g., runtime-1.18-lts)n- all lts patch versions (e.g., 1.18.1-lts, 1.18.2-lts)nndoes not apply to:n- mainline runtime releases (non-lts)n- product/console release notes (separate taxonomy)nn---nn release note document requirements (per patch)neach lts patch must publish a single release note entry with the metadata and sections below.nn required patch metadata (must be present verbatim)ninclude a release metadata section near the top with the following fields.nnrequired fieldsn- lts version: (e.g., 1.18.1-lts)n- release date (utc): yyyy-mm-ddn- branch: (e.g., runtime-1.18-lts)n- git tag: (e.g., runtime-v1.18.1-lts)n- source commit: (git sha of the release tag target)n- build provenance: (link to ci run provenance attestation location)n- artifacts:n - runtime image tag(s)n - private installer bundle version (if applicable)n - helm chart version(s) that can select this runtimen- checksums/signatures:n - sha256 (link or inline list)n - signature verification instructions (link)n- sbom:n - status: available pending not_applicablen - location/link (if available)nnoptional but recommended fieldsn- release manager: namen- approved backports: count link to backport trackern- rollout policy: hosted/dedicated/private notes (if relevant)nn required sections (in order)n1) summaryn2) release metadata (required fields above)n3) compatibility matrix (runtime driver/cuda model constraints packaging)n4) changes by category (taxonomy below)n5) performance notes (benchmark summary known tradeoffs)n6) upgrade notes (hosted / dedicated / private)n7) known issues (with mitigations / workarounds)n8) security notes (cve format if applicable)n9) appendix (optional): full pr list, links, reproducibility detailsnn---nn taxonomy (categories and definitions)nlts release notes must use the following categories. categories are intentionally narrower than mainline to keep changes comprehensible and auditable.nn category a securityndefinition: vulnerabilities, hardening changes, dependency updates with security impact, security mitigations.nninclude:n- cve(s) fixed (if assigned)n- severity (cvss if available otherwise redwood severity)n- affected versions (lts mainline if known)n- mitigation guidance (if customers can mitigate without upgrading)nnnon-examples:n- pure refactors without security impact (use reliability/correctness if needed)nn category b reliability / correctnessndefinition: fixes for crashes, data corruption, incorrect outputs, deadlocks, scheduler starvation, memory safety bugs, and other sev1/sev2 issues.nninclude:n- customer impact symptoms (what operators would see)n- scope (which models / gpus / workloads)n- risk notes (why backport is low-risk test coverage)nn category c performance / efficiencyndefinition: changes expected to measurably affect latency/throughput/cost, including stabilizing autotune parameters or disabling experimental heuristics.nninclude:n- expected impact (direction approximate range)n- whether change is predictability first vs speed firstn- perf gate summary reference (see performance notes section)nn category d compatibility / packagingndefinition: changes affecting build, artifacts, container images, private installer/helm behaviors, version pinning semantics, gpu/driver/cuda support, or model compatibility constraints.nninclude:n- breaking changes (should be rare in lts if present, must include explicit upgrade notes callout)n- required operator actions (pinning changes, config updates)nn category e observability / operabilityndefinition: slo dashboards, logging changes, new counters, trace fields, error classification improvements, rollback guidance improvements.nn category f deprecations / behavior changesndefinition: any intentional behavior change that can impact customer workloads even if correct (e.g., default scheduling parameter changes).nnrules:n- must include a behavior change calloutn- must include rollback path (config or downgrade)nn category g documentationndefinition: docs-only updates related to lts operationalization.nn---nn required change entry formatnwithin changes by category, each bullet must follow this structure.nnformatn- impact short title (1 line)n - what changed:n - customer impact:n - risk level: low medium highn - validation:n - references: pr(s) / issue(s)nnimpact values (choose one)n- fixn- improvementn- hardeningn- behavior changen- no user-visible changennrisk level guidancen- low: minimal diff, localized fix, strong regression coverage, no perf sensitivityn- medium: touches hot path or scheduler logic, but with targeted tests and perf validationn- high: multi-file core behavior change should be avoided for lts unless eviction rate returns to near-zero post-burst.n- p99 latency does not show synchronized spikes that align with compaction bytes moved.nn rollout guardrails (operational)nsre guardrails for hosted canaries:n- auto-rollback if p99 latency regression exceeds slo guardrail for a sustained window and correlates with compaction/eviction activity.n- page on elevated eviction rate accompanied by rising fragmentation ratio and falling free bytes.nnfor dedicated pools:n- use pool-specific baselines confirm no sustained throughput degradation and no increase in cancellation-related errors.nn---nn rollout plan (runtime 1.22)nphased rollout (typical):n1. internal canary (single region/pool runtime-owned workloads)n2. hosted subset (small of shared pools latency-sensitive routes prioritized)n3. dedicated pools (opt-in by pool validate with customer success when needed)n4. broader enablement (expand by region/model profile)nnall phases require:n- metrics present and dashboards wired.n- confirm kill-switch propagation tested in the environment.nn---nn operational controls (kill-switch troubleshooting)n kill-switchnif you suspect compaction/eviction is contributing to latency spikes or allocator instability:n1. flip kv.kill_switch true for the impacted pool/cluster.n2. confirm within 12 config propagation intervals that:n - runtime_kv_compaction_steps_total stops increasingn - runtime_kv_evictions_total stops increasingn3. if the pool remains unstable, follow standard overload/backpressure procedures (route shifting, capacity adjustments).nn common symptoms and first checksn- symptom: p99 spikes during burstsn - check: compaction bytes moved/sec and compaction step time histogram during the spike.n - mitigation: reduce kv.compaction.budget_ms_per_step and/or increase kv.compaction.trigger_fragmentation_ratio slightly if severe, kill-switch.nn- symptom: elevated eviction raten - check: runtime_kv_free_bytes trend and fragmentation ratio confirm tier breakdown.n - mitigation: raise kv.eviction.min_free_bytes_target (evict earlier to avoid emergency shedding) or adjust tier weights validate pinned session behavior.nn- symptom: oom / forced sheddingn - check: allocator headroom, fragmentation ratio, and whether compaction is making progress.n - mitigation: temporarily enable eviction (if off), or adjust thresholds consider capacity.nn---nn customer-facing notes (support / cs)nsuggested messaging (when asked):n- runtime 1.22 adds kv cache compaction and safer eviction behavior to reduce fragmentation-related tail latency spikes during bursty workloads.n- there are no api changes improvements are in the serving runtime memory manager.n- for dedicated/private environments, tuning is available if workloads have extreme churn or unusually long-lived sessions.nnwhat to request from customers reporting tail latency spikes:n- time window region/pooln- model route details (chat vs generate)n- evidence of burst pattern (rps, concurrency) and sequence length distribution if availablen- traces (request ids) so we can correlate with compaction/eviction spansnn---nn known risks / limitations (runtime 1.22)n- if budgets are set too high, compaction can become visible as latency spikes. defaults are conservative for hosted.n- eviction is intentionally conservative around pinned sessions in some workloads, this may limit eviction effectiveness under extreme pressure.n- very high churn frequent cancellations can stress relocation bookkeeping the cancellation edge case fix is included in 1.22, but continue to monitor cancellation-related error rates.nnfor details and mitigations, see the kv cache compaction known risks page.nn---nn owners / contactsn- tech lead (kv): omar el-sayedn- scheduler integration: kernel benchmarking sprint plan (runtime 1.22), content: overviewnthis page is the execution plan for the focused fp8/int8 kernel benchmarking sprint. the sprint produces a reproducible benchmark matrix across our top hosted models and primary gpu skus, and converts results into shippable runtime decisions:n- kernel auto-selection updates (fp8/int8 vs baseline)n- scheduler knob defaults/tuning for mixed prefill/decode workloadsn- quantization profile guidance for the hosted model catalogn- perf canary gates, dashboards, and regression triage playbooksnnsprint window: 2 weeks (targeting runtime 1.22.0)nn goalsn1. build a defensible benchmark matrix comparing fp8 and int8 kernel paths against current baselines across realistic production-like workloads.n2. translate benchmark outcomes into actionable runtime changes (dispatch heuristics scheduler defaults), shipped behind flags and rolled out safely.n3. ensure changes are safe and repeatable: measurement stability, artifact metadata, and regression thresholds suitable for ci and perf canary.nn non-goals / out of scopen- training-time quantization, fine-tuning, or distillation work.n- broad model catalog expansion. this sprint focuses on top hosted traffic.n- multi-node tensor-parallel scaling studies beyond the configurations already used in hosted.nn owners and stakeholder mapn core ownersn- program (sprint source_type: confluence, title: sequence length scaling and kernel breakpoints characterization and operational playbook, content: overviewnnthis page documents an empirical characterization of how sequence length distribution interacts with kernel selection and scheduling in the redwood serving runtime. it consolidates the benchmark design, observed kernel breakpoints, profiling steps, and an operational runbook for diagnosing and mitigating performance cliffs that appear when request token lengths cross specific thresholds. the goal is to provide a reproducible approach for teams to:nn- quantify per-model breakpoints where the runtime swaps execution kernels or changes memory strategy,n- map those breakpoints to tail and p50 latency regressions under realistic traffic mixes, andn- provide a low-friction remediation path (config, routing, and rollout guidance).nnwhy this mattersnnsequence length interacts with many runtime subsystems: attention kernel selection, kv-cache allocation, beam/decoder loop scheduling, and cross-gpu shard placement. small shifts in length distribution (e.g., 64 - 96 tokens) can cause:nn- kernel fallback to slower attention implementations,n- increased temporary gpu memory pressure that triggers spilling or allocator pathologies,n- larger per-request batching mismatches that break latency slos, andn- degraded model quantization code-paths (fp16-int8 fallback) on older kernels.nnthis doc summarizes controlled experiments and provides playbooks to identify and mitigate these effects in production.nnprinciples and definitionsnn1) breakpoint: a sequence length value at which the runtime changes kernel, memory allocation pattern, or scheduling policy.n2) hot path kernel: the primary highly-optimized kernel chosen for the majority of requests below the first breakpoint.n3) slow path kernel: fallback kernel or non-optimized path taken above a breakpoint.n4) effective length: request length expected generated tokens when the runtime preallocates kv or scratch.nnexperiment summary (high level)nn- workload: 10k synthetic prompts per model, sampled across prompt templates used by product teams (short chat, multi-turn context, doc summary). generation budgets: 16, 64, 128 tokens.n- models: two llama-family variants (7b, 13b), a non-sharded 70b, and a trimmed 3b quantized.n- hardware: a100-40gb (single-gpu runs), a100-80gb (single and 2-way sharded), h100-80gb (single-gpu), and rtx-6000 for legacy stack tests.n- metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, kernel name (telemetry tag), gpu mem high-water, scheduler queue depth, batch composition, and kv-cache hit/miss rate.nnkey observed breakpoints (example)nn model observed breakpoints (tokens) typical effect notes n--------------------------------------:-----------------------n 3b-quant 96, 256 96 triggers slower attention kernel (vectorized-scalar), 256 triggers allocator spilling quantization path causes extra memory copies on gpu_legacy drivers n 7b-sharded 64, 192 64-192 increases per-shard kv footprint above 192 scheduler switches to larger slice size causing 40 p95 shard placement tuning recommended n 13b 80 kernel switch to tiled attention p99 spikes for small batch sizes tiling increases kernel launch overhead n 70b 64, 128 64 increases async memcpy contention 128 often requires 2-shard execution which changes network rtts check nccl tuning nnbenchmark methodology (repro steps)nn1) environment setupn - use the perf harness in tools/runtime-bench. ensure cuda visible devices set and driver/harness versions recorded.n - commands (example):nn bashn export cuda_visible_devices0n git checkout main bazel build //tools/runtime-bench:bench_runnern sequence sweepn - sweep effective lengths: 8, 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 128, 160, 192, 256 with fixed gen budget where applicable.n - for each length record: kernel_name, batch_size, queue_wait_ms, gpu_mem_mb, p50/p95/p99 latency.nn3) mixed traffic testn - construct realistic traffic mix from product telemetry (ratios e.g., 70 short-chat (1 of requests call that l1.n- plot p95/p99 by length and overlay kernel.name. breakpoints appear where latency changes sharply with correlated kernel switch.n- correlate alloc.high_water_mb with p99 spikes: if mem rises by 10 at a breakpoint, consider quantization/alloc path investigation.nnoperational playbook (triage remediation)nn1) detectn - alerting: create an alert when model.route p99 latency increases by 25 vs 7d baseline and kernel.name for 5 of requests is a known slow path. use telemetry query:nn sqln select kernel_name, count() from runtime.eventsn where model_name llama-7b and ts now() - interval 5mn group by kernel_name order by count descn nn2) triage steps (ordered)n - confirm whether p99 increase maps to shift in request length distribution (compare api.request_effective_length histograms).n - check scheduler.queue_depth and batch.composition to rule out batch skew.n - verify kv-cache hit rate a sudden drop can inflate effective length due to upstream re-fetching.n - inspect gpu alloc.high_water_mb for leaking/spill behavior.nn3) immediate mitigation (fast path)n - if kernel switch caused regression and a faster compatible kernel exists for longer lengths, enable temporary model override to force that kernel for this model/route (use route-level config). example: set runtime.override_kernel attention-tiled-opt-v2 for routes matching /chat/ .n - if kv-cache is the issue, enable short-term per-route prefix-caching or reduce prefix size to avoid crossing the breakpoint.nn4) medium-term remediationsn - add a routing rule: split traffic by predicted effective length (l1) and route long requests to a node pool with larger gpus or a kernel-optimized pool.n - adjust autoscaler warm targets for nodes that serve long sequences to avoid cold-shard placement during bursts.n - work with runtime team to prioritize kernel optimization (see section below).nn5) postmortem itemsn - add failing prompt examples to the models regression set and schedule quantized-kernel compatibility test in nightly perf suite.n - update per-model sequence breakpoints table in team wiki and annotate deployment manifests with expected l1/l2.nnkernel scheduling and compilation action itemsnn- for each runtime kernel variant, maintain a short compatibility matrix: supported sequence ranges, preferred hardware, and quantization compatibility.n- where a kernel has a small but expensive launch overhead (tiling kernels), include a warm-start micro-benchmark in the perf suite to measure amortized cost vs per-request overhead.n- add compiler flag matrix to ci for kernels that use vendor-provided fused ops this prevents unexpected fallbacks when new drivers are rolled.nnprofiler playbook (how to collect actionable traces)nn1) light-weight trace (25 mins under live traffic)n - capture telemetry tags listed above at 5s granularity.n - export top-3 kernel_name occurrences with latency percentiles.nn2) full gpu profile (for repro)n - use nvidia nsight systems and measure kernel launches, memcpy, and occupancy. command example:nn bashn nsys profile --tracecuda,cudnn --sampletimer --output seq-breakpoint-7b n -- ./bazel-bin/tools/runtime-bench/bench_runner --model llama-7b --length 96 --iterations 1000n nn3) kernel-level microprofilen - capture kernel-level flamegraphs and symbolized traces. correlate with allocator calls to find allocation hotspots that precede kernel fallback.nnconfiguration kernel tiling defaults.n- quantized models showed more frequent kernel fallbacks on legacy drivers driver upgrades removed one observed breakpoint in the 3b-quant tests.nnrunbook snippets (quick production models and records l1/l2 breakpoints to a central table.n- track kernel regressions as part of release gating for runtime releases a change that introduces a new breakpoint must have a documented mitigation and perf test.nnappendix a reproducible artifacts and resultsnn- benchmark configs: gs://redwood-perf/seqscale-2026/llama-3b,7b,13b,70b.yamln- raw telemetry snapshot (airgapped): known caveatsnn- breakpoints are sensitive to driver and compiler versions do not copy absolute token values between clusters without running the sweep.n- mixed-batch workloads can mask breakpoints due to amortized kernel launch costs both isolated and mixed tests are required.n- some models employ decoding-time length conditioning that changes effective length distribution ensure input generation in benchmarks replicates production preprocessors.nnif you have questions, want the raw experiment logs, or need help adding a model to the nightly sweep, ping the runtime-kernel-team in operational audit indexing and residency playbook, content: overviewnnthis playbook defines operational patterns for indexing audit events, mapping audit storage to geographic residency and retention policies, and integrating rbac/authorization signals with compliance evidence workflows. it is intended for sre, security, and infra teams who operate the audit pipeline, and for engineering teams that must produce forensic-quality evidence during incidents.nnobjectivesn- ensure audit events are indexed and queryable within slos required by compliance and incident response.n- attach authoritative residency and retention metadata to each audit event.n- provide deterministic evidence collection runbooks for incidents that preserve chain-of-custody.n- integrate secure-sdlc gates so releases cannot remove required audit telemetry.nnscopen- applies to: service-to-service auth logs, user-level authorization events (grant/revoke/role-change), model-serving inference audit events, admin console actions, and orchestration job logs.n- excludes: ephemeral debug logs written to developer laptops or external third-party saas logs (those must be ingested via connectors described below).nndefinitionsn- event ttl: configured retention period for a given event type (see retention matrix).n- residency tag: a canonical tag on each event indicating the legal region of custody (e.g., eu, us, apac).n- evidence bundle: a time-bounded collection of events and artifacts used for a compliance request or forensic analysis.nnownership and rolesn- audit pipeline owner: eng-platform/audit-team (primary) responsible for ingestion, indexing, and retention enforcement.n- evidence custodian: security-ops owns packaging and legal handoff for evidence bundles.n- service owners: individual service teams ensure their services emit the canonical audit schema and residency metadata.n- sre oncall: operational response and temporary retention extension during incidents.nnindexing and storage patternsn1) canonical schema (required fields)n- event_id (uuid v4)n- timestamp_utc (iso8601)n- service (string)n- event_type (enum: auth, authz, admin, data_access, (enum: us, eu, apac, other)n- retention_policy_id (string)n- trace_id (optional)n- tx_payload_hash (optional sha256)nn2) indexing requirementsn- primary index on (timestamp_utc, service). secondary indexes on (event_type), (principal_id), and (residency).n- events must be available for query at 1s latency for last-24h and 30s for last-7d under normal load. these are operational slos.nn3) partitioning and hot-pathsn- partition by residency/residency_region service date (utc date). this simplifies geo-fenced exports and legal holds.n- hot-path telemetry (admin console, role-change events) should be forwarded to the immutable cold-storage write-ahead log in parallel to the searchable index.nnretention and residency policy matrixn retention_policy_id event_types default_ttl residency_affinity legal_hold_extension n----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------n rp-90d admin, authz, auth tag is set at emission time (see emission checklist).nncompliance evidence workflow (operational steps)n1) evidence request intaken- security receives request (internal ir, legal subpoena, shape calibration and cost envelope analysis for serving runtime, content: overviewnnthis document defines a repeatable framework for calibrating concurrency shapes for model serving workloads and mapping observed performance to a cost envelope. the goal is to provide teams with a concise procedure to: (1) translate production traffic patterns into benchmark shapes, (2) tune runtime batching/slotting parameters to meet latency slos at minimal cost, and (3) compute a cost-vs-latency envelope that guides deployment choices (hosted vs dedicated vs private).nnwhy this mattersnn- production traffic is rarely constant: bursts, ramps, and diurnal cycles change effective concurrency and the optimal batching strategy.n- incorrectly calibrated concurrency models cause either wasted gpu capacity or slo violations during bursts.n- a compact cost envelope lets product and infra teams pick capacity commitments and autoscale policies with predictable unit economics.nnscope and audiencenn- audience: serving runtime engineers, performance sres, product platform owners, and solutions engineers running customer pilots.n- scope: end-to-end benchmarking procedure, observability signals required, calibration experiment matrix, cost envelope derivation, and a short runbook for troubleshooting failed calibrations.nnkey definitionsnn- concurrency shape: a time series pattern describing requests-per-second (rps) per model/route over a window (examples: steady, bursty spike, sawtooth, poisson-workload).n- effective concurrency: the number of concurrently in-flight token-generation contexts that consume gpu resources, accounting for average sequence length and token emit rate.n- cost envelope: a curve mapping latency percentile (e.g., p95) to minimum cost (gpu-hour normalized) under tuned runtime parameters.nnrequired telemetry and signalsnncollect the following metrics during all experiments (per model/route):nn- request.rps (gauge, 1s)n- request.latency.p50,p90,p95,p99 (ms)n- kernel.utilization.gpu_pct (percent)n- runtime.batch.size.avg and runtime.batch.size.p90n- kvcache.hits and kvcache.miss_raten- queue.length and queue.wait_time_msn- gpu.memory.used_mb and fragmentation_pctn- kernel.queue_time_ms (time requests wait for kernel dispatch)n- cost.token_usd (derived using current pricing model)nntest harness and artifact requirementsnn- harness: use bench-runner v2.3 or later. bench-runner must support: synthetic workload playback, sequence-length sampling, and prefix-caching enable/disable toggles.n- artifact: a representative request trace (preferably 16 hours) showing traffic variability anonymize customer data for compliance.n- model: use the production model artifact and the exact serving configuration (quantization profile, padded sequence length, kv cache policy).nnexperiment matrix (minimum)nnrun the following matrix for each model/route:nn1) concurrency shapes: steady (constant rps), spike (10x for 30s every 5m), sawtooth (linear ramp 0.2x - 2x over 5m), poisson burst (lambda tuned to 80 of target capacity).n2) sequence length percentiles: 25th, 50th, 75th, 95th.n3) kv cache settings: warm (prefilled), cold (empty), partial (50 hit).n4) batching configs: batch_max_tokens in 256, 512, 1024, batch_window_ms in 2, 8, 20.n5) slotting/quota profiles: single-tenant slot sizes small, medium, large and predictive preemption on/off.nncalibration procedure (step-by-step)nn1. baseline capturen - start with a steady-shape workload at a conservative rps (e.g., 40 of nominal capacity).n - verify metrics are healthy and kv cache warm where applicable.nn2. single-dimension sweepn - sweep batch_max_tokens with batch_window_ms fixed at 8ms and measure p95 latency and token-cost.n - log the batch.size distribution and kernel queue_time_ms for each point.nn3. shape-sensitive sweepn - replay spike and sawtooth shapes and evaluate: latency tail, queue length, and recoverability after burst.n - if p99 increases 2x over baseline during spikes, enable conservative preemption (slot steal threshold 90).nn4. kv cache sensitivityn - run cold-cache variant of the spike shape measure delta in kernel.utilization and latency.n - for models showing 15 p95 regression on cold cache, add pre-warm policy or increase reserved slots.nn5. full matrix run and pareto front extractionn - combine promising batch and slotting configs from previous steps across all shapes.n - for each config, compute cost_per_1000_tokens_usd and p95 latency.n - build the pareto front (configs not dominated on both axes) this forms the cost envelope.nnexample tuning config (json)nnn model: redwood-opt-13b,n batching: batch_max_tokens: 512, batch_window_ms: 8,n slotting: profile: medium, preemptive_threshold_pct: 90,n kvcache: partialnnninterpreting the cost envelopenn- plot p95 latency on x axis and cost_per_1000_tokens_usd on y axis. each point is a config/shape pair.n- the lower-left pareto frontier is the desirable region (low latency, low cost).n- choose operating point by policy: e.g., product may pick config at p95120ms with minimal cost increase when moving to p95100ms requires 30 more cost.nnquantitative example (text table)nnconfig p95 (ms) tokens_per_gpu_hour cost_per_1000_tokens_usdn--- ---: ---: ---:nbatch256, window2ms 95 1,200,000 0.0028nbatch512, shape.n- shape replay dashboard: playback timeline of rps, queue_length, kernel.queue_time_ms, and p95 latency.n- regression alert: if production p95 moves outside the configured envelope for 10m, trigger sev3 for platform.nnkernel scheduling considerations (practical guidance)nn- batch window tradeoffs: larger windows improve throughput but increase kernel.queue_time_ms and tail latency for spike shapes. use adaptive batch_window_ms where sawtooth or spikes are frequent.n- preemption policy: enable preemptive stealing for multi-tenant runs where tail-latency is critical set threshold to dsid_e78c51f152be4f8f81d7afc28c063076, source_type: confluence, title: burst slo simulation and cost sampling methodology, content: summaryn-------nthis document defines the canonical methodology we use for simulating short-duration (burst) traffic patterns to validate latency slos and surface per-token cost amplification effects in the runtime. it combines a workload model, kernel-scheduler assumptions, kv cache warmup dynamics, and a cost-sampling strategy so experiment results are comparable across teams and releases.nngoalsn-----n- provide a repeatable experimental recipe for measuring impact of bursts on p50/p95/p99 latency and per-token cost.n- quantify cost amplification (extra gpu cycles or tokens) caused by cold kv caches, scheduling preemption, and cross-tenant contention.n- produce sampling guidance so cost estimates converge within 5 for 95 of runs.n- tie results to clear operational mitigations (routing, cache warming, priority shaping).nnscope and non-goalsn-------------------n- in scope: latency slo regressions from 10s30s bursts, kv cache cold-warm transitions, kernel scheduling backpressure, and short-window autoscaling behavior.n- out of scope: long-term capacity planning (multi-hour), per-customer billing reconciliation, and model-quality degradation.nnkey concepts and assumptionsn----------------------------n- burst window: contiguous arrival period where qps baseline by 3x for at least 10s. default burst window used in experiments: 15s and 60s.n- cost amplification: ratio of observed gpu token-cost (compute memory overhead) to steady-state per-token cost. expressed as a multiplier (e.g., 1.45x).n- kv cache hit-rate curve: we model cache warming as an exponential rise: hit(t) h_inf (1 - exp(-t / tau)), where tau is warmup time constant (default 8s for a single shard).n- kernel preemption latency: scheduling pause introduced when a higher-priority request preempts a kernel. default preemption penalty: 1.8 ms per preemption event on ampere a100 80gb nodes (profiled).nnworkload modeln--------------n1) arrival processn - poisson baseline with lambda_b (e.g., 50 qps). bursts are injected by superimposing a short-duration spike modeled as a log-normal multiplicative factor.n - configurable burst shapes: square (instant increase), ramp (linear increase over 25s), and fat-tail (pareto-distributed dense tail).n2) sequence length distributionn - empirical histograms from production: short (512) 10.n - for burst sensitivity tests use parameterized scale-up factors for long sequences.n3) prefix reuse / kv localityn - hot prefixes: small set of user prefixes that account for high fraction of tokens. we simulate hot-prefix ratio h_frac 0.05, 0.15, 0.30.nnkernel scheduling and resource modeln----------------------------------n- scheduler abstraction used by the simulation mirrors primary runtime decisions: continuous batching (cb), preemptive priority shepherding (pps), and kernel crediting. each simulated request consumes a schedule quantum proportional to tokens x compute_profile.n- priority classes modeled: latency-critical, standard, background. preemption rules: latency-critical can steal up to 30 of kernel credits standard requests are throttled when queue depth q_thresh (default 120).n- gpu resource model includes occupancy and tensor-core efficiency drop when active concurrent sms 0.7 events/sec per gpu or kvcache.global_hit_rate 0.25 within 90s.nnrelease tracking and experiment reproducibilityn---------------------------------------------n- each experiment must be linked to a runtime-release tag (git commit) and a kernel artifact version. store experiment.yaml, seed, and the full result tarball in the artifacts bucket under path: s3://redwood-bench-results/release/experiment_name/timestamp/.n- example metadata record to attach to results (csv-friendly fields only): release_tag, git_sha, kernel_version, seed, config_sha256, runtime_image, notes.nnknown limitations and open questionsn----------------------------------n- simulation abstracts network jitter and rpc fanout we recommend correlating with a small on-cluster canary for every major change.n- cost model sensitivity to gpu spot pricing is not captured. separate sensitivity sweep is required for billing impact.n- multi-tenant cross-customer interference is modeled only via synthetic priority classes we lack a labeled corpus of production cross-tenant interference events.nnownership and escalationn------------------------n- primary owner: eng/serving-runtime/benchmarking (priya nair)n- secondary: eng/sre (owen martinez)n- for release gating: product-owner signoff eng/sre verification required.n- escalation path: pager - eng-sre source_type: confluence, title: shadow kernel emulation benchmark protocol (skeb) - 2026, content: summary:nthis document defines the shadow kernel emulation benchmark protocol (skeb): a standardized lab procedure, metrics contract, and release-gate checklist for evaluating experimental gpu kernel behavior using an emulator/shadow runtime prior to any production rollout. skeb reduces risk from kernel regressions that affect tail latency, kv-cache correctness, and scheduling fairness by validating kernels in a controlled shadow environment that mirrors production traffic shapes.nngoals and non-goals:n- goals:n - provide a repeatable protocol to compare a candidate kernel against the incumbent across cost, latency tails, and failure modes.n - surface subtle interactions between scheduler admission signals, kv cache warmup patterns, and kernel memory fragmentation.n - produce a deterministic artifact (bench report) to inform release gating and rollback criteria.n- non-goals:n - this is not an exhaustive functional test suite for model correctness or model artifacts.n - skeb does not replace live canaries it reduces the failure surface before canarying.nnwhen to run skeb:n1. new preventing tail-latency regressions in the redwood serving runtime. it covers measurement methodology, diagnostic commands, quick mitigations, kernel-scheduler knobs, benchmark repro recipes, canary/rollout guidance, alerting rules, and a checklist for post-incident follow-up.nnwhy tail latency matters:nn- slo impact: p99 and p99.9 directly affect user-facing latency for streaming and non-streaming workloads a small number of high-latency requests can cause downstream timeouts and user-visible errors.n- cost and capacity: excessive tail latency reduces effective throughput and increases idle gpu time (kv cache churn, smaller batch efficiency).n- regression vectors: model changes (longer context), quantization shifts, kernel changes, misconfigured batchers, network spikes, and kv cache thrash.nnslos and thresholds (company-standard baseline):nn- p50 p99 threshold, inspect span timeline for long gaps.n5) reproduce with targeted load: run the micro-workload for the failing route at 2x p99 arrival rate to reproduce.n6) mitigate (see quick mitigations).n7) root-cause analysis and permanent fix.nnquick mitigations (emergency steps to restore slos):nn- route-level rollback: pin the route to previous model_variant (fastest rollback if regression due to model or quantization).n- backpressure tuning: reduce max_concurrency for the route to reduce batching head-of-line blocking (example: max_concurrency 32 - 16).n- autoscaler pulse: scale up dedicated pool by 20 capacity for 1030 minutes to absorb tail churn.n- batcher drain and restart: rotate batcher playbook.n, doc_id: dsid_e821df837cf246e6b98e0c54244aab14, source_type: confluence, title: policy-driven load probe and scheduler feedback protocol, content: summaryn-------nthis page documents the policy-driven load probe and scheduler feedback protocol (plp-sfp). the protocol is designed to safely surface scheduler and kernel behavior under controlled, policy-shaped load while providing deterministic feedback signals that the runtime scheduler can consume to adjust admission, backfill, and priority heuristics.nnintended audiencen- runtime engineersn- benchmarking and perf-sig membersn- oncall and sre rotation responsible for scheduler incidentsnngoalsn- provide a reproducible method for injecting targeted load shapes into the serving runtime without violating customer slas.n- produce canonical telemetry artifacts (probe reports) that map directly to scheduler decision signals.n- define automated feedback actions the scheduler can take when probes indicate a regression or resource pressure.nnscope and non-goalsn- in scope: admission/backfill behavior, kv cache warmup under shaped bursts, per-kernel latency distribution under mixed-concurrency, slot coalescing effectiveness.n- out of scope: long-running model training, hardware-level failure injections (handled by infra chaos team).nnglossaryn- probe: controlled synthetic traffic pattern exercised against a target model and route.n- fingerprint: compact summary of latency/cost distribution for a probe (see probe fingerprint format).n- decision signal: normalized metric emitted by the probe runner that the scheduler consumes (e.g., kernel contention score, slot-utilization drift).nnarchitecture overviewn1) controller: probe-runner service (bench-probe) that schedules probes and collects traces. owned by benchmarking team.n2) collector: high-throughput telemetry pipeline that annotates traces with request-provenance and kernel hints. uses the runtime trace bus.n3) aggregator: offline/nearline job that produces a probe fingerprint and decision signals. runs in namespace perf-aggregator.n4) consumer: scheduler decision fabric subscribes to decision signals via the signal bus and maps signals to policy actions (admit/reject/backfill/tier-shift).nnprobe types and recommended usagen- smoke probe: short (30s) steady qps at nominal concurrency. use for ci verifications.n- burst probe: 560s high-intensity spike aimed at stressing kv cache and kernel preemption. use for degradation mode tests.n- ramp probe: linear ramp from 10 to 110 nominal qps over 510 minutes to find nonlinear breakpoints.n- cohort probe: multi-route correlated traffic that exercises cross-tenant memory eviction and kernel-sharing.nnprobe configuration (recommended defaults)n field description playbook, content: overviewnnthis playbook describes the slot synthesis simulator (s3) a reproducible lab harness used to synthesize gpu slot allocation, kernel contention, and scheduler behavior to fuzz-test sla boundaries. the purpose is to find edge cases where our scheduler, kernel selection, or cache warmup interacts to cause slo regressions or degraded output fidelity. s3 is intended for benchmarking, pre-release safety gates, and targeted post-incident verification.nnwhy we built s3nn- production traffic has complex concurrency shapes, prefix-sharing, and mixed model families (fp32/int8/quantized). traditional replay and unit microbenchmarks miss combinatorial scheduling interactions.n- s3 allows us to simulate: heterogeneous accelerators, slot preemption, admission spikes, varying sequence length distributions, and kv-cache warmup patterns.n- results feed into kernel/operator rollouts, scheduler policy tuning, and gating decisions for quantization/feature releases.nnglossarynn- slot: logical gpu allocation unit used by the scheduler (can map to cuda context / compute slice).n- slot synthesis: creating synthetic slot occupancy patterns over time to emulate real request mixes.n- slo fuzz: intentionally varying traffic and system parameters beyond expected ranges to find brittle decision boundaries.n- fidelity cliff: abrupt quality degradation (latency or output) when scheduler or kernel changes occur.nnhigh-level architecture of s3nn1) input generator: consumes a workload profile (sequence-length histogram, model mix, kv-cache hit curves) and emits a timeline of synthetic requests.n2) slot modeler: maps requests to slot occupancy using configurable policies (co-location, isolation, preemption windows).n3) kernel stressor: simulates kernel handoffs, warm/cold kernel latencies, and queueing at kernel dispatcher granularity.n4) metrics sink: collects per-request synthetic metrics (simulated service time, queue delay), aggregates into slo windows, and emits experiment reports.nnsimulator configuration reference (key fields)nn- experiment_name: short id for the runn- duration_seconds: wall-clock duration of the simulationn- models: ordered list of model stubs with per-model latency and token-cost distributionsn- slot_topology: definition of slot counts, types (cpu, gpu_a100, gpu_h100, tpu), and heterogeneity mappingn- admission_policy: policy id (e.g., conservative, balanced, aggressive) to exercise scheduler branchesn- preemption_profile: probability/time-window parameters to synthesize preemption eventsn- kv_warmup_curve: mapping from time to hit-rate for prefix cachen- sequence_length_distribution: empirical histogram or parametric (p95, mean)nnsample yaml experiment (copy/paste into simulator cli)nn---nexperiment_name: s3_sla_fuzz_canary_2026_02nduration_seconds: 3600nmodels:n - name: lm-medium-quantn mean_token_ms: 6.8n token_std_ms: 1.2n kv_sensitivity: 1.6 relative slowdown when kv missn - name: chat-largen mean_token_ms: 12.3n token_std_ms: 3.1n kv_sensitivity: 1.0nslot_topology:n - type: gpu_h100n count: 8n slots_per_gpu: 4n - type: gpu_a100n count: 12n slots_per_gpu: empirical:seq_hist_2026_q1.jsonn---nncli examplesnn- dry run (no metric sink):n ./s3 run --config examples/canary.yaml --dry-runnn- full run with metrics upload: n ./s3 run --config examples/canary.yaml --metrics gs://redwood-s3/experiments/2026/nnprimary metrics and acceptance criteriann- p50 / p95 / p99 tail latency (per-model and global) baseline delta tolerated: p95 15 req/s/min sustained).n- preemption-induced failure probability: fraction of preempted requests that miss deadline (1 requires investigation).n- cost signal (simulated gpu-seconds): used to catch regression in per-token cost.nnexperiment recipes (start here depending on intent)nn1) canary kernel rollout simulation (safety gate)n - purpose: measure effect of new kernel variant on tail latency under mixed traffic.n - steps: pick production model mix set 10 of slots to new_kernel profile run s3 for 1 hour with several admission_policy values (conservative, balanced, aggressive) compare per-model p99 and p95 to baseline.n - gate: no model-level p99 regression 10 and global slo violation 2x latency slo.n - gate: debug any observed requests, capture decision traces and slot assignment timeline.nnrunbook: executing a baseline s3 experimentnn1) prepare baseline artifacts: workload profile, seq_hist, and baseline_p95 numbers (from production telemetry).n2) upload config to experiments eng-serving-runtime.nnsafety and preconditions (must be satisfied before risky runs)nn- all kernel rollout experiments must be run with a baseline reference and known-good commit id.n- long-running fuzz runs (6h) must be signed off by the runtime lead and scheduled to avoid infra contention.n- secrets and pii: s3 must never be run with production user data use anonymized or synthetic request shapes only.nninterpreting s3 outputsnn- regression matrix: rows models, cols metrics (p50/p95/p99, slo rate, cost). flag cells that exceed gate thresholds.n- decision trace artifacts: a sequence of slot assignment events kernel hints. use the trace viewer (link in appendix) to step through abnormal requests.n- heatmaps: slot occupancy over time look for correlated increases in kernel queue time and kv-miss spikes.nncommon failure modes and troubleshooting checklistnn- symptom: p99 regressions concentrated on quantized modelsn - likely cause: kv_sensitivity underestimation or inadequate kernel warmup for int8 kernels.n - actions: increase kv_warmup_curve, re-run gpu affinity packing test.nn- symptom: sustained queue growth under balanced policyn - likely cause: admission_policy implementation mismatch with production (policy parameters differ).n - actions: export production admission snapshot, reconcile parameter differences, re-run.nn- symptom: flakiness between runs (non-deterministic results)n - likely cause: rng seeds not pinned or sequence_length_distribution referencing mutable live corpus.n - actions: pin seeds in config and use archived seq_hist confluence, title: sdk connection pooling and fanout quickstart, content: overviewnnthis quickstart describes recommended connection pooling and request fanout patterns for redwood sdk clients. it targets backend services that make high-throughput calls to the redwood api (generation, embeddings, reranking). the goal is to reduce tail latency, avoid connector saturation at the network layer, and provide predictable token-cost accounting when fanout is required.nnuse cases coverednn- high qps microservices that call redwood for short-lived generation requests.n- batch/parallel embedding workloads (concurrent tenants).n- fanout workflows where a single user action triggers 310 parallel model calls (e.g., multi-hypothesis generation reranker).nnprinciples and tradeoffsnn1) keep a modest, bounded pool per process prefer many small pools over one global unbounded pool.n2) prefer async concurrency primitives with backpressure (semaphores, rate limiters) over naive thread-per-request models.n3) when fanout n (where n is configurable), consider sequential or staged execution to preserve latency slos and cost budgets.n4) instrument both pool usage and request-level downstream metrics so capacity issues are observable before customers notice.nnquickstart patternsnnpattern a single-host connection pool (recommended for stateless api servers)nn- maintain a fixed-size http/http2 connection pool to the redwood endpoint.n- per-process pool size min(64, max(8, cpu_cores 8)) as a starting heuristic.n- combine with an async semaphore to cap in-flight api calls to the pool size.nnexample: node.js (axios generic-pool)nnconst axios require(axios)nconst genericpool require(generic-pool)nconst httpsagent require( agent new httpsagent( keepalive: true, maxsockets: 64 )nconst client axios.create( baseurl: process.env.redwood_url, agent, timeout: 30000 )nn// simple semaphore (toy example)nconst sema require(async-sema)nconst poolsemaphore new sema(32) // in-flight capnnasync function callredwood(payload) n await poolsemaphore.acquire()n try n const res await client.post(/v1/generate, payload, headers: authorization: bearer process.env.redwood_key )n return res.datan finally n poolsemaphore.release()n nnnnotes: tune maxsockets to match process-level cpu and expected concurrency. keep separate agent/client instances for long-running worker vs short-lived request handlers.nnpattern b controlled fanout (recommended for multi-call ux flows)nn- limit simultaneous branch calls with a bounded concurrency pool.n- stagger start times slightly to avoid synchronized bursts across instances.n- if branches are independent but result sizes vary, prefer pessimistic token budgeting adaptive early cancellation.nnstaged fanout algorithm (recommended)nn1) sort branches by predicted cost (if available) or worst-case estimate.n2) reserve slot tokens equal to branch concurrency cap (k).n3) start first k branches in parallel as each completes, start the next.n4) if cumulative token usage exceeds a configured budget, cancel lower-priority branches and return partial results.nnexample: python doc_id: dsid_f5c25101dccd4d3784ad43431b92346a, source_type: confluence, title: shadow cohort fidelity stitching protocol, content: summaryn--------nthis document defines the shadow cohort fidelity stitching protocol: an experiment and analysis pattern for running mirrored (shadowed) production traffic across multiple runtime cohorts to validate fidelity, kernel-scheduling and quantization impacts, and end-to-end user-visible regression risk before rollout. the protocol is designed for validating changes that affect execution kernels, scheduler policies, kv cache behavior, quantization profiles, or model variants.nnscopen-----n- applies to runtime experiments that change kernel selection, scheduler configuration, quantization profile, or model variant.n- intended for mid-to-large scale shadow runs (from single-node to fleet-wide depending on risk).n- not for synthetic microbenchmarks this protocol relies on production-shaped traffic.nnobjectivesn----------n1. detect regressions in output fidelity (semantic divergence, hallucination rate) introduced by kernel/scheduler/quantization changes.n2. measure operational impact: latency p50/p95/p99, tail amplification, token cost delta, and memory pressure.n3. provide clear pass/fail criteria tied to slos and risk budgets.n4. produce automation-friendly artifacts: config snippets, analysis queries, and dashboard templates.nndefinitions and termsn---------------------n- primary cohort: live production serving path receiving real user traffic.n- shadow cohort: non-responding mirrored path that receives copies of requests for analysis only.n- stitching: aligning outputs from primary and shadow for token-level and semantic comparison.n- fidelity delta: measured difference in quality metrics (embedding similarity, logprob delta, downstream evals).n- cohort window: contiguous time range used for comparison (recommended 60120 minutes per experiment).nnownership and rolesn-------------------n- experiment owner: eng-serving-runtime feature lead (creates config, runs experiment).n- observability owner: eng-platform (dashboards, sampling traces).n- quality owner: applied-ml-and-evals (defines fidelity metrics and acceptance thresholds).n- oncall / runbook owner: eng-sre (prepared to abort if operational thresholds are breached).nnpre-requisitesn--------------n- canary availability of shadow cohort image/version with kernel/scheduler/quantization change.n- traffic mirroring capability at the dispatch layer with request context preservation (headers, timestamps).n- stable sampling and replay hooks in tracing and kv cache to capture divergent behaviour.n- baseline corpus of prompts and a lightweight eval harness to run offline checks for severe regressions.nnexperiment matrix and cohortsn----------------------------nuse a combinatorial matrix to cover realistic differences:n cohort name model variant kernel set quantization scheduler profile notes n primary redwood-v1.4 stable-kernels-1 q8_compat standard baseline production n shadow-a redwood-v1.4 new-kernel-optim q8_compat standard tests kernel changes n shadow-b redwood-v1.4 new-kernel-optim q4_ffnx adjusted-batching tests quantization scheduler n shadow-c redwood-v1.5 stable-kernels-1 q8_compat priority-synth tests model variant scheduler nnsampling strategyn-----------------n- mirror 100 of a low-risk subset (e.g., read-only assistant queries) for correctness experiments.n- mirror 520 of general traffic with deterministic hashing (request_id mod n) for operational metrics to limit cost.n- ensure session affinity keys are preserved so session-level kv cache behavior is comparable.nninstrumentation and telemetryn----------------------------ncollect the following per-request:n- request_id, timestamp, cohort_id, model_version, kernel_tag, quant_profile, scheduler_profilen- latency_ms (dispatch, kernel, end-to-end), token_count_in, token_count_outn- model_logprob_sum, per-token logprobs (sampled), response_embedding (1281024 dim depending on model)n- runtime signals: gpu_util_pct, cuda_mem_free_mb, cpu_load, kvcache_hit_rationnmetrics and acceptance thresholdsn-------------------------------nquality metrics (primary gates):n- embedding cosine similarity median 0.995 and 5th percentile 0.95 between primary and shadow responses (for single-turn responses).n- mean per-token logprob delta 0.15 nats/token across stitched tokens.n- downstream task auc / exact-match must not degrade 1.5 relative.n- severe hallucination rate (as flagged by eval harness or heuristics) increase 0.1 percentage point.noperational metrics (secondary gates):n- delta p99 latency 12 ms (absolute) or relative increase 15 (whichever is smaller).n- p95 latency amplification factor 1.25.n- increase in gpu tail stalls 10 requires immediate abort and triage.n- token cost delta per 1m tokens 5 for production budget-sensitive customers.nnprocedure: runbook-style stepsn-----------------------------n1. preparation (owner 2 reviewers):n - create experiment config and register cohort ids in dispatch.n - pre-run offline golden-corpus checks (1000 prompts) using the shadow image.n - confirm observability dashboards (latency, embeddings, traces) are available.n2. ramp stage (1030 minutes):n - start mirroring the low-risk hashed subset to shadows at 1 of traffic.n - monitor p50/p95/p99, memory, and kvcache heatmap.n - if operational thresholds breached, pause mirroring and escalate to eng-sre.n3. validation stage (60120 minutes):n - increase mirror to target sampling rate (520).n - persist request/response pairs to stitched storage with retention 14 days for analysis.n - run automated fidelity-check jobs every 15 minutes (embedding similarity, lm logprob deltas).n4. analysis stage (post-run):n - aggregate metrics by cohort, request class, model_version, and kernel_tag.n - run stratified analysis by sequence length (short/medium/long), session-affinity (cold/warm), and request type.n - generate a report with pass/fail and recommended mitigations.n5. decision rollout:n - if all gates pass: prepare canary rollout (10 traffic to new cohort) following standard canary checklist.n - if any gate fails: create issue with reproduction artifacts and assign to kernel/scheduler owners.nnanalysis recipes and queriesn---------------------------n- stitching key: use (request_id request_timestamp session_id) to join primary and shadow. if multiple shadow responses exist, align by token offset.n- example sql-like aggregation (pseudo):nnselect cohort, percentile(latency_ms, 50) as p50, percentile(latency_ms, 95) as p95, n avg(embedding_cos_sim) as mean_emb_sim, percentile(embedding_cos_sim,5) as emb_sim_p5nfrom stitched_responsesnwhere run_id shadow-2027-02-10ngroup by cohortnn- semantic regression triage: for requests where emb_sim 25 or gpu error rate spike 3x baseline or emb_sim cohort median pager duty escalation per sre rotannacceptance criteria (high level):nn1) functional: all sample generation and embedding endpoints return valid responses for the test corpus (no 5xx/errors)n2)
